526. William Charleton to Locke, 27 January/6 February 1680 (465, 531)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, ff. 35-6.
Montpellier the 6th. February 1680
Deare Sir
It is a considerable time since I received your letter and present of one of the finest Meddalls Europe can shew, and yet I have thanked you for neither till now, you see Sir how I abuse your kindnesse, I advice you therefore for the future to be more sparing and not to throw away your favours on such as my self that do so little deserve them. The 19th: of December I sent you a letter with an Inclosed for my Lord of Sussex†1 from his brother Mr. Leanard and his thanks as well as mine for the trouble you tooke in delivering a former one, I should be verry glad to heare that it came to your hands, since Sir John Chichley acquainted me that you had left the towne, this comes notwithstanding—adressed to you as the former beleeving that your Landlord will be carefull to send it to you. I have met with a sermon preached by the ArchBishop of Albi when he was Bishop of Mende in the yeare 1670 but know not whether it be that you desire.†2 I shall indeavour to find out the others if he preached any, either before or since, and send them you by the first oportunity. Mr: Tufton is growen a new man since he came hither being much amended, I thanke you most kindly for the news of Sir John Chichley's encreased famyly, which he never yet told me of nor of his Lady's great belly, pray when you see them make my service acceptable to them both. and let him know that I shall write to him shortly to thanke him for the fine Tobacco box he sent me by Mr. Tufton. My Lord Bruce and his Lady†3 are at length arrived here, but intend to stay but 2 or 3 months at most and then intend for Bourbon,†4 the best news that I can send
― 152 ―

you from hence is that all our nation are in indifferent good health and Ile assure you no one of them is more your servant then
Sir
Your most obliged and affectionate freind
WILLIAM CHARLETON
Mr: Tufton Dr. Barbyrac, Dr. Magnoll, Dr. Paul†1 who is returned from Usez, and mr. Pati†2 present you their humble service. My humble service to Mr. Digg's†3 to whom I wish much joy.
Address: These For His worthy freind Mr: John Locke at Mr: Hicks's a tailer below the King's playhouse in Bridges street London port payè jusques a Paris
Postal note: franc pour paris
Postmark: FE 12(?)
Endorsed by Locke: (i): Mr Charleton 6o Feb: 80; (ii): Charleton 6o Feb. 80
527. Nathaniel Hodges to Locke, 28 January 1680 (459, 737)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, f. 211. Locke was in Oxford from about 20 December to 3 February. Hodges was perhaps at Thanet House; if so, his companion is likely to have been Stringer or John Hoskins. For the names Carmelin, Lysis, and Musidore, see i. 324, n. 1.
Dear Carmelin
I Received both yours, one by the Carrier, the other by the Dean,†4 for which as I send you many thanks, So likewise an honest acknowledgment that I ought to return you two for them; But when I reflect upon the weaknesse of my head I am apt to think one enough, and I am affraid when I reflect upon the weaknesse of my understanding, That a man of any thing lesse generosity than Carmelin would be as apt to think one too much. I have been extremely dull and low these two or three daies, and though the gent†5 were very pleasant, and seemed to shew the effects of your good
― 153 ―

wishes to us both, yet for all his haste he was fain to be contented with that rate of Musique the Fiddle he was to play upon would afford. If you had been with us you would have thought it a very near resemblance of a brisk French Mounseiur's making a Tabor of a Tub. I read your Letter to him because the raillery of it was equally obliging to us both, unlesse I had in one particular the advantage, That whilst it gave me the kind thoughts of an absent freind, it furnished me at the same time with the onely acceptable things I had to entertain an other that was present. What we said of you I can no more tell you than your own eares that tingled without doubt whilst we were at it. Much inward joy I am sure I had, whether the rest of my outward expressions were agreable or no I cannot tell, but this I know, my head rang more than a long peal or two. Yet for all the din, Chamber rent†1 I remember we talked of, which I promised not to exact, But I must tell you I have such a hankering after somewhat of the French dominion as well as my neighbours, That I cannot but a little bristle up my selfe when I hear my freind means to come in person and doe me homage for it. Why should the lame horse stand so much upon it? doth he not know that there are Aldermen to be met with as well as there were Senatours at Rome?†2 Though I cannot promise his Master good company, yet I can assure Rosinante he shall not fail of his choise of Dapples.†3 If neither Lysis nor Carmelin can work any thing with him, let him be delivered up to the Secular powers of the Ferrier.†4 And that is all my head, my paper, and my bed will now permitt me, unlesse it be to remember honest Musidore who must stay for his cherishing 'till some more easy and gamesome time of
LYSIS
Jan: 28th. 1679
Endorsed by Locke: Lysis 28 Jan 79

February
528. John Hoskins to Locke, 5 February 1680 (77, 753)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 230-1. For the writer see nos. 76, 308. Locke left Oxford on 3 February and arrived at Salisbury on the 4th. He left Salisbury on 12 February.
London 5th: Feb: 1679
Dear Sir
I have yours of the 1st: and 2d: Instant; togeather with a Book, which I have delivered according as you directed me in the paper wherein 'twas wrapt; my Lord†1 received it with great joy; and bid me give you a thousand thanks, he perused it greedily, and I see him at it very intent last night again, I told him you desired you might know, if there were anything in it, he would have further satisfaction about. how he likes the whole I cannot yet account to you, for I have not spook to him of it. But before I acquainted him with what you writt relating to the Schole at Mrs: Birches.†2 he is well pleased with the offer you make of going over to her, being desirous to know what in her own mind she is most inclind to; whether she had rather keep the boording her self and a Master to teach them; or quitt all to an other that shall be commended to her. and when you have found her own Inclination, to sound likewise what she may be perswaded to, but how this business will comport with your removall from Oxford I cannot tell; however I thought best now to discharge myself of my Lords command, because I goe into Norfolk†3 the next week; and what you doe in refference to it I must desire you to give an account of to Mr: Stringer; I am in no good state of health, those symtoms I have still of a Rumatisme, tho not in so great, yet in a troublesom degree. I am sorry for our little Godson,†4 I wish you good success in his recovery, besides my greif for his Son, I am troubled it will keep him from coming to town, I hoped to have seen him before I went. my humble service to him and his Lady. My Lords indifferent, but by dringing a Milk water is very apt to have the Gout in his stomach. my Lady is well. Mr Stringer told me he writt to you by
― 155 ―

Tewsdays Post,†1 not being able to give you an account of your business till then. Publick news I have as little as I have taken time to write it; I perceive by J:Ts: Letter†2 (which he tells me was to come with the book that came from you, but came the day after) all the news I can tell you is what of those things you hear, are fals, or are suspected. 1st: the D: of Y: is not come. nor is there any reconciliation made between him and the D: of M: nor how confidently so ever it is talkd, doe we beleive the former will capacitate himself for Admirall, nor the latter be restored.†3 the report of the Generall Pardon is over, twas said at first it should extend to all but the Lords in the Tower, but tis hush'd.†4 there is no Inditement yet brought in against Sir Ro: Peyton. so that tis expected he shall be baild the last day of the Term;†5 Harris that Publishes the Protestant Intelligence was Indited to day for selling a book calld the Appeale, which was found against him; so we shall see who will be fined highest the Protestant Pamphleteers or Popish subborners.†6 Mr: S: Coventrey has leave to sell his Place. we hear tis a great dispute whether my L: Sunderl: or L: Hide shall be L: high Treasurer. if the former then the latter and S: Godolphin shall be the 2 Secretarys. confident rumours we have had that Sir L: Jenkings, or a Bisshop neer you shall have the great Seale; but Mr: Finch being made first Commissioner of the Admiralty and P: Councillor stounds that report. my Lord Bronkerd, and Sir T: Littleton come in the places of Sir H: Capell and Mr: Vaughan that have both quitted.†7
― 156 ―

There is a great Alteration making in the Commissions of the Justices of the Peace, but tis carried very secrettly, and will be so till the whole be finished.†1 these heads of news J:Ts: Letters puts me in Mind of; I wish I knew or could think of anything that would make my Letter savory to the D:†2 whose appetite to news I take to be sharper then yours. I am
Yours most affectionately
JH
Direct to me at Mrs Forgys a Hosiers at the Leg and Star neer Somerset house in the Strand
Address: These to Mr: Lock at Dr: Thomas's house in Salsbury
Postmark: FE 5
Endorsed by Locke: J Hoskins 5 Feb. 79/80
529. Thomas Stringer to Locke, 5 February 1680 (430, 618)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, ff. 145-6.
Feb: 5th. 1679.
Deare Sir
Hearing by mr Hoskins you are gon from Oxford and fearing the letter I sent thether should miscarry I have therefore sent this Extraordinary to Salisbury, only to acquaint you that as yett I heare noe news from Wilson†3 about your money in the Exchequer, though mr Rychards†4 did not only promise to send him to me, but did undertake to use his best endeavours to gett you a Chapman himselfe. I have receive your money for Kingston from my Lord†5 and have Lodged it with mr Percivall†6 for you as you desire. I
― 157 ―

have spake to Ben:†1 about my Lady Windhams Interest†2 whoe doth promise to procure it. I am just takeing Coach for Bexwells and therefore pardon the hast of
Your very humble servant
THO: STRINGER
Address: For mr John Lock at Doctor Thomas his house in Salisbury
Postmark: FE 7

530. Thomas Tufton, later sixth earl of Thanet to Locke, 14/24 February 1680 (454, 591)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 32-3.
Montpellier the 24 of February 80
Sir
I finde it very nessesary for mee now to lett you know the occation of this long silence, my first reason was the long staye you made in the Country,†3 the second was that I might lett you know they effects of Montpellier aire which I owe in great measure my life to for I came hiether very ill and by experience finde I can live in a hott Country though all the ill consequences of that cold†acannot make mee repent that I am of it for I know nothing that I would change with them but aire, maye I but endure to keep here 2 yeare as I designe you will see mee returne and not lessen the reputation of the Country for relieving miserable Creatures that cannot live at home, I am Lodged at the Cannourg†4 very well where I keep house alone and endeavor to finde the content of a temperate life I have not lesse care of my servants for I have learned the Frenche waye to preserve there health in keeping them to a spare diet, wee have here my Lady Meathe and hur Brother who this
― 158 ―

night desiered mee to returne his thankes for conveying his letter to his Brother who forgetts him to much†1 last post I wrote to my Brother†2 to speake to him, our faithfull mr Charleton will ever diserve that name hee wrote to you last weeke but is as farr from quitting this place as the daye hee arrived. hee will not promise to goe any where with mee but a Coursing wee enjoye here that diversion often, allowed to my Lord Bruce†a by†a the Duke of Verneull†3 which wee are to take as a very great favour, I am very gladd to oblige my Country men with horses which I finde add much to our satisfaction here, I am now quite out of hopes of seing you except the sea coll and rotting small beere should occation the returne of your old ennemye which is not the part of a Frend to wishe I had much rather returne well my selfe and finde wee maye bothe endure old England, I wrote a monthe agoe to Sir James Rusworthe†4 to whom I desiere my service and this post doe the same to Sir John†5 whom I here is soe well that hee needs never more see this place, I disposed of all your presents as directed and at Paris made offer to that Gentleman†6 of what hee had disbursed for you which surprised him for hee sayes you made him severall presents and' hee is in paine how to bee quite with you it tis not his case alone for manny of your Country men are sensible of it, a letter from my Brother Thanet informes mee that you have the mildest winter that ever was know wee are here surfieted with fine dayes and for variety I could almost wishe for ill weather, I could bee gladd to see him here for I here hee is in a dangerous condistion I used all endeavors to make him thinke of it in time, if you meet with him pray give your oppinnion of it, Sir the last favour is to present my service to my Lady and Sir John Bankes and the young Gentleman that was to goe with us into Italye and to the Ladyes and mr Finche, yours
TUFTON
Address: For mr Locke at Thanet house in Aldersgate Street London
Postmark: FE 26
Endorsed by Locke: Mr Tufton 24 Feb. 80

531. William Charleton to Locke, 2/12 March 1680 (526, 559)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, ff. 37-8.
Montpellier the 12th: March 1680
Deare Sir
It may justly seem verry strange to you since it do's to my self, that I have let a letter from so good a freind ly unanswer'd by me so long a time, Dr: Paul's indisposition ha's prevented me from giving you an account of the weight of water, but he being now on the mending hand I hope shortly to satisfie you in that particular, in the mean time I send you on his part the way of preparing leven,†1 with his service, I have procur'd as I supose the only sermon of Monsieur D'Albi and shall send it you by the first occasion, Inclos'd you have a note of what Dr. Magnol desires of the many plants you mention'd together with his thanks,†2 and the manner write by himself of the making use of the Cynaria Aculeata and he ha's added that of the Gallium,†3 I am troubled that I am not as able to serve you as I am willing and then you might be sure of being punctually comply'd with in your desires, we have many English here though few of great quality except My Lady Meath My Lord Bruce and his Lady both designed shortly to leave this place, Mr. Tufton intends for Barcelona with mr. Bard an English gentleman that you have formerly seen here. Mr. Morris†4 ha's received little benefit by the journey he ha's made hither though he ha's been verry temperate, your humble servant is still at the old rate neither verry well nor verry ill but as you have obliged him
Sir
Your most cordiall freind
WILLIAM CHARLETON
My humble service to Sir John chichley and his Lady pray acquaint him that I shall suddenly give him an account of it.
You will oblige me in letting me know if you have received notice of Mr. Leanards letters having been delivered to mr. Morgan, and in favouring me in the delivery of this.

Madam la princesse Caietan is the Lady that lodged at the Louvre in 77.†1

532. Sir Anthony Ashley Cooper, first earl of Shaftesbury, to Locke, 20 March 1680 (322, 561)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 72-3. Written by an amanuensis apart from the signature. Printed in King, p. 36.
London: March 20o: 79/80
Mr: Locke.
We long to see you here; and hope you have allmost ended your Travails. Somersetshire no doubt wil perfect your breeding; after France and Oxford you could not goe to a properer place. My wife finds you profit much there; for you have recover'd your Skil in Chedder Cheases and for a Demonstration have sent us one of the best we have seene. I thank you for your care about my Grandchild,†2 but haveing wearyed my self with considerations every way, I resolve to have him in my house: I long to speake with you about it. — For news we have little. onely our Governors here are soe truely zealous for the advancement of the Protestant Religion as 'tis established in the Church of England; that they are sending the Common Prayer-book the second tyme into Scotland.†3 No doubt but my Lord Lauderdale knows it will agree with their present constitution; but surely he was much mistaken when he administred the Covenant to England.†4 But we shall see how the Tripodes,†5 and the holy Alter will agree. — My Lord of Ormond is
― 161 ―

said to be dying;†1 soe that you have Irish and Scotch News: and for English you make as much att Bristoll as in any part of the Kingdome.†2
Thus recomending you to the Protection of the Bishop of Bath and Wells†3 (whose strong Beere is the onely spirituall thing any Somersetsheire Gentleman knows) I rest
Your very affectionate and assured freind
SHAFTESBURY
Address: For John Locke Esq. Att Sutton Courte To be lefte att mr: Matt: Walters a Grocer upon the Brid In Bristoll.
Endorsed by Locke: E Shaftesbury 20 Mar 79/80
May
533. Mrs. Anne Grigg to Locke, 8/18 [May] 1680 (320, 535)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 122-3. The writer from the contents and handwriting. The month from Locke's endorsement.
Paris the 18th 80
Deare Brother
As there is nothing in the world I priz like an old friend you may well conclude it of great concerne to me to give them all the content I can; before your letter came to my hand I determin'd to say more to you than to any of my familiars and by this post dispatch an account of myself and all that relate to me here, and first I thank God we are all very well, indeed poor Will†4 came ill from London with a cold which the Sea did not cure by reason of the short pasage, he has bin dull and oprest with flegme which now threatens no mischief, he liv'd upon Tissan till he fear'd starving and when he return'd to flesh rather improved than lost his temper,†5 we both wish'd you near, and as well as I could gues us'd him as you would have me, for I need none to tell me good things of Mr Locke to make me value his judgment and his kindness, and I doe with great sincerity thank you for the particular directions you give me, but
― 162 ―

my heart pains me to think of the unhappy accedent at Bristol,†1 especially now I hear the evil is not over, I wish your side as well as my own, and shall with great joy receave every little officer that brings me good news from you. this day I was with Monsieur Justel who speaks of you as you doe of him we agree mightly and tomorrow he with Monsieur Toinard will be with me, and then owe†2 be to you; Mr Marshall†3 is your servant and punctually observ'd all orders, so that I am in your Lodgins and have in the honest Scotchman a diligent and usefull acquaintance. pray in a line let my Bristol friends know that we are well and tell yourself that I am so much in disorder for want of time and setlement, that I cannot so wisely nor so handsomly as I would tell you that I will ever be your most affectionate sister
Address: To Mr Locke at the Earle of Shaftsburys at Thanet House in Aldersgate Street London
Postmark: — 15
Endorsed by Locke: A Grig 18o May 80.
534. Henri Justel to Locke, 11/21 May 1680 (524, 537)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 12, ff. 84-5. Locke listed the contents by making marginal notes and repeating them in the endorsement, as explained in the note on Toinard: i. 582. The marginals are omitted here.
le 21 May 1680
Monsieur
Jay appris avec déplaisir laccident qui vous est arrivé qui a touché tous ceux qui ont l'honneur de vous connoitre. Vous m'avez obligé sensiblement en me donnant la connoissance dune personne aussi raisonnable que celle que vous mavez recommandeè.†4 Jaurois esté bien aise de scavoir son nom que vous avez oubliè de me dire. Vous pouvez estre asseuré que je la servirai en tout ce que je pourrai. Jaurois bien de la joye de pouvoir luy estre utile et de luy témoigner lestime que je fais de son merite. Je vous remercie tres humblement du globe dont vous mavez envoyè la description et la figure.†5
― 163 ―

On attend ici avec impatience le livre de Mr. Morison. Monsieur l Evesque de Londres†1 ma envoyè le livre de Malpigi qui est curieux, la seconde partie nest pas si considerable que la premiere. Nous navons de nouveau que les petits livres de Mr. Pereau†2que Mr. Thoinart vous a envoyez. on travaille a ruiner les Cartesiens et a empescher quon enseigne leur doctrine qui paroist contraire a la creance de Rome sur le suject de la transsubstantiation.†3 les Janssenistes et les Reformez ne seront pas espargnez. toutes les nouveautez en matiere de philosophie seront supprimeés. les docteurs ont enfin eu lavantage et Aristote aura le dessus. On envoye ici une belle statue dapollon Pythien quon dit estre parfaite. Elle represente un corps nud qui a la teste dapollon, le bras gauche appuyè sur un tronc darbre entortillé dun serpent et le bras droit elevé et tourné derriere la teste.†4 On vous aura parlè du miroir ardent de Mr. Vilete qui est fort grand et sans tache.†5 Jen ai marquè la grandeur a Mr. gale Secretaire de votre Societé.†6 Le livre du Pere Simon est imprime en Hollande. il y a une response dun docteur de Sorbonne a la lettre de Mr. Spanheim que vous aurez veue. Ce docteur a faict une Analyse du livre de ce Pere qui est tres bien faicte et tres exacte.†7 On a veu un petit traitté de la regale, mais il est devenu si rare, quil est difficile de le pouvoir seulement lire.†8 Mr. Litlebury†9 qui vous rendra ceste lettre vous dira de nos nouvelles. Tous ceux qui ont eu le bonheur de vous voir a Paris vous baisent les mains et vous sont obligez de l'honneur de votre souvenir. Je ne doute pas que vous ne voyez souvent Mr. Brisban que je Vous supplie de vouloir asseurer de mes respects. Je
― 164 ―

ne luy ecris pas parce que je scai bien quil naime pas a recevoir des lettres de personnes. Chacun a ses raisons en ce monde et il ne faut rien faire qui puisse choquer nos amis. Je vous remercie de la peine que vous avez prise de vous informer de la famille du nom de Blowin, cest pour le Secretaire de lambassade de Suede qui porte ce nom la, lequel a interest den estre informe. Il vous en sera tout a faict obligé. cest une personne de merite. quand je scaurai quelque nouvelle litteraire je vous en ferai part. cest Votre tres humble et tres obeissent serviteur
JUSTEL†a
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Loke at Mr. Hick tayler below the Kings play house in bridges street London
Endorsed by Locke: (i): Justel 21o May 80; (ii): Morison / Malpigius / Cartesians / Statue d'Apollon / Miroir ardent / P Simon / Regale / Blowin†b
535. Mrs. Anna Grigg to Locke, 12/22 May 1680 (533, 539)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 124-5.
My Deare Brother
Tho I will not venture often by the post, you are never to scape my hand when a civil person offers me his service; I hope the person that is to deliver you this†1 will have a quick passage, for I long to give you the satisfaction of knowing againe that we are in perfict health, and that the friendship you have procur'd me with Monsieur Justell is like to doe me considerable service, we have allready entred into deepe talk and remember you withall all imaginable good Will: I will not undertake to tell you the storys of France, I meane what concerns us, our friend will I am very sure doe that part, but this I must venture to tell you that some with whome you have formerly converst easily, become sower and severe against Protestants and you will find things worse then you left them, however you are often wish'd for here, by men a woman and Child; I cannot wish you a Cough but I wish you at Someurs†2where your friends advise me by all meanes to pitch my tent, indeed they urge it with such strong reasons as will infalliblie determine me for that
― 165 ―

place God willing, and next week I designe my departure from hence; but pray remember that Mr Reneu†1 will convey your letters and that I receave none with more joy than yours, and therefore gratifie me as often as you please, and consider me as one that dares never forget kindnesses, and take it as a sure signe that I am sincere in all that I have profest, that in twelve yeares time†2 the fickle Nature of women has not betray'd me to be faint hearted in any intregue of friendship with you, nor is it in the power of any intrest to make me indifferent what becomes of you, my letter is cal'd for and therefore farwell
Your affectionate sister and servant
A GRIGG
May the 22th 80
Address: For yourself
Endorsed by Locke: A Grig 22 May. 80
536. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, 12/22 May [1680] (525, 538)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, ff. 43-4, and c. 31, f. 32 (enclosure). Year from Locke's endorsement. Answered by no. 538.
+
ce mercredi 22. May
Jamais aucune des votres, Monsieur, ne ma donné tant de joie que cele qui m'a eté rendue par une Dame de vos amies, qui va à Saumur, mais en meme tems j'ay eté saisi d'une extreme afliction pour l'acident qui vous est arivé, et je voudrois que ce vous fust une ocasion pour venir revoir mr notre Abbé Gendron. Il etoit ici ce carême dernier, et jalay avec lui au Palais demander a madame Varenes ceque pouvoien<t>†a etre devenus les livres que je lui avois donnéz pour vous des leté dernier puisqu'ils ne <vous>†b avoient point eté rendus. ce netoit pas la dixieme fois que je lui avois fait cete demandé mais adhibueram testem fidelem,†3 afin qu'il vous pust
― 166 ―

assurer que j avois satisfait a ceque vous aviez desiré de moi. elle me dist cequ'ele mavoit toujours qu'il etoit vray qu'aiant manqué une ocasion ele les avoit gardéz tres long tems, jusques au depart de mr Charas auquel enfin ele les avoit donez,†1 mais cela ne me contentoit pas a cause de votre silence sur cet article et je ne vous dissimuleray point que j'ay eu pour ce retardement beaucoup de chagrin aprehendant que vous pussiez penser que je navois executé lhonneur de vos ordres qui feront en tout tems et en tous lieux ma plus grande joie. Vous ne me mandez point avoir receu la maniere de faire du Levain†2 ny si ele vous a reüssi et le pain aussi avec ce Levain. Il y en a d'excelent a Saumur qui se fait a un vilage voizin, et lon atribue cela a l'eau, car la Reine fit autrefois suivre la cour au meilleur Boulanger de ce vilage qui ne faisoit plus come chez lui. Je vous ai envoié trois in 8. d'essais de Physique de mr Perraut†3 que l'autheur ma donnéz si bien reliéz que je voudrois qu'ils fussent entre vos mains, mais je me suis contenté de vous les envoier en blanc a cause des rigeurs de votre Doüane et que le Sieur Littlebury n'auroit pas voulu s'en charger autrement.†4 je vous ay envoié par le même des epreuves de mon harmonie des Rois, des Paralipomen et des prophetes; qui est bien plus dificile a faire et a imprimer que cele des mêmes livres avec les Pseaumes.†5 Vous me direz votre sentiment sincere sur cete maniere, qui me donne bien de la peine, et je nescay si la satisfaction qu'en poura avoir le Lecteur, la poura egaler ou au moins en aprocher. Peu de persones savent que je me suis ataché a cet ouvrage, et je n'en ay montré les epreuves qu'a deux de mes amis, qui en les voiant s'etonnerent de ce quil y a tant d'harmonies des Evangiles, et que lon n'en ait point encore un des rois et des Paralipomen, quand même on n'y ajouteroit pas les Pseaumes ny les Prophetes come je fais. J'ay commencé a faire les epreuves de tout cequi regimbe le plus dans limpression, et quand jen auray encore environ une douzaine de pages, le reste sera assez facile. je crois avoir fixé des evenements et des propheties assez heureusement, et pour peu que vous vouliez vous doner la peine
― 167 ―

d'examiner le tout, come vous avez fait cele des Evangiles, le public vous en sera un jour bien obligé.
Je ne scaurois pas vous entretenir plus au long parceque je vais au service dun de nos amis et parents qui avoit eté tout notre conseil pendant notre proces contre Monsieur et nos religieuses. Je n'ay jamais eu de ma vie une si cruele semaine, que me fut la derniere. Cet ami demeura malade le Dimanche, je receus nouvele le vendredi que mr Perier l'aisné etoit mort a Clermont†1 et le samedi j apris que vous aviez deux côtes cassées. ce mr Perier etoit une personne d'un grand merite, et navoit que 38.ans. il etoit neveu de mr Paschal, et vous aurez pu voir quelquefois dans ma chambre quelquun de mss ses freres. Je devois aler a la fin de cet eté faire avec lui lexperience de la pezanteur de lair avec les barometres simple et double sur le Puy de Domene, dont il est parlé dans l'ecrit <du>†a Sieur Hubin, que vous avez.†2
Je suis telement acoutumé a recevoir de vos presents que j'oubliois a vous remercier du dernier paquet. j'ay aussi receu celui ou etoient les cartes de Londres dont j'ay doné une a mr Auzout, qui vous salüe. celes a joüer sont droles.
Je voudrois bien que vous voulussiez faire imprimer votre mani<ere>†b de faire des receuils et des cabinets, je lenseigne a tout le monde, <et>†b dis qu'ele est de vous, et l'on la trouve admirable.†3
Mr Justel m'a dit par deux fois que la Dame Angloise avoit de largent a me doner de votre part, dont je suis etonné car ce seroit a moy a vous en envoier, c'est pourquoi j'ay interest que nous ne venions point a conte. J'en avois desja remercié un gentilhome qui m'avoit dit la même chose de votre part cet Automne derniere.†4
Hier vinrent ici me voir deux jeunes Anglois que je juge etre le fils de la Dame et un autre jeune gentilhomme que je vis chez elle

samedi dernier.†1 je n'ay pas eté assez heureux pour les recevoir. j'etois a l'observatoire ou nous parlions bien de vous, et vous en avez cy joint une temoignage de mr l'Abé Picard, ou est lobservation des macules.

538. Locke to Nicolas Toinard, 20 May 1680 (536, 541)
B.M., Add. MS. 28,835, ff. 1-2. Printed in Ollion, Notes, pp. 68-72; Ollion, pp. 47-52. Answers no. 536; answered by nos. 541 and 545.
(English ) 
London. 20 May. 80
Ictus ille calcis equinæ qui adeo afflixit costas non tantum ex contusione mihi attulit dolorem, quantum ex timore, ne longum silentium me tibi negligentiæ suspectum redderet. infortunium
― 171 ―

enim illud exteriora cutem scilicet et ossa solum, hoc intima pectoris et cor ipsum pupugit. Sed decumbentem tua ut vidio defendit humanitas, et jam data occasione consolata est amicitia, utroque nomine tibi gratias quantas quantas possum et habeo et reddo. Cæterum mihi valde valde molestum est, nugas meas tibi tantum facessere negotium, ut necesse tibi fore putares iterum atque iterum Vareniam adiere, et adhibito teste fideli de libris depositis sciscitari, quasi aut tu minus promptus in amicitiæ officiis aut ego id suspicari possem. istud certe mihi dolet te istuc posse inducere animum. Ego libros illos (sc. les Essays de Morale les 3 premiers volums et les remedes de Madame Fouquet) reversus Londinum domi meæ reperi, sed uti fit domesticorum oscitantiâ nec quando nec per quem allati sunt scire poteram.†1 et si festinatio me fefellit, nescio, hoc scio me ultimis meis literis per Dominam Grig missis te de hac re certiorem facere destinaveram.†2 Infortunia rarò venire solitaria et dicimus nos et sentio ego. Solatium enim et fructum quem ex literis tuis cæpisse oportuit me una cum ipsis litteris ex ultimis tuis nimis constat. Nihil enim de modo conficiendi fermentum nec de paneficio unquam ad manus meas pervenit, et qui istum mihi
― 172 ―

tum animi tum corporis nutrimentum interverterunt opto ut fame pereant vel saltem pane furfuraceo pænitentiam agant. Philosophiam Perautii aliquid habere in se eximium non dubito. et quia ex familiaribus tuis author est et quia hanc ignorantiæ meæ medelam mihi transmittendam curasti. quod si vero appulsum navis in qua advehitur anxiè expecto inde est quod aliquid Philosophiâ majus simul asportatur, Paralipomenωn scilicet harmonia. Hujus prima mentio me adire fecit Litleburium patrem,†1 <filium>†a modo inveni e Galliâ vestrâ reversum sed libris velociorem, et me, impatienter de harmoniæ adventu rogantem, aliquot adhuc dies expectare jubet. Hæc ipsius verba meis auribus parum harmonica. Avidè enim cupio istius operis primitias videre et degustare, et ex iis spem concipere me aliquando visurum hanc etiam harmoniam animo meo tam diu exoptatam a tam peritâ a tam doctâ manu concinnatam. Noli igitur me hortari ut schedas hasce prolusorias perlegam, fac solum ut cum hasce iterum atque iterum perlegi, ne aliæ desint usque dum peragatur opus. Tibi enim persuasum velim, nihil parturiente prælo in publicum prodire posse quod huic operi
― 173 ―

meâ quidem sententiâ conferri possit. Itaque impensè rogo ut schedas omnes mihi transmittendas cures ut tandem in integrum perfectumque volumen coalescant, ut fratri suo Evangelico adjungatur hic alter aureus. fiantque simul musæi mei cimelia, argento auroque pretiosora. Ignoscas rogo huic petitioni parum modestæ. Aliis in rebus fateor servandus est modus. Sed in re tam eximiâ tam desideratâ quis est qui sine culpâ sibi potest temperare. Judicium meum tibi curæ esse non debet quia nihili est, quia non opus erit, et si opus esset non defuturum. nosti in me libertatem loquendi minimè fucatam. Et si mea censura tibi aliquid esse possit incitamenti ut me hisce paginis locupletes, scias quod amicitia, gratitudo, benevolentia, quæ lenitatem et mansuetudinem aliis solent suadere me hac in causâ judicem reddent severiorem. En tibi igitur alter Minos, qualem velis, fac solum ut coram appareat reus nunquam ex manibus meis in libertatem iterum elapsurus.

(Original Text)
London. 20 May. 80
That kick from a horse's hoof which knocked my ribs about so severely did not distress me so much by the battering I received as by the fear I felt that my long silence might be leading you to suspect that I was neglecting you;
[p. 171]
for that misfortune affected only the outside of me, to wit my skin and bones, but this pierced my inmost breast and my very heart. But your kind-heartedness, as I now see, has been my advocate whilst I lay sick, and your friendship has comforted me when the occasion has arisen. On both these accounts I am deeply grateful to you, and I give you the warmest thanks I am capable of. For the rest, I am exceedingly vexed that my trifles should give you so much trouble as to make you think it necessary to call again and again on Mme de Varennes, taking a reliable witness with you, to inquire about the books left with her; as if you were in any way backward in rendering friendly services, or as if I could suspect you of it. I am certainly sorry that you could think of doing such a thing. As for those books, i.e. les Essays de Morale les 3 premiers volums, et les remedes de Madame Fouquet, I found them at my lodging when I returned to London, but owing to the negligence of the servants, as so often happens, I was not able to discover when or by whom they were brought there.†1 I may possibly have omitted to mention it in the hurry of writing, but I know that I had meant to let you know about this in my last letter, which was sent by Mrs. Grigg.†2 Misfortunes seldom come singly, as we say and as I now realize; for the comfort and profit which I ought to have received from your letters together with the letters themselves are made all too clear by your last. Nothing about the method of making yeast or baking bread has ever come to my hands, and I hope that the people who have
[p. 172]
defrauded me of that sustenance both of soul and of body may perish of hunger, or at least may do penance by living on bran-bread.
I do not doubt that there is something of especial merit in the science of Perrault, both because the author is a friend of yours and since you have arranged for this remedy for my ignorance to be sent to me. My real reason, however, for eagerly expecting the arrival of the ship that is carrying it is that it is bringing at the same time something greater than science, I mean your Harmony of the Book of Chronicles. The first mention of this made me go to see Littlebury père;†1 but I found only the son, who had returned from your land of France, though quicker than the books; when I asked impatiently about the arrival of the Harmony he told me I must wait a few days longer. These words of his did not ring very harmoniously in my ears; for I am all agog to see and taste the first-fruits of that work, and to conceive from them the hope that I may one day see also the harmony that my soul has so long yearned for, attuned as it is by such a skilled and scholarly hand. You need not therefore urge me to peruse these precursory sheets; only see to it that when I have read them through again and again there may be no lack of others to follow until the work is finished; for I would have you feel certain
[p. 173]
that the labours of the press can give the public nothing able to compare with that work, at least in my opinion. I beg you therefore most earnestly to have all the sheets sent to me, so that they may finally be brought together in a complete and finished volume, with this second golden brother joined to his brother of the Gospel, to become together the treasures of my study, more precious than silver and gold. Forgive me, please, for being such a shameless petitioner; in other things, I admit, one should observe moderation; but in a matter of such importance and so much the object of our desires who can restrain himself and remain blameless? My own judgement must not concern you, since it is nothing, and since there will be no need for it, and if the need should arise it will not be wanting. You know my unvarnished freedom of speech; and if reproof from me could help at all in inciting you to enrich me with these pages, know that friendship, gratitude, and goodwill, which usually move others to lenity and forbearance, will in this case make me a severer judge. There, then, is a second Minos for you, of the sort you would wish; only see to it that the accused appears before me, never again to slip out of my hands into liberty.

Meanwhile I thank you for giving me light from these spots that darken the sun himself. (Original Text) I find two or three names of measures employed at Montpellier, and it would be useful to me to know their contents. They are une Truquette d'eau, une Piche d'eau et une Hemine de Farine.†3 If you should happen to meet anyone from that city who can explain these terms, please ask him to do so, so that I can decide about these values with certainty. I come across many such things which give me occasion to wish that people might some day agree upon the philosophic foot. I should therefore be glad to know what conclusion our friend Römer, to whom I send my best wishes, has finally come to about it, as when he was leaving this country he seemed to me to have some doubts about the length of the pendulum. But I ought to stop some time and not go on wearying you; may I tell you just one thing before I do so? Last Tuesday
[p. 176]
hailstones of enormous size fell all over the city here. I myself measured one lump of ice (for that is what they really were) which had a circumference of 420 grys; it was rounded in shape and slightly flattened on both sides, so that it was not perfectly spherical. I hear that others were measured by various people and found to have twice as great a circumference; but the middling specimen that I handled myself sufficiently astonished me, and I should be glad to know from your philosophers up to what weight solid bodies of such bulk can be suspended in the air. I doubt whether the Cartesians can have any contrivances to help in this matter, and whether the Occult Qualities of the Peripatetics may not break down under such a load. But enough of all this. Please give my best respects to those admirable and distinguished gentlemen Messrs. Gendron, Formentin, Renaudot, St. Colombe, Bernier, Picard, Justel, and the rest of my well-wishers who are accustomed to gather at his house. Please forgive me for writing in Latin, as I am not well versed either in it or in French; but I thought that your refined ears would be less offended by solecisms in a foreign tongue. Good-bye, and continue to love me
Your most obedient
JL

539. Mrs. Anna Grigg to Locke, 26 May/5 June 1680 (535, 555)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 126-7.
Soumeurs the 5th of June 1680
My Deare Brother
I cannot denie but since my last to you I have mett with some little tediousness, but all hinders not my health and I bless God my satisfaction; I could not from Paris give you a perfict account of your friends, especially Monsieur Toynard, whome I had seen but once when I write to you from Paris, but imediately after he obliged me with his good company and gave me very plaine demonstrations of your power over him, for never did I see a man more substantially usfull, he sav'd me money very ingeniously, and without begging it procur'd me the assistance of the civilest persons in Orleans that ever I mett withall,†1 so that by your intrest here I have such obligations as will charme me into a greater respect for France than I imagin'd I could be capable of; as to the paying your debts tis soone done for Monsieur Toinard will not be prevailed upon to own that you owe him anything, but rather complains that you play tricks with him and will not instruct him how he may gues at what is due to you from himself, the differance is such between your accounts that t'will be hard to make them answer either of your endevours, for Monsieur Toynard desires the satisfaction of paying you part of the great things are due to you; Is not this a very plesant scene for one that knows herself to be an old debtor to you? I wish it may be as wisely demonstrated that I am sensible of your affectionate care of me as it is easie for me in all places to find persons that speak honestly fine and good things of you, but whatever fate disturbs my acknowledgments, I will love you as becomes an innocent friend and an upright sister, who thinks of your misfortune with a sigh, and of your distance with harmeless desires that you were eating Straberies with her; I must needs informe
― 178 ―


you that Soumeurs is one of the prettyest places I ever saw and the House I am in not onely good and plesant but the diet excelent and the owners of it wonderfully civil, they have as good a reputation as can be imagind, and persons of our own Nation by long experiance teach me to write thus handsomely of them; but my fortune is perticularly to be remark'd, for others pay fiveteen and eight Crowns a months for lodging and diet, I have the very best in all respects for three Crowns less; I think the termes of living hard in France, but I must not repine when I am favoured on al sids.
But after all I am sometimes in pain, when Mr Crofts who is here with Mr Cesar†1 for a few days longer, dispars of the childs ever learning French or anything else. the task I see will take up time and brains, I will not grudg him mine so it may serve him, but should the expence prove great and his improvement smale I shall be concern'd more then enough, but at presant I doe not dispond whatever is sugested to me, so that I begin to hope that I am endued with a little more patience then I have sometimes bin mistris of And indeed I live in an age wherin there is need of a large provission of this vertue, God preserve sweet England and all my beloved friends there, you know who I most value among them, pray preserve me in their memory and for your satisfaction I must tell you that by your means and Mr Reneus I have even in this remote corner very great civilitys from the most desirable persons, and in good ernest there is so much differance between the reasonable comforts of this town and my abode at Brentwood†2 that I cannot bemoan myself in the change I have made. The evils the protestants feel and those they fear makes them more considerate then they are in a place that shall be nameless, The youth are taught more carefully to be religious in this Colledge,†3 then in our English schools, it may be thay may not brag of that exactness of learning that other places may, but yet they make a shift to produce persons well tempor'd and fit for busseness or conversation. You see deare Brother by the report I give of things that I have noe fancy to be out of humour with my presant state of life, I confess I think it very ungratfull to be contemplating the night and never reflect upon any thing but
― 179 ―

what creats terror, I thank God the sun shins sometimes and many are the occassions I have dayly to sing prayse, in this sense of things I will chuse to conclude this long letter in which I must request you to doe as I have don, turn over leif, for when you were in France you charged me to doe so by you, pray remember, that I prize your letters and favours very particularly and that I am without other designs than those of simplicity and kindness
Deare Brother
Your most humble servant and much obliged friend
ANNA GRIGG
my good sister Betty†1 will rejoyce to hear that we are well when you say or write it tis enough

You will here receive two bills for thirty pounds, which I was willinge to accept of, though I could contrive it noe more to your convenience. I consider'd that Shandoy's street was neare Mr Herberte, though farre from Thanet house.†3 I had return'd all your
― 180 ―

money in my hands, could I have met with those whose occasions would have allow'd them to have receiv'd it; but I was forc'd to doe it as I could.
I have sent a state of your account; and must acquainte you that in the money you left with Mr Thomas,†1 there was a bad halfe crowne; which I could not desire him to change, beinge onely a depositary of it and pleadeinge it to bee the numericalle†2 money hee had of you the morninge you went to Salisbury. that money you may please to remember I did not receive for you. and now I take my selfe to bee enteringe on the preferment of beinge your steward; soe that if any accidents happen of that nature, my master (as is reasonable)†a shal never bee concern'd in them. I have proceeded with Mr Bernard accordeinge to instructions. hee gives you his humble service and thanks for the sheets of the Evangelists†3 I gave him by your order. I enquir'd who was at the charge of the edition of Josephus, and gave him the reason of my soe doeinge, which as you had stated it was (as it ought to bee) extreme kindly taken. hee told mee twas my Lord Bishop,†4 and shew'd a great forwardnesse to acquainte him of the expence you had beene at in promoteinge that worke; but I desir'd him (and at last prevayl'd) to forbeare soe doeinge, till I had heard from you; beinge willinge to give you the trouble of many letters, rather then doe any thinge you may possibly dislike. hee would have paid mee the money, (with much earnestnesse), and ask'd it againe of my Lord, but I would not allow of it. I have done nothinge in this affaire that (I am sure) you will dislike; and have carried it with great respecte and tendernesse to my Lord and Mr Bernard and withall left the way open for any proceedeings you shall thinke fitte to practice. Mr Sessions†5 will goe out of towne on Munday, soe that if you can shew him the bill before that time twill not bee amisse, though I doubt not but hee will leave order for the payment of it. bee pleas'd to have mee in your thoughts; and take it not amisse if (as if I mistake not you gave mee l<eav>e†b to doe) I put you in minde of my Lord Grey.†6I remember you once wish'd mee parson of Bishopston (which though scarce any thinge lesse then a
― 181 ―

miracle can effecte) Ile acquainte you that I am inform'd that one has gotte Dr Clutterbucks title of Cambridge after Coldicut, who may possibly attempt to get a confirmation of his title (beinge it belongs to the Erldome) from Mr Herberte.†1 this I thought fitte to mention to you; that you might make some use of it, if you thought it necessary. I will hereafter (if you please to leave the time to mee) contrive better the returnes of your money; and am
Sir
your most oblig'd servant
G: WALLS.
Address: For Mr John Locke at Thanet house in Aldersgate street this. London

541. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, [c. 27 May/6 June 1680] (538, 545)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, ff. 45-6. Locke's date in the endorsement is that of receipt; he received the letter on 7 or 8 June: no. 546. It answers no. 538 of 20/30 May. It was intended to arrive in London a day or two before 5/15 June (that Toinard's date for the sun-spots is new style is shown by no. 545). Allowing five days in transit in either direction, the date of the letter falls between 25 May/4 June and 29 May/8 June. Toinard's statement about the date of Mrs. Grigg's arrival in Saumur is loose: see below, p. 184, n. 1. Answered by no. 546.
+
Je me suis aquité, Monsieur, de ceque vous m'avez ordonné aupres de tous nos illustres amis, a la reserve du capitaine marin que j atens de jour a autre. mr Bernier vous envoie le Salamalek,†2 et ma donné un ecrit qu'il a fait depuis peu contre un monsieur dit De la Ville, touchant laparence des especes du pain et du vin dans le Saint Sacrement <suivant>†a l'opinion des Gassendistes.†3 mr Thevenot a vu un catalogue de la Bibliotheque de Cambridge ou
― 182 ―

il y a numero 19 un livre intitulé Turquestanæ regni descriptio.†1 il vous prie de vous informer ceque ce peut etre que ce livre que je crois manuscrit, et sil est gros, et si cest une traduction, ou une relation faite par le voiageur et en quel tems. Il en a une en Persan qui est admirable, et cela pouroit lui donner ocasion d'en regaler le public. Mr Picard come nuntius sidereus†2 vous donne avis que si les macules ne sont dissipées, elles doivent reparoitre le 15. de ce mois parceque vous savez qu'etant com'elles sont tres proche du soleil, eles suivent le cours qu'il fait sur son centre. Vous en donnerez avis a vos messieurs afin qu'ils les observent. mr Romer est telement ocupé a finir un globe pour monseigneur le Daufin ou lon voit le mouvement de toutes les planetes,†3 qu'il na pu me donner contentement sur cequ'il doit depuis si longtems me metre au net pour vous touchant linstruction du triangle que je vous ay envoié.†4 mr de ste Colombe qui est a de retour a Brest vous salüe tres particulierement et vous prie de lui envoier sil se peut les hauteurs exactes des principaux endroits de la manche comme cap Lezard Portland Douvres, lisle de With, etcæt. cest a savoir sil y en de plus precises que celes qui sont dans nos cartes dont il vous fait de nouveau les remerciements.
A legard des choses que vous desirez, j'ay demandé a mr lAbé Picard le nom de ces mezures de monpelier, mais il ne lest scait pas, et j'en feray ecrire sur les lieux. Je crois que vous desirez savoir cela a cause de quelques doses de remedes que vous aurez apris en ce païs la. je scay seulement que leur livre est de 4. onces moindre que la notre. Je voudrois que cela plutost que la consomption ou un coup de pié de cheval vous portast a en aler examiner lez proportions sur les lieux. Il est tres a souhaiter que lon convient dune mezure et dun poids, mais il n'y a pas lieu d'esperer cela que dans la Caroline ou lon taille en plein drap. je n'oserois vous mander ceque j'ay apris depuis peu sur ce sujet a legard de ceux qui pouroient et
― 183 ―

devroient lintroduire dans un etat qui inviteroit peutetre le reste de l'Europe a cete conformité et uniformité universele. Je vous renverray l'histoire du Dutroa, et vous auriez il y a long tems les brizûres d'Italie pour les regles, si Bouterfild m'avoit tenu parole. Il y a un endroit de votre letre que je ne scaurois lire ou que je n'entens pas ou il y a. et neudi machinam descriptione velim. cela suit les brisures d Italie et je nescai ceque cest que neudi.†1 Mandez moi si vous ne voulez simplement que les cahiers des nouveles decouvertes de seul mois d Avril 1679, et pourquoi non toutes celes de cete annèe courante. J'ay eu tort de ne vous avoir pas envoié le petit Almanach†2 qui est fort curieux cete anneè et sera le dernier de ce genre come je vois les choses se tourner. Il y a des fautes de l'année passée qu'ils ont eté si negligens que de ne les pas corriger. je les marqueray sur ceux que je vous enverrai. Je vous prie aussi de m'en envoier un pareil a celui pour mr Auzout qui vous baise les mains.†3
On acheve d'imprimer un petit in folio au Louvre qui contient les voiages de mr L'Abé Picard a Uranisbourg, a Monpelier, a Brest, celui de mr Romer en Angleterre. et cæt. le tout aux depens du Roi. S'ils se vendent je vous en enverrai un. Il y a de belles figures et de belles choses.†4 J'avois porté mond. sieur Abé (inter nos) qui est l'auteur de ce livre de doner un projet de la reduction de toutes les mezures au pié naturel, mais il a eu ses raisons pour ne le pas faire, et je ne les ay pas aprouveès.
Au reste vous voulez bien que je vous dise qu'en exhortant vous mesme les autres a une uniformité dans les mezures afin que lon se pust entendre vous vous etes bien oublié de me doner cele de votre gresle par une que personne ne comprend ici, non pas meme les Anglois a trois ou quatre desquels je l'ay fait voir sans conter nos amis Anglicanisans come mss Tevenot, Auzout Renaudot et c. Vous ecrivez: commensuravi (globum unum) cujus circuitus erat 420 grys forma erat r<otunda>.†a Vous serez sil vous plaist l'œdipe de ce mot de grys qui est un gryphus†5 pour tous ceux qui l'ont lu. Vous pouviez vous servir de la mezure d Angleterre ou de France ou des parties du pié universel. et d'ailleurs ce nombre de 420 est si grand quelques petites que soient les parties qui le composent que nous ne pouvons rien imaginer qui nous le fasse entendre.
― 184 ―

Madame Grig est ariveè aparemment en bonne santé a Saumur des il eut Samedi dernier quinze jours.†1 Je me chargeay ici de lui faire tenir ses cofres a Orleans surement, prontement, et a bon marché et l'adressay a un de mes meilleurs amis pour un bateau particulier et des bateliers pacifiques dont il pust repondre. Je voudrois avoir frequemment des occasions plus importantes pour vous marquer ceque je voudrois faire ici et par tout ailleurs en consideration et en reconnoissance de toutes vos graces.
A legard de l'harmonie je vous en ecriray une autrefois plus amplement. ne prenez pas garde a la chronologie de la tête, il y a des pages ou il sest glissé bien des fautes par limpatience que jay eües de les faire tirer. je continueray jusques a la fin du Roy Amon pere de Josias, et vous enverray le tout. j'en ay desja douze pages nouveles. J'ay fait refaire la 36. de la premiere collection que vous avez.†2 Un gentilhome Anglois m'a dit que vous deviez venir en france, Je voudrois que tous les Anglois, aux moins ceux qui sont a Paris, disent toujours vray
Vous voulez bien que monsieur et madame Brisban trouvent ici les assurances de mes tres humbles respects. J'ay pris la liberté de donner a un de mes amis qui est parent a celui a qui jadressay madame Grig, une letre pour lui, et une autre pour vous.†3

542. Dr. Edward Pococke to Locke, 29 May 1680
Dr. Paul Mellon's collection. Transcribed from photograph. The letter mentioned by Pococke may be one summarized by Dr. Leonard Twells (D.N.B.): 'About this Time <August 1671->, Mr. Locke, ..., in a Letter to the Father, mentions his having engaged his Son at Salisbury, in translating and printing a Part of Maimonides, and that he had spoken with Mr. Boyle about it: He desired also to have it printed, just as that Piece translated by Mr. Prideaux was. He further assured Dr. Pocock, that it would greatly encourage those, who wished well to the Work, if he could assure them, that it should be done under the Father's Direction': life of Pococke prefixed to his Theological Works, 1740, i. 69. Twells's date is wrong: Prideaux's translation was published in 1679: p. 72.
Worthy Sir
I received your kinde letter of May the 15th, and heartily thanke you for it, and for those many expressions of your good affections to me and mine which I have, allwayes found reall and cordiall. I had thought that I might have had opportunity before this of speaking with my sonne Edward†1 and acquainting him with what you had written, but he having not in this time come hither I could not longer deferre writing to returne my thankes to you. He had translated a piece of Maimonides, but there was that unhappines in it that it was such that the Jew Abendana†2 here had before translated and made ready for the presse, how ever it be not yet printed. I shall exhort him to set on some other having so good incouragement to it. He hath been of late much troubled with sore eyes. I thanke you for speaking with Mr Boyle. Sir my wife thankes you for your kinde remembrance of her, and for your many kindnesses, which none more heartily acknowledge then we do, though none lesse able to requite them. With both our best respects and love, I commend you to Gods blessed protection and rest
Sir Your most affectionate friend and servant
EDW: POCOCKE
OX: ChristCh.†a
May 29. 1680.
Endorsed by Locke: E. Pocock 29o may. 80

543. William Stratton to Locke, 30 May 1680 (550)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, f. 4.
William Stratton, d. 1695, probably a tanner; married (1) Mary, d. 1678, daughter of Peter Locke; (2) Elizabeth Grigg, probably a sister of the Revd. Thomas Grigg. He took over most of the business of Locke's Somerset property from Peter Locke probably early this year: see no. 511. Some notes on his accounts for 1679 and 1680, probably written by Edward Clarke, form B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, ff. 1-3.
Dear Cosin
I yesterday spake with Marke Heale and his partners about the Cole worke†1 hoe now desirs that Articles may be mad of the agreement and a bond of performanc on each side. the ground at Casebrook is Caled as they say by the name of Satry they say it is but one ground that the brook runeth thorow it soe that it is yours on both sids of the brook becaus you gave mee Instructions of Consenting two one and it semeingly two be two I would not Consent to articles till I heare from you that you Consent that they shall have both sides which as yet I doe not know any reson why they should not have the preveledg of both if there bee ocation and as for your estate at buck hill the paish of Publow have made a A Rate for the poore and raised you two 1l:5s: although water Flatcher remains at 1l when I hard†a- of theyr-†a doeing of it I prevented Esq Langtons†2 signing the rate soe they got Mr Haringtons hand and doe Intend two strain†3 for the mony. If you think fit two writ two Sir Tho: Bridges†4 Conserning it it is of great Consernment, for I know not when they will give of a raiseing and shall Indever two prevent it Sir Tho: Bridges suns hand is two the rate Mr Joanes†5was Conserned about you buisnes and did wright two Mr Langton which was a means of preventing his signing the rate I suppose Mr Henry Bridges†6 did not Consider of your Conserns when he put his hand I desire two heare from you the first return of the post Conserning this and your Consent two the Colework in both grounds becase

they are willing to make a begining My Father Locke and Mother†1 desires kindly two be remembred two you allsoe my Wife presents her servis two you hopeing you had received her letters

544. Dr. John Fell, bishop of Oxford, to Locke, 1 June [1680] (303, 643)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 105-6. Year from Locke's endorsement. Printed in King, pp. 152-3.
Sir
You are not to excuse your address by letter, as if it could give a trouble to me. I assure you I have that respect and friendship for you, that I should be glad to have heard from you, alltho you had no other business then to let me know you were in health; especially since you left this place in such a condition, as might make your friends apprehensive for you. As to the proposal concerning books; we have about two years since quit our hands of our stock to men of trade, so that the interest is now with those we dealt with. I have spoke this morning with one of them, Mr: Pitt who within few daies will be at London, and will there attend upon you. he seems to approve of the terms offerd, so that I presume he will close with them.†2 I have no more at present to add, but desire that when you
― 188 ―

write to Mr: Justell, you would represent the esteem which I have for him. Let me also desire you to be assurd that I am
Sir
Your Affectionat friend
Jo. Oxon̄
June 1.

545. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, 9/19 June [1680] (541, 546)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, ff. 47-8. Year from Locke's endorsement. Answers no. 538; answered by no. 556.

mercredi ce 19 Juin
Je n'entends, monsieur, que d'hier au soir un endroit de votre letre, ou il est parlé d'un Abacus arithmeticus, car monsieur Justel me le donna chez lui, laiant receu de monsieur Link.†1 Je suis de plus en plus confus de tous les bienfaits dont vous m'acablez, et je ne scai comment y repondre. cete machine est tres bien executeé. Mr Paschal en est le premier inventeur. Mr Perier l'aisné son neveu, nouvelement decedé, la perfectiona de beaucoup etant a Orleans, ou il la fit faire en cuivre par un nommé Dek, horlogeur.†2 Je la feray voir au plutost a messieurs ses freres qui sont ici qui l'entendent fort bien, Je crois que vous les avez vus quelquefois dans ma chambre. Grillet†3 en a aussi fait une a sa maniere, et mr Leibnits†4 une autre que j'ay vüe lorsqu'il etoit ici. Jiray cete apresdinée chercher
― 189 ―

monsieur Link pour le remercier. Je vous fais metre a part une teuïlle de chacune de mes epreuves, ou il sest glissé bien des fautes. par exemple dans toutes celes que vous avez il y a Jubilæus XIV. au lieu de XV. ainsi vous graterez l'I qui est entre le X. et le V.†1
Je vous souhaitois bien hier au Jardin du Roy a l'ouverture des leçons que fit mr Du Vernay anatomiste de lacademie. Il y avoit belle et grande compagnie, et bien de vos amis. mr Labé Picard qui vous salüe, me dist que des deux dernieres taches du soleil, il y en avoit eu une de dissipée, et que l'autre reparoissoit avec une nouvele plus grande que les precedentes. J'ay une extreme impatience que son livre soit achevé pour vous l'envoier si jen peux avoir prece vel precio.†2 Apres qu'il m'eust dit ces nouveles, je m'en alay chez Mr Justel ou il y avoit grand monde, et come chacun disoit des sienes et que lon disoit qu'il couroit de mauvais bruits de Tanger,†3 je dis qu'il couroit aussi de mauvais bruits du soleil, tout de nouveau; et come la compagnie comprit bien que je voulois parler des taches, cela fit rire. Vous avez cy joint la maniere de faire du pain a la mode de France, mais si vous lavez trouvé bon, il faut revenir en gouter sur les lieux, car vos ouvriers, fussent-ils Suis<ses,>†a n'en feront jamais de pareil.
[Enclosure:]
+
Pour avoir du Levain
℞. De la farine petrie a l'ordinaire avec de l'eau simple. metez en environ gros come la tête d'un homme dans une ecuële de bois, et puis la couvrez de quelque chose come etofe de laine ou dun drap de toile.
cete pâte s'aigrira et sera votre levain.
Nota qu'ele s'aigrira plus tost ou plus tard selon le tems et le lieu. car en tems et lieu chaud cela fera plus tost mais ordinairement cela se va a trois jours ou environ.
Led. Levain etant fait, se peut garder quinze jours. et si lon veut le garder davantage on peut le saler un peu.
― 190 ―

Pour faire le pain, on petrit la pâte a l'ordinaire et tant plus ele est petrie, tant meilleur et plus leger est le pain.
Lon prend de ce levain environ gros com'un œuf, et lon le mele bien avec de la pâte, gros ou environ come les deux poings, et le tout se distribue ensuite dans de la pâte qui peut faire dix ou douze livres de pain. et ainsi de suite.
Quand tous vos pains sont faits, vous les couvrez bien avec de bonnes couvertures ou choses equivalentes, et le pain se leve en deux ou trois heures de tems plus ou moins selon le tems et le lieu. et apres le metez au four, dans le tems convenable.
Il est a remarquer que†a quoique l'on puisse faire du Levain avec toutes sortes de bléz, il est bon neanmoins de n'en faire que de froment, qui est meilleur que celui de segle pour le pain même de segle, quoique le levain de segle y puisse servir, mais non pas aux pains que lon fait de blé froment.
Une personne qui entend bien le menage de la campagne, m'a dit qu'il faut environ la 50. de levain pour le pain, et que neanmoins cela depend du goust, les uns le voulant plus fort de levain et les autres moins.
Je crois que votre Suisse†1 vous executeroit bien cete maniere qui est presque la seule en usage en france. A propos de Suisse un gentilhomme arivé d'Italie debitoit dernierement plusieurs manieres pour courre la poste sans les incommoditez ordinaires. Je lui demanday s'il en sovoit une pour ne point tomber ny lui ny pas un de sa compagnie, il se tut, et je lui apris, <comme>†b une chose eprouveé, votre secret, qui etoit de courre avec un Suisse, parcequ'il n'y a que lui qui tombe pour toute la troupe. Il m'en remercia bien.
Je nescay si j'auray le tems de vous copier aujourdhui le Dutroa, mais ce sera pour la premiere ocasion, parceque voila que lon m'envoie querir pour une afaire a quoi je ne m'entendois pas. Madame de Bouïllon†2 est a Orleans entre les mains de Notre ami pour une fistule lacrymale. Je receus hier de ses letres. Il est prest d'avoir un procez contre ses moines.†3 J'espere enfin revoir la patrie, ou
― 191 ―

je n'ay eté il y a tantost trois ans et demi. Si j'y trouve la tranquillité, que je n'ay presque jamais eüe de ma vie, je finiray toutes les choses que j'ay ebauchées. Je commenceray par metre en etat d'etre imprimeé, l'Harmonie G-L†1 des Evangiles, en sorte que des sommaires, on en poura faire un livre de poche que je pouray intituler Evangeliorum Enchiridion Harmonicum, ou quelque chose de semblable.
J'ay rendu ici et faire†2 rendre a Orleans a Made Grig tous les ofices que j'ay pu, et voudrois servir vos amis en tout cequi poura se presenter.
Address: For Mr John Locke Angleterre At Mr Hicks's a tayler, below the Kings play house in Bridges street London
Postmark: IV 14
Endorsed by Locke: Toinard 19 Jun. 80

Nudius tertius literæ tuæ mihi redditæ sunt quas paulo tardiores venisse suspicor quia solis maculas (nisi interim dissipatæ essent) 15° hujus mensis iterum comparituras dicis, qui dies ante adventum literarum tuarum præterlapsus est. Te enim non inire rationem Calendaris nostri exoleti et erronei mihi peruasum est. Sed isto spectaculo facile carere possum dummodo tanta tam illustrium
― 192 ―

virorum constellatio me respicere non dedignetur. Constellationem quid ni dicam, cum sublimia illa et splendida ingenia et immortale decus longe exsuperant quicquid in cœlestibus illis corporibus suspicimus. Eos omnes datâ occasione meo nomine iterum iterumque salutatos velim. Suumque Berniero nostro Salamalek quanto possum cum <fænore>†a reddo. quem etsi inter philosophos disputantem libenter et cum fructu audirem, mallem tamen, si dicere fas est, ut nos populorum orientalium mores et facta resque illuc observatas nos edoceret. London. 10 Jun 80
I received your letter two days ago; I suspect that the reason it was somewhat slow in reaching me was that the sun-spots were, as you tell me, due to appear again (unless they were dissipated in the interim) on the 15th of this month, which day had passed before the arrival of your letter, for I feel sure that you take no account of our obsolete and erroneous calendar. But I can easily forgo that spectacle so long as such a constellation of illustrious men
[p. 192]
deigns to look upon me. I may well say a constellation, since their sublime and brilliant talents and their imperishable glory far surpass anything that we see above us in those heavenly bodies. Please greet them all from me again and again as opportunity offers. I return our friend Bernier's Salamalek with all the interest I can. Though I find pleasure and profit in hearing him disputing amongst the philosophers, yet I should, if I may say so, prefer him to tell us something about the manners and doings of Eastern peoples and the things he has observed in those parts. We have long been overloaded, it seems to me, with philosophy and disputations, whilst we have little or nothing in the way of trustworthy accounts of happenings amongst foreign nations, those at least which are at some distance from us. But this is between ourselves, and because I know that you have the same desire; if only you could persuade our excellent friend, who is so eminently fitted to deal with these things, to fall in with our wishes.

(Original Text) As to the spinning machine, I am sorry that these words were so badly written that you could not read them. But the description of machines is not only very laborious but also difficult to understand; so I think that this request of mine can be dispensed with, the more so as there is a bed here in our house which is very useful for gouty people or for those lying sick with any complaint; any sick-nurse can easily adjust it in any position, the feet or head being raised without the least discomfort to the sick person. I meant to give you a description of it, but the difficulty of the task has so far

the more useful anything new is the more difficult it is to make it available; hence I am inclined to acquiesce in the opinion that of all the spirits that drive us this way and that and mix themselves up everywhere in human affairs the bad ones, if not in the majority, nevertheless surpass the good in industry.
