655. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, 24 August/3 September 1681 (648, 656)
B.L., MSS. Locke c. 21, ff. 113-14, and c. 31, f. 47. Answered by no. 665.
+
A Paris Mercredi, ce 3. Septembre 81.
Depuis ma derniere la terre ne m'aiant rien fourni qui fust digne de vous, j'ay atendu les graces du ciel pour me remetre dans l'honneur de votre souvenir. Je crus jeudi au soir qu'il me seroit favorable, et j'allay coucher à l'observatoire chez monsieur L'Abé Picard ou tout etoit disposé pour observer une eclipse que l'on avoit crüe par le calcule devoir ariver, les deux luminaires etant sur l'horison, par un efet de la refraction. Ceque Pline en raporte ne vous est pas
― 433 ―

inconnu, cest pourquoi je commenceray par vous dire que jamais il ne fut ici une plus belle nuit. nous y fumes regaléz de Jupiter et Saturne en atendant, ceque quelques autheurs ont apeléz, Adulterium Solis et Lunæ, que nous vimes fort a notre plaisir, et vous en avez cy joint l'observation.†1 à quoi j'ajouteray cequ'un Gentilhome de mes amis plein de merite et digne de creance me mande entre plusieurs choses extraordinaires qu'il a observées proche de Barege aux Pirenées qu'il y a des ponts de nege d'un rocher à l'autre par dessous les quels passent des torrents.†2 Il en a vu un qui embrasse deux torrents, et qui a vingt neuf toises de long et autant de large par dessus. Il y a par dessous ce pont neuf toises et demie entre les naissances de la voute. ces ponts sont tellement forts qu'il estime que du Canon y passeroit, et il y a fait rouler de grosses pierres par dessus.
Le Livre de mr Papin pour cuivre les viandes est traduit ici,†3 et je me veux doner une de ces machines ou je crois pouvoir rectifier quelque chose qui fera un plus grand et plus pront efet, et cependant ele sera plus simple.
ce mien ami qui est à Barege s'y trouvant sans instruments ny barometres ny niveau pour prendre la hauteur des montagnes, s'est avisé de faire tirer en montant de distance en distance des coups de fusil pour juger des elevations par la progression du son suposant 90. toises pour demie seconde du pendule.
Comme vous vous interesséz pour tout cequi touche les personnes de merite et particulierement quand elles sont du nombre de vos amis, je ne puis ometre de vous mander que les afaires de mr Römer vont fort bien, et qu'il doit epouser la fille de mr Bartholin Conseiller d'etat son ancien patron.†4 Je l'en ay felicité. Je ne vous ay pas temoigné mon deplaisir, craignant d'augmenter le votre, sur la facheuse conjoncture ou vous etes,†5 et m'etant d'ailleurs persuadé que vous me rendiez assez de justice pour ne pouvoir douter qu'il
― 434 ―

ne peut vous rien ariver de quelque nature que ce soit qui me puisse jamais etre indiferent.

656. Locke to Nicolas Toinard, 30 August 1681 (655, 659)
B.M., Add. MS. 28,753, ff. 22-3. Printed in Ollion, Notes, pp. 137-9; Ollion, pp. 105-8; both with wrong date 17 July [1681]. Answers nos. 642 and 648; answered by no. 659.
J'etois en pein avant l'arrivè de vostre derniere du 17 Juillet de peur que le Noldius qui avoit tardè si long temps icy à <commencer>†a son voiage ne s'eut perdu en chemin. Je suis fort aise s'il vous a servi à quelque chose, et sur tout al'harmonie à la quelle vous n avez pas plus d'atachment que je n'ay d'inclination et d'estime. je ne scay si j'ay dit dans quelque autre de mes lettres que je tombe d'accord avec vous, que dans le corps de votre harmonie vous ferez bien de rendre le meme mot Hebreu par le meme mot Latin tant qu'il sera possible et faire la traduction mot pour mot, ce que monstrera d'avantage la genie de la langue Hebreu et aussi l'accord del harmonie c'est pour quoi je prefer 11 Par XIV. 13 ad neutiquam eis victum†1 à tout autre traduction, et quanquam hujusmodi locutiones parum Latinæ doctas et eligantes forsan aliquantum <offendent>†b aures præsto tamen erit in margine remedium si illic affigas narrationem pure Latinam, cui rei consultè a te provisum intelligo.†2 J'ay etè depuis quelque tems si embarassè dans des affaires qui n'ont guerre d'harmonie avec l'estude et les lettres que vous me devez excuser oud'avoir trop dit, en le repetant, sur l harmonie ou trop peudes autres choses dont il fallut deja long tems vous avoir repondu. Mais je suis nouvellement reveneu d'Oxford ou j'ay etè obligè d'aller quand j'y songeois le moins.†3 Les Requiems sont bien Gallant
― 436 ―

dans la Cour de Neptune de ne point faire d'afront aux dames Negresses qu y vont les derober de leur monnoie, et on peut bien soupsoner que ces poissons font la guerre à les hommes non pas par cruautè mais par amour et jalousie quoiquil en soit Je baise les maines tres humblement a Monsieur Massiac dont la conversation vous fournira bien de choses à vostre Adversaria, et il faut le remercier de ma part de celle cy que je vien d'ecrire dans les mien,†1 et je vous prie aussi d'assurer Monsieur Ste Colombe de mes tres humbles respects

657. Richard Roderick to Locke, 5 September [1681]
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, ff. 29-30. Year from Locke's endorsement. The writer, c. 1648-1730, matriculated from Christ Church 1665; B.A. 1669; etc.; D.D. 1690: Foster.
Sir
I thought it convenient to defer my answer to what you wrote concerning me in Mr Wall's letter 'till I had somewhat longer tried Cumner waters.†1 I have taken them eleven times, three quarts a morning except the last, when I drank but two. They have all along passt very well both by stool and urine. That faintnesse all over the body which before I was troubled with presently abated, but I find some remembrances of it especially in the morning, when at my first rising 'tis hard to keep my head from being heated and my thoughts scattered. The risings and pimples I had on my leggs and elsewhere are at length gone; but the pinchings there and in other parts of my body, and the dull pains chiefly on my left side are not yet removed, though indeed not accompanied with such faintnesse as heretofore, nor soe troublesome. The stiffenesse in my left arm and hand has it's frequent returns. I am as formerly better after dinner then in the morning. Be pleased to remember that I said the obstructions complain'd of affected my lungs, which I have always found sensibly cleered and opened upon violent exercise. Whenever I have indulged and sunk under the lazy humour, the hypocondria and the head ne're failed to be very much heated: the latter always at such times muddy and dizzy, has at all times been ready to turn round upon my looking down a precipice but can now somewhat better endure such a sight since my taking the waters. I shall continue drinking them 'till you please to send directions what's next to be done by
Your most humble servant
RIC. RODERICK
Sept. the 5t.
I have constantly been and still am very drousy morning and evening, especially when the spleen is moved. I am sensible of the change of weather, and very much troubled in an hot season with faintnesse and other symptomes.
― 439 ―

I think I must now be forced to leave off the waters, for they were not brought this morning.
Address: These For Mr John Lock at Thanet-house in Aldersgate street London.
Postmark: SE 7
Endorsed by Locke: R: Roderick 5 Sept. 81

Deare Sir
It is full 2 months since I received your kind and obliging letter of the 9th June and after my usuall custom now I have use of you take the oportunity of returning you my thanks for it. Ile assure you I was verry sorry to heare you had been confined to your bed, but hope if I am so happy as to see England, whether I fully intend shortly (God willing) I shall find you in a verry hale condition. Dr. Magnol gave me some seeds to send you but my things having been packt up before he delivered them I intend to bring them along with me, he ha's sent you a parcell or 2 of seeds of Africa and I hope before I goe he will procure me more. 659. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, 24 September/4 October 1681 (i) (656, 660)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, ff. 118-19. Answers no. 656; answered by no. 665.
+
A Paris, Samedi, ce 4. Octobre 81.
Je ne scaurois, Monsieur, vous <ex>primer†a combien j'ay le cœur serré de la perte que la France vien<t>†a de faire de Mr Justel. Je
― 441 ―

sors de lui dire Adieu, et il est parti en carosse pour Calais avec ses deux enfans, en atendant que madame Justel suive des qu'ele aura doné ordre a quelques afaires.†1 Je vous avoüe que je veux du bien à l'Angleterre de nous avoir donné quantité de galans hommes qui m'honorent de leur bienveillance, mais je ne lui pardoneray jamais le larcin qu'ele nous fait à moins que Londres ne rende prontement à Paris mr Locke en echange de mr Justel. Je suis redevable de plusieurs obligations tant à sa personne qu'à son cabinet, et come je mets au premier rang celle de votre connoissance, jugez qu'ele est ma desolation pour son absence et pour la votre. cela va me rendre provincial pour longues années, à moins que le mauvais sort qui continüe de me persecuter, ne me rapele ici pour des sollicitations de procez, ou j'ay eté miserablement ocupé depuis si long tems, ou bien si ce n'est qu'une meilleure Etoile ne me rende Ultramarin. Mr Justel n'est pas fort eloigné d'un etablissement la ou votre nom est entouré d'eau. Nous en avons souvent parlé ensemble, mais aiant bien examiné les loix de cete Colonie, nous avons trouvé bien des choses embarassantes, et tres contraires à la tranquillité que des subalternes cherchent dans ces sortes de païs. Il en conferera avec vous, et si l'on pouvoit les modifier, ou les oter en tout ou en partie, je ne fais nul doute que la douceur du gouvernement, jointe à la bonté de lair et des eaux, et a la fertilité de la terre, n'y atirast beaucoup de monde en peu de tems. Souvenez vous qu'il y a la une certaine Ile sur laquele on pretend en France dans le faubourg st Germain par hypotheque speciale ou privilegiée, autant ou plus de droit que sur celle de Bourbon, puisque le Titulaire a fait d'ofre de l'une, et que le Senhor fulano de Mascarenhas†2 n'a jamais parlé de même pour la siene.
J'ay doné a mr Justel un petit paquet pour vous, ou il y a quelques additions au livre de Mr Papin que lon a traduit et imprimé ici. Il y a aussi des ep<reuv>es†a d'une harmonie in quarto des deux livres des Machabæes.†3 Je <les>†a fis l'eté precedent en me joüant, pour ne pas perdre tout à fait lesprit harmonique, pendant une maladie, parcequ'il m'etoit expressement defendu de me trop
― 442 ―

apliquer. J'en ay obtenu un privilege pour dix ans, en grec et en latin, conjointement ou separement.†1 si j'ay du repos en province, ou je vais enfin en peu de tems, je pouray l'y faire imprimer, et une autrefois je vous entretiendray d'un bien autre ouvrage. Je vous suis obligé des livres que vous m'avez envoiéz, et vous en remercie tres humblement, en atendant que ce païs me done lieu de me revanger de toutes vos honetetez. J'espere que la personne qui a bien voulu sen charger,†2 me les rendra bien tost. Nous avons ici le Wilkins, et je nescai pas pourquoi ce mien ami demande si fort l'Algarno et l'autre. Je voudrois desja l'avoir pour lui remetre entre les mains. Je vous rendray bon conte du Gouvernement du C. de chinchon,†3 et de quelque chose du Kinkina.
Je vous ai envoié l'observation de l'Eclipse du 29. d'Aoust, ou j'etois. mr Picard sera le 15. de ce mois à st malo pour les longitudes par les satellites, et mr de la Hire a Donkirke. donez en avis à vos giboieurs.
Le petit animal devorateur de tous les autres, sans excepter les Tigres ny les Lions, lequel va par petis plotons†4 dans les terres d'Angole, et dont vous avez pu voir un peau que j'ay donée a mr lAbé Gendron, s'apele Zambuigi,†5 et non pas d'un certain autre nom que nous avoit dit mr de ste Colombe qui n'est pas si grec†6 sur cete matiere que mr de massiac son frere.
J'ay outre deux facheux procez et le depart de mr Justel, une autre afliction, cest que j'avois une possession plus que centenaire De motu continuo acus magneticæ ab ortu in occasum in partibus Europæ,†7 et il y a un mois que mr l'Abé Picard trouva qu'a Paris l'Eguille est retrogradée de 35. minutes, n'etant pl< >†a de 2.D.15'. au lieu de 2.D.50'. qu'ele avoit il y a un a< >†a est porté dans le petit Almanach, page 85.†8
― 443 ―

Cela m'a fort surpris, et j'en demande confirmation. Il m'ecrit de la Fleche en date du 30. de septembre dernier, qu'il y a fait à ma priere une observation de la variation, et qu'il la trouvée de 2.D. à lOüest. qui est la même quil y avoit il y a deux ans, en tout cas voila à philosophie, car pourquoi retrograder à Paris et ne le pas faire à la Fleche, ny peutetre ailleurs. Je voudrois que vous eussiez assez de repos pour l'observer à Londres, car elle aura augmenté ou diminué. ne vous tourmentez pas pour la machine à remolquer. Je vous en suis autant obligé que si je l'avois. Je vous prie de faire pour moy des remerciemens à mr Hoocke pour le livre qu'il m'envoioit par un Suisse qui dit luy avoir eté volé. mr Picard me mande qu'il m'ecrira de st Malo. Il ne me refusera pas ses observations, quand je lui diray que cest pour vous.
Ne laissez pas de m'ecrire à l'adresse de mon hote, qui me remetra tout ceque l'on lui adressera pour moi.
Si vous voiez Monsieur et Madame Brisban, assurez les de mes tres humbles respects. Je les prie de boire une petite fois à ma santé avec monsieur Justel. Il me semble que je m'en ressentiray ici.
Madame Grigge part aussi demain. j'eus l'honneur de la voir hier, et je la verray encore sur le soir. Mr Justel poura aler de compagnie avec elle de Calais a Londres.
Je m'en vais voir penser un pauvre enfant d'un de mes meilleurs amis, Il a une plaie a la poitrine par un abcez interne. mr l'Abé Gendron m'a doné par letres de bons avis. entr'autres de songer a oter le douleur, et pour cela ne se point opiniatrer a metre de tantes,†1 parcequ'il ne faut pas craindre que cela se ferme le malade sen est parfaitement bien trouvè. Il y a dix ans que j'imaginay une petite machine pour faire des injections. Je nescay si je vous lay dite, vous la scaurez une autre fois. Je suis —
Address: For Mr John Locke Angleterre At Mr Hicks's à tailer, below the Kings playhouse in Bridges Street London

661. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, 28 [Sept.]/8 [Oct.] 1681 (660, 662)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, ff. 115-16. The passages relating to Justel and Mrs. Grigg were written later than nos. 659 and 660. In 1681 the new-style 8 September fell on a Monday; 8 October, on a Wednesday; this, with the postmark, indicates 8 October, N.S., as the correct date. Answered by no. 665.
+
mercredi 8. Septembre 81.
Je vous ecrivis samedi precipitamment le sujet de plaintes qu'avoit la France contre l'Angleterre pour nous avoir enlevé mr Justel, et comment nous etions bien fondèz a demander des letres de represailles. Il n'y a que vous seul, monsieur, qui puissiez prevenir la rupture entre ces deux couronnes, en nous restituant par vous même cequi nous est du de remplacement pour monsieur
― 445 ―

Justel. Je vis le Samedi au soir madame Grigg, qui se plaignit etrangement à moi de ceque je ne luy donois rien a vous porter, J'en avois desja assez de chagrin; et come j'avois atendu vainement un petit livre du Kinkina, imprimé a Lyon,†1 Je courus encor le dimanche au matin chez le Libraire qui me l'avoit promis; et n'aiant rien de meilleur, je pris chez lui deux journaux,†2 dans lun desquels il est mention dudit livre, et les donay tous deux a madame Grigge, sans etre empaquetéz, et une letre qui etant faite auparavant que jeusse pris ces journaux, n'en parle point. Dans la page 390. de celuy du 8. septembre†3 Il y est parlé de l'ouverture qui se fit d'une femme morte, du ventre de la quele il sortit un grand bruit — acompagné d'une flamme de feu tres promte qui grilla les cheveux et brula le vizage de la Sage-femme. Je scay parfaitement cete histoire, qui est tres veritable, mais a legard de la flamme, il faut entendre que ce fut un vapeur qui prit feu a la chandele que tenoit la Sage-femme. l'odeur de cete vapeur etoit tres puante. on travaille a une relation ou il doit y avoir quelque chose de beau. cela est arivé a Vitri, village a une lieue de Paris. En vous faizant present de ces deux journaux je vous donne beau jeu pour dire que ce ne vous envoie que des titres de livres pour des livres efectifs que vous m'envoiez, mais il y a longtems que vous m'avez mis à lepreuve de toute confusion, par lexces de vos honetetez. Le dernier paquet dont vous m'avez regalé, ne m'a pas encor eté delivré, et si je savois le nom de celui qui a bien voulu sen charger,†4 je tacherois de la demeler. Jy regreterois principalement d'entre les trois livres qu'il contient, l'ars signorum d'Algarno, puisqu'il vous a doné tant de peine a trouver, et par consequent aussi couté à acheter. Je pretendois me delasser amplement ce matin en vous fatigant par une longue letre à laquele j'avois destiné tout le tems jusques à midi, mais come je suis, ce semble, né pour mille choses facheuses qui n'arivent a personne qu'a moy, J'eus hier une afaire au Palais qui est sans exemple, et de la part dune persone qui est constituée dans une tres grande dignité, et aupres de qui j'avois de bonnes recommandations outre que j'en suis connu tres particulierement. Je lui demandois une chose qui est dans l'ordre, et que lon n'a jamais refuseé au
― 446 ―

plus etrange d'Alemagne, cependant on ne me lacorda pas, mais le magistrat ne croiant pas que je m'assistasse de conseil en pareilles ocasions, en a eu la confusion, et a eté obligé de reformer cequ'il avoit fait. Jen ay plus de chagrin que lui, car je contois sur sa protection, et il aura du ressentiment de cete rencontre, qui a d'ailleurs servi à me le faire connêtre. Si je contois la choze a mr Justel qui le connoit, il feroit je m'assure, tout transplanté qu'il soit pour la religion puritaine, un grand signe de croix. Apres cela je m'en vais faire ceque je n'aurois jamais fait, cest de me defier de mr Locke, tout mr Locke qu'il soit.
Si vous n'avez pas receu l'Observation de leclipse de Lune du 29. Aoust, a laquelle jassisté, et que je vous envoiay dans son tems, je vous la renverray. A propos de cete Eclipse, lautre jour en plaisantant, j'embarassay fort un medecin, auquel je dis que la flamme qui etoit sortie du ventre de cete femme, etoit un efet de l Eclipse parceque cela etoit arivé au même tems, et que puisqu'il n'en pouvoit doner de raison il faloit qu'il prist celle la pour bonne, dautant plus que les femmes avoient bien des choses communes avec la Lune. ce grand bruit qui sortit de son ventre a fait mentir le proverbe françois, qui dit: Femme qui pete, n'est pas morte.
Je suis obligé de rester encor ici <ju>sques†a à la fin du mois, de peur de surprise par nos parties, qui me desolent par leur chicane et mauvais foy. J'aurois bien a vous entretenir dautres choses, et en particulier de mon Harmonie du Pentateuque,†1 dont je me veux plus de bien à proportion que de ceque j'ay fait sur les Evangiles, quoiqu'il ait semblé meriter votre estime.

663. William Charleton to Locke, 4/14 October 1681 (658, 664, 670)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, ff. 44-5.
Montpellier the 14th October 1681
Deare Sir
Since the writing of mine of the 20th September I received yours of the 27th August where it lay by the way I know not, I had
― 448 ―

thought ere this to be nearer England then I feare I shall be in November, though still I am fixt as to my returne, my not moving so soon as I fully resolved to have done is the reason why I send you Dr. Magnols seeds with some few that I have got of a freind that tooke the paines to gather them himself in the Pyrenean mountaines in one of the boxs that I shall send towards Mr. Richards this weeke, where likewise is a small box with 6 bottles of the Queen of Hungarys water, and 3 bottles of perfumed water to wash the hands with, 2 of eau de mille fleurs, and one of eau d'Ange, and 4 bottles of cyprus powder 2 of white and 2 of grey which I entreate your acceptance of. The 2 boxes that I now send are marked No: (4) No. (5).
Box No: 4 contains 4 boxes marked 1.2.3.4. in the box no:1: are 5 Embroydered purses, and 9 sachetts. Box No. 2 contains†a7 bottles of the Queen of Hungary's water, 2 bottles eau d'Ange, and one of mille fleurs, and 6 bottles of cyprus powder. Box No. 3 contains†a the small present I make you and the Box No: 4 the seeds Dr. Magnol and I send you. in the papers marked with a P are those seeds that come from Catalognia. In the Box No: (5) are 17 pictures of Toloses painting in gilt frames of birds, Insects, and plants,†1 which with whatever else I have formerly sent you If I returne not I shall desire you to keep in memory of a verry humble servant of yours, I most humbly thanke you for the way you have taught me of preserving Insects which I'le assure you I shall communicate to no person. I acquainted you in my last of my having sent you 2 of Dr. Magnols books. I wish you had been more free with me and had given me the liberty of sending you something more worth your acceptance. Dr. Barbyrac, Dr. Magnol, Dr. Paul, and all your freinds here salute you kindly no English famyly is arrived as yet here, neither do I heare of any that are expected. Mr. Tufton is not as yet come but I beleeve he is at Lyons and may be here towards the end of this month. Farewell Deare Sir tell I see you and conserve me your freindship I beseech you since no one can be more then I
Sir
Your devoted servant
WILLIAM CHARLETON
― 449 ―

In the Box No:(5) besides the pictures are some few plants in loose sheets of paper.
Mr. Tufton is arrived and presents you his service.

B.M., Add. MS. 28,835, ff. 7-8. The sentence 'Dieu vous donne le repos ... un style plus addouci' is printed in J. C. Brunet, Manuel du libraire, 4th ed., 1842-4, art. London 14 Oct. 81
Vous pouvez bien conter parmi vos bonheurs Monsieur que vous n'entendez pas la langue Angloise, cela vous epargne bien de la peine, et la cause que vous ne recevez pas chasque semaine de mes letres c'est que la difficultè de m'exprimer en langue Chrestienne areste l'inclination que j'ay de vous parler touts les jours. et je vous ay tant d'obligations que ce seroit de mon devoir de vous fair mes reconnoissances par chasque poste. mais j'apprehende bien que le jargon de mes letres vous seroit plus ennuyex que ma silence seroit coupable. Je ne puis pourtant me taire tousjours. apres trois ou quatre de vos letres et tant de belles choses que vous m'envoiez il faut vous remercier de telle maniere qu'on le put
― 452 ―

J'ay regalè nos espions du ciel del'Eclyps de lune que m'envoiasts le 3me Septembre mais pour vous dire la veritè il me semble que ces gens la sont un peu malitieuse, qui adulterium solis et lunæ tam curiosè observant, miror ego quod spicula non metuant ἑκηβόλου Ἀπόλλωνος†1 mais ils prendent bien garde d'avoir toute la terre pour boulever†a enter eux et Monsieur Apollon qui sans doubt en seroit fort enragè
Ce que vostre ami vous ecrit des ponts de neige proche de Barege aux Pirenées m'a oté une scrupule que j ay eu long temp de la peine a resoudre (viz) Comment dans les montaines et autre lieux ou il y a une froid qui gele perpetuellement, l'eau de fontaines pouvoit couler puisque elle seroit gelèe aussitost qu'elle sorteroit dans l'air, d'ou il en suiveroit bien de difficulties, mais la sagesse de la nature a bien pourvieu à toute chose, et l'eau meme bastit à soy meme une couverture pour escorter son voyage dans sa route. comme font les Fourmis en Ceilon†b narrante Knoxio.†c †2 Vostre ami s'est servi d'un tres belle invention pour prandre la hauteur mais croiez vous que 90 toises pour demie seconde du pendule soit la difference de la progression du son d'avec la progression de la lumiere
Les bons nouvelles que vous m'ecrivez touchant Mr Romer me donnent bien de la joye, je prens part à tout le bonheur que lui put ariver et je vous prie de m'envoyer son addresse parceque je voudrois aussi le feliciter au sujet de son mariage. Vous m'avez donnè de si grands preuves de vostre generositè que je ne puis pas doubter que vous ne vous interessez en tout ce que me touche faitez moy la justice de croir la meme chose de moi
Je vien à la vostre du 8me Sept.†3 et je ne puis pas m'empecher de vous dire la dessus que vous n'etes pas content de m'accabler de vos bainfaits, mais vous ajoutez tant de belles parolles, comme si vous m'etiez reduables de toutes les honetetez que vous me fitz. Sur cete chapitre vous me parles de l'ars signorum d'Algarno
― 453 ―

comme de quelque chose dimportance. Si j'avois quelque peine a le trouver c'estoit parcequ il estoit un bagatel negligè et non pas pour avoir du prix, scombris enim et piperi reservabatur potius quam docti cujuspiam scriniis.†1 et j'aprehende que vostre ami aura plus de peine à y trouver quelque chose que je n'avois a trouver le livre. Je vois bien qu'on vous avoit fort mal traitè au Palais et que le chagrin en estoit grand quand même il a pu m'attirer vostre
(English ) supcon ce la ne me chocque point de tout, donandum hoc offensionis paroxysmo qui his in casibus omnia plerumque concutit, sed cum ad te ipsum <redieris>†a me alterius mali contagio infici minime suspicaberis. memento quibus venales sunt linguæ cor in vicinio locatum haud nimis tutum est. nescio ego an ætatis ingravescentis sit morbus an hominum justior æstimatio hoc cértò scio si Toinardus meus et hujusmodi aliqui antiquæ fidei viri me non conciliabant humano generi ego alter prorsus Timon†2<evaderem>,†b verum cum tanto minor sit bonorum numerus convassendum est aliquando et in Insulam Bourboniam proficiscendum ubi Justellum nostrum simul possedebimus. Dieu vous donne le repos que vostre harmonie merite, je suis ravi que vous la commencez par le pentateuque ce que me fait esperer que vous parcourerez toute la bible et en ferez un ouvrage achevè, et je crois qu une traduction literale sera la plus commode pour l harmonie, avec un Synopsis à cotè dans un style plus addouci.
― 454 ―

Vous n'avez rien perdu de ce que les trois liveres vous ayent etè rendus si tard puisque il n'y avoit rien dans ces livres ou faut du matiere ou faut de la langue qui pouroit vous entretenir mais comme les pauvres pays payent leur tribut aux plus grand roys de ce que leur terre produit quoique il ne soit que de peu d'importance. si bien que quand je vous importune en vous envoyant de nos bagatelles je vous prie de vous souvenir que je suis d'un pays qui n'est pas fertil en de belles choses et qui meritent vous etre presentes
Tout ce que vous avez mis entre les maines de Monsieur Justel ou de Madame Grig m'a etè rendu et je vous en rende mille graces. mais je serois bien aise de scavoir la machine à amollir les os de vostre facon. Je vous ai mille obligations al egard de moy même et al egard de mes amis Madame Grig m'a parlè de vos honetetez d'une maniere digne de vostre character qui est d'estre l'homme du monde le plus obligeant. Vous avez tant d'amis et de serviteurs acetheur en Agleterre que je <m>'etonne†a que vous ne songez jamais d'aller voir vos gens icy et d'en recevoir l'homage du a vostre merit et a vostre vertue. laissez un peu Orleans (car je pu bien croire que vous ne trouvez grand difficultè de quitter le Palais et les processes) et venez prendre un peu l'air parmi des gens qui sont toutes a vous et qui tacheront de vous divertir. Amenez avec vous Monsieur l'Abbè Gendron, parceque je ne le puis pas assez le remercier de ses honetites à si grand distance, quoique je lui fisse toutes les reconnoissaces imaginables. Je ne croi pas que vous mavez parlè de la millieme part<i>e†a de belles choses que vous connoissez, faut du temps et d'occasion. cela a etè la cause que je n'ay pas scu la machine pour infuser de la liqueur dans les fistulas. Tout ce qu est de vostre invention a quelque chose de commode au de la de l'ordinaire et merite bien d'estre scu de tout le monde
Je baise les maines tres humblement a Monsieur le capitaine, Monsieur de St Colombe, Monsieur Thevenot. jespere q'uil a estè satisfait du commencement et de la fin del' histoire Turquestani que je vous a envoyè il y a quelque temps. Je vous prie aussi de saluer de ma part Monsieur Bernier et de vous informer de lui si il y a parmi les Orientaux tant Turcs que Paiens quelque Sorcelerie. Spectre, Oracles ett et si le Diable se fait vaire a ces gens la comme en l Amarique, la Lapponie et autre part parmi les paiens. Je vous suis infinement obligè touchant la Kinkina. J'ay l'honeur de
― 455 ―

estre connu de Monsieur le Comte de Peñalossa†1 et si vous le voiez encore je vous prie de lui faire mes tres humble baisemaines son histoire aura sans doubte quelque chose de fort particulere et de fort agreable et il nous pourroit donner bien des eclaircissements touchant l'Amarique. Puisque la machine a touer n'est pas publièe j y ay estè encore une fois pour l'observer plus particulierement et je vous en envoyeray les mesures comme je les ay pise sur le lieu, et la description le mieux qu il me sera possible
(Original Text) [l. 8]
such a thing is forgivable as arising from acute vexation at an offence, which in such cases is apt to upset one entirely; but when you return to yourself you will never suspect me of being infected by contagion of another's evil. Remember that for those who have venal tongues the heart, being situated close by, is none too safe. I do not know whether it is a malady of advancing age or a juster appreciation of human beings; this I am sure of, that if my Toinard and some other such men of old-fashioned honesty did not reconcile me to the human race, I should become a regular Timon†2 the second; seeing, however, that good men are such a small minority we must pack up some day and betake ourselves to the Île Bourbon, where we will have our friend Justel with us too.

[Toinard:]
Ce fut, monsieur, a la belle journée d'avant hier jeudi, 23. de ce mois d'Octobre que vous futes bien souhaité dans ma chambre, non pas pour une ocazion passagere, mais comme habitant de Paris ou d'Orleans. mr L'Abé Gendron m'a fait lhonneur de loger chez moy pour etre incognito à Paris. Il a preferé la mediocre chere que je lui pouvois faire aux grans regals de monsieur Colbert de chez qui il s'etoit retiré avec lagreement du Seigneur sous pretexte d'etre plus
― 456 ―

en repos et plus en liberté. Il etoit venu a sa priere pour une indisposition de madame Colbert,†1 qui a plus receu de soulagement par la confiance qu'ele a en mr lAbé Gendron que par les remedes qu'il luy ait ordonéz. On avoit disposé de frequens relais sur la route, et il sest rendu en huit heures d'Orleans a Seaux en chaize roulante, qui est une diligence extraordinaire dont mond. sieur†a Abé a eté incommodé quelque tems.†2 J'ay taché de repondre a la bienveillance dont il m'honore, par les compagnies que je luy ay procurées, Voiez combien lui et moy avons perdu par votre eloignement. Il nous faloit encore le Capitaine de marine qui fait a prezent par terre la reveüe de l'armée navale dont il est le bon gros vizamiral.†3 Quand vous voudrez tout cela se rencontrera ensemble à faire des observations avec chacun sa Lunete à la main, Dont le verre sera blanc ou rouge selon le tems et le lieu.
A propos de mr Gendron, je nescai si je vous ay autrefois dit qu'il a fort aprouvé une petite machine que j'imaginay il y a dix ans pour infuser de la liqueur dans les fistules ou dans les plaies profondes, au lieu de se servir de Siringue. cequi m'en fait souvenir cest que je l'ay prié ici de voir un jeune enfant d'un de mes amis, auquel il sest fait une fistule dans la poitrine apres un abcez, mr Hubin a fait plusieurs de ces machines de diferentes grosseurs. Si je ne vous en ay donné, c'est que l'ocasion d'en parler ne s'est pas prezentée, outre que lorsque†b- je vous-†b possedois, j'avois plus d'interest d'ecouter les belles et grandes choses dont vous me regaliez, que vous n'auriez eu davantage a aprendre mes petites inventions. Si davanture je ne vous ay point parlé de cecy, je l'ajouteray suivant vos ordres à un paquet que jay à vous envoier des que jen auray trouvé une ocazion.
J'ai fait faire pour un de mes amis une ormoire suivant votre dessein.†4 Il en est admirablement contant, et comme bien des gens l'ont eté voir ausquels il disoit que jen etois l'Inventeur, je leur ay dit qu'a moi n'apartenoit tant de braverie, et que cetoit uniquement de vous de qui je la tenois avec bien d'autres choses, et que lon devoit lapeler le Cabinet de monsieur Lock. Si javois cru rester si long tems ici je men serois doné un, mais je n'y manqueray
― 457 ―

pas en province. Vous avez cy joint une reponse historique a votre memoire de Kinkina.†1 Je puis repondre de la bonne foy de celui de qui je lay eüe, et de sa connoissance en ces matieres. Sa vie est un Roman que lon traduit, et qui doit etre bientost imprimé. Il y aura des choses fort agreables. J'ay lu la meilleure partie de l'original, qui est parfaitement bien ecrit en Castillan.
Songez serieuzement à la restitution pour monsieur Justel que je salüe.
Dans la recete du Kinkina j'ay bien voulu metre que le pois†2 dun ecu, cest a dire d'or, car il ariva un jour que manque d'avoir ajouté ce mot, lors que les patagons†3 ne valoient que 58.s,†a un malade prit une de ces pieces avec deux sols, en d< >†b pour faire l'ecu, et en pris le pois d'une < >†b qui luy avoit eté ordonée au pois d'un < >†b
Mr l'Abe Picard ma ecrit de Vitre qu'il devoit samedi dernier lorsqu'il seroit a st malo en doner dans l'aile a l'un des satellites. Il y a un observateur de l'Academie à Donkerke pour cela, et mr Cassini a Paris, ny correspondra ton point en Angleterre?

670. William Charleton to Locke, [December 1681] (663, 664, 691)

Deare Sir
though I have been unmindfull of my concerns I see you have not, Mr: Kirby shewed me a letter he received from you wherein you are pleased to make them to much your own and the aprehensions of that ought to have kept me from giving you the trouble I did about them, you see the advantage I have got by living in France, a modest Englishman newly come over would never have had the confidence to have been so troublesome to his freind, but since I have begun I must beg your pardon if I continue, I send you therefore the bill of lading for the 2 last boxs I sent to Mr: John Richards No: 4. No 5:, in the Box No: 4. are 4 Boxs markt 1.2.3.4. in the box no: 1 are 5 Embroydered purses and 9 Sachettes. Box No: 3. is for your self and contains†a 6 bottles of the Queen of Hungary's water, and 3 bottles of parfumed waters, and 4 bottles of cyprus powder.
Box No 4 contains†a the seeds Dr. Magnol and I sent you. in the papers markt with a P: are those seeds that came from Catalognia.
Box No: 5 contains†a 17 pictures of birds Insects and plants, and some few plants in loose sheets of paper. You had heard from me since the writing of my last of the 14th October but that I have been verry ill, and truly am not well yet and I fear never shall, yours not mentioning any thinge to the contrary makes me hope your health is established, which I should be extream joyfull to heare. I may stay possiblely here a moneth longer, so that if you chance to be in towne and that you think I can be usefull to you let me know it, your letter directed to me at Mr: Kirby's will be sure to come to my hands. Since I draw nearer England I hope at last I may kisse your hands there, and give you my personall thankes for all the kindnesse you have shewen to
Sir
Your affectionate humble servant

671. Sir Thomas Lynch to Locke, 6 December 1681 (649, 673)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 186-7.
Wee have Dear Mr Lock bin here already 5 or 6 Weekes, our Merchants are stil in the Downes, and the Frigat at Cowes, and the Wind not disposed to favour us, nor like to do it as the People here say till Candlemas, Becaus it blew Westerly on Alhollanday,†1 you may imagine, by this, wee have leasure enough to inquyre after our freynds, Especially†a such, as have been so bussy as you;†2 Pray let's know if it's not over, or whether it has not put al thoughts of thother World out of your head, Were the warmth and Peace of that preferrable to the freyndship and troubles you have in this, I do not see but yo'le have tyme enough to come to us, That you may not want meanes or information, I have desyred my freynd Coll. Beeston†3 (an Ingenuous Man) to deliver theis. He'le advise and serve you in al thats needful. Tho I confess I do not know you ever seryously thought of such a Voyage, or that you can so soon quit the freindships, Bussiness, and engagements you have here, Yet I cannot forbear doing my part towards the compassing what I so much desyre, for like this Age I aym at the satisfying my own passions and interests without having any regard to anothers, or it may be to Justice or Reason. But I'le say no more, for I would
― 463 ―

receive your freyndship as the Kings Honours ex mero motu,†1 But I may tel you, If your Constitution can bear the heates, and your mind il Company, yo'le se Maderas, BB,†2 Jamaica,†a and Cartagena, and may come back with the frigat That must return assoone as possible, Whether you go or stay pray beleive I am most affectionately
Sir your freynd and Servant
T LYNCH
Plymouth. 6. December 1681
Address: To John Lock Esquire at Thanet-hous in Aldersgate-streete In London.

673. Sir Thomas Lynch to Locke, 16 December 1681 (671, 719)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 15, ff. 188-9. Lynch sailed about 3 February 1682: Cal. S.P., Dom., 1682, p. 69.
Plymouth.16.December 1681
D Mr Lock.
Just now I have yours of the 10th and 13th Instant, so ful of Expressions of freyndship and kindness, That nothing but your Company could have obliged me more; you have don me right in judging what I wryt was sincere, and yourself in glosing so ingeniously on it, That has turn'd your Letter into an Oracle, for wee cannot agree about the Meaning, one sayes you wil come another not, I conclude you know I cannot Comand the Wynds, But I may the frigats, if you wryt me by the Post you were coming; Wee have no more hopes of a fayr Wynd then wee had 7 weekes ago, and are as bussy making Cloathes for Christmas, as if wee were at the End, rather than the beginning of our Voyage, you may therfore fancy us as well and in as good humour as crosse Wynds and the want of good Company Can make us. It's true you are very reasonable in preferring the tranquillyty and Conversation of Oxford to the Dangers and Incertayntyes of the Winds and Seas and it's as true we are not unreasonable in covetting the Conversation that would
― 466 ―

Sir
Your most aff freynd and Servant
THO LYNCH

A Orleans ce vendredi 26 Decembre 81. Lendemain de noel†b Vous avez cy joint, Monsieur, trois petis morceaux de verre que je vous envoie pour matiere a philosopher sur les couleurs en general et sur la couleur rouge en particulier. Ces trois morceaux faisoient partie d'une plus grande piece qui a eté tiré d'un pot a notre verrerie en ma presence, et l'un des trois etant mis sur une pelle de fer dans le fourneau y est devenu rouge, et le seroit encore devenu davantage, si l'on l'avoit tenu plus long tems au feu. Les deux otres morceaux qui sont de cristal blanc, prendront la même couleur en leur faisant la même chose, sur quoi vous observerez qu'il ne faut pas metre tout d'un coup la pelle dans la bouche du fourneau, mais l'avancer peu a peu, afin que les cristaux s'echaufent par degréz, parcequ'autrement ils peteroient. Vous avez faire cet experience a vos verreries, sinon chez un orfevre en metant lesd. morceaux dans un moufle, et donant le feu.
C'est ce me semble u<ne>†c chose assez singuliere que cela, mais il y en a bien une autre qui me semble plus admirable, c'est que ces mêmes morceaux etant devenus rouges, vous lez metrez dans un creuset au fourneau; et par la fusion ils deviendront blans com'ils
― 468 ―

etoient auparavant, et les remetant de nouveau au feu comme cydessus ils seront rouges une autrefois, et puis blans si lon les remet en fuzion; et ainsi de suite.
La dessus on demande d'ou vient le rouge et ou il va. Je vous prie den consulter monsieur Boyle, que je n'oze pas prendre la liberté de vous prier d'assurer de mes tres humbles respects, n'aiant pas l'honneur d'etre connu de lui. Je chercheray une occasion pour vous faire tenir quelques ouvrages de cete matiere, comme tabatieres, fioles, et c.
Vous savez bien que la maniere de faire la couleur rouge des ancienes vitres des Eglises est perdue il y a long tems, et la voila retrouveé plus belle qu'elle n'etoit.
Je vous enverray aussi des cabochons de cete même etofe sur les quels vous ferez bien plus d'experiences à cause qu'ils seront un peu gros et solides.

675. John Richards to Locke, 22 December 1681
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, f. 20. There is nothing to show whether or not no. 280 and the present letter were written by the same man. The present writer is mentioned in nos. 529, 658, and 663; in no. 664 he is described as a merchant. He was sometime keeper of the East India Company's warehouse in Leadenhall Street. The present letter shows that he was connected with the Shaftesbury household. He died at sea on 2 February, five days out from the Downs: Sir William Hedges, Diary, ed. R. Barlow, etc. (Hakluyt Soc., vols. lxxiv, lxxv, lxxviii, 1887-9), i. 16, ii. (273-4). Letter from his widow below, no. 756.
The East India Company having taken Richards into its service, Locke was bound with him in the sum of £250 for his rendering true accounts to the Company, etc. Richards signed a counterbond on 9 November obliging himself and his heirs to pay Locke and his heirs £500; it was witnessed by Peter Percival and William (?) DAMARIS CUDWORTH, LATER LADY MASHAM
Damaris Cudworth was born on 18 January 1659. Her father was Dr. Ralph Cudworth (no. 422); her mother Damaris, daughter of Matthew Cradock. Cradock, who died in 1641, was sometime governor of the Massachusetts Bay Company; he was an opponent of Charles I and a member of parliament for London in 1640-1. Mrs. Cudworth was married first to Thomas Andrewes, the son of the notable financier of the same name who was Lord Mayor of London in 1650-1, and governor of the East India Company in 1659, a republican and knighted by Cromwell in 1657. There were several children by both marriages. Nothing is known about the younger Damaris's early life and education except that, as her letters show, she grew up in her father's circle, the Cambridge Platonists. She met Locke probably towards the end of 1681, shortly before the date of her first extant letter to him. In 1685 she married Sir Francis Masham, a baronet, a widower with eight sons and one daughter, and henceforward lived at Oates (or Otes), an estate in High Laver in Essex, about 25 miles from London and 34 from Cambridge. There was one son of the marriage, Francis Cudworth Masham, born in 1686. Locke, returning to England in February 1689, found the London winters injurious to his health. He spent Christmas 1690 and most of the early months of 1691 at Oates, paying Masham for his keep. Thenceforward he had permanent quarters there and the greater part of his library. At first he spent the summers in London attending to political duties. Later his visits to London became shorter and in his last years he remained continuously at Oates. Lady Masham tended him in his last illness and was reading the Psalms to him when he died. A few weeks later she wrote an account of him for Jean Le Clerc. She herself died at Bath on 20 April 1708 and is buried in Bath Abbey.
― 471 ―

Lady Masham's views or her connection with Dr. Henry More won for her the regard of John Norris (no. 1492), who dedicated to her The Theory and Regulation of Love, 1688 (dedication dated 26 March 1688) and addressed to her Reflections upon the Conduct of Human Life, 1690 (dated at end 2 September 1689). In 1696 Lady Masham published without her name A Discourse concerning the Love of God, in which she expressed her dissent from views put forward by Norris and Mary Astell (D.N.B.) in Letters concerning the Love of God, which he published in 1695. Norris attributed the Discourse to Locke, with whom he had quarrelled, and in a reply complained of the 'Disdain and Contempt' with which the author had treated him, and of his free 'Indulgence of his Spleen and Prejudice': Practical Discourses, vol. iv, 1698, pp. 382, 424. In 1705 Lady Masham published, again anonymously, Occasional Thoughts in reference to a Vertuous or Christian Life, an appeal to women to study the grounds of religious belief.†1
Sir Francis Masham was a descendant of Sir Henry Cromwell 'the Golden Knight'; his father's mother was a first cousin of Oliver, the Protector. Thanks to Mark Noble a large amount of genealogical information is available for Sir Henry's descendants. Noble compiled this from printed materials and manuscript pedigrees, registers, and family papers. There are errors but he deserves well of his successors. What is not clear is how far Sir Henry's descendants cohered; whether the third or fourth generations felt any ties of consanguinity. In the seventeenth century connection and patronage were important. The name of Cromwell was hateful after the Restoration, but ability and social position were valued. Charles II employed a son-in-law of Oliver and a niece's husband as diplomatists, while a brother-in-law became a bishop. After the Revolution Sir Henry's descendants were noticeable in parliamentary and political life; among them are Archbishop Tillotson, John Lord Cutts, and Henry St. John, Viscount Bolingbroke.
The available evidence for cohesion is inconclusive. Martha Lockhart writes about her cousins Joanna Cutts and John Hampden; they were her third cousins. She may have been exceptional. Esther Masham in her letterbooks is concerned almost entirely with her cousins on either side; Locke enters it as a family friend, an inmate of the house; Esther appears to have found her friends among her cousins and to have taken little interest in her neighbours. It seems likely that consanguinity was a stronger bond than it is today and provided opportunities for establishing friendships; they, however, would depend for their growth and maintenance on mutual affection.
Lady Masham was brought by her marriage into this circle, and in turn brought Locke into it. The loss of her letters and papers makes it impossible to estimate her feelings regarding it. She is unlikely to have known at all well the most famous new entrant, Queen Anne's Mrs. Masham, Abigail Hill, as the latter married her youngest stepson Samuel, later the first Lord Masham, only in the September preceding her death.

677. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 6 January [1682] (684)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 77-8. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Sir
Be it under whatever pretence you please that you have sent me a letter, you ought not to feare that it should be ill taken, since nothing can be liable to a Misinterpretation that you say, who as I beleeve you would not really Deceive, so perhaps should you designe it you might not find it very easie, there being something necessarie besides Witt to make one succeed in it. You might therefore without any Apprehension have writt to me all that you Pleas'd. The Idea that I have form'd of you in my Mind, could you have design'd ill, would have secur'd me, and otherwise I am not unwilling to Contribute to your Diversion, in which I have found so agreable an entertainment. But methinks Monsieur Scudery being discarded as you say he is†1 (for which I am very glad if he will not allow one to be pleas'd with the Esteeme of those for whom all the World has an esteeme) you should have let me knowne what new and better forms are introduc'd instead of those Antiquated ones of his which may be as convincing as Folded Arms and the sullens. I have beene told Lately by a Person for whom I have a greater Esteeme then for Voiture†2 that he is as much in the wrong too in makeing his Grand Cyrus and Aronces entertaine Clelia and Mandana with discourses so full of sence and write them letters so Witty and so Handsome, it being impossible as he said for those who love so to do. You thought not of it I beleeve when you
― 473 ―

writt yours, nor do I desire that you should, should you ever write to me againe, for besides the difficultie that it would be to you to write otherwise then well there is nothing that I love better then good letters, and I would with all my Heart never receive an ill one upon any Account whatever. I am willing that expression of your Respect for me (if it be one) should be Defer'd till that revolution of time you speake of, when perhaps I as well as you may have different sentiments from those I now have. In the meane while permit me to think that it will be acceptable to you that I reckon you in the number of those of my Friends for whom I have a more particular Consideration, and I shall think my self sufficiently recompenc'd for all the Raillery you may pass upon me who am
Your Obedient Servant
PHILOCLEA.†1
Jan: the 6th.
If you knew but in what paine I have writt this letter you would not doubt but that I have Charity enough to wish you a good new yeare and every thing else that is really desirable.

679. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, 15/25 or 16/26 January 1682 (674, 686)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, ff. 128-30. 25 January 1682, N.S., fell on a Sunday.
+
A Orleans ce Lundi 25. 82.
Je vous envoiay il y a quelques tems un paquet par la poste dans lequel entre des cartes coupées il y avoit des morceaux de verre dignes de votre curiosité. Ils sont d'une nouvele composition que l'on fait à notre verrerie, et com'ils auront peutêtre eté perdu avec le recit que je vous envoiois de leurs proprietez, je recapituleray ici quelque chose de ma derniere.
Ces morceaux sont de cristal blanc ordinaire auquel on a ajouté une drogue, par le moien de laquele led. cristal etant tiré blanc du pot qui est dans le fourneau, et etant presenté pendant quelque tems à la bouche dud. fourneau, devient d'un beau rouge, et d'autant plus enfoncé que l'on le laisse de tems a la bouche du fourneau.
― 475 ―

Voila la premiere matiere à philosopher, car on demande ou etoit ce rouge qui ne paroist dans le verre que par la cuisson que l'on lui donne à la bouche du fourneau.
La seconde matiere à philosopher est que ce cristal devenu rouge, etant remis en fusion dans le fourneau, en est retiré blanc comme la premiere fois, et l'on demande qu'est devenüe sa couleur rouge.
La troisiême matiere à philosopher est que ce cristal redevenu blanc, etant remis à la bouche du fourneau, redevient rouge comme la premiere fois, et l'on demande qu'elle est la source de ce rouge qui paroist et disparoist alternativement, et ainsi à l'infini.
J'estime que Monsieur Boyle ne sera pas faché d'aprendre ces experiences, et qu'il nous en donnera les raisons. Il est à remarquer que cela n'arive que dans ce rouge inventé de nouveau, qui est le même que celui des ancienes vitres des Eglises, qui avoit eté perdu depuis plus de deux cents ans.
A la Ste chapele de Bourges†1 il y a des vitres rouges au travers des queles les raions du soleil ne passent point mais seulement la lumiere, et ils vantent cela com'une merveille. Nous en avons ici decouvert la cause en faisant des bouteilles rouges qui n'ont qu'un doublet rouge fort mince au dessous du cristal blanc dont le corps de la bouteille est composé. Ainsi ces vitres sont de trois feuïlles de verre, dont il y en a deux de cristal blanc, et une qui est un doublet rouge entre deux, le tout joint et comme colé et incorporé ensemble par le feu, et ces trois corps rompent le raion.
mr Perrot a aussi trouvé depuis six jours une couleur admirable d'Agathe. Elle est si belle qu'ele eface la nature. J'en ay fait tailler des pierres, et je voudrois trouver une ocasion pour vous en envoier avec des bouteilles tant rouges que d'Agathe.
Notre amy mr Romer est aujourdhui le tout en Dannemarck. Il entre dans tous les colleges comme mathematicien du Roy. Il me mande que l'on travaille etrangement pour l'embellissement de Copenhague et l'augmentation et perfection de ses ports, et que les occupations de la mer et de la terre troublent celes du ciel. Il a epousé la fille de mr Bartholin, qui est belle et riche.
Je vous ay autrefois bien rompu la tête de mon systeme du mouvement continu de l'aiguille aimanteé, a l'entour du compas. j'avois une possession plusque centenaire,†2 mais l'aiguille a retrogradé de 15. minutes à Paris, et si l'observation est sure, cela marque que
― 476 ―

l'aimant a dans ses declinaisons orientales et occidentales un mouvement irregulier de libration vers le Pole. mr Tevenot a fait depuis peu graver une carte canadoise depuis le lac des Ilinois et la baye des Puans jusques à la baye du st Esprit dans le Golfe de mexique.†1 Il y a une admirable riviere qui va nord et sud p<resque>†a depuis le lac Superieur jusques aud. Golfe. Il se trouve dans un endroit proche de ses bords des chevaux et des chameaux.†2 Il y a beaucoup de cuivre dans ce païs. Mr Tevenot en donera aussi la relation entiere, avec autres belles choses. Il faudroit des ocasions pour vous remetre cela et cequi pouroit tomber sous ma coupe afin de vous donner au moins quelques petites marques de ma reconnoissance pour tous les bienfaits dont vous m'acablez.
Un de mes a trouvé dans les Pyrenæes une grande abondance d'Alun de Plume†3 dont il m'a envoié. Il y en a des filaments tres longs dont je crois que lon faisoit l'Asbestos des anciens tiré de la pierre Amianthos.
J'ay fait cete letre chez mr lAbé Gendron qui s'est purgé ce matin, et n'a voulu voir personne que moy. Quand il a dejeuné apres que sa medecine a operé, il a bu a votre santé et a la miene.
Address: For Mr John Locke Angleterre at Mr Hicks's à tailer, below the Kings playhouse in Bridges street London
Endorsed by Locke: Toinard 25 Jan 82

680. Dr. David Thomas to Locke, 8 February 1682 (678, 702)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 20, ff. 42-3.
Sarum Feb 8 81
Deare Freind
I had sooner answered your letter but that I wayted the course of a pleurisy which I find as all coughs†a- and other acute deseases not curable without respect to the Epidemick in which bleeding purgeing etc prove ineffectuall without Cortex-†a I doe therefore try the same method with my little consumptive patient†1 whom I find too much emaciated to be kept in bed what the successe time must shew. All I find is that shee doth not grow worse nor mend. I hope you have payd the writeing Master.†2 If your affayres would permitt I would fayne see you here to try if Chymestry might not be improved to the cure of Agues. I wish the honourable†3 would by you impart his cure of a Cancer, I haveing 2 or 3 patients to try it upon. I am
your affectionate ADRIAN
Parthenice is your servant
Address: These For Mr John Locke at Thanet house in Aldersgate streete London

EDWARD CLARKE
Edward Clarke of Chipley in the parish of Nynehead near Taunton in Somerset belonged to a family long settled in that neighbourhood. The Edward Clarke of Bradford who was captured among the royalists in Bridgwater in 1645, and fined £40 as a delinquent, was probably the father of Locke's friend. He married first Anne, daughter of Mark Knight of Buckinghamshire. She died in 1652. His second marriage, to Elizabeth Lottisham, brought the Chipley estate into the Clarke family. He died in 1679.
Clarke was born about 1650. He entered Wadham College, Oxford, as a fellow-commoner on 30 March 1667, matriculating on the same day, and remaining in residence probably until 1670. While he was there he may have met John Freke (no. 874), who entered the college in 1669 and who was to be a life-long friend. He also entered the Inner Temple and was called to the bar on 20 April 1673. About two years later he married Locke's kinswoman Mary Jepp, niece of John Strachey. Probably before the end of 1675, whether before or after his marriage, he became acquainted with Shaftesbury. His later career shows that he must have held political views close to Shaftesbury's, but his only recorded service to him was his appointment in 1680 as one of the four trustees for part of the earl's estates; after Shaftesbury's death he continued to act as a trustee for the dowager countess and then for the third earl. He was probably a candidate for Taunton for James II's parliament but was defeated. On 8 June, at the time of Monmouth's rebellion, he was taken into custody. This was probably a simple precautionary measure; he petitioned the king and was released on security.
With the Revolution he came into public life. To Locke's disappointment he did not stand for the Convention. About April, thanks to Locke's influence with Lord Bellomont, he became Auditor-General to Queen Mary. He entered parliament in 1690 for Taunton and continued to represent it until his death. At the outset he was an active member, serving on many committees; this probably continued until he was hampered by ill health. Surviving records indicate that he spoke frequently in debate; they suggest
― 480 ―

that he was not outstanding as a speaker. In July 1694 he was appointed a director of the newly established Bank of England, but refused to serve. A few weeks later he was appointed a commissioner of Excise, an office that he held until 1699, when members of parliament were disqualified for it. About the end of 1694 he and Freke combined to form 'the College'; that being a fanciful name adopted by them for their private enjoyment. Freke appears to have been a close friend of Somers; he could lay Locke's views before him while Clarke could vent them in the house of commons. The most active period was in 1695 and 1696, when the problems of the recoinage were to be discussed; to this period also belongs the ending of the Licensing Acts, an achievement in which Clarke took an important part.
During these years he had the cares of an increasing family and of his wife's and his own ill health. It is impossible to list all the children. The first, who died almost immediately, was born in 1676. The most important for Locke's correspondence are Edward and Elizabeth. It was in the first place on Edward's behalf that Locke wrote the letters which he later shaped into Some Thoughts concerning Education. Locke was devoted to Elizabeth, the eldest surviving daughter, whom he styles his 'wife'. Mrs. Clarke died at Chipley on 10 January 1706 and was buried on 8 February among her own folk at Chew Magna. Clarke died probably at Chipley on 20 October 1710 and was buried at Nynehead.
In his will he names five of his children: his eldest surviving son Jepp, who inherited Chipley; he was sheriff of Somerset in 1700 and died in 1741; Samuel, who is mentioned in Locke's correspondence; Elizabeth, now married to John Jones; and two further daughters, Anne and Mary. Elizabeth's husband is said to have been a Welshman; in any case he is not traceable in the pedigree of the Jones family of Stowey. Anne married William Sanford of Nynehead Court, who died in 1719; she died in 1744. Mary married George Musgrave, a nephew of Dr. William Musgrave of Exeter (no. 1248, etc.); he died in 1724; she, on 2 May 1739, aged 52.
Authorities: Collinson, Somerset, ii. 99*; iii. 261, 268-9, 549, etc.; Abstracts of Somerset Wills (F. Brown), iii. 33-5; Rand, pp. 1-73 passim (some statements appear to be based on manuscripts belonging to the Sanford family); Cal. Committee for Compounding, p. 914; Registers of Wadham College, ed. R. B. Gardiner, 1889-95; Calendar of the Inner Temple Records, ed. F. A. Inderwick 1896-1901; Haley, Shaftesbury, p. 727; Cal. S.P., Dom., 1685, nos. 248, 777; C. J.; Anchitel Grey, Debates of the House of Commons, 1667-94, 1769 (1763?), x. 73, 206, 237, 277, 379; Narcissus Luttrell, Parliamentary Diary, ed. H. Horwitz, 1972 (Grey's reports after 1689 are fragmentary; he reports only one of Clarke's speeches at much length; Luttrell gives abstracts rather than reports of debates; he gives only one of Clarke's speeches at length: p. 272; frequently he merely lists him among participants in a debate); Charles Talbot, duke of Shrewsbury (Shrewsbury Correspondence), ed. W. Coxe, 1821, pp. 43, 417, 426, 479.

683. Locke to Edward Clarke, 16 February 1682 (682, 685)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 2. Clarke wrote a draft of his answer at the end of the postscript; it is here printed as no. 685. Printed in Rand, pp. 83-4. Answers no. 682.
Ch: ch: 16 Feb: 8½
Deare Sir
I beleive the kinde expressions of your letter in the utmost latitude you can meane them. But what assureances soever you give me of your freindship you will but ill performe what I expect from it, unlesse you take care to use a freind of mine that is in your hands something better then I feare you doe. If you continue to persecute your self with your owne thoughts I shall complaine of you as one that takes delight to torment me in the most sensible part, and you will be sure to receive all the reproaches from me that you can expect from a man who findes himself injurd in what is extreamely deare to him. Tis possibly but ill breeding to returne grumbling and threats in exchange for soe obleigeing a letter as you sent me. If therefor you doe not thinke I am naturally very rude and quarlesome you must conclude that the cause is of importance
― 483 ―

which makes me goe contrary to my custome and inclination. But I hope I talke all this more out of concerne then need and I am willing to thinke you doe not wholy neglect your self since you enquire after the Spa waters. where they are to be had I doe not certainly know. But Dr. Goodall†1 I remember told me he knew of some in towne, and tis by his direction and under his conduct that I desire you to take them. I have formerly acquainted him with some litle of your case and I dare answer for him he will be carefull in ad viseing you as I know he is able and discreet. he lives at the Colledge of physitians in Warwick lane†2 and pray goe to him in my name. The murther of Mr Thin is soe barbarous a thing that I finde it abhorred by all sober men. I finde in your letter an other inclosed to me which by the superscription I judge to come from Thanet house,†3 which yet I cannot reconcile to your refering me to Mr Stringer for other news. for I conclude he sent you this letter to be inclosed in yours. since he writt not to me him self. Pray present my humble service to Mrs Clarke who I hope is got well out of the affaire of the Nurse†4 and has noe thing now to divert her from the great businesse of the gold and silver petticoat my humble service to Mrs Cudworth and the rest of your good company I am Sir
your most humble and most affectionate servant
J LOCKE
If you thinke fit to make use of Dr Goodall, I will if you please to let me know it, write to him at large my thoughts and give him an account of what I have donne, but should have been glad you would have consented we three might have talked togeather whilst I was in town.

684. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 16 February [1682] (677, 687)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 79-80. Year from Locke's endorsement. On 11 February, perhaps at Philoclea's suggestion, Locke bought a copy of Select Discourses, 1660 (2nd ed., 1673; L.L., no. 2701), by John Smith (1618-52; D.N.B.) of Queens' College, Cambridge; he was now reading it, and was especially interested in the first discourse, 'The true Way or Method of attaining to Divine Knowledge'. In his Journal for 19, 20, and 21 February he commented on the Discourses: (i) on Enthusiasm; he probably sent part of this to Philoclea on 6 April (no. 696); (ii) on the Immortality of the Soul (Smith's fourth discourse); (iii) on Knowledge, which he apparently sent her about 21 February (no. 687) in answer to the present letter.
Feb: the 16th.
Sir
It being for your Honour that your Governess should have something in her more then is Common to the rest of her Sex I do not much wonder if you should really indeavour to fancy that she has soe But She who knows her self too well to be guiltie of so great an Errour knows that there is nothing she can Boast of but the Title that you are pleas'd to give her, of which I assure you she is not a little Proud, and which (how great a Friend soever she be to Truth on other occasions) rather then lose she would very willingly owe to your too advantageous opinion of her. I suppose by this time you have made a farther progress in the Book of which I would gladly know your thoughts but you must remember to tell me them truely, and to let me know what those things are that you dislike in it, without applying your self (I beseech you) any more to mee to make you understand any thing which you did not before. What you Comprehend not I am not very likely to make you, and you may be still ignorant if the Author have not sufficiently explaind himself, I did indeed beleeve before I heard from you that you would think of this section as I now imagine that you doe But whether that fourefold kind of Knowledge that he talks of†1 be soe or not, methinks that that Division which you have made of Mankind†2seemes to be something too general, and there are a number of Persons in the World (at least (I think) ought to be) which I find not included in any part of it. But I know not what you may call
― 485 ―

Vision†1 nor how much you may attribute to the power of Reason, onely as I understand them it seemes to mee that there may be something betweene these†a two things, there being (I think) such a Degree of Perfection to be attain'd to in this Life to which the Powers of meere Unassisted Reason will never Conduct a Man, not that I think more meanely of Reason I beleeve then you do, much less would lay aside the use of it as many do. But I would faine know whether you think not that by imploying it the best one can, and by constantly adhereing to the Dictates of it, they may not at length come to be acted by a Higher Principle, Or whether it is by that alone that we are capable of becomeing those new Creatures so often spoken of, it seemes to mee I confess that it is not, and I beleeve that my Author was of that mind, neither do I know how to understand several places in St Paul (which seem'd not difficult before) if hee Himself were not as much an Enthusiast†2 as this comes to. But I shall quite tire you as I have alreaddie done my self, you know I cannot write short letters, but if you ask me questions they'l be twice as long. Pray take care for the Future or I shall write you out of all Patience. You may be able to judge what I am like to do by this, since I am lame at present, and thought I could not have writt at all when I took the Pen in my Hand, haveing almost broke my Arm to day besides three or foure mischeifs more that I got all with a fall as I was standing still. Poore Mr C —†3 was almost scar'd out of his Witts at three Roomes distance and had not he come to my aid directed by the noise most certainly I had laine there till this time you see how carefull a Governess you have of me, that I neglect you not notwithstanding all these†a disasters, but it is no more then you ought to expect from one who is so much your Friend and servant as Philoclea.
Pray if you expect any more letters from me let me know how I must direct them, since upon Mr Clerks asking his lady how, I undertook to tell and was corrected.
Address: These For Mr Lock at Christs Church in Oxford
Postmarks: FE 16; G (?)
Endorsed by Locke: Philoclea 16 Feb. 8½

687. Locke to Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, [c. 21 February 1682] (684, 688)
B.L., MS. Locke f. 6, pp. 33-8: Locke's Journal, 21 February 1682. Incomplete copy of a letter sent to Philoclea about this time: it answers no. 684 and is answered by no. 688. Printed in An Early Draft of Locke's Essay, ed. R. I. Aaron and J. Gibb, 1936, pp. 123-5.
[Locke considers that the four kinds of knowledge enumerated by Smith are only several degrees of the love of God and practice of virtue. Opinions in the mind that are not founded on reason are not knowledge, 'but if they concerne God and religion deserve the name of Enthusiasme'. Reason is assisted by 'education discourse contemplation or otherwise'; all the improvements come from God. 'Whatever is known, however sublime or spirituall is known only by the naturall faculty of the understanding and reason, however assisted. Though there may be this difference that one perhaps has got an help to see and discerne heavenly objects which an other never soe much as looked after and therefor I cannot quit my former division of men who†a- either thinke as if they were only body and minde not soule or spirit at all, or those who in some cases at least thinke of themselves as all soule seperate from the commerce of the body and in those instances have only visions or more properly imaginations. and a third sort who considering themselves as made up of body and soule here and in a state of mediocrity make use and follow their reason-†a untill you tell me what sort of persons those are who are not included in any part of it. I hope they will not be his fourth which to deale truly with you seeme to me very much to savour of Enthusiasme and soe will be very litle different from my Visionarys I meane in respect of their opinions and knowledg.' These men may exhibit 'Seraphyke love and Heroick vertue', excellent qualities, but irrelevant in a discussion concerning 'the destinction of men in respect of knowledg'. Locke approves of Smith's second discourse, of Superstition; he will discuss the third, of Atheism, with Philoclea later.]
― 489 ―

688. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 27 February [1682] (687, 690)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 81-2. Year from Locke's endorsement. Answers no. 687.
Feb: the 27th
Sir
If I could have beleev'd that that Account which I gave you of my self in my last could have put you in any Paine till you heard from me againe I should not have neglected the first opportunitie of leting you know that the Harms which my Fall did me were soone recoverd, and that I have since beene in Indifferent good Health. It would have beene but Justice to have done this, since I beleeve that I owe much to your good wishes, I should be very glad if you knew how to increase my Obligation to them and that it were in there power too to restore me to as good a Humour as I am at present in an Ill one. I know not very well how it comes about, but I am extreamly Angry with my self, and have a strange Disposition to be soe with all the World besides. I wonder at you that knowing as you doe how subject I am to these kind of Fitts, at sometimes, that you would not so order it that I might have found some occasion of quarreling with you in case the fit were on me, and that I was dispos'd to it. But you have taken no care at all of that, so that in the present Humour that I am in I can find nothing at all to write to you about, unless it be to contrive a Quarrel against next time, which perhaps might succeed if I should tell you that it is my Authors fourth Division of Men that I all along meant,†1 which if you will call Enthusiasts in your next I shall think my self much concern'd, and will resolve to take very Ill, this perhaps might do well enough, but however I do not tell you this, not being dispos'd to write any thing about the subject, nor knowing the Reason wherefore he calls this a 4fold kind of knowledge rather then as you say. But why would you put me upon this againe when I told you in my last that you must not? were you not affraid that in Revenge I should have ask'd your advice about makeing me a New Petticoate?†2 Have sent you an Account of all the new Fassions that have beene since you left the Towne? told you what my new Manto is made of? and a Thousand
― 490 ―

things more of the like nature that I have all in store for you if you provoke me to it againe.†a For the present haveing better consider'd it and finding that my Letter is like to be sufficiently Impertinent without I resolve to reserve it till then, therefore pray take care and remember that you are only freely and Plainly to tell me your thoughts of my Author without ever examining mee about him, who am so far from being able to explain His Opinions that I cannot give you an Account of my owne Actions which was the other thing that you desir'd of me, all that I know being onely that I got such a Fall as I told you of, but which ways I cannot for my Life immagine. You will see by this that I am the worst in the World at Answeareing Questions. The truth is, I have of late so Mortall an Aversion for it that twoo Hours Practice every night is so far from reconcileing me to it that I almost wish sometimes that I were Dumb, and am in a Fright every time that any Body begins to speake to me. I thought the other Day that if I lock'd my self up in my chamber I should certainly be free from this trouble, when before I had beene at rest an Houre in comes <your>†b Letter and another of three sides of a sheet of Paper all questions from one end to t'other, I have not answear'd it yet, nor beleeve I shall not these three months. Pray have a care that you provoke me not so much, and write any thing to me rather then ask me one question more, since I am so far out of Patience that I prefer'd being sick last Night before it. I am almost so too now with the length of this letter therefore shall onely add that I am
Your Friend and Servant
PHILOCLEA.
There is a Brother of mine†1 whom you have seene with me sometimes that is now going to France with my Lord Preston.†2 if you have any thing to command him he would be very glad to serve you, and you may do him a great Favour in it since he cannot be in my Lords Familie there, and will be much a stranger.

Postmarks: FE 28; G

680. Mrs. Anna Grigg to Locke, 28 February [1682] (647, 703)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 141-2. Year from Locke's endorsement. Mrs. Grigg's next communication with Locke was by a letter written by her son: no. 701.
Sir
Last night I come to London on purpose to hear what was the matter with some of my very kind friends and what they had to object against my thoughts of carrying my Son to Oxford, you know what were my reasons when we last discoursed together they are the same still and I hope time will make it evedent that I dont move in obedience to fondness, nor durst I atempt an unusuall methode had I stood alone in my sentiments, tis true my whole bussness has almost bin to be a true spie for my boy, I know now by experience that tis not without risking the present and future state of children that we venture them in a Croud, I have often told you with concern the particular evils that threaten youth in publick,†1 And you know me two well to think that slight inconveniences would prevaile upon me to reflect upon those affairs that wemen hardly have leave to pry into, but God having placed me in a state wherein I am to Act more warryly, I must not for feare of being reputed singular venture my whole Estate against those rocks I have by constant care and experiance discovered to be dangerous; None objects strongly against me when I plead that tis pitty a youth of any parts should be ten hours every day getting what is obtainable in one, nor can I device†2 why it should seeme strang if I chuse to have my Son rather imploy'd in reading excelent books such as acquaints him with the plaine and most speedy ways of becoming wise; (Since few boys loves hystory more or can give a better account of what he reads,) I had much rather find him turning over Dr Hamond†3 and Dr Cave†4 etc then be digging in an Emptie Nodle for poor rimes and imparing his health for to please an Angry master who expects an Epistle upon some subject a boy may have noe genious for; No brother I have had two good an aprobation
― 492 ―

from yourself and others to faint now at one years greater expence, besids I have set down and soberly calculated this expence, and have greater hopes to prosper then if I resolved to be blindly led a more celeberated†1 way; Deare brother pardon a sister crouded with company and thoughts and to ease my care be pleas'd to try what you can doe for a tutor, Mr Adams of Lincon Colledge†2 was this day by Mr Fisher mentioned to me as a most excelent person, but tis not known where he would be tempted by 10 or 20 pounds to hear and assist Will Grigg dayly, at lest he will be faithfull in helping us as a friend; And pray Sir what doe you think of mentioning this disign to the Presedent who may in Trinity Colledge supplie us, I could trust no body to bespeak me the good Opinion of the Deane like yourself,†3beleeve me my pen now wrongs both my head and heart, and were I to be gues'd at by this paper I am the veriest woman that ever was heard, and the mans politicks that Dr Fowler†4 fancyed sometimes frisking in my brains is no way disernable, but I hope your next will so recrute me that I shall be able to express myself more suitable to my own and your wish, all that I will ad is that mrs Cox requests you to accept her service and to acquaint mrs Eglton who keeps an Apothecarys shop in the high street that nothing can be determined aboute the Lodgins, (for till the Tutor be found out tis to no purpose to fix on a habitation). I will stay all this week in twon and part of the next in expectation of hearing from you obtain for me the kindness of Deane Bathurst and his Lady†5 and perswad them as you may most honestly that tis they draw me to Oxford and that I desire to live near them with a resolution to pay them all the respect and Obedience Mr Grigg himself did, ile tell you another time more decently that I am Your sensible friend and servant
the last of February
Address: For Mr Lock Student In Christs Church in Oxon
Postmark: FE 28
