March
690. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 9 March [1682] (688, 693)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 83-4. Year from Locke's endorsement.
March the 9th
You were in the right I beleeve when you thought that none of all those that you saw weare Leeks on St Taffy's Day†1 was nearer of Kin to Kadwallader†2 then my self, and you have furnish'd me with an excellent excuse for my Aversness to be ask'd questions in telling me that Hee was of the same Humour since I assure you I am Descended from him and begin now to beleeve that it runs in the Bloud and is Natural to all his Posteritie. You will not I hope ask me to prove that I am one of them, which perhaps might be more difficult to do then that I was not Fuddled when I got my Fall, to which notwithstanding I have but very little to say in my owne Defence all Appearances makeing so much against me that of the twoo I beleeve you will be righter in thinking that it was so then that I was in any such rapture as you speake of, being never subject to any such, nor haveing ever pretended that I know of to be in the number of those Metaphysical Contemplative People.†3 That I have no Ill Opinion of the Platonists I confess, nor ought you to wonder at That seeing I have spent the Most of my Life amongst Philosophers of that Sect†4 in whom I have always found the most Vertue and Friendship. But as to what I writt to you certainly I did no more then onely tell you which way I thought we might come to quarrel, and not any thing else, and therefore you are very unkind in abuseing, as you have done, your Poore Governess so Cruelly. However not haveing now the leisure to be Angry I resolve for once to forgive you, though not without expecting that you should some time or other acknowledge your fault, which I think is but a Reasonable sattisfaction. If you have any service to Command my Brother he is very readdy to Obey you. When He goes he does not yet know, but my Lord†5 talks of being in Paris
― 494 ―

before the Twenty fifth of this Month. I have received the Parcel you writt about and shall give it my Brother who will be sure to take care of it. I know not whether I ever told you that I writt to Dr C—†1 for you, from whom I received an Answeare not long since in which he presented his service to you.—You were almost expected here on Tuesday Night by some of your Friends, I know not for what reason, but seeing you not come I resolv'd to let you know that notwithstanding all my Quarrels I am
Much your Friend and Servant
PHILOCLEA.

691. William Charleton to Locke, 13/23 March 1682 (670, 722)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, ff. 50-1.
Bourdeaux the 23th March 168½
Deare Sir
I am extreamely to blame in deferring the return of my thanks for your most kind and obliging letter of the 16th January past till now, the lazyness of my temper is far from being an excuse, and the Indisposition of my crazy body not such but that I might have writ to you sooner. Lent is now drawing to an end†2 and as soon as it is finished (God willing) I shall go towards Paris and take Orleance in my way, and waite upon Mr: Toinard and his brother Monsieur de Villemblin, and on Monsieur L'Abbé Gendron and Monsieur Formantin and Dr. Godfroy to whom I could wish that I could render my Conversation as agreable as yours was and then I should not despaire of bringing Mr: Toinard and Mr: Formentin to England with me. Besides the extream wet weather which alone would have hindred me from removing hence, an unhappy accident fell out which obliged me to stay longer then I intended. My corrispondent at Paris a relation of Mr Selapris dyed, and it was
― 495 ―

some considerable time before I received the news, and as I have been Informed since he had severall letters for me amongst which a letter of Credit for 2000 ll.†1 and I cannot certainely tell yet whether they have not been sent for Swisserland, all my feare is least my letter of credit should light into ill hands and that I should loose my money for I have taken care to have new credit. I beleeve I shall be gon from hence before I can receive an answer to this so that I shall desire you when you are pleased to write to direct your letter after the following adresse
A Monsieur
Monsieur Guillaume Ord†2 Banquier
A
Paris
pour faire tenir s'il luy plaist a vostre serviteur Charleton
When I return for England I am confident I should be verry welcome to severall of my relations houses, but being not in so good a state of health as I was formerly and so not able to comply so far as I was wont, I should rather encline to have lodgings in some private house that might not be far from your residence when you are in town, not that I intend to be troublesome to you with to frequent vissits, but that when I have the advantage of your good Company you may not take a journey to see me. If therefore you would Inform yourself in that particular and send me word to Paris at what rate I may have 2 Indifferent chambers with Indifferent furniture at a month it would be a favour, above all pray let me know where I may enquire after you when I come to town for I intend my first vissit to your self. Mr: Kirby his Lady son and daughters give you their services and I am
Deare Sir
Your verry much obliged and most affectionate servant

692. John Bonville to Locke, 18 March 1682 (694)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 4, f. 47. The writer was the son of Locke's aunt Anne Locke and her husband Humphrey Bonvile. Her father and friends disapproved of her marriage, and her children, apart from John, were in poor circumstances: Cranston, p. 4; no. 767. John was now setting up as a pewterer. He evidently remained a small tradesman, and appears not to have held any office in the Pewterers' Company; his standing is shown by his continuance in Houndsditch, a street for joiners, brasiers, dealers in old clothes, and the like: Strype's Stow, ii. 27. He now apparently wanted to borrow money from Locke; Locke wanted a signatory as security for the loan.
London March the 18th: 8½
Honoured Sir
I have Received yours Wherein I understand your Desire is to have one bound with me, I could have Asked my Master Hicks with whome I served my time and I think he would not denied me such A kindnes but I Am very Loath too make my Case knowne because it ware Ever Reported that I had A great deal more of my owne when I Came to him, There for Deare Sir doe not stay your hand In doeing of me this great kindness for In soe doeing you will make A man of me: my Cousin keen†1 will Lett me have As many tools As will come to 14 or 15 <l>†a which make me Loath to desire Any for there ki<nd>nes,†a But If I knew my self not In A Copacity Too pay Too whome I Ame Obliged I should think my self wors then Ann Infidell:†2 to desire Either mony or goods, Dear Sir In A word it is well known that Am soe neare Related to such A worthy person as your self And my unkle,†3 shold it be knowne that I have Nothing it wold be such A disparegment to me that it will be my Ruen, Sir I Am now in my new habitation, I am Cumpeld for to Lay Aside That Little In which the Lord have blesed for I Cannot goe noe forether, without your Asistanc. Deare Cousin I now Live The next dore to the signe of the Crowne In Hounsditch, Pray Sir be plesd to Let me heare your Comfortable Answar with speed that time may not be Lost, soe I Rest your Kinsman And very Humble servant.
JNO BONVILE

693. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 23 March [1682] (690, 695)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 85-6. Year from Locke's endorsement.
March the 23.
If my zeal for those of whom I have always beene disposd to think very well, and in the number of whom my most particular Friends have hap'ned to bee, has made me appeare, too much concern'd for them, or seeme to apprehend without reason that they were Unjustly reflected on, you will Pardon me I dare say and (now I assure you that it was soe) will impute the unnecessarie seriousness of my reply to the Dulness of the Humour that I was then in or to any thing else rather then to a beleefe that I could be in good earnest displeas'd with any thing that you said. However if it Appeard so I begg your Pardon a Thousand times, assureing you that I shall much sooner chuse to disowne my Welch Bloud, and renounce all Kindred with Kadwallader, then ever to run the least hazard of being less your Governess then you were pleas'd to allow me to bee. My Brother desires me to present his Humble service to you, and returns you his Thanks for the Favour you offer him, for which I must account my self equally Oblig'd. Hee will obey your commands as neare as he can when he goes into France, but it is yet so uncertaine when that will be (it depending upon my Lord P—†1 who is at present at Newmarket) that I have beene in great doubt whether or no I ought not to have sent your Letter by the Post. If you would have it so pray let me know and I shall do it. Had it requir'd more hast I suppos'd you would have said so, which not doing I have indulg'd so much to an Idleness caus'd by some returns of my late Indisposition as not to write to you about it all this while. I know not how it happens but Dr Lower†2 has not had all that good success with me which he uses to have, but he perswades me the Waters†3 onely are wanting to compleat it, for which I attend with great impatience till the Weather is a little warmer. I shall give your service to Dr C—†4 if I have any occasion of writeing to him. Shee who writt to him for you is very sensible of her great Obligations to you which it is not
― 498 ―

more certaine she has never merrited then that they have renderd her with all sinceritie (as well as I)
Your Obliged Faithfull Friend and Humble Servant
PHILOCLEA.

April
695. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 1 April [1682] (693, 696)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 87-8. Year from Locke's endorsement. Answered by no. 696.
Apr: the 1rst
Haveing beene so Happy as to have my Health well enough almost ever since my last to you methinks I am under some kind of Obligation of leting you know soe, it seeming not Just to make you a sharer in my Evill Fortune, without makeing you also a Partaker in my Good, which that Friendship that you profess to have for me perswades me you will in some sort bee. Sinceritie being a Vertue that I have always had a particular Value for, I could never have any yet for any Person whatever that I beleev'd not posses'd of it. Haveing therefore consequently perswaded my self of yours I can attribute to no other cause then Friendship those advantageous Thoughts which you have of me, and indeed when the Judgment of my Friends is such as all the World will acknowledge unquestionable methinks I can have no more certaine Proofs of there Kindness then there haveing Opinions of me which I cannot have the Vanitie to beleeve they could have if they excersis'd it Impartially. You see now that you will have a double Obligation upon you to be very sincere in whatever you say to mee Since I shall draw those Inferences from it which perhaps others would not that might less beleeve you, or not know so well as I doe the Pleasure of haveing Friends whose Merrit is extraordinarie,
What one Desires one easilie Beleeves I have heard said very often, but how false soever I have experienc'd it on divers occasions it is certaine that in doing thus I find it so in this. I was mightie sorry when I had read your Letter that I had not writt to you sooner last time least your letter should be sent too late, I sent them both on Monday Night to the General Posthouse†1 and should be very glad to heare that it prove not soe, as I am that you are so readdy to beleeve that I was not in good earnest displeas'd. But if you find not some time or other more faults with my Author†2 I shall suspect that you do not truely give so much Credit to my word as you pretend to do, and then I dare not assure you that I shall not indeed be Angry, which if you value you would not do
― 500 ―

well to runn the Hazard, although I do not beleeve that either in Jest or Earnest wee can have any Quarrels which will ever make me less then I am
Your Friend and Servant
PHILOCLEA.
Address: These For Mr Lock at Christs Church in Oxford
Postmarks: AP 1; G
Endorsed by Locke: Philoclea 1o Apr. 82
696. Locke to Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, [6 April 1682?] (695, 699)
B.L., MS. Locke f. 6, pp. 20-2. Locke's Journal, 19 February 1682. Part of some remarks on Enthusiasm, commenting on John Smith's Select Discourses: pp. 484 n., 488. Printed in Locke, Early draft, ed. Aaron and Gibb, p. 119. From no. 699, Philoclea's answer, it is clear that Locke sent her a copy of some part of this passage; a note in the Journal, 'hactenus April 6' suggests the date. The letter answers no. 695; answered by no. 699.
A strong and firme perswasion of any proposition relateing to religion for which a man hath either noe or not sufficient proofs from reason but receives them as truths wrought in the minde extraordinarily by god him self and influences comeing immediately from him seemes to me to be Enthusiasme, which can be noe evidence or ground of assureance at all nor can by any means be taken for Knowledg.†a For I finde that Christians, Mahumetans and Bramins all pretend to it (and I am told the Chineses too) But tis certain that contradictions and falshoods cannot come from god, nor can any one that is of the true Religion be assured of any thing by a way whereby those of a false religion may be and are equally confirmed in theirs.†b For the Turkish Dervises pretend to Revelations Extasies vision Rapture. to be swallowed up and transported with illuminations of god. Discourseing with god. seeing the face of god. v. Ricaut 216 (i e Of the Ottoman Empire folio London 70
― 501 ―

1.2 c.13 etc) and the Jaugis amongst the Hindous talke of being illuminated and intirely united to god Bernier. 173 (i e memoires Tome 3. 8° London 72) p. 36†1 as well as the most spiritualised Christians
697. Mrs. Jane Stringer to Locke, 8 April 1682 (618, 748)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, ff. 97-8.
Aprill the 8th: 1682:
Deare Sir
I received yours and sent the inclosed as you orderd me. this is the 19th: day of Mr Stringers spitting it hath succeeded extream well and kept up to a good height without taking any thing to continue or raise it since the first three dayes the last of which is now 17 dayes agoe he took the last dose and yett his spitting is now as much as att any time since he began my brother†2 sais it has bin the most kindly and gentle sallivation that ever he knew in his life we hope the efect will be as fortunate to him though truly I cannot yett boast much of any great allteration in his legs they tell me I must not so soon expect that till he has recruted strength again and used an artifitiall bath sumtime: he has spitt three gallons since he enterd into this course which his brother†3 thinks a sufficient quantity therefore he intends to give him a purge to morrow to carry the humour another way. I must needs say the strength of his Fancy and faith has carryed him most gallantly through it with all the patience and regularity Imaginable my thinks it were great pitty he should not obtain his desired end since he has so carefully pursued it. I beleeve you will think me a prety indiferent wife that am noe more concerned about the matter but the truth is as the case now stands I have an equall if not a larger share of the government and that you know is a very pleasant thing. att least I am willing allways to beleeve my presant condition best and make it all my choice rather then my nessicity this you know allso that I am Joan Easy that loves not to be
― 502 ―

disturbd. your valintine†1 was hear this affternoon. she presents her humble serviss to you and orderd me to lett you know thare are few good lodgings about alldersgate street†2 she has seen two pretty little chambers two story high in an upholsterers house they may be furnished as you please the price will be 8 shillings a weeke but you must lett her know the time when she must take els they may be gon for none will save there lodgings unless they be paid for it. Mr Stringer presents his humble serviss to you. it is now so very late that I cannot be so perticular as I ought, but in short my lord and lady†3 your frends in salsbury court†4 and hear long to see you so dose
your very humble servant

699. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 20 April [1682] (696, 704)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 89-90. Year from Locke's endorsement. Answers no. 696.
April the 20th
It is neither to excess of Devotion in me, or defect of Charitie, that you ought to impute my silence, the occasions of which have been so many that I should tire both you and my self if I should recite them. I shall therefore onely assure you that they were unavoidable with which if you are not sattisfy'd I will next time send you a Catelogue of them, which I am sure (when you see) will be allowd by you for Just and Lawfull Impediments, although my want of Health will not be included in it, for your concerne of which I am extreamly Oblig'd to you, as also for your beleeveing that I have some Kind of Title to what I thought I had held merely from your free Gift, which Opinion how much soever you have confirm'd in me I shall dispute with you no longer, but returne (since you have done so) to the Occasion of our former Difference which I designd not to have reviv'd againe but onely to have knowne your thoughts of the following Discourses†1 which as I conceive have no Dependance on the Foregoing whatever the number of Sancho's Goats might have to the story he was teling his Master,†2 which I do not remember. The thing I suppose then in question betweene us was whether or no my Author were an Enthusiast (since we are agreed in the Opinion of Enthusiasme to which I hope I am as much an Enemie as you), But as to That, I have nothing more to say onely that when I read his Book I did not at all apprehend him to be soe, but that if I should beleeve him so upon any Body's Authoritie it would assoone be yours as the Churchmans you tell me of,†3 who I suppose without any Disrespect to his Worth or Order was Fallible like other men, and that I am no more Oblig'd to beleeve as he does, then to reject for That reason any Opinion that is held by those of the Church of Rome, truth and Falshood being still the same from whom ever they are receiv'd, which I say not because I agree with the Jesuits in that Opinion of theres†4 (if it be so) since I neither well know what they
― 504 ―

meane, nor think my self a fit judge of these things.
But that I may Answeare the Authoritie of your Churchman with another, there is one who giveing reasons why there is no Communication betweene Good Angells and the Vertuous, gives it for one That God Himself affords his Intimacies and Converses to the better Souls that are prepar'd for it, That the Proud and Phantastick Pretences of the conceited Melancholists of this age to Divine Communion had indeed Prejudic'd many very Intelligent Persons against the beleefe of any such thing, They looking upon it but as a High flowne Notion of Warme Immagination as he acknowledges himself formerly to have done, But that haveing since consider'd it he is convinc'd, and does now abundantly beleeve That the Divine Spirit does afford its Sensible Presence and Immediate Beatifick touch to some Persons so and soe Qualify'd.†1 They are his owne words, but whether they amount to what was condemn'd in the Jesuits, or whether it be a Truth and Reallitie or not, is more then I know, and I only tell it you because it was from a Churchman who had the Reputation of Learning as well as yours, and was Esteem'd a more then ordinaryly Ingenious Man. As for my self being not in the number of those fitly Qualify'd Persons I can be no judge of it, Things of inward sense being not to be Deny'd (as Hee says) because wee our selves do not feell them, nor can form any Apprehension of them, Nor are they to be Judg'd of by the noetical exercises of speculative understanding, but by the Sentient and Vital Faculties.†2 whatever therefore another professes to Experience in this kind How should I be able to Deny? and Provided that they Act not nor Admit any thing but what they can give a Rational Account of, That they Pay a Universal Obedience to all the laws of God, and that they beleeve the Holy Scriptures I do not see any Reason why there opinion should be quarrel'd with, or themselves Condemn'd as Persons who let themselves be impos'd upon by there Immaginations and by the Suggestions of unbridled Phancie since thus long they do not quit there Reason; (as the Enthusiast does, who pretends to leave that light for a better (in which I suppose is there great Mistake, there being no suggestions of the Holy Spirrit but what are always agreable to, if not Demonstrable from Reason) But if to any this great Priviledge be Vouchsaf'd
― 505 ―

I do not know why it may not as well be so, to all who are as Sincere and Devout lovers of God and Vertue, and who do Faithfully adhere to that light which they already have, of which I suppose there are many amongst the most Barbarous Nations and Professors of the Wildest Religions in the World, as well as reall Enthusiasts every where, as I suppose those Ricaut and Monsieur Berniere speake of might bee, but in the number of whom I did not indeed beleeve Mr S—, looking upon the designe of that whole Discourse in General as no other then to recommend Puritie of Life as the onely true way of attaining to Divine Knowledge in which are made the greater advances by how much the more the Mind is purg'd from all Impuritie, there being a Natural Cohesion of Truth with impolluted Souls,†1and also, as Dr More says, a Principle Antecedaneous to Reason which he calls Divine Sagacitie which is onely Competible to Persons of Pure and Unspoted Minds†2 and without which Reason is not succesfull in the Contemplation of the Highest matters. I am quite tyr'd else should (like you) add something more on this subject although I be sufficiently sensible how much this will excercise your Patience, and would need your Pardon had not you your self occasion'd it, which is all that can excuse it on my part, who have a Blind Obedience for all the Commands of my Friends especially when they are so much dispos'd to be in Choller as you tell me you are at present, which I assure you is not Indifferent to me, much less soe that concerne which begets it and which has made me as well out of acknowledgment as Esteeme
Your Friend and Humble Servant
PHILOCLEA.
My Brother goes for France on Monday but I do not designe to give him the Pacquet of Seeds because you say the Gentleman†3 will be gone.
Address: These For Mr Lock at Christs Church in Oxford.
Postmarks: AP 20; G
Endorsed by Locke: Philoclea 20o Apr. 82

700. John Pickering to Locke, 23 April 1682
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 156-7. Locke's former pupil: no. 144.
Sir
I Wil not omit this opportunity of soe sure a hand to present my servise to you by, altho by the suddennesse of the bearers goeing and some necessary affaires of my owne at this time I am not allowed a leisure to say much more, when I was last at Oxford my enquiries after you and your welfare (which by great Obligations) I am Concerned for, gave me then the account of your being at London, as formerly made after you when at London that then you were at Oxford, if any affaires of travel Curiosity or Businesse Incline you towards the North, I shold thinke my selfe mighty happy in your good Company the Influence whereof is with very great satisfaction often remembred by Sir

703. Mrs. Anna Grigg to Locke, 2 May [1682] (689, 707)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 143-4. Year from Locke's endorsement. Mrs. Grigg alludes to her son's letter, no. 701.
Sir
About a fortnight agoe I writ you a long letter, (that is to say as soon as I could recovery my little wits which had bin so long disordred by a thousand cros accedents) I began my conversation with you thus — Deare brother manefest that you realy value me by a severe reprof for not telling you that I was out of humer with every thing and could endure no body but old friends and such as were like to prove such etc. Now had I sent that letter it had not I imagin procur'd me either the tittle of madam nor could you for your life have bin so grave in your resentments, but foolish thing that I was I read over what I had bin a whole hour writting which if I once doe and conceipt any word too youthfull, there is no mercy for my own letters, this proved the ruen of many kinde expressions, and so put me upon employing my little secretary, from whome you had formerly bin willing to hear, and in whose wellfair you have bin so faithfully concern'd that I was willing the child should understand it as well as myself and learn betimes to acquaint his friends with the great intregues†1 of his fortune; but very seriously I am sorry I have bin silent when your care made my writting necescary, but first I knew not when you would be at Oxford and than the resigning up of my two beloved Wills†2 when Oxford was so much resolved on cost me some pains and would not let me presently give you an account of my being vanquish'd, but when once overcome by others, I thought it fit to master all those plesant raveries which I had of my boys vaster improvement (then I thought possible in a Croud) before I could tolerably satisfie myself in doing or saying any thing, thus without malice I er'd, and without wickedness you dare not continue to be Angry, Nay I defie you so much as to think hardly of me, and you shall be my brother and my friend in spite of all the Wit and Whigisme in England,†3 thus dare I write from the Iron key†4 and were I not a good
― 509 ―

natured Tory, I should conclude that your darling mrs Cox had provok'd you by uncharitable Lybells. She would fain have me present you her service and say she is in danger of being kindly melancholy if you make not hast to town, had her pritty daughter†1 made me such a conffession, I might to ingratiate myself have revealed secrets but she is the same reserv'd Lady she was many years agoe and I the very selfsame friend and servant
A G
May the 2d
Address: For Mr John Locke Student of Christ-Church Oxon
Postmark: MA 2
Endorsed by Locke: A Grig 2o May 82
704. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 6 May [1682] (699, 710)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 91-2. Year from Locke's endorsement.
May the 6th
Though I am at this time in a very Unusual Humour, and not at all dispos'd to write Letters, Yet seeing no likelihood of being soone in any other, I have resolv'd however to tell you soe, that I may not any more runn the risque of provokeing you to Anger, which I would not willingly do, notwithstanding what you say of your haveing no good Facultie at Chideing, to which if you had but the lest inclination in the World you could certainly never doe with mee at a better time then now, Since the Dispensation†2 I am at present got into would not so much as permit me to quarrel with you againe, but has within these Six Days made me the Meekest, Humblest, Quietest, Creature you ever saw. Let People say what they will, or Doe what they will, I take all with Submission, and like those whom Use and Custome has harden'd am become almost capable of indureing all things. Should you therefore take a Phancie to be Angry with me without a cause, Or should you interpret the best intentions I could have Perversly, Or what would be more Cruel then either of them should you have
― 510 ―

such Thoughts of me as I should beleeve Inconsistent with that Esteeme which necessarily accompanies a Durable Friendship, All this would be no more then I have beene taught to suffer, and that without murmuring. You will not I suppose think that I have beene able to be brought to this without haveing a Profound Indifference for all things in the World besides, and it is certaine that at this time I have soe. I have beene thinking therefore that the best improvement I can make by my Misfortunes will be to take advantage of my Temper and turne a Stoick. It is now certainly if ever that I shall be able to do it, since being not by Nature Quarrelsome I should never have the Power to fall out with the World if That did not first begin with mee. You must not now therefore expect that I should any longer Pursue a Discourse which perhaps would not be approv'd by the Philosophers of that Sect which I am going to embrace, besides that if I would I should find it almost impossible, since my Afflictions have had that effect upon my Memory that I remember not any thing of that Letter but the Subject, nor scarsely any thing else that is above Nine Days Old, and therefore since wee are so far agreed I think it will be best to end that Dispute. I do not expect any more then you that the World should be all of one Mind, neither do I desire that they should, provided that I my self could but be soe. But I am at present so far from that, that I beleeve I have not for these many Days chang'd my Dress so often as my thoughts, nor knowne any thing so little as my owne Heart. There are but twoo things in the World that I can find to which I remaine always Constant, and those are the Love of Vertue, and my Friends, whom in all tempers I experience that I equally regard, and value, and Therefore should the Phantasticalness and Inequalitie of my Humour, which you will every Day discover more then other (besides a Thousand other Faults and Weaknesses) make you to be less one of them, then now you are, I assure you I must make greater advances in Stoicisme then I feare I shall doe not to be sensibly troubled at it, since by a double Obligation I shall always bee
Your Faithfull Friend and Humble Servant
PHILOCLEA.
Address: These For Mr Lock at Christs Church in Oxford.
Postmarks: MA 6; G
Endorsed by Locke: Philoclea 6o May. 82
― 511 ―

705. Locke to Mrs. Mary Clarke, 7 May 1682 (709)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 6. Printed in Rand, pp. 84-6. Answered by no. 709. Edward Clarke's latest preceding extant letter is no. 685.
Ch: Ch: 7o May 82
Madam
Wit and good nature meeting in a fair young Lady as they doe in you make the best resemblance of an Angell that we know: and he that is blessed with the conversation and freindship of a person so extraordinary enjoys all that remains of paradise in this world. For certainly the difference betwixt that happy place and this untoward world, did not lie in the tast of fruits and smell of flowers: in more musicall notes of birds, or a better landscape to enterteine the eye. But man kinde there should have been angels to one another, Their wit should have delighted without hurting, and their knowledg instructed without vanity. Every ones vertue should have made a satisfaction to himself and an example to others, prudence and good nature should have preserved an universall harmony without leaveing any roome for envye by lookeing ill upon anothers happynesse to disturbe ones owne. Good will should have given rise to all was don there and sincerity vouching the intention to be good had banishd all feares and jealousys and kept out that worst of tormentors Suspition which makes even sweet things bitter, and what in its self is good, uneasy and hurtfull to him that has it. Since then 'twas not shady walks or groves of mirtle; the gaudy colours of some, or perfume of other flowers, that made the happynesse of that garden, but the Innocence beauty knowledg and vertue of the company there, Bethinke your self what a stock you have left of this lost treasure to bestow on those you will thinke worthy of it. I'm sure it is enough to justifie all the importunity I can be guilty of in sueing for some part of it, espetially when you have encouraged me to hope that for a few good words if I could light on them to send you you would dispose your self to thinke a litle more seriously of your comeing hither. I confesse those I have put into my letter are not peeked†1 words, which tis thought are not always the best, but I tooke that which I imagind was the surest way to have good ones, which was to set before my thoughts your vertues and excellent qualitys and then if I could but remember the names of them, I should be sure to send you a letter filled with
― 512 ―

the best words in the world. and if I have not tis because our imperfect language wants names for severall of those uncommon accomplishments are to be found in you. However I may faile in the maine, this I shall always have cause to thanke you for, That you have once in your life given me the oportunity to speake some part of my thoughts of you without being able to condemne what I say either of flattery or complement haveing your self given me leave to doe it, and therefor you must allow me with confidence to assure you that I am
Madam
Your most humble and most obedient servant
J LOCKE
I am Mr Clarks humble servant and shall be glad to heare that he is returned safe and well, And pray give my humble service to your overhead neighbour†1 this you can doe in better words then I can what ever you say of mine.
Address: These present To Mrs: Clarke at the Lady Kings in Salisbury court neare Fleetstreet London
Postmark: MY 8

707. Mrs. Anna Grigg to Locke, 9 [May] 1682 (703, 732)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 145-6. The correct month from the postmark, Locke's correction, etc., and contents.
April†a the 9th 82
Deare Brother
Not long since I heard this story, A poor woman being to bee tried for a witch an inquisitive damsel luckely ask'd her how long she had bin one; t'was answred that her accusars were wiser then she, and from them she might be informed, for till they told her she was one she knew it not; Nor indeed could I have gues'd at my being one myself, had you not proved so many things against me, and for your farther satisfaction in this point: what but some magiccall inspiration could keep off the violence of your resentments, and oblige you in spite of my incivility and the neglect of my own affairs, to turn all your sharpness into the most taking reflections; who would not transgres to be so rebuk'd? I am glad you demand so peremtorily the letter I formerly design'd you, I hope my courage in refusing to obey you will bring me the rattle you promis me, tis the onely way to pleas the chit, who was ever better pleas'd with your railing then the finest complements she ever heard, but I am an arrent child for telling you so, for if you be spitefull you will change the theam and then I shall be put to new shifts? but tis no great matter for by puzling me you will diliver me from the danger of being hang'd for a Sorceres, and if my littleness be farry†b Like tis well for you I have not the knack of being invisible, for I have spite enough to pinch, but I have not wit enough to mentain an agreeable contention; just now pases under my window
― 514 ―

Your most humble Servant

708. Samuel Thomas to Locke, 10 May 1682 (304, 523)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 20, ff. 134-5. Thomas was instituted vicar of Chard on 3 August 1681.
Chard. May 10.82.
Sir,
This is to thank you for the intimations with which yours begins of the inconveniences likely to attend my conveying my goods from Oxon by water; and tis easy to believe that the loading and unloading 3 times may prove much more mischievous to them then the doing it but once; but that it will be very much cheaper by Sea is the opinion of all whom I talk with here; and yet I believe your contrary opinion would be right, if I could get a wagon at as cheap a rate from this, as I did (after my Father's death) from Ubley†2to Oxon. when the carriage of two and twenty hundred
― 515 ―

weight did not come to 4l̷l̷, the owner of the wagon requiring but 3-6d the 100. But if I could get my bookes, and other goods, hither for 12l̷l̷ I should be glad; for I doubt my bookes and the Boxes in which they are will weigh at least forty hundred. But whensoever I remove 'em I must come to Oxford my self having the Keyes of all with mee here. and whensoever I doe so, which I intend soone after Whitsontide†1 (if our Bishop's visitation hinder not) I shall be glad to find you at Ch: Ch: In the meane time as to your Boxes I am very confident that if there were 7 lodg'd by Jer: Bates†2 in my chamber, and you had but 6 from mee, the seventh was onely a little empty thing, the cover of which was broken in the middle; and of such a one I seeme to have some Idea, which possibly was left behind as not worth removing as well as that large map in a Frame which still remaines there. That there was no such mistake as you suggest there might be when I parted with mr Ward's†3 goods, I am as confident; for he and I both were upon the place when his goods were remov'd; and besides his and yours I have had none in my custody but H: Bagshaw's†4 which were gone out of my hands long before yours came into them. And therefore supposing there was another Box, of books, and of any considerable bulk, put into my hands, I can surmise but 2 things, 1, That I might possibly lodge that also at Dr. Pocock's, or else 2, in the roome beyond the study belonging to our common-fire roome†5 (where I lodg'd an old Trunk and some other things) but that I did so, I have no, the least, Idea. and therefore all that I can say farther is that I am sorry there should be any occasion for your making this enquiry. my humble respects and service I pray to Dr. Pocock and his Lady.†6 hoping that he receiv'd mine of April. 25. However that Box is mis-plac'd. the newes of your retrieving it will be very welcome to
your reall Friend and humble servant
S. THOMAS.
Address: For his much esteemed Friend mr John Lock this I pray.
Endorsed by Locke: S. Thomas 10 May. 82

709. Mrs. Mary Clarke to Locke, 23 May 1682 (705, 724)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 177-8. Printed in Rand, pp. 86-7. Answers no. 705.
London May the 23th. 1682
Deare Sir
I Receved your Letter of the 8th. of this Instant,†1 and knowing the hand to be yours I hastily Broke it open, being in hopes then to have knowne the certaine time of your returne to London, but insteede of haveing that sattisfacktion, I wase surprised with soe many fine words, that I wropt it up a Gaine and wase forsted to read the superscription ten times over before I Could sattisfiye my selfe that I had not opened the Letter that wase desined for my prety over head Neighbour†2 which deserves them all, but on me you ought not to have throne away halfe soe many of your best words If I had writ you forty Letters to bespeeke them, without it wase to make Roome for somthing better worth your thoughts to Entertaine you, for I doe assure you Deare Cozen halfe a word att any time would make me seryouse in a Journey to waite on you weare it ten times as far to do you the Least service, but now I hope to see you in towne wheare wee will discorse of a Journey to Tunbridg that being more proper for this hott seasen and Leave the Billett subjeckt†3 till the next winter and in the meane time I must tell you tiss a Great peice of Charrity to Lett us see you now we are under Great Malloncoley for the Loss of Mrs. Cudworths Company, who is Lattley Gone to Cambridge, I could have wished you had bin heare when she went to have shared with us in our troble, and by this you may se I have mischeffe towards you in my heart and If I can will be revenged on you for all the trickes you play mee. but however you use me I find I cannot possobley bee other then
Deare Sir,
your Truley affecttionate and Faithfull humble servant

710. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 23 May [1682] (704, 714)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 93-4. Year from Locke's endorsement. The letter relates to Cambridge.
May the 23d
I onely write to you now to let you know that you have a Governess who cannot forget you. otherwise being so lately come to a new place, Haveing parted with so many Persons who are Deare to me, and Being now with others who are to leave me within these three Days, I find not my self at all in a Humour of writeing any more then I was the last time, nor of being much better pleas'd with my self or the World, although for the designe of turning a Stoick I begin to suspect that it will not doe, notwithstanding that I have just Bought Anthony Le Grand of the Passions,†1 and am reading over Seneca the second time, who is so far from haveing taught me more Patience then I had before that in an Houres reading Hee has awaken'd mee out of that State of Insensibleitie that I seem'd to be in, and Provok'd me to Cholor above Half a Dosen times. What amends he may make me in his succeeding Discourses I know not but this has beene a great Disappointment to me Hitherto who incounterd him as an Old Freind almost sent by Providence for my releife. But Seneca I suppose is still the same that he was three Yeares agoe, and it is I that am alter'd, who cannot Deny the Changableness and Inconstancie of my Nature, how bad a Character soever I give of my self by it, nor alter it, how great soever the Inconveniences are that I suffer by it and the Mistakes that it runs me into. It is not above a Fortnight since that I
― 518 ―

beleev'd I could have liv'd as well pleas'd in one place as another, that I stood not in need of any Body, and that I was a whole World to my self, and now I experience so much the Contrary that Methinks I am Divided into as many Parts as there are Persons that I love, and that it is intollerable to live in a Place where it is not possible to spend one Houre in an agreable Conversation without being beholden to the Dead or the Absent Liveing for it, and that too in one of the most Famous Universities in the World. For Heavens sake if you know such another place as this is tell me some what of it, and of some Body that ever sufferd as I do, and if there should never have beene any such I beseech you however dont scruple telling me so Pleaseing a Falshood, since I love some companion in all Conditions, and Have not Vertue enough to wish that I may be the onely Unfortunate. My Paper no more then the sullen Humour I am in will give me leave to add any thing more but that I am Sir
your Freind and Servant
PHILOCLEA
Address: These For Mr Lock at Christs Church in Oxford
Postmark: MA 24

713. William Locke to Locke, 7 June 1682 (735)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 229-30. The writer is identifiable as a son of William Locke, d. 1611, tanner, of Cerne Abbas, a brother of Locke's grandfather Nicholas Locke of Pensford. According to his own statement he was born about 1605. In 1655 a William Locke and Richard Churchill were patrons of Broadmayne rectory, and presented it to one Robert Locke, sometime of Queens' College, Cambridge (Venn). On Robert's death in 1663 the elder John Glasbrooke became rector; he was succeeded in 1678 by Joseph Studley; these two were the successive husbands of William Locke's daughter Elizabeth: Notes and Queries for Somerset and Dorset, xx (1930-2), 47-8; Dorset Natural Hist. and Archæol Soc., Proc. lxx (1948), 113.
Sir perhaps it may seeme strange unto you to receive lines from a person you have scarse ever knowne or heard of although I am one of your neerest kinsmen—yet considering my daughters occasion and heareing of your abilities and love to your kindred I have written this to desire you if you can to shew your kindnes to her sonne John Glasbrooke†1 who is a youth now at schoole at dorcshester†a and wilbe shortly fitt for oxford, and the kindnes that I desire of you is to assist him what you may—I cannot propound what you should or will doe—but I want a friend for him and know none so neere and able and I hope willing to pleasure mee herein. hee hath the next advouson of the parsonage at Broad Mayne†2 after his father in Law (by my purchase) only hee wants ability—I cannott write more nor need to so neere a friend: pray sir lett mee have your answere and whether you can or will or cannott I shall accept it and count my selfe obliged. Thus resting
Your unknowne kinsman and humble servant
WILLIAM LOCKE
Cerne Abby in dorsett
7th of June 1682
for mr John Locke living with the right honourable the Earle of Shaston†3

714. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 10 June [1682] (710, 720)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 95-6. Year from Locke's endorsement.
June the 10th
What ever you think of me I assure you it is not my Way to Complaine without Reason, and you may always conclude that I am certainly in a bad Humor whenever I tell you so, since I never accuse my self falsly of things which I cannot beleeve it should be to my advantage to be thought Guiltie of. However since you beleeve that an Ill Humor may sometimes be agreable for the sake of Varietie, I may not perhaps henceforwards take so much care to avoid it as I have hitherto done, since the desire of pleaseing my Friends is always much more Prevalent with mee then that of being pleas'd my self. But pray remember now that it is You who have put me upon this, and that if you should find any Ill effects of it hereafter you will have no body to thank for it but Your self. At present I am well enough pleas'd, and beleeve notwithstanding what you say to the Contrary That I am not onely as good a Physitian as I am a Philosopher but something a better one, since not being able to returne to my Usual Humour by the exercise of all the Reason I was Mistress of, I have at length found out another expedient to effect it, which has beene by Diverting it another way, in which I have succeeded by injoyning my self a certaine task in the Performance whereof I take much sattisfaction, but you being my Puple, and not I yours, I think I am not Oblig'd to give you any Account what that is. It suffices that you kno it has prov'd so effectual that I question whether the Aire of London could have beene much more so, notwithstanding that if it were convenient I could not forbeare haveing a most Vehement Desire to see divers Persons who are there. I doubt not at all but you find it as agreable a Place as you left it, if every body that uses to be there be so still, except mee. However if it be not so, I feare I shall not be very sorry for you, since how much soever I am your Friend I must confess that I cannot surmount that infirmitie of my Nature which makes me on such occasions as these glad when other People are no better pleas'd then my self, and upon this account to confess the truth to you it would have beene much to my sattisfaction to have had you have continud at O—†1 still. You cannot easielie immagine what a Tenderness
― 522 ―

the Parellel betweene our twoo Conditions was begining to have begot in me for you. But now considering you quite otherwise with some Kind of Envy as one Happier then my self I find I know not how that that new sort of Affection for you Insensibly decreases and that you will be to me but just what you use to bee. For after all that I have told you of my good Humour you must know that Philosopher like I owe it wholly to my self, finding it convenient at this time to scorne to be beholden to any thing without me for it, not haveing†a so much as that conversation you mention to contribute any thing towards it, so that the present state that I am in you may conceive to be rather that of Quiet and contentment, then of any mightie extraordinarie Delight or Pleasure. But as I take it that is most Stoical, and therefore as it should be, that designe being not yet quite abandon'd. And now should I conclude my letter but that I have a request to make to you which though not very Philosophical according to my present Genius Yet considering that you love Varietie, and that it will be agreable to a Certaine Humor of mine which usually takes place once in Twenty foure Hours, I shall not Omit it. It is (heareing that you go soone to Tunbridge) that you will for my sake be as Impertinent there as ever you can, and that as a Consequent of that you will take care to Informe me in all the little News of that Place, As who is the most celebrated Beautie there, who loves who, and all That, which it is needless to tell you. In the meane time I have another Favour to beg of you in the doing of which you will much Oblige me too, and that is, that you would instruct mee a little How it is that one ought to write Letters of Consolation, especially those in which one beleeves there is not much of it needfull. I have such a one lays upon my Hands now which I would faine Have Dispatch'd but have offer'd at it twice or thrice and cannot for my Life tell what to say. I beseech you do not beleeve that I am in jest since I assure you I was never so put to it in my life before, and know not what I shall do if you be not so Kind as to send me a Form or twoo which may serve for this and the like occasions hereafter. I am quite tired†b and can onely add that I am
Your Faithfull Humble Servant
PHILOCLEA.
I beseech you Pardon mee if I have not writt sence, since I have not Light enough to see to read what it is, and am in hast.
― 523 ―

Address: These For Mr Lock at Thanet House in Aldersgate Street London.
Postmark: IV 12
Endorsed by Locke: Philoclea 10 Jun. 82
715. James Tyrrell to Locke, [c. 10 June 1682] (645, 750)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 44-5. The date is a few days after the Moroccan ambassador's visit to Oxford, which ended on Thursday 1 June, and while the newspaper accounts of the visit were fresh (there is a notice in London Gazette, 5 June). On 8 June Locke paid for a letter to Oakley: Journal, p. 67. It is probably the letter mentioned by Tyrrell. It was not necessarily written or dispatched on 8 June, but is the best available guide to the date of the present letter.
Dear Carmelin
I have received yours, and to tell you the truth had not answered it so soon had it not bin for a little businesse I forgot in my last, and know not how soon your occasions or Stars may call you out of Towne, though this is no very inviteing weather for the waters†1 whilst the heavens afford so much. but to come to the businesse, it is that you would doe remember to Speake to my Lord†2 for Jack Ridley, if he have any imployment for him, at any of his parks or Chace: or if not, at present, yet if you could get him a grooms, or footmans place you would doe him, and his Mother a great courtesy. though the obligation would be to my self: I know no fault the boy has but that he does not love hard Countrey work, which he will not be troubled with in a Lords service. I pray let me have your answere in this before you goe to the wells, and when you goe I suppose you will doe me the favour to let me know it, and how to direct a letter to you; I have writt to you thither a letter of Complement to give you an occasion to be acquainted with my neighbour Mr: Jephson,†3 who will deliver it you at the wells. if you hold your resolution of goeing thither. since you say nothing of it: I am very well pleased with your Moral reflexions upon your Sorrell;†4 and for my owne part endeavour as much as I can to imitate his unconcernednesse for to morrow, much lesse for next year: and
― 524 ―

therefore avoyd as much as I can the conversation of those melancholy politicians who with the fear of future ills keep us, and themselves from enjoying all the minutes wee can call our owne, viz. the present. as for Sorrell he had a great affliction befell him yesterday which was that he was (with the asistance of some three or 4 men) let bloud: which (to speake like a methodist†1 and not an Empyrick) was very adust,†2 and cholerick; insomuch that he gave very clear demonstrations of his owne mettall by flinging himself, and the man and all to the ground (that was fain to sit upon him), as also of his owne experience in that processe: as for the Entertainment of our Moorish Embass:†3 since you expect a farther account of it, all I can tell you is that the Collation was in the well Arbour,†4 which was the more surprizeing†5 because he expected nothing there, which stood all ready against he came in being onely sweet-meats and milkmeats; Tarts†a etc.†a he eat of many things but drank nothing but milk and water and seemed by what I hear, much better satisfyed with this runing banquet then with that which was much more costly that my Lord Bishop†6 made him.
his carriage was very civill and obligeing; and his parting complement I shall not forget. which was, his prayers that wee might all (of that Family) live long to enjoy that pleasant place, and that our good K.†7 might live as many years as Adam, and when those were past live them over agen, that wee might alwayes live in peace.†8 as for his
― 525 ―

entertainments at Oxford, and at my Lord Norris's†1 I shall say nothing of them because I suppose they have bin already the subject of the Mercuryes.†2
onely He was not well satisfyed with his reception at Oxford, and refused to take his Doctors degree which was tendered him because a Cambridg Gentleman who came over with him out of Barbary, and whom he recommended was refused it by the convocation.†3 in which I think he did well. as for the Musick, and speeches I heard them not; but by the Character of them were highly Asiatick,†4 and so the fitter for him to whom they were intended. Dr: Hyde†5 presented him with some Arabick MSS: but to make the best use of that little paper is left: I can tell you that your wood was all carryed this day, and on saterday, and safe layd in. as for your boxe I have not sent for it yet but will†a with the caution you give me by the first oppertunity. as for the theà†6 I have it not yet but will inquire for it to morrow when I goe my self, and whether my wife has it, or not yet she presents her service to you, and looks upon her self as much obliged to you, as if she had, onely you might have spared robing your self of that which will be I hope one of our cheif Entertainments when you <come>†b downe agen. though I doubt by this boxe of books you have thoughts of staying a good while since you send for your company to you. as for sorrell my wife with John Clerk†7 will be in Towne within this fortnight, and then if you please to have him he shall bring him up, if not, he is very welcome here: I suppose I shall know your mind before he goes up. my wife is better I think in her stomach since she took the cortex, and rides sometimes; but she had a terrible fit of the spleen and wind, the other day. but is now well. and so is all here, and your servants as much as
MUSIDORE.
― 526 ―

716. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, 16/26 June [1682] (686, 717)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, ff. 133-4. Year from Locke's endorsement and contents.
+
ce vendredi 26. Juin
Je vous suis sensiblement obligé, Monsieur, de linquietude que vous me faites paroitre avoir eüe a cause de mon silence. Elle n'a jamais eté meilleure depuis plus de vint ans, mais il n'en a pas eté de même de celle de notre Capitaine de marine qui nous a fait ici grand'peur depuis six semaines. Il est a present entierement hors d'afaire, et m'a tres fort recommandé de vous faire des complimens de sa part aussi bien que mr l'Abe G.
J'ay eté depuis un mois assez heureux pour voir plus de vint Anglois ou Ecossois passant par ici, tous honetes gens. monsieur Coxe†1 fils d'un fameux medecin a eté lun de ceux la. Il a avec lui madame sa femme qui est tres bien faite, mais qui ne parle point encore de langage chretien, car cest ainsi comme je vous ay desja dit que j'apele ceux ou jentens quelque peu de chose. Nous avons aussi gouverné ici monsieur Fall,†2 gouverneur des deux fils du Grand Tresorier d'Ecosse†3 qui eurent ici bien de l'inquietude pour monsieur leur Pere sur la nouvele du Naufrage de monsieur le Duc d'Yorke,†4 mais il avoit eté sur le plancher des vaches.†5 nous avons aussi vu un Anglois chargé des depouilles d'Orient ou il a demeuré douze ans.†6 Il scait fort bien les langues et les rits de ces nations la. Je l'ay adressé à monsieur Tevenot et a monsieur lAbé Renaudot. Nous avons ici de residence monsieur Jonston†7 Ecossois fort galant homme, parent de monsieur le Docteur Brunet,†8 auteur du livre
― 527 ―

Anglois de la Regale, et ami de monsieur Justel. Il est gouverneur de mr le Chevalier Bernard†1 qui est d'aupres d Hogtinton. Au reste. pour justifier en quelque maniere mon silence je vous diray que jatendois de Paris le retour de monsieur Perrot pour faire des bouchons a visse pour vous et pour monsieur Boyle, et que j'ay aussi fait faire de petites bouteilles a goulet ecroué, lesqueles sont d'une nouvele composition d'Agathe, qui est tres belle. j'atens une ocasion pour vous en envoier mais je voudrois bien mieux les porter moi même, dont je ne desespere pas dans quelque tems, aiant eté retenu ici par une afaire qui n'a pas eté terminée si tost que je le croiois. Jen ay une envie plus grande que vous ne pouvez vous le figurer. Je vous ecriray bien tost de Paris, mais d'avance je vous diray que monsieur Perrot de notre verrerie, que je tiens pour le premier homme de sa profession, travaille enfin a un ouvrage auquel je le porte depuis long tems, cest un traité de la vitrification.†2 Il m'a montré cequ'il en a desja composé, et il y a des Choses singulieres, et inconnües a tout autre qu'a lui, Il en voudra bien regaler le public. J'ay fait ici manque de meilleure exercice quelque chose qui ne vous deplaira pas peutêtre quand je vous le feray voir. cela a fort plu a monsieur Fall, et a notre Capitaine de marine. Je nescai si je vous ay dit que j'ay trouvé le petit discours des Balenes†3 dont j'avois fait lecture a mr Southwel.
Je vous prie d'assurer de mes respects monsieur Boyle, et messieurs Justel et Brunet.†4 J'ay receu ici depuis peu deux letres de monsieur Justel, qui a sa niece mademoisele d'Heucourt entre les mains de mr Gendron a qui je la recommande bien.
Address: For Mr John Locke Angleterre At Mr Hicks's a tailer below the Kings playhouse in Bridges street London
Endorsed by Locke: Toinard 26o Jun. 82
Perrot de la vitrification / Whalefishing.†a

We have had Dear Mr Lock a Voyage so tedious and unfortunate That you were as lucky as prudent in not coming with us, at Maderas I left my wife very il having miscaryed, I have synce heard hyr feauvur and agu had left hyr and she was out of al danger, soe I expect hir by the first ship touches there which is bound hyther If†c- she returnes not,-†c I have bin troubled with a giddiness and vyolent payn in my head ever since I came betwixt the Tropicks, I aryved the 14th last month, and am now somthing better, not having been able to wryte til within this weeke, otherwise you had sooner heard from me, Mr Hickman†1 I supose tels you he's farmer

720. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 1 July [1682] (714, 726)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 97-8. Year from Locke's endorsement.
July the 1rst
Methoughts†6 it was very pleasantly spoken on that occasion that it was by a certaine Lord a Friend of yours,†7 That it much pleas'd him to see that the Learned could be Out, and the most Knowing Mistaken, as well as others. I remember that I was then of the same Opinion, and it is since, from a Phancie not very unlike it, that I have so much desir'd that you should be Impertinent.†8
― 531 ―

Wonder not therefore any more (I beseech you) at a request that I renew to you againe now that you are going to the Waters, where I wish you all the Pleasure that you can expect or desire, and should have done it something sooner but that I thought I might have sent you a Book before you went which my Brother†1 has sent me for you, but which I have not yet received. When I do I shall take the Pleasure now of reading it before you see it, although I have alreaddy design'd my self so much Work of that Kind that I know not when I shall finish it, and All to keepe my self in a good Humor, which yet methinks I need not take so much Pains to doe, since I find the Good Innocent Aire is like to have all the blame of my Ill ones. You are very Obliging indeed in laying all the fault upon that, since you make me thereby perfectly <Guiltless>,†a But however I think in Honor I ought not to let it suffer Unjustly and therefore do assure you whatever your Opinion of it is, that it is as quiet <and>†b Harmless an Aire as ever you came into in your Life and Absolutely the fitest place in the World for a GrandChild of Kadwalladors to become a Stoick in, it being so far from Disordering the Heart as you say that I assure you there is nothing here that ever offers to have any thing at all to do with it, and indeed in this Place a Heart is one of the most useless things in the World.
You see now that you have a Governess that will be strictly Just though to her owne disadvantage. I hope therfore this letter will restore me to your good Opinion and Attone for all the Envy and Ill Humour you found in my last, for which the truth is I cannot repent, that being a thing which you Know is naturally my Aversion, and Besides that if I should ever do it I would willingly do it once for all which I find would be impossible to do now, that you are going to Tunbridge, and that it is not yet long Vacation.†2 However I assure you this that mine is an Envy after a new Mode which will never hinder me from wishing you those Pleasures which I grumble for the want of, nor from being Sir
your Obliged Friend and Humble servant
PHILOCLEA

722. William Charleton to Locke, 22 July/1 August 1682 (691, 728)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, ff. 52-3.
Paris the 1th August 1682
Deare Sir
Having received 2 such kind letters from a person I am so much obliged to as yourself dated the 4th and 30th Aprill and likewise a commission from you, I cannot almost beleive otherwise then that I must passe in your esteem as a verry ungratefull person, but on the other hand when I tell you that I came hither but the last moneth, and that I found both your letters at my arrivall, and that I have been verry ill for someday's and verry desirous likewise of performing your commands before I writ, I hope you will entertaine more favourable thoughts of me. I waited on Mr: Toinard, and Mr: Formentin, and Dr: Godfroy, and on the Abbé Gendron, all of them much your freinds, and extreamely civill to me upon your account, but for the 2 former I never met with more worthy persons, you hold so constant a corrispondence with the former that I doubt not but he ha's told you that he intends not for England, he ordered me to send you 2 small boxs the contents I question not but he ha's given you an account of, but howsoever Inclosed I send you a list of them,†2 I have been verry much Concerned that I could not meet with a pleasing oportunity of sending them to you till now that I do it by the bearer, a person that I can confide in one mr Moll who ha's lived with a freind of mine Mr Buxton†3 for some time
― 534 ―

abroad (and formerly with Sir John Hobart)†1 the Gentleman being lately dead at Orleance he returnes to England. I have been so unfortunate as to have lost Mr Toinards adresse which I had in my table book†2 and left in a Hackney coach, I desire the favour of you to let me have it when you write to me. With much difficulty I have got Moreri's historicall Dictionary†3 in 2 large volumes indifferently well bound, I indeavoured to have had it in sheets having heard that no books are permitted to come over bound into England,†4 they are to big to be sent by the bearer so I shall send them with some I have bought which I must so far trespasse upon you as to desire you to lodge with some freind of yours till I come over, which will be Infalliblely (God willing) in October. Informe me if it be needfull to rip of the Covers, I vissited all the booksellers shopps in the rüe St. Jacque's and in the rüe de la harpe†5 and else where and could find not one more, they say they will be shortly reprinted but some freinds of mine tell me they will not passe the presse this 6 moneths. Sir I am in a verry weak and languishing Condition but shall ever continue
Sir
Your most affectionate humble servant
WILLIAM CHARLETON
The Inclosed is from the Abbè L'Engendre.†6
please to adress your letters to me as formerly chez Mr: Guillaume Ord banquier A Paris
Pray Sir let me know if my Lord Meath or Mr Cheney be in London.
Address: These For His worthy freind Mr: John Locke at Thanet house in Aldersgate Street in London
Endorsed by Locke: Charleton 1 Aug. 82

724. Locke to Mrs. Mary Clarke, 2 August [1682] (709, 774)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 171. Year from contents. Printed in Rand, pp. 558-9 (with year as '[1700]'). Clarke's next extant letter is no. 739.
London Aug. 2
Madam
Had you been by when I just now read your obleigeing letter you had certainly thought me the most unreasonable and outragious man in the world for I had certainly scolded at you like anything and all the returne you had had to your civilitys had been noe thing but wrangleing peevishnesse and choller, and how it will fare with you yet before I come to the bottom of my paper I cannot be over confident. For when I recollect that haveing sent for my horse†1 into Oxford shire on purpose to come and wait on you at Tunbridg, and since that spoke for a place in a freinds coach which failed me I more easily bore the disapointment of both horse and coach out of consideration that I should inconvenience you in a place where it was said abundance of company had very much straitend every bodys lodgings, and now you tell me you have all this while kept a chamber for me on purpose. Had you not a minde at any rate to have an advantage of reproaching me how is it possible you should hire a chamber only to lock up this secret in and not let me know any thing of it? I intend not to loose the oportunity of revengeing my self on you there, and therefor the begining of the next weeke I intend to make you a visit.†2 How the sight of you may alter my temper I know not, but this I am sure I am at present too full of Belingsgate to discourse with a Lady for whom I have soe peculiar a respect as I have for you and to whom in what humor soever I am truth forces me to say that I am
Madam
your most humble and most obedient servant
J LOCKE
― 537 ―

Pray present my most humble service to Mr Clarke, with whome I conclude the waters agree since I heare noething to the contrary
Address: For Mrs Clark at Rusthall near Tunbridg Or at the Wells at Tunbridg
Postmark: AV 3
725. Dr. David Thomas to Locke, 5 August 1682 (723, 769)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 20, ff. 50-1.
Sarum Aug. 5: 82
Deare Freind
My wife by the use of Sy papav Rhead and sometime ol. Amigd d and sometime water and drinkeing water is pretty well recovered which would not have beene if her pthisis had not beene the effect of an inflammatory feavor. If Mr Hobs wants not an apprentice soe soone pray enquire for another master in that faculty. Mr Sneton I thinke spoyled by drunkenesse. I thanke you for your care of my sonne John. I entend to leave him wholly to your management. I am not concerned at the breadth of the Cedar plankes if 16 Inches soe they be 2 Inches thicke and 8 foot long for the price I must beare with though I thinke it deare. If he will cut one planke and send the other wholl 8 foot long. For 16 square feete is as much as I neede. Therefore one way or other I desire you to send the Cedar and one planke of 16 Inches broad and 8 foot long is equally good to me as of 12 Inches broad: the length and thickenesse of one planke being what is considerable to me. My freind is come downe by whom I desired you to send me your opinion de morbo gallico I am
your affectionate A D R
Parthenice presents her service and thanke to you for her sonne John

726. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, [c. 14 August 1682] (720, 730)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 99-100. Date from the postal note and Locke's endorsement.
Haveing as I think formerly Confest to you that it was my Custome very often to prevent the Accusations of my Friends by begining first with them when I knew my self to be Guiltie, I shall not Therefore do so now, Although I could take my Choise at this time of three or foure several ways that would all serve to prove the fault Yours that I have not writt to you all this while. But besides this, I have a Mind to let you see too, that under the Name of Friends, which in Conformitie, I as well give to People that I do not much Care for as to those that I doe, are Compris'd a number of People whome I treat very Differently, and whom for Convenience sake I divide into foure or five Orders or Distinctions of Friends, finding my self capable of so many Different Degreese of Friendship. Not to Consider then in which Rank of them you stand, I do†a undoubtedly find you in the number of those to whom I look upon my self as under an Indispensible Obligation of useing sinceritie. I shall therefore very freely acknowledge my self faultie, assureing you that if I had not a great Opinion of your Goodness I should hardly know how to ask Pardon for so much Rudeness and Incivilitie as I have beene Guiltie of. Not but that perhaps I could say something that might extenuate a great part of it by leting you know that we have had those here to whom I was oblig'd to pay a Tiresome Attendance That I have beene very much Indispos'd with an Unusual Paine in my Head, and still am soe, Besides that I have twice beene out of the Towne, with other things of this kind. But because that I Naturally have an Aversion to all Excuses, and Excuse Makers, and am willing to increase the Obligation I shall owe you, I shall not insist upon these things, nor indeavour to take from the Merrit of that Faith, whose Impliciteness is not of less Value in Friendship, then it is in Religion. But who can assure me that you are not a Heretick in both? For the last it is I think your owne Concerne wholly, and therefore I shall Leave it wholly to you, but for the first it is at Present become so much Mine that I Beg it of you, who though I am very Carefull in Denouncing Damnation, must needs assure you, that this is no Venial Sin, at lest I could
― 539 ―


produce a great Author or twoo for it, who methinks in this matter should be of some Authoritie with you, Though it would indeed be the more Obliging to beleeve me upon my owne, who I perceive you think may be One, in time, if I am not Pretty well towards it already.
But since the Conceptions of Friendship for†a- such only are mine-†a (as I take it) hold no agreement with Baby Clouts methinks that Curiositie which you once had to have inquir'd more narrowly after them, should still Continue, Nor should you so easilie be put off by an excuse which I cannot allow for a just one, in the Lady who made it,†1 who as I have beene inform'd, does not use to be prevented by such Occasions from doing things of the like Nature. But you are resolv'd I see still to put me in need of the Old Remidie from which I have but Lately received a Cruel Diversion, and therefore to Answer your question the best that I can, It is now so long since I writt to you last, that I know not very well what I did then, But for this Present time, and for a good while past, I do assure you, that I have not only Thought, but have found it some Paine to me, to doe any thing else beside thinking, which should I give a stricter Account of it, would be found none of the lest causes of my not Writeing to my Friends. I should presume too much upon your Friendship should I entertaine you with things in which you could take no Part, but what your Natural Goodness, and Compasion would give you, and therefore I shall onely tell you in short, that I am upon the point of loseing in a Brother†2 the Dearest Person in the World to me, to whose Advantage (as I am perswaded) I have Sacrific'd all Considerations of my owne Sattisfaction, in Consenting to a Voiage from which I have but small Hopes of seeing him returne. If you have ever knowne what it is to Love so Tenderly as I doe, or knew but Half my Weakeness, You would not doubt but that I have had many thoughts before I could come to such a Resolution, and as many since I have done it, which are so little Pleaseing to me that you would lay the Greatest Obligation in the World on me if you could teach me to live with out any at all. As for your second question whether I think that the Lady who writt to you†3 Left her
― 540 ―

Heart at London, or No, when she came from thence, If she has Witt, as you say she Has, I do assure you, that she did not, But though perhaps (for all your Complement) she may not have very much, Yet I assure you that those who know her, doe her the Honour to beleeve, that she takes as much Care of her Heart, as many Wiser People. However it be she nevertheless thinks her self much Oblig'd to that Friend of Hers that would be so Carefull of it for her, and I dare not be assur'd, that it may not be an occasion of makeing her more Negligent for the Future, then she has ever beene for the time that is past; — But to returne to my self, Is it possible that you should be Angry with your Governess, and that for no other Cause but not reading your Books. I must Confess indeed that beleeveing at present I should have no use of the Art of Navigation,†1 the first look into it Discourag'd me from proceeding farther, But if you are of an other Mind, and think it is as usefull to me, as some here do Architecture, and Trigonometri, I shall set about the understanding of them all, as fast as I can. In the meane time My Deare Pupil Pardon my Error if I have beene in one, and excuse all the other faults of your Faithfull Humble Servant
PHILOCLEA.
Address: These for Mr Lock at Thanet House in Aldersgate street in London
Postmark: AV 16
Postal note: Agust 16 Left
Endorsed by Locke: Philoclea Aug: 82
727. Dr. John Fell, Bishop of Oxford, to Locke, 15 August [1682?] (643)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 101-2. The year is problematical. Locke's endorsement is wrong. By the signature and the address the year must be between 1679 and 1682. In 1679 Locke had not seen Fell probably for some years; the letter seems to presuppose some oral discussion. In 1680 15 August fell on a Sunday, an unsuitable day for a business letter. In 1681 Locke apparently resided in Oxford from 1 to 18 August. Though an incorrect address is possible Fell is unlikely to have written to Locke in the present terms on 15 August 1683 after the discovery of the Rye-House Plot. This leaves 1682 as the only year to which there is no objection.
― 541 ―

Sir
You formerly told me that you should be able to dispose of twenty books of the sorts†1 which were printed here. If it still stands with your convenience to undertake that trouble, I shall accordingly consign it to you, and remain Sir
Your Assured friend
JO. OXOn̄.
Aug. 15.
Address: To The worthily esteemd Mr: John Lock at Thanet house in Aldersgate Street These D.
Noted (postal?): August 16 Left
Endorsed by Locke: J:Oxon 15 Aug. 72

729. Andrew Percivall to Locke, 22 August 1682 (317)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, f. 59.
Carolina†a the 22d: august 1682
Deare Sir
As I cannott omitt wrighting youe by every opertunity so give me leave onely to enforme youe that I live. As to the afaires of our Country wee are like the other worldes: as wee increase in nombers of people and Estates so more Crosse accidents and troubls attent us wee have had some losses lately by Indians perticularly two men by westoes†1 and one by wynyahes.†2 the revenge wee have of the westoes is that nine of them fell in and after the action the rest forced to flight, since which I have gott fower of them brought in alive now prisoners. 730. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 29 August [1682] (726, 731)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 101-2. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Camb: August the 29th
Though I am indebted to you for twoo Letters, yet I beleeve I should not have writt to you to Day, were it not that I might be something more so. You will make no scruple I hope to give snuff to one that desires it, and that so importunately, that I can scarse find Patience to waite till it is Possible you should send it me. there is none in this Towne but what perfectly fuddles me, and I fancie almost gives me the Palsie, though I find so much good in it too, as
― 544 ―

tempts me to take it notwithstanding that Dangerous qualitie, and a severe Prohibition besides. If you would know now what it is that I ail, that makes it so necessarie for me, I should find it very difficult to tell you, since I can describe it no otherwise, but that without being much Paine, it is something in my Head which is as troublesome as that, and has all the same effects, as makeing me much a Sott, and depriveing me almost of the use of that little understanding which I us'd to have, so that at present there is no great danger of my applying my self much to the study of Trigonometri, at lest you will say with Likelihood of much success. But I am so far from it that it is certaine at this time, that I cannot speake three words of sence, at least if I do, it is but by Chance, and is more then I know when I have done, in this Condition now I have eleven Letters to write, and which way do you think I shall be able to do it, if you knew but what Paine I am in to Day, for one that I writt Yesterday, I am sure you would extreamly Pitty me, since writeing it to one that I have but once seene, and never writt to before I remember that I have said a Hundred things that are not to be understood but by one that knows me Perfectly well, besides that there is some part of it, that should I be ask'd I have absolutely forgot the meaneing of my self, and therefore am not able so much as to write Notes upon it should I be desir'd, which I expect I shall be by the next Post. If you have any Pitty contribute what you can to help me out of this sad Condition, till when I shall not be able to apprehend any thing that you can say, or to write one Word of Answeare to all the Letters that you send me, though I am nevertheless, now as at other times
Your Obedient Humble Servant
PHILOCLEA.
I have much Curiositie to know the Poetess you speake of, alsoe who was this Yeare the most Celebrated Beautie at the Wells.
You may send to me on Monday by Martin at the Bull in Bishopsgate Street.†1
