731. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 9 September [1682] (730, 734)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 103-4. Year from Locke's endorsement. Locke has concealed some names; there is no apparent reason for his having done so.
That you may have no Cause for Repentance (which you know is a Melancholy thing that I hate) this is to let you know that had the Snuff not come, I should have taken snuff most certainely, but that I am now, if I am not Mistaken, in a very tollerable good Humour, for which I give thanks to you since how much soever you disparage snuff I am very sensible that I am Oblig'd to Hippolito†1 for a great part of it. But since I have got a Custome of makeing all my Complaints to you, I cannot forbeare telling you, that notwithstanding this, I have very little Reason to be Pleas'd, and that I beleeve within these twoo Days I shall be Downeright sick, with the Croud of Impertinent Company that this Place is always full of at a Sturbridge†a Faire,†2 it is a Persecution of the kind that I am Confident exceeds all Immagination, and if you have any good Nature in you, you will at lest think upon me once a Day with Compassion, the Truth is by that time it is done, I am affraid every thing will look so much like Winter, that though I shall be much at ease then, yet I shall not fancie to stay long in the Countrey, unless Necessitie drive me to it, Since my Sisters Familie†3 is so increas'd that I cannot be there and doubt it will the same at my Lady Kings,†b where the good Company would induce me to overlook great inconveniences if it could be, though hardly all that I indur'd the last Winter. When I am resolv'd to leave this Place, which perhaps may not be yet a good While I will send to you to know whether you think I had best propose it or not, though I do beleeve it will not be possible, or if it be, that my Lady will not like to make any alterations which should put her upon the lest unnecessarie charge, though it would be very convenient for her self, as well as others, but however I shall not inquire what she will doe till I know my
― 546 ―

owne Mind, and what Mrs Clark†a does, to whom pray take not any notice of what I write, but onely let me know, when you can tell, whether she has not little Master†1 Home this Winter. If you heare at any time of any Convenient place that would be fitt for me with onely my maid to Board in Pray do me the favour to send me word of it. I am in hast being to Dress me you must know to go to the Faire, haveing perswaded my Mother†2 to see the German Jugler†3 which Dr. More†b †4 and my Father likewise have promis'd me to do, if I will send for him hither, which I intend assoone as my Father is return'd from London, where he at present is, being Oblig'd to give Securitie to the East India Company for my Brother, who leaves his Master to go over as a Factor for them. I hope to see him one Day before he goes, and intend to make use of all the Philosophy that I have to take leave of him as I ought, that is, like the Daughter of a Philosopher and your Governess. I have roome onely to add that I am
your obedient servant
PHILOCLEA
Sep: the 9th

734. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 25 September [1682] (731, 740)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 105-6. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Since I love Companions in my Misfortunes, you could not have done me a greater Pleasure, then to let me know how deeply you have beene a sufferer in the same Cruel Persecution, that I have so lately indur'd, though as far as I perceive, you came off upon much easier terms, if one Day excus'd you. However since it is now past, I look upon it as some recompence for mine, that it has Contributed to your Diversion, and given you as much Pleasure as I received from the first Knowledge of yours, since when I have not beene in the Laughing Humour, haveing not beene Perfectly Well ever since, and some part of the time, very sick, it being onely in my Power to Governe my Mind, and not my Body, which I beleeve you know is of a very UnPhilosophical Constitution, and has not the power to beare Up under any little Disturbance. I suppose you will understand by this that I have taken my leave (as I told you in my last I was to do) of my Deare Brother, and I really am, and have beene, so Dull ever since, that I cannot immagine what one can have to say to make up a Letter, to any Body, without haveing something to Desire of them, or some News to tell them, or Business, or the like, All which I am now destitute of, and therefore I hope you will Pardon me for once, for writeing to you, merely to let you know, that I have nothing to say to you, which I have not at this time, unless it be to tell you That you were in a mistake concerning little Master, since I understand by a letter from Mrs C—†1 Yesterday, that she does designe to have him Home ere it be long, so that at present I cannot tell whether I can come to Towne,
― 551 ―

or no, till Spring, for want of Convenient Lodgings. I can think of none at all at present, unless at Dr Kgs†1 in Hatton Garden, to whose Lady I think to write something about it the next weeke, who I fancie will not be unwilling to it, But if she be not, whether or no I my self shall be pleas'd in being there, Or when I shall make Tryal of it, I cannot yet tell, but suppose it will hardly be before the Terme†2 if so soone. I have nothing more to say, but that your Governess thinks her self much Oblig'd to you, that you can be reconcil'd to Winter for her sake, and that I am Sir
Your Faithfull Humble Servant
PHILOCLEA.
Sept: the 25th
Address: These For John Lock Esqr at Thanet House in Aldersgate Street London.
Postmark: —E 25
Endorsed by Locke: Philoclea 25 Sept. 82

735. William Locke to Locke, 2 October 1682 (713)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 231-2.
Kind Cosen I received your Letter dated July 22: 82 from Thanet house and confesse my selfe deeply ingaged for your kindnes but have delayed my answere partly because I knew not where Thanet house were in London because London was not mentioned and especially till I had conference with my daughter I could not relate the particular of my desire: Shee hath a sonne by a former husband now at schoole at dorchester neere 16 yeeres old whom I judge a towardly and comely youth and (if capable) is to succeed mr Joseph Studeley (her now husband in the parsonage at Broad Mayne and is at schoole to that end but wanting ability and especially a freind to relie on proves deficult and made mee remember you. unto whom I am so neere related and of whom I heare so much desireing your assistance in placeing him where hee may be fitt for oxford: and no schoole like westminster†3 if it may bee done, and what I am able to
― 552 ―

doe in continuing him there awhile I will not faile to doe because his genius is bent that way and hee is now in virgills Aeniods and other Latine bookes and I apprehend that mr Joseph Stoodly though but a father in law†1 may doe something—pray Sir consider the occasion of this boldnes unto you because if you faile I am out of hopes of effecting it: or if you would see the ladd hee shalbe sent upp to you, howsoever pray faile not to give mee your answere in which I shall acquiesse what ever it bee but till then shalbe in hopes and without rest As concerning my family I had sonnes and daughers seaven: but all dead except my daughter Elizabeth now at Broadmayne who hath 6 children to succeed in my family the residue I have survived, and am now neere 76 yeeres of age (being elder then my Cosen Peter Locke by neere 2 yeeres) my kinsman william Locke at dorchester†2 hath children men and women. Sir I have bene bold in writing and you cannott but judge of the necessity and I trust it will come in an acceptable time: I have no more but to desire your answere, and so I rest
Your neere kinsman and affectionate friend and servant
WILLIAM LOCKE
Cerne Abbas neere dorchester:
October 2d 1682.

I now send you by 2 of my freinds that are lately Come from Bourdeaux, Mr Butteris, and Mr Dix, all the mapps you desired except that of the Maldives, and I have added 7 to them so that they are in all 22, a large map of Picardy is one, if you like it, as fast as

the rest of the Provinces are finished which are to be done in the same manner I shall get them for you, for I see I must set up my staff here this winter though I fully resolved to the contrary. I have at last got Alp: Borellus de motu animalium printed at Rome in quarto: the first part in the yeare 80 and the second part (which came hither but lately from thence) in the yeare 81 which you will receive with the mapps, for the Moreri's Dictionary in 2 large folios I atend only your answer and shall take care if you see fit to have it sent you by Roan,†1 for I shall not remove my bookes as yet. I know not whether you hold a Corrispondency with mr Kirby, if not; the death of his Lady may be news to you though somewhat stale, she dyed the 17th of September about 8 a clocke in the morning sudenly of an Apoplexy, she was opened, and there was found a great quantity of congealed bloud in her head, her lungs were much wasted, and exulcerated, and in her kidneys were severall stones, the old gentleman lay's her death greatly to heart. Montpelier I perceave looses much of its reputation for lately (besides others that went before) my Lord Ferrers†2 and his famyly are gone for Aix, and thither intends to set out this weeke my Lord Manchester and his Lady.†3 I am much beholden to Mr Tufton for his kindness in remembring me. pray be pleased to give him, and Sir John: Chichley and his Lady, my service when you see them. wishing you health and hapyness I take my leave and am
Sir
Your most obliged humble servant
WILLIAM CHARLETON
pray be pleased to Inform me if my Lord Meath or mr Chiney be in London.†4
Address: For Mr John Locke to be left at Mr Hicks a Tayler below the King's play house in Bridges street in Covent garden

740. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 28 October [1682] (734, 744)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 107-8. Date from Locke's endorsement.
If you could have had your wish, and beene Present when I received your Letter, I know not whether my Looks would have appear'd to you any otherwise then they us'd to doe, But this I am sure, that if you could have seene my Heart, You would have found that it was a great Consolation to me for the Loss of one Friend, to know that I was not depriv'd of Twoo together, And that I was much better Pleas'd to heare news of You from the Elizian Feilds,†1 then I should have beene from either France, Germanie, or Holland, Although I am very sorry to hear that you Cannot be Happy in a Place where all the World is so. And yet perhaps, if the Truth were knowne, you are not much Otherwise, or surely so small a thing as my Idea in your Mind, could never have put you in so good Humour. If it did, I must needs think (whatever you tell me to the Contrary) that Experience has convinc'd you, that (at least) there are some things that are better in the Idea, then in themselves (However as Good) for certainly my Real Presence could not have done more at that Time then that did, if it were as you say, and therefore I think it will be better to let you Continue still in Elizium by your self, then run the Hazard of an Unprofitable Journey to keepe you Company there, Besides that I am not of the Mind that it is so great a Misfortune to want a Companion, For in this long time since I writt to You last, in which some People perhaps would have changd there Minds above Twentie times, I have chang'd mine once, and instead of thinking (as I us'd to do) that the Happyness of life consisted Principally in Societie, and Friendship, I now beleeve otherwise, and that to be Happy One must Care for Nothing, nor Nobody, Have no Friends, Love onely ones self, Nor ever take Concerne in the Good, or Ill, of other people whoever they be. According therefore to this Opinion you
― 558 ―

cannot be Unhappy, and I am just now so mightilie perswaded that it is a Right One, that I am upon the very point of resolving immediatly to indeavour all that I can to reduce it into Practice, although I should have beene very glad to have had it received your approbation first, which I dare say you would give it upon farther Consideration, there being a Thousand Conveniences in it that I have not time now to Mention, who then shall never trouble you with such long letters as this, at lest if to do so, it be necessarie to have either Witt, or Kindness. For as for the First, I have it not already, and for the second, to be sure Then I shall not, nor can you complaine of me for it, when all the World besides will be alike indifferent to me, and since that till then I shall always be very much
Your Friend and Servant
PHILOCLEA.
Cambridge Oct: the 28th
I had almost quite forgot to Answeare your question, nor can well tell how to do it now I have remember'd it, But I think I shall not go to London sooner then the end of next Month, Where I shall chuse much sooner to be at my Lady Ks†1 then any where else if she be free to it, and that I shall not incommode any Body else.
Address: These For Mr Lock at Christs Church in Oxford.
Postmark: OC 30
Postal note: P P 2d(?) to London.
Endorsed by Locke: Philoclea 28 Oct.82

744. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 28 November [1682] (740, 751)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, f. 109. Year from Locke's endorsement.
I have at Present some extraordinarie occasions of Business, and am otherwise so little Dispos'd to write, that did I not feare you would think me sullen, or Rude, or something or other almost as Bad, I should not let you heare from me till I came to London, where I shall be on Thursday sevennight, staying here this Weeke to see the solemnities of Sir John Finches Funeral over First, for whom all here, are true Mourners. ― 562 ―

now to give you none of my Thousand Reasons and it is like have forgot many of them by this time, But I am sure I shall always know one good one to make me think nothing in this World deserves Half the Care we usually Bestow upon it, and that Happiness is not to be look'd for in any thing without us. I thank God I have never in my Life beene much of any other Mind, and therefore it is not any Disappointment that makes me more so now then ever, no more then that in some Melancholy Humour I am faln out with the World, so that I would not have you expect if ever you see me againe you should find me worse Company then I use to be, or less then I was, your Friend,
PHILOCLEA.
I suppose you will perceive that I am in hast and accordingly excuse me for what I know not well what I write.
Novem the 28th

745. George Walls to Locke, 15 December 1682 (742, 1132)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 47-8. Hamburg used the old-style calendar until 1700.
Hamburgh December 15th. 1682.
Sir
Though I know noe excuse sufficient for my not writeinge to you since I came to Hamburgh (which was the first of December) yet I can trulie lay before you that the varietie of offices that were to be done for women and children, a fast sermon, besides two on the sunday, and those respects that were to be paid at my first comeinge hither to the members of the companie, together with somewhat worse then all this the drudgerie of beinge at extravagant entertainments have occasion'd somethinge soe like busienesse ever since I came here that I hope you'le make some allowance for
― 563 ―

the omission. Tis not reasonable to desire more kindnesse then has hitherto beene shewne me uppon all accounts, from the kings Envoy†1 and the whole companie. and tis beyounde the rate of the kindnesse of a country parish in England to be paid from michaelmasse for service that did not begin till the 3d of December.†2 A courte was call'd the monday after my arriveall, in which I was chosen minister to the Companie with verie particular instances (and somewhat unusual) of unanimitie in the election, and soone after the Treasurer, secretarie (who is verie much yours) and two of the principale members of the companie sent to me to acquaint me of it, that a house was order'd me and £50 appointed to be paid me for this quarter, in consideration of the trouble I had beene at and hazardous journey I had undertaken at this season of the yeere. I shall not trouble you with the accidents of my passage which were somewhat unusuall; nor can I tell you anie news, but that this day the Envoy receiv'd an order from Counsell to commande the deputie to arrest anie estate or goods of mr Pilkingtons†3 that should be founde in Hamburgh. I hope you'le have noe occasion to come hither, but if you should, be assur'd that I have a gentile house that I'le give you as much right to as the Companie has given me. I begge, (Sir) youle take some paines in giveinge my respects to my friends, dutie to my Lord Bishop,†4 most humble service to my deare Lord Clancartie, good Dr Pococke and his familie, my true friends Mr Prideaux, Mr Woodward and George Martin with all the rest. Deare Sir
Your most affectionate, oblig'd humble servant

746. Richard old to Locke, 26 December 1682 (599, 749)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 172-3.
Sir
I cannot impart any thing to you worth your notice from hence, but only how our Colledg affairs have gon since your absence, and in what posture they now stand. Five Westminster scholars of this years election were admitted students last week, in the vacancies made by the preferment of Mr Wyatt and Mr Morley, Mr Barbours death, and the expulsion two non-graduates, Brady, and Cooper,†1 the former for deserting the Colledg at Act last, going to London without leave, and rambling there ever since without taking any notice of his dependance here, setting up there for a witt, and being a small retainer to the Play-House, the latter for being caught about a fortnight ago, in a scandalous house, and in very bad circumstances, by Mr Charlett†2 Proproctor of Trin: Colledg, who complained of him to the Vice-Can:†3 and he to the Bishop of Oxon.†4 in the removes of this year Mr Isham, Mr Altham the Procter, Mr Morgan now at Tangier Chaplain to the Garrison there, and Mr Prideaux are advanced to our table.†5 The officers for the year ensuing are Dr Hammond Treasurer, Dr Jane Subdean, Mr Isham Catechist, Mr Breach and Mr Taswell Censors, Mr Evans Rhet. and Mr Sparkes Graec. Reader.†6 yesterday morne the Bishop of Oxon entertained the University with an excellent Sermon in the
― 565 ―

Cathedrall, and today he treats all the Noble men and Masters of his own Colledg with a magnificent dinner at his own Lodgings. At quarter day I received for you from the Butler £05.08s.09d. and from the Treasurer £01.03s.04d. if there be any service I can do for you relating to this or any other affair during your absence, I hope you will with the greatest freedom engage the endeavours of
Sir
Your faithfull freind and humble servant
RICHARD OLD
Ch:Ch: Oxon. December. 26. 82.

749. Richard Old to Locke, 6 January 1683 (746, 1352)
B.L., MS. Locke. c. 16, ff. 174-5. The letter mentioned by Old is lost.
Ch: Ch: Oxon. Jan. 6. 82
Sir
It concernes me to do both you and myselfe right, by endeavouring to rectifie some mistakes, which it seem's severall passages of my last letter have occasioned. I confess I wrot in great hast, and had not possible leisure to be accurate in my choise or placing of words, but the buisness I was to acquaint you with was in itselfe so very plain, that I wonder how I could possibly so far obscure it by the most imperfect expressions, that you should not know well how to understand what I sayd concerning it. By the best recollection I can make of what drop't so hastily from my thoughts into my pen, what I then imparted to you was only to this effect, that I was commanded by the Bishop of Oxon†1 to let you know, that tho he could not gratifie you in the request you made formerly for a particular chamber, being unwilling to disoblidg Dr Aldrich†2 who had bin earnest with him that Mr Breach might have that chamber, when he left it, yet that he should be very ready to give you the liberty of pleasing yourselfe in any other choice, either of Mr Wyatts chamber, now vacant, or if you did not like that, of some others
― 568 ―

which would ere long fall into his disposall.
Now laying it down as a principle (which I am sure you will readily admitt) that every true freind endeavours the advantage of his freind, in any fair and legall way, with the same reall and affectionate concerne as he would his own, it must necessarily follow that Dr Aldrich was Competitor with you for that chamber, into which he desired Mr Breach might succeed after his removall. I question not but my Lord Bishop was unwilling to disoblidg you as well as him, but could not possibly gratifie you both in the same request. And I am apt to beleive that Dr Aldrich would judg, that he had the very same, or at least as good reason as you, to say, that he had thought he might have pretended to this favour without a disobligation to any body. I must own what you say, as a most certain truth, That the world must think Dr Aldrich a strang man, if my Lord cannot dispose of a chamber as he thinks fit, for fear of disoblidging him, but I am confident I wrott nothing that could give just occasion to make any such supposition, for tho I am perswaded my Lord was willing to have oblidged you both, if it had bin possible, yet I cannott think that he was fearfull of disoblidging either of you, or that so mean and slavish a consideration was any motive, or did in the least degree influence his Lordship to dispose of that chamber otherwise then he thought fit. The true state of the case is plainly thus Dr Aldrich had but lately laid out so considerable a summe of mony on that chamber, as would make any apartment (where there were room enough) handsome and commodious, and he was desirous to use his best interest with the Bishop, that an intimate freind of his might enjoy the benefit of those great expences he had bin at. And 'tis probable he might farther think, that he had reason to presume, that it was but equitable that he should have some such consideration and allowance made him for so publick a benefaction, that would extend to all future successions, as therby to gain an opportunity of befreinding a person, by whom he had bin signally oblidged in severall things of great importance. I am sure my own circumstances being in this respect the same with his, I should think it no presumption to hope for the like favour, whosoever should then chance to have the power to dispose of my chamber when I had any occasion to leave it. especially considering that this I beleev is the only Colledg in town, where the custome prevails not, that some reasonable allowance should be made to the former incumbent by his next successor for mony laid out in usefull and
― 569 ―

decent alterations and improvements. neither would favour of this kind much divert the ordinary course according to which chambers are usually disposed of, there being few if any besides Dr. Aldrich and myselfe who have any considerable reason to insist on the pretense I last mention'd.
What ever comes from you to me by letter, I receive as it were sub sigillo confessionis, and esteem my obligation to secresy to be little less sacred then that, And therefore though I have taken this liberty to declare my reall sense of this affair to you, which I hope you will look on no otherwise then as such a freedome which a freind may inoffensively use when he thinks he hath just cause so to do, yet I am confident you have a better opinion of me, then so much as to suspect that I would give but the least hint of any thing expressed here, to either of the parties concerned therin. this evening I presented your humble service and thankes to his Lordship for the favour of his present offer of Mr Wyatts chamber and the choise of others when they fall, and told him that in a little time you hope to wait on his Lordship and yourselfe pay your thankes for his favours. His Lordship's reply was, that this remove would reach to the bottom of the Colledg, and that he was in some present distress how to settle the Westminster scholars last elected, whom he could not dispose of till others had made vacancies in severall upper chambers. but however that he would tarrie in expectation of your coming hither as long as he could with any tolerable convenience. What letters are directed hither in your absence shall carefully be transmitted to you by
Sir
Your most faithfull freind and humble servant,
RICHARD OLD.

750. James Tyrrell to Locke, 16 January 1683 (715, 768)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 46-7.
Dear C.†1
I thank you for your speedy care of Jemmyes†2 lungs, and wish you could have as much of your owne (which you tell me are
― 570 ―

indisposed) as for your prescription it shall be given him as soon as he is in a condition to take it; for your suspition of the measles was not in vain for this day seavenight he fell ill of them, but had them not much in his head, face or any where els, because I suppose the greatest part of their malignity discharged it self upon his lungs in a violent Cough.
wee were fain to send for Dr: L.†1 who has bin very carefull of him all the while. and wee observed your directions about hot things, and no more then needs for he had a high hectick feavour all the while, which is not quite gone off yet though the measles have bin dead ever since Friday. but God be thanked it much decreases, and wee give him an opening pectoral drink which does very well with him. wee have twice endeavoured to purge him with Manna dissolved in snail water, but it seems it does not agree with him, it onely makeing him sick, and comeing up again in great part without any other effect, so that wee were fain to give him glysters to bring it away. it has had no better successe with poor Tommy†2 neither, who fell ill of the measles about Okeley just at the same time, and has bin very ill but is now well again: wee must be fain to purge them both with somewhat els. I have put on Jemmy a Flannell wastcoat†3 next his skin. which I hope will doe him good. as soon as he is well wee intend to send him to Okeley for some time. Mally†4 holds well yet (save for her stomach) though how long she will doe so God knows. Your Patient†5 is pretty well and remembers her service to you and says she has often wisht for your company but never more then last week when the Children were both so ill. so you may see I have had my disappointments as well as you, for first I depended upon your good conversation whilst I stayd here,†6 and have bin almost all the while deprived of it, and then I thought to have had some comfort in my boys company here this Christmasse; and to allay that have found Jemmyes Cough increased. and both of them have caught the measles here. As for Sorrell I have upon better consideration turned him out into my owne meadow, where he may run without hurting his Cornes, I hope 6 weeks, or 2 months runing will set him up again. he was not foundred onely much battred, and heat in his
― 571 ―

feet by a long journey with bad shoes. I hope this will be the last I shall have need to write to you before I see you, which I much long for my service to J.H.†1 if in Towne: Sir F.†2 is well and the rest of our Friends which is all from
yours heartily
M.
Jan: 16.-83.†a
Pray bid Syl: goe to Hicks,†3 and fetch my coat and let it be put up in your box. and let him buy me a ream of 6d. paper. and bring it downe with him. Dr: L. advises an†b issue for Jemmyes cough but I tell him I will consider farther of it: not thinking it convenient to tell him what you say.
Address: For Mr: John Lock at Thanet House in Aldersgate street. to be left with the Porter. London.

751. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, [January 1683?] (744, 752)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 32, f. 19. In Damaris Cudworth's hand. Undated, but a copy with Locke's reply (ibid., ff. 20-1) is endorsed by Locke with the date 1682/3. The date is problematical. If Damon's flight alludes to Locke's departure from London at some time when Philoclea was resident there, and if Locke's date applies to both poems, the allusion is probably to his removal to Clapham on 17 January; he was ill while there, but not necessarily unable to write the answer; his departure for Salisbury on 23 February to attend Shaftesbury's burial seems less appropriate, and in any case his answer is unlikely to be later than 26 January, when he learnt of Shaftesbury's death. But Locke's date may apply only to his answer, in which case Damon's flight may allude to a visit, apparently to Oakley, between 24 and 28 December: Journal, and the two poems could belong to late December and early January. If Damon's flight is figurative early January is the most appropriate time.
On Damons Loveing of Clora
Say wherefore is't that Damon flys,
From the Weake Charms of Cloras Eyes?
― 572 ―

Weake Charms they surely needs must bee,
Which till this Houre he could not see,
Nor is she now more Faire, then when
Theire first acquaintance they began,
When the Gay shepherd Laugh'd at love,
Swore it no Gen'rous Heart could move,
Disease of Fools, Fond Lunacie,
To Cloras Face oft would he Cry,
on mee your Friendship but bestow,
(Friendship, the onely Good below)
Faire shepherdess Ile ask no more,
Since more to give, exceeds your Pow'r.
Damon the Mightie Gift then gain'd,
With Witt exalted now maintain'd
No Happy lovers greatest Bliss
More then a Shadow was to his,
Which all Refin'd, found no alloy,
And like to Fate, nought could destroy.
Long did the Happy Youth thus live,
Hee could not ask, nor could shee give,
Till wandering the other Day
Lo, on the Ground the Shepherd lay,
Pensive, as unseene Clora thought,
Whom heedless steps had thither brought
To heare bewail his Miserie,
Complaine of loss of Libertie,
Curse his owne Stubborn Pride, and then
With Teares, and sighs, begin againe,
Ask Pardon of Philosophy
For Passions rude Apostacie,
Resolve he would no Captive bee,
But set Himself by Reason free,
He Paus'd on this awhile, but strait
Ah Damon Cry'd, it is too late,
Thou yesterday the Will didst lose,
To Day the Power to refuse,
Condemn'd a Sacrifice to bee,
Oppose not then thy Destinie,
Appease loves God, let Clora know
How much to thee her Charms do owe,
― 573 ―

Her Pitty shee cannot Deny
Though all her Powers thou didst Defy,
More difficult the Conquest is
The Nobler sure esteem'd it is.
Mistaken Damon, she Reply'd,
Nor did herself no longer hide,
Conquests so Hardly Gain'd do show
Wee nothing to the Conquer'd owe,
Nor can I challenge any part
In Captivateing thy rough Heart,
Since I am still the same as when
My Powers, and loves, you did disdaine,
Just Destinie thy love does Cause,
Submiting thee to Humane Laws,
Who Proudly would'st exempted be
Through Ignorance, or Vanitie.
The Friendship once I gave retaine
But think from me no more to gaine,
To whom thy Passion comes too late,
That scorne a Conquest giv'n by Fate.
With this she left the trembling swaine
Half Dead with Greife at her disdaine,
Who for his love no Cure can find
But Breaths his Plaints unto the Wind,
Not Dareing Cloras Eyes to see
Since her Unjust Severitie,
Who still insensible remains, }
His Constant Passion still Disdains, }
And Laughs at all his Greife, and Pains. }
Endorsed by Locke: Verses
752. Locke to Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, [January 1683?] (751, 760)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 32, ff. 20-1. Draft or copy. On f. 20 there is a copy, written by Syl Brounower, of no. 751; Locke's answer, in his own writing, follows on f. 21. For the date see no. 751 n.
But this disdain could not yet move
The Constancy of Damons love
― 574 ―

Her hand in his he gently tooke
And with a kinde but dying looke
He thus replyd
If Conquest hardly gaind doe shew
You noething to the conquerd owe
Much doubt she of her charmes must have
Who would owe all unto her slave
Robbers may boast an easy prize
Resistance sets off victorys
And she has none or knows not how to use
Her power that none but willing hearts subdues.
If you can't challenge any part
In captivateing my rough heart
Why d'ee refuse the sacrifice
I make of it to your faire eyes?
The fates you say forced me. And soe
They will what ever others doe
And she but litle glory gains
Whose slaves from others tooke their chains.
My freedome I to you resigne
The freedome which you know was mine
A freedome once soe great soe strong
T'was blamd for holding out soe long.
I freindship beg'd and did obteine
And thought my self a happy swain
But 'twas not ignorance nor pride
Made me ask noe thing els besides
He that asks freindship asks the heart
Unlesse there be some better part
And that were made only a toy
To please some idle wanton boy
I thought by this 'twould well be known
I now noe longer was my own.
Yours Freindship made me: from that hower
Was I not always in your power?
Freindship first warmed me with desire
And lodgd in me a secret fier
― 575 ―

Which either time or some kinde blast
Was sure to make flame out at last
If with kinde words you breathd new heat
And made it soon the mastery get
Or a look like lightning came
That on a suddain raisd the flame
It matters not now to enquire
Your power prevaild and all's on fire
[This ends the first column on the page; it is not clear whether the following lines, in the second column, are a continuation or an alternative poem:]
Love without his bow and dart
Like Freindship stole into my heart.
Did Conqueror e're a place disown
Because unstormd he tooke the town?
Tell me Clora what will please
A Victory that comes with ease?
What easier conquest can you have
Then what soft freindship to you gave?
Or like some Hero would you toile
In armes, before you ceizd the spoile?
Tis your complaint I kept the feild
And struggld long e're I did yeild.
Must I not love because a freind?
Who begins there must he there end?
With as much reason you may say
That those faint colours which doe lay
Foundation for the nobler die
Ought imperfect thus to lie
Dull and uselesse fade and waste
Without the flameing Scarlet dip at last.
Your cold disdain bids me no longer live
Your Freindship bids me hope all you can give
Pray tell me Clora with what art you will
Preserve your Freind and yet your Lover kill
Then with a sigh closeing what he had said
Upon her boosome dropd his drooping head
Endorsed by Locke: Verses 82/3
― 576 ―

753. Locke to John Hoskins or Thomas Stringer, 26 January 1683 (528; 653, 754)
Victoria and Albert Museum, Forster collection, MS. 363. Torn, but probably no part of text lost; some words affected by creases. Locke was at Clapham from 17 January until 8 February, visiting London for the day on 3 February: Journal. Hoskins was probably in London; Stringer at Wimborne St. Giles: Christie, Shaftesbury, ii. 459-60.
Claph<a>m†a 26o Jan 82/3
Sir
You will easily imagin what a sad surprize the news of the inclose was to me here this morning.†1 where I have been by my indispotion confined to my bed ever since wednesday was seventh night.†2 The circumstances I was in both of body and minde made me very uncapeable of adviseing in such an occasion of this, all the returne I was able <to>†a make to the Gent letter was to write to Mr Anth: Shepheard†3 at Amsterdam that I thought they would there thinke it best to Land as neare as might be to St. Giles's and therefor would thinke Poole the fitest place to come to. But least y<ou>†b might thinke fit to direct other wise there and because the matter may require other considerations in reference to other circumstances I have thought it best to send away to you the inclosed with all possible speed and have writ word <i>nto†b Holland, that if the body will keepe soe long it might be convenient to stay till they heare from St Giles's. I am
Sir
your most humble servant
J LOCKE

754. Thomas Stringer to Locke, 12 February 1683 (753, 1028, 1038)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, ff. 153-4.
Feb: 12th. 1682
Deare Sir
I am very glad to heare that you are soe well as to come againe to London, having gott soe much grownde of your distemper in Cold weather I hope with carefull usuage you may in a little time perfect your Recovery. My Lady†1 thanks you very kindly for your friendshipp and readynesse to doe her service in this time of her great affliction, She hath ordered me to tell you that your Company would be very acceptable to her, but yett she would not have you by any means to undertake such a jorney to endanger your health, for she sayth you cannot doe her better service then by being kinde to your selfe, and endeavouring to sett your selfe firm upon your leggs. I did sometime sinc order a Copie of the Trust to be delivered to Sir William and mr Clark,†2 (which mr Eyre†3 hath sinc writt he hath delivered them), and alsoe hath given Sir William Some Generall account of the Trust, and could I but come to speake with them I should easily Convince and satisfye them about it. I was in great hopes that you was in soe good a Condition that Travelling might have been usefull to you, and that we might have been soe happy to have seen you all three here together. besides the great advantage it would have been to my Poore Ladys buisnesse, it would have been some enterteynement to you to heare the account both mr Heighmore†4 mr Cheswell†5 and my selfe should have given you of our old friend mr Hoskins, the Strangenesse would appeare very surprising to you, and if we could not bring very good witnesses of the truth of it an Exact relation would seem very incredible. But I am in great hopes when Sir William and mr Clark doe know the
― 578 ―

whole State of that matter, mr Hoskins's Capriciousnesse will have but little influence upon them, lett them not apprehend any greater danger from his not acting then what he hath discovered, for I dare to sweare he hath given them his best reasons. it may be the principle thing he will kepe to him selfe not because he thinks it will deterr them for Acting but for feare they should be feircer in it, and more violent against him then I have been. of this I have given Sir William Some accout. My Lady doth own exceeding great obligations to mr Clarke for his kinde offer to come out of Somersettshire hether. I could hartily wish it would be agreeable to Sir Williams Health and other Concerns to meete him here, And that you were in such Circumstances that you might be the better for Travelling, but upon noe other score we cannot desire it. I beleive my Ladys occations will keepe her here yett this month or five weeks before she wilbe able to dispatch to returne for London. There is all possible respect payd to my Lord of Shaftesbury and his Lady,†1 and what ever returns they are pleased to make, they are sure of nothing but Civill and faire treatment from hence. I hartily wish you health and subscribe in much sincerity
Deare Sir
Your most affectionate and Faithfull servant
T: S:
you have all good wishes from hence.
Address: For mr John Lock at Thanett House in Aldersgate Streete London Postmark: -E 14
Endorsed by Locke: T. Stringer 12 Feb. 82/3

756. Mrs. Deborah Richards to [Edward Clarke?], 19 February 1683
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, f. 17. Copy in Edward Clarke's hand. Michell is perhaps a fictitious name used by Locke in place of Clarke's. The copy is unlikely to have reached Locke before the end of the year. The writer is the widow of John Richards (no. 675); she is mentioned as being in Balasore Road on 22 July 1682; she engaged in trade in Balasore (in Orissa) and died there on 20 May 1683: Hedges, Diary, i. 31-2, 70, 91.
Ballosore February the 19th 1682.
Honoured Sir
I suppose you long er'e this have hear'd of my most sad misfortune which has proved allmost too heavy for mee to beare, for after my sad deplorable Condition that I was left in which was in three dayes after wee sett sayle from the Down's That my Deare Mr. Richards Dyed†1 and left mee with Child, but soon after I miscarryed, And as soon as I Landed a most violent Flux seised upon mee, and continued verie bad for five moneth's which rendred mee uncapable of serving any of my Freinds, or my owne selfe, or else I had Returned this yeare my selfe, For the whole Countrey is in soe much disturbance that there is few or noe private Concerns sent home this yeare, And therefore must begg yours and your Lady's Pardon hopeing the next Shipping it will make up the Losse of this yeare, which God willing I will send or Bring home my selfe to you and All poore Mr. Richard's's Adventurers verie truly and justly, soe Remaine with my humble service to your selfe and Lady, I am,
Sir
your most Faithfull servant
DEBORAH RICHARDS:
Deare Sir
I humbly Begg that you would see Doctor Locke and tell Him the same that I have Writt to you, which shall bee Fathfully performed, with my humble service to Him:
This is a true Coppy of Mrs. Richards her Letter taken from the
originall by mee: E:C:
Endorsed by Locke: Mrs. Richards 19 Feb. 82 to Mr Michell an Apothecary in Covent Garden

757. Locke to Edward Clarke, 20 February [1683] (739, 758)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 177. Year from contents. Printed in Rand, pp. 88-9.
London 20 Feb:
Deare Sir
I have not seen a businesse goe easier then that about litle mis's remove to Ditton, nor more jumbled then mine with mr Clark. We were at Ditton your Lady and I the day after you went. we found Mas: very well and lusty and soe he continues for such was the news Charles brought to Salisbury Court last night. Nurse is to bring Mas: Hadley to town on thursday next to be weaned, and the same day Mis will be sent for from Stanmore and be put into her hands soe that all that businesse will be as well as is possible, and I hope the event will be as successfull as the begining has been in all the parts lucky and as far as I can guesse Mistris's minde is at rest about it†1
I have had two or three deeds ingrossed for my Mortgage to Mr Clark,†2 wherein the trouble has been his, the fault other peoples. The first thing that disturbd the draught you left, was that the Rectory was left out of the recovery which was sufferd of Overton and soe it could not be well conveyd to him by my Lord P.†3 nor the rent thereof to me by him. To supply this defect my mony being ready he resolvd to give me Sanford for security. when that deed was ready for the seale and upon the point of being executed in comes one of my Lords Officers with whom Mr Clark goeing to Mr G. Eyers†4 returns satisfied to goe on with the payment of the mony, which he was at a stand in before and then returning desires me to take my security on Overton for that he should have need of Sanford for the raiseing of more mony and a greater sum. I that desird noe thing but to be securd and willing to ease as much as I could the perplexity of a man to whom I could impute none of this
― 582 ―

uncertainty and seemd to me to act very candidly. I tooke the rents of Overton, with the Reversions of the farme and manner for my security and that only for three months Mr Clark being earnest to have it for noe longer time, because he thought it too great a security for such a sum. and I was willing to oppose none of his conveniencys that might consist with my security. Soe that the matter is as good as left to be setled between him and you when you come to towne. I have yet noe Copy of any of the deeds but of Tregonills lease and release.†1 those with the Mortgage in your name and his bond are left with your Lady. If noe new thing happen I shall goe out of town on Thursday next†2 with Dr Thomas and then the next news you heare from me will be from St Giles's. Your Lady and the rest of the company at Salisbury court are well. I am
Deare Sir
your most humble servant
J LOCKE
I am commanded by your Lady whom I am now with to send you her kinde remembrance. I have taken place in Salisbury coac<lb/> .†a
758. Locke to Edward Clarke, 22 February 1683 (757, 759)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 4. Printed in Rand, pp. 89-91.
Salisbury court 22 Feb. 82/3
Deare Sir
Your Cosin Clarke tells me he has now pretty well setled his businesse and is goeing out of town to morrow. he has now all the writeings in his custody with a receit and releases from Mr Fowles. He has not yet given me the copys of them only of Tregonhils lease and release as I told you in my last but he has promised me to send up attested copys of all that you shall thinke necessary by you.
I write this in your closet your Lady by me and mis in the Cradle in the next roome. She was sent for to day and Nurse Edeling came with her though not sent for. The child is thriven since wee saw it there, but yet your Lady has resolvd to put it into Nurse Trents
― 583 ―

hands to morrow who is also come to town with Mr Hadley to leave him here, and that for these plain reasons. First because the thriveing of the child since your last seeing of it, argues some neglect in the nurse before, which the dissatisfaction appeard in you†a for her not thriveing has made her mend since, and should have been the effect of her care and tendernesse sooner. 2O Tis agreed that Nurse Edeling has very litle or noe milk and Nurse Trent plenty soe that if sucking agrees with her there she may have it. and if Feeding does better Nurse Trent can doe that as well as the other. To which you must adde a third noe lesse considerable and that is that upon long experience your Lady can with more satisfaction and confidence trust Nurse Trents care then the other, who never gave her soe much reason to suspect her neglect in two yeare as this has don in three months. This resolution I hope will be of good successe to the child and in the meane time put both your mindes at rest haveing donne that which upon consideration was thought best and most reasonable to be don
Sir James Edwards†1 tells your Lady that Mr Cawleys son is well approved of the company but yet is like to misse his imployment in the East India company unlesse some body else give security for him as well as his father hath donne since they admitt none without two give bond, and the ships will in a short time be goeing. Your Lady sends you word of this without any direction from Sir James Edwards but only out of charity to a lad she has seen you concerned for and thinks you may take some order with his father about it now you are pretty neare him. I shall god willing be on my way to St. Giles's to morrow morning and I am now pleased with the accident that hinderd me from goeing with Dr Thomas to day since it gave me the oportunity to be here to see the child and discourse with your Lady about it before I left the town. I am
Deare Sir
Your most humble servant
J LOCKE

759. Locke to Edward Clarke, 2 March 1683 (758, 761)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 5. Printed in Rand, pp. 91-2.
St Giles's 2 Mar 82/3
Deare Sir
Tis great pitty that a man who hath soe much reall freindship as you have should put it in a dresse which is commonly made use of to cover the defects and failings of that which is lesse sincere. And did I not know you very well I should be at a losse how to understand the great thanks you send me which soe litle belong to me. But I allow those expressions I finde in your two letters of 21. and 24 Feb: to the concernement I know you have for those things wherein I have donne litle more then shew my willingnesse to serve you, And†a- must not-†a yet in the meane time (whilst you talke soe much of my favours) forget those greater obligations I have to you. But to put an end to discourses of this nature give me leave to assure you once for all, that I beleive of your kindenesse whatsoever you desire I should. and I beg you to beleive of me that I cannot have greater satisfaction then to finde occasions of acknowledging it. My Lady†1 is very sensible of your kindenesse to her and returns you her thanks. But things goe on now soe well here, that I thinke there will be noe need of presseing Sir William C.†2 to come down and without that I suppose he will scarce come, and therefor you may not be much affraid of any summons to meet here, if it should happen such care shall be taken as you desire. Tis thought my Lady will be able to get hence by Lady day, pray send me word how long you intend to stay at Chipley.
The proceedings of mr H†3 here have been wonderfull, the storys soe many and soe stra<nge>,†b that if they were not confirmd by every body and severall sober and ...†b twould be impossible to bel<eive them>.†b Your C<osin>†b Clark I beleive will have spoken with you
― 585 ―

before this come to you and thereby you will understand how our businesse was setled at last. I refer my self wholy to you in the affair In whose hands I count it as safe as my owne, and I doubt not but you will take care that the security shall be good and sufficient in all the parts of it. Mr Stringer presents his service to you and desires you would remember to pay to his man Simons sister at Spaxton†1 the mony you had of him in Mich. terme last. I hope ere this you have received an account from your Lady of her satisfaction in the remove of Mis and I hope the next news will be of her thriveing well at Ditton. I am
Deare Sir
Your most affectionate humble servant
J LOCKE
Address: For Mr Edward Clark at Chipley To be left at the Posthouse at Taunton post paid

760. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 20 March [1683] (752, 763)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 110-11. Year from Locke's endorsement.
I could never have thought that you who use so often to Commend the Countrey to us, would ever have Complain'd of its being Dull, and of its makeing You so. For my Part I have always found the quite Contrary Effect from it, and therefore have lately had some thoughts of trying for a few Days whether the fresh Aire neare Hamstead†2 would not better my Invention, to the Badness of which you are Oblig'd that you have not hitherto received one Impertinent Line from me. Nor is it any thing now but Pure Crossness which makes me write to you, it comeing into my Mind that you would not have me to do so, and therefore told me not how I might Direct a Letter to you, beleeveing I would be so stout as not to ask. But if this was your designe, you will see that it did not succeed, Or that I can Devine when I have an Occasion, and a Mind
― 586 ―

to do so. That I should be so Spightfull now, cannot sure seeme Strange, Since they say it is Natural to Ilnatur'd People when they are Vex'd themselves to take Pleasure in makeing Others so, And you may easilie imagine that none of the East-India Merchants are in very good Humour at Present.†1 However with all my Crossness I am nevertheless
Your Humble Servant
PHILOCLEA.
March the 20th.

Deare Sir
I hope you got safely to town last night and found your Lady and all well at your arrivall, whereof I shall be very glad to receive the good news. I got yesterday a returne†2 for your mony at Ten days sight. I could not meet with any that could doe it sooner, and Mr Minifie who was Major of this place the last yeare Dr Thomas assures me is a very good man, and will be in London himself the begining of this weeke. Your mony upon two or three tellings wanted a shilling which I added to it to make just Thirty seven pounds Besides fourteen shillings and six pence which he refusd as not good mony, I made up with other of my owne which yet I doubt not but I shall part with before I see you in London. We had here yesterday a foot race, if it can be called a race where there is but one and he not to run neither. for the wager was that he would walke twenty miles†3 in five howers. The Walker won by an hower
― 587 ―

and seven minutes. My service to your Lady and the rest of your good company. I am
Deare Sir
Your most humble servant

762. Locke to Edward Clarke, 27 March 1683 (761, 770)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, nos. 8 and 9. The letter is written apparently on a large sheet of paper, the prescription on a small one; either or both may be incomplete. Printed in Rand, pp. 93-4.
Salisbury 27 Mar 83
Deare Sir
On Sunday last I sent you a bill for 37l drawn on one William  †b at the Sarazens head in Friday street by his master Mr Minifie of this towne, who went hence for London yesterday and soe will be in town to pay you himself. I repete this to you here again, that if the bill and my last letter should have miscaried, you might goe to Mr Minifie for the mony by the same token he promised to tell it again on Saturday last to see whether there were noething over, which yet he did not.
I am troubled for your Ladys and sons cough but I hope neither of them will be of any longue continuance and I am very glad the Children are gon again into the country ayer for soe I conclude they are ere this time. If your Ladys cough continues I would advise her to take about seven ounces of bloud, and purge the next day, takeing five of the pills prescribd, and the cordial draught at night after it. if she has six stools or more with the pills it will be well enough, else let her take them agen two days after addeing one or two proportionably as she found them worke before and take again the cordiall draught at night, after that the Lambative and emulsion
― 588 ―

I doubt not but will perfectly put an end to her cough. I am sorry I am forced to send soe long <a>†a bill, which I feare will be apt to fright her from doeing any thing, but this I am sure is the safest way and though there be much writeing tis in effect noething but a purge lambative and emulsion
For your son if his cough does not abate of it self let him be purged with half an ounce of manna dissolvd in beere or posset drinke, which if it worke not to 5 or 6 stools increase the dose and repeat it again a day or two after. Let him continue the use of the syrup or mixture for his ague according to the direction I have here sent, only after every purgeing let him take at night goeing to bed three spoonfulls and†b the†b next morning three spoonfulls twice resting fower howers between, and then let him take it after wards again in a smaller quantity as he does now, I am Sir
your most humble servant†c
I thinke of returning to morrow to St Giless and hope our stay there will not now be long if there be occasion pray send for me, in the meane time let me heare. Dr Thomas is your humble servant. My service to your Lady and the rest of your good company
[Enclosure:]

763. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 7 April [1683] (760, 779)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 112-13. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Were it to any Body but you (from whom I expect Thanks) I should beg Pardon for not writeing all this while, Notwithstanding that my concerns in Merchandise†1 has neither put me out of Humour for That, or any thing else. It has not beene that I have thought I should be less Spightfull in doing it now, then I beleev'd I was about three Weeks since (for with Mee (who have no faith in Astrologie) it will not Pass, that you foresaw what would be the Consequence of giveing me no Direction) I beleeve still that you had the same Designe, notwithstanding that you would now seeme to disowne it, because it succeeded not. But haveing let you see that I understood you, and knew how to be Spightfull if I would, I have ever since had so little Disposition to be so, that in Continuing it I should certainly but have beene so to my self most. You see how much a little Time may Alter one, And that in Spight of Spightfulness good Nature will at last Prevail. However do not attribute it wholly to Excess of Goodness, since I beleeve if I was to be Examin'd about it It would not be found the onely Cause.
I am your humble servant
PHILOCLEA.
April the 7th

765. Locke to Charles Cudworth, 27 April 1683
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, ff. 35-6. Draft. Printed in King, pp. 249-51. For Cudworth see p. 539, n. 2. Locke had returned to London on 7 April: p. 593 n.
London. 27 Apr. 83
Sir
Though you are got quite to the other side of the world yet you cease not to make new aquisitions here, and the character you have left behinde you makes your acquaintance be sought after to
― 591 ―

the remotest parts of the earth.
There is a commerce of Freindship as well as merchandise and though noe body almost lets his thoughts goe as far as the East Indies without a designe of geting mony and growing rich, yet if you allow my intentions I hope to make a greater advantage by another sort of correspondence with you there. In the conversation I have had the happynesse to have sometimes with your sister here I have observed her often to speake of you with more tendernesse and concerne then all the rest of the world, which has made me conclude it must be something extraordinary in you which has raisd in her (who is soe good a judg,) soe particular an esteeme and affection beyond what is due to the bare ties of nature and bloud. and I cannot but thinke that your soules are akin as well as your bodys and that yours as well as hers is not of the ordinary alloy. I account it none of the least favours she has don me that she has promised me your freindship and you must not thinke it strange if I presume upon her word and trouble you with some enquirys concerning the country you are in, since she incourages me in it and assures me I shall not faile of an answer. Some of those who have traveld and write of those parts, give us strange storys of the tricks donne by some of their Juglers there, which must needs be beyond leger de main and seeme not within the power of art or nature. I would very gladly know whether they are really donne as strange as they are reported, and whether those that practise them are any of them Mahumetans, or all (which I rather suppose) heathens, and how they are looked on by the Bramins and the other people of the country, whether they have any aparitions amongst them and what thoughts of spirits, and as much of the opinions religion and ceremonys of the Hindos and other heathens of those countrys as comes in your way to learne or enquire. It would be too great kindenesse if you could learne any news of any copys of the old or new testament or any parts of them which they had amongst them, in those easterne countrys, in any language, before the European trade thither by the Cape of good hope.†1 I should trouble you also with enquirys concerning their languages learning government manners and particularly Aurange Zebe†2 the Emperor of Indostan, since I could promise my self a more exact account from you then what we have in printed travells, but I feare I have beene more troublesome then what you will imagin will become a man that does but
― 592 ―

now begin to beg your acquaintance.
If I have trespasd herein you must excuse it to the litle destinction I made between you and your sister, you must conclude I forgot my self and thought I was talkeing to, and (as I use to doe) learning some thing of her, and tis to the same account I must beg you to place the obligation you will lay on me by procureing and sending hither an answer to this inclosed letter directed to Mrs Richards.†1 Her husband†a died goeing to the East Indies in a ship that set out hence about Christmas was twelve month, where he was to have been factor somewhere in the bay of Bengale for the company: his wife and two daughters who were with him went on the voyage, where she setled herself and remains now you will easily know. I beg the favour of you to get this inclosed conveyd to her, and an answer from her which be pleasd to direct to be left for me either with Mr P. Percivall at the black boy in Lombard street or Mr J. Cox at the Iron Key in Thames street London. And now haveing been thus free with you tis in vain to make apologies for it. If you allow your sister to dispose of your freindship you will not take it amisse that I have lookd upon my self as in possession of what she has bestowd on me, or that I begin my conversation with you, with a freedom and familiarity suitable to an establishd amity and acquaintance, besides, if at this distance we should set out according to the formes of ceremony, our correspondence would proceed with a more solemne pace then the treaties of princes and we must spend some years in the very preliminarys. He that in his first addresse should only put of his hat make a leg and say your servant Sir to a man at the other end of the world, may, (if the windes sit right and the ships†b come home safe to bring back the returne of his complement,) may I say in two or three years perhaps atteine to some thing that looks like the begining of an acquaintance, and by the next Jubilee there may be hopes of some conversation between them. Sir you see what a blunt fellow your sister hath recommended to you, one as far removd from the Ceremony of the easterne people you are among as from their country, but one that with great truth and sincerity says to you I am
― 593 ―

One thing which I had forgot give me leave to adde which is a great desire to know how the severall people of the east keepe their account of time as months and years and whether they generally agree in any periods answering to our weeks and whether their arithmatike turns at ten as ours doth.
Endorsed by Locke: JL to Mr. C: Cudworth 27 Apr. 83
766. Locke to [Anthony Ashley Cooper, second earl of Shaftesbury?] [late April 1683?]
London, Victoria and Albert Museum, Forster Collection, MSS. 363 and 364. Presumably from the Shaftesbury collection. Draft or copy? In poor condition, with some loss of text by decay or tearing. The addressee from the endorsement and contents. Locke returned from Wimborne St. Giles to London on 6 and 7 April. The present letter suggests that he was in the company of the dowager countess of Shaftesbury; it was evidently written a little while after their arrival in town. It was perhaps submitted to the dowager countess for her approval and so came from her to the third earl and the Shaftesbury collection. There is nothing to show whether a version was sent to the second earl.
My Lord
As I always very readily imbrace all occasions of serveing your Lordship, Soe I am glad I was not hinderd by my wearynesse and some businesse of my owne from giveing your Lordship an account of my Ladys health and safe arrivall here, the night we came to town. For had I staid till the report, which soon followd us, had filled the town with the proceedings at St Giles's as soon as ever my Lady was gon I <would>†a have been at a perfect losse and not known how to write: Since it would have appeard very impertinent if not perfect mockery, to have sent in all hast news of my Ladys welfare to a place, where, things were soe managed (if repor<t>†b say true) as if it were to give the world a declaration, that she, her wel<fare>†b or any thing that belongd to her were very little valued. Those marks of kindenesse to your Lordship and family which my Lady douager left there at her comeing away (to that degree that your Lordship and my Lady could not but expresse great sense of the obligation and call it great bounty) could not but be very pleaseing to all those who looked upon them as pledges of her future kindenesse and strong engagements to suitable returns. And noe body
― 594 ―

who has the least respect for your Lordship can thinke they wish well either to your self, your family or reputation who put you upon such actions as (to say noe thing els) seeme to bid defiance to all my Lady douagers Kinde Inclinations. It is not in the power of good nature, religion or freindship to make any one soe stupid as to be wholy insensible of continued ill usage and indignitys, And when repeated actions have made impressions of that kinde what other <r>esolutions†a they may in time produce everybody knows.
My Lord I beg your Lordship pardon for giveing you this trouble. your Lordship I am sure knows how litle apt I am to medle in other peoples matters, but I must professe my selfe soe much an humble servant to all that are related <to>†b my Lord your father that I cannot but thinke it my duty to advise your Lordship of what is soe visible that all the world talks of it and to assure your Lordship that I am
Endorsed (not by Locke): to my Lord.
Noted (a seventeenth-century hand?): Mr Lock Lord Shaftesbury about the year 1684- or 5

768. James Tyrrell to Locke, [c. 27 May 1683] (750, 775)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 48-9. Locke's endorsement gives presumably the date on which he received the letter.
Dear Carmelin
I was in good hope I should have heard from you this week how you did and when you will come downe; but perhaps either your comeing is like to be very quick, or els, your expectations of my being in Towne may have hindred you from writeing to me, to remove which obstacle I shall let you know, that Sorrell is not yet in a condition for the market, neither if he were is the weather so inviteing as to make me venture upon a Journey on horseback at a time when it raines more, or lesse every day: I suppose my Father and Mother,†2 and brother and sist: Cavendish†3 will be in Towne this week if possible if†a my brother could get well of a fit of the gout which he is at this time much tormented with. as for the state of things here, your Patient†4 is not like to be well this half year, for I doubt she is breeding, haveing besides other symtomes a constant sicknesse in her stomach after meat, but†b- this inter nos.-†b here is fallen out a very sad accident A Dog fell mad last†c- week, and-†c has bit divers Children, and amongst the rest Jo: Clerks little boy, (a very pretty Child) by the hand, wee are all in great care for it. and have given it divers medicines, and have lett it blood, and purged it; and I would have given it the broad leaved
― 597 ―

mosse you shewed me could I have told how to have presently had it. but my Mother says that you shewed her the same sort in our bowling green walk; which I have gatherd, and intend the Child shall take it powderd, in beer, but I would be glad to know how long or how often he must doe it. I have one favour more to beg of you. if it stand with your convenience John Hicks I suppose you know has bin in some trouble, and writes to me for some money I owe him. I have returned him up 10l. this week, and would have sent him more could I have spared it from my owne occasions: but if you can doe it (without straitneing your self) pray pay him ten pounds more, and place it to my account, and I will pay it you againe either at Midsummer or Michaelmasse next at farthest, and I will in the meane time give you a note of my hand for it. I have sent this by him that He may know your answere, and that if you cannot doe it I may provide it some other way for him. pray remember to send or bring downe the books, and French maps with you when you come, I am
yours heartily
MUSIDORE

770. Locke to Edward Clarke, 24 August 1683 (762, 771)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 12. Printed in Rand, pp. 94-5.
The following documents preserved with Locke's correspondence belong to the period between 31 May and 24 August:
Two drafts for indentures, 12 and 13 June, both in Clarke's hand: Locke buys from Clarke for £800 the manor of Bradford in Somerset, and some
― 599 ―

other land; he redemises the property to Clarke in return for an annuity of £100. MS. Locke b. 8, nos. 173-4.
Receipt (fragment), 2 August, signed by Locke for sum of £31 11s. 2d. received from (William) Stratton. MS. Locke c. 19, f. 21.
Power of attorney, 10 August, Locke to William Stratton in respect of his Somerset property; witnesses Charles Cheswell and Michael Hook. Ibid., ff. 22-3.
Assignment of bond, 15 August: Charles Morgan, gentleman, and Maurice Hunt, esquire, both of St. Martin in the Fields, by their obligation dated 2 February 1682 are bound to Locke in the sum of £300 for the payment to him of £150 with interest on the third day of August next following the date of the obligation; Locke now for a consideration grants to Clarke the obligation, with full power to act in his name in regard to it; same witnesses as last. MS. Locke b. 8, no. 10.
Power of attorney, 22 August, Locke to both Clarke and Stratton, or either of them, in respect of his Somerset estates: same witnesses as last. Ibid., no. 11.
Locke left London on 14 June; he spent some time at Oxford, with visits to Oakley, Cirencester, Purton, and perhaps Salisbury; was probably at Sutton on 1 and 2 August, and then perhaps at Purton and Salisbury: Journals and the documents noted above. He appears to have visited Chipley also in this period: below.
Purton 24o Aug. 83
Deare Sir
I hope this letter will meet you and your Lady at Sutton soe far safe on your way to London, whether I wish you a good journey and then your Lady a happy delivery there of her great belly†1 but I hope to see you there before that time.†2 I have by the same hand writt to my Cosin Stratton to pay you what money he has of mine in his hands. I hope it will be noe inconvenience to you to receive it at Sutton for I suppose if you should not need it yet Mrs Strachey†3 has money in London and soe it will be a convenient way of returne for both her and me. I am soe used to trouble you that you would almost beare it out of custome as I presume upon prescription, but I must ascribe it to the true cause your extraordinary kindenesse to which it is but a poore but all the returne I can make to assure you that I am with perfect esteeme and affection
Deare Sir
Your most humble and most obleiged servant

771. Locke to Edward Clarke, 26 August 1683 (770, 773)
Rand, pp. 95-8. Locke was with Dr. Thomas on 25 August: Journal.
26th Aug. 1683.
Dear Sir,
Would your friendship or my occasions permit it, this paper might be with more decency employed in the return of my thanks for the kindnesses you have already done me than in putting you upon the trouble of doing me more, but so it is I can only increase the score and with far better opportunity of acknowledgment. I have herewith sent you many papers. You will know how and how far and in what occasions they are to be made use of better than I. What you dislike you may burn. I have sent amongst them a letter of attorney to Mr. P. P;†2 if you think that a fit place to lodge money in pray give it him, for I thought it convenient to have somebody in London to lodge and return it: if you should leave the town you must be judge whether this be well contrived, and so I pray order it accordingly.
My Lady Shaftesbury has, I suppose, money in one Mr. Prince's†3 or some other hands in Amsterdam. Pray talk with her about it, for that probably may both suit her and my occasions, but mention not me but a friend of yours you will be responsible for, for I would be private at least till you hear from me again. For I would gladly have all the money I could returned to me as soon as conveniently may be, and that for several reasons; and therefore I would be glad you could get the money of Mr. Morgan†4 to be returned with others as soon as you can. If he will not pay it presently, I think it
― 601 ―

would be best to put it into your or P. Percivall's or R. <Smithsby's>†a name†1 by changing the bond.
You remember the word papers. This enclosed will guide you to a gentlewoman in whose hands are lodged the writings concerning my annuity.†2 Those I think were best to be sealed up and left with her still. In another paper sealed up you will find a bond of Dr. Thomas's for fifty pounds,†3 which pray deliver him, with other writings of the like kind which dispose of as you think fit, though I think they will be best there till you have occasion to make use of them. There is an other paper also sealed up which what it contains I suppose you will guess by the shape of it from what I have formerly told you. You may consider whether you think it best to lie there or no. There is also a purse of gold, about 100 guineas I suppose in value. The ruby ring in it give her, and all the other pieces that are wrapped up in little papers to keep them for me. The onyx ring with a seal cut in it, if you please, accept from me. This purse with all in it I would also have lie there till you have an opportunity to return the money to me; for if that cannot be done I would have it rest all with her, only the two rings there I would have you take, the one for your self, the other for your Lady. It will all be ready there for you to call for at any time whenever you have an opportunity to return it. I would desire you to enquire of Mr. Bray, one of the storekeepers of the East India storehouse at Leadenhall, whether he hath had any news from <Mrs. Richards>†bof anything concerning me, and to take order in that matter as it shall require. When Syll comes to town  †c for his subsistence or journey pray supply him. I have ordered him to
― 602 ―

receive money in other places, of which if you will ask him he will give you an account.†1
In the same place as Dr. Thomas's bond you will find a bond of my cousin Bonville's for twenty pounds. I lent it him to help set him up, and design to receive nor use nor to call in the principal till my own necessities force me. And if I die before I call for it, and he behave himself well to me, which you will know from Dr. Thomas, I would have the bond given up to him. I have given order to Mr. <Pawling>†a to send up to you when he sends you your coach glass with a little red trunk of mine, in which you will find my book of accounts, which I put into your hands for two reasons, first that you may see how my moneys stand, and so get in what money you find owing to me where the sums are considerable enough to give you the trouble, and next to let you see therein my method. Pray keep this book as safe as you can. Stands ready cased. Dr. Thomas has paid me now at Salisbury fifty pounds, and therefore pray deliver him up his bond: how our account stands you will see by that book. I have ordered Mr. Pawling to return you some money he has of mine. I think it is not much. What he sends take without asking any account from him, for I am sure he will keep back nothing that is mine.†2 Dr. Thomas, who brings you this, comes almost on purpose about my affairs, whom pray advise in my concernments. What news the Old Bailey affords from time to time I would gladly receive from you.†3 The key of that little red trunk before mentioned Dr. Thomas has: it serves to that and a little leather standish I have in Oxford. I have writ to Mr. Pawling to send you also my hat and clothes, which I should be glad to receive if they can be sent me. Mr. Ashurst†4 or some such man will advise you how. If Dr. Thomas remove my things to a good place, I think you were best lock my book of accounts up in my scriptor†5 when you go out of town; and to this purpose keep the key of the
― 603 ―

scriptor till then, and then you may be pleased to leave it with Mrs. Grig, from whom Dr. Thomas had it. Mrs. Grig may be heard of at the Dean of Canterbury's†1 or Dr. Blomer's, but this as all other I leave to you wholly, only I would be glad to have that book safe.
Pray talk with Dr. Thomas about the best way of securing the books and goods in my chamber at Christ Church if there should be any danger. There is a pair of silver candlesticks, too, and a silver standish of mine in Mr. Percivall's hands. When a safe and sure way of returning money to me is found, I would have them also turned into money and returned to me. Upon consideration I have thought it best to make a will, which you will find amongst the other papers, by which you may be legally entitled to whatsoever I leave; and it being uncertain whether that may be more or less, I can without making another formal will give you new directions to dispose of what I shall leave as occasions and circumstances may vary. I have assigned over my annuity, due from my Lady Shaftesbury, to Dr. Thomas, who has promised to leave the assignment with you and a declaration of trust,†2 and if there be occasion to assign it to Mr. Tyrrell.
I am, perfectly yours,
J. L.
All my wearing linen, flannel shirts, waistcoats, stockings, either at Dr. Goodall's or Oxford, I would have sent to me.
My old suits and a cloak at London I would have sold forthwith†a for
