773. Locke to Edward Clarke, 21 November/1 December [1683?] (771, 776)
Rand, pp. 98-100. Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. The date is problematical. According to the text the most recent letter from Clarke that Locke had received was dated 3 October; according to Locke's Journal Clarke wrote to him on 5, 9, and 19 October; he made notes of these letters on 9, 15, and 23 October, O.S. The contents of the letter in general fit 1683 and do not fit any other likely year. If the mention of Cambridge alludes to Philoclea the letter cannot be later than 1684 as she married Sir Francis Masham in June 1685 and went to live at Oates; and it can scarcely belong to 1684 as Philoclea wrote to Locke on 25 August and 8 October of that year. The discrepancy is perhaps due to an error in the text, Rand's or Locke's, '3rd Oct.' for 23 October, Locke giving the date of entry in his Journal instead of that (19 October) of Clarke's letter. The 'long month' would then be an expression of his impatience and not a simple record of the lapse of time. As Locke uses either old-style or double dates in his Journal until 18/28 December 1683, the date here is presumably old style.
Locke wrote to Mrs. Clarke about the beginning of February: no. 774.
21st Nov.
Dear Sir,
I begin now to be in pain by your silence. The latest date I have from you being the 3rd Oct., which I may now call a long month
― 605 ―

since. For as there is nobody to whom I have greater obligations than to you, so I can truly say that whether I consider gratitude, friendship, or inclination, there is nobody in the world can upon any of these scores be more concerned for you and yours than I am upon every one of them. And if I may with freedom tell it you, I can with great sincerity assure you that that which most sensibly touches in my own private affairs is my absence from a man I so perfectly love and esteem and my being out of the way of giving him those marks I would of it. I think you know me so well that you will not suspect this to have the least of compliment. And if you reflect upon my former letters, and consider with what a blunt confidence I have troubled you in my affairs, you will have reason to think me guilty on the other side, though you put in some allowance for the reasons that made it almost necessary for me to write to you in such a style. But now in truth I could hold no longer, and I must tell you again I am in pain till I hear from you. I know that the painful hour must by this time have overtaken your Lady, and I long to hear that 'tis safely over: when you assure me of that, and that she and you and the little ones are well, I shall be at rest and be at much more ease than I am at present.
About the middle of October I sent you a letter wherein were four others inclosed, whereof one was to Mr. Tyrrell at Oakley and an other to Mr. Paul.†1 They were open that you might read them and then convey them if you thought fit, for that authority I give you over all my letters that come to your hands, you being a better judge in the place than I can be at this distance. I shall [not] trouble you with any petition or anything more concerning those letters till I hear from you again. I writ to you also an answer to the advise you gave concerning Roberts and Sheldate, and desire you to consider whether upon the whole matter if the gent. had still any business here that you should [acquaint] her that the person whom Roberts talked so simply of is ready to serve her, and that it was declined no longer than whilst he thought he should not stay long enough in that place when that business lay to do it, having at first designed to make but a very little stay in it; and that if there be any occasion still, and she thinks still to employ him, he desires she would keep both his being there and his being employed in her business private even from Mr. Sheldate. The reason why he thought this offer fit to be made her was that he feared she might
― 606 ―

take it amiss that she had not had the offer of his service when he was in a place capable to serve her, which she will undoubtedly come to hear of. But, as I said then, this is wholly left to your discretion to do in it as you think best, since you said you were almost out of countenance upon this occasion.†1
Michaelmas is now over, but I have not a word of Morgan:†2 it is not intended that you should run the risk of that affair: 'tis enough that you have the trouble. If therefore it be not paid or secured to your satisfaction there will be £50 to be paid at Christmas by Mr. Cheswell,†3 and to balance the account the remainder shall be remitted from hence to you. But however that matter stands I desire you to consider whether you or I or Adrain Thompson†4 were best to give the receipt for that £50 at Christmas, that order may be taken accordingly.
Honest Adrian writes me word that the chest that is now in Mrs.  †a custody was not opened, though he had the key and directions to do it.†5 Neither do I ask whether any thing else in her custody was opened, only give me leave to tell you that I either think or dreamt you enquired of me concerning the title of a treatise, part whereof is in Mr. Smith's hands, and it is Tractatus de morbo Gallico.†6 If there were another copy of it I should be very glad to have that at any reasonable rate, for I have heard it commended and shall apply myself close to the study of physic by the fireside this winter. But of this I shall write to you more hereafter, when I hear there are more copies than one, for else it will not be reasonable to desire it. I desire also to know whether Dr. Sydenham hath published any thing this year.†7
Though I would not give you the trouble of public news which gazettes and news-letters tell of, yet I would be glad to hear sometimes
― 607 ―

of my old friends, how Thomas†1 does and where he is, how the trust goes on,†2 and how J. H. plies.†3 What news from Cambridge,†4and whether there be no complaints from thence of a friend of yours, for something of my particular acquaintance and friends [will be] welcome to me. For I perceive, let me be as much a hermit as I will, let me endeavour to separate myself from the world as much as I can, that part will not stick to me as long as I have any life, any thought, left, and I shall still have a sensible part left for the concerns of my friends and acquaintance. And truly, could I have but the conversation of some few persons I could name, with quiet and freedom, I could well forget all the gaudy superfluity of this life; nay, I should think myself very happy if I could but tell you once a day to your face how much
I am, Dear Sir,
your most affectionate and most obliged servant,
J. LOCKE
There are four of mine besides this, of which I am uncertain whether any of them be come to your hand.
1684
February
774. Locke to Mrs. Mary Clarke, [early February 1684?] (724, 777)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, nos. 163 and 164. Printed in Rand, pp. 101-2. If no. 164, a printed slip, is the 'litle peice of frost worke' mentioned in the letter, it could not reach Locke before 29 January, and, allowing for post-days, probably not before 1 February, O.S.
Madam
If your lieing in will as you say produce long letters as certainly as I finde it does fine children I advise for my own sake as well as that of your family that master and you would get to worke again as hard as you can drive that you might lye in again as soon as may be, for I long as much as ever you did for mulberys that you should have two or three boys more, and for a long letter that should tell me how good a time you have had and how the litle one thrives for methinkes you doe soe very well at both that tis pitty but you should keepe your hand in. But pray doe not mistake and conclude
― 608 ―

from hence that I shall expect a letter but once a yeare from you. If I have a great letter noe oftener then you have got a great belly perhaps I shall not fall out with you but I shall grumble shreudly if you will not afford me a few words oftener then that. I am exceeding glad to heare the good news of your haveing passed your time soe well and being soe well up again. I was I confesse in peine when I heard noe news of you about that time and though my silly lungs doe but ill brooke your aire in the winter yet I wishd my self often in the warme chamber and the good company you mention, I thinke I could make as good a gossip as any in your parish for savoury discourse and keepeing the fire warme, Indeed I have not yet much perfected my hand in drinkeing, But I hope soe to harden my lungs this winter with turfe smoke that they will be able by the springe to defye the stoutest of your gossips boules and then have at you. I thanke god I have not been soe well these many years in winter, If you please to come hither you shall not heare me cough once in <a>†a whole day togeather and into the bargain you shall see new fashons, new housewifery, new cookery, new sights, too much to be put into a letter. I am glad to heare the litle one is soe lusty a girle,†1 but I take it amisse that all your talke is of her and soe litle of My pretty Mistresse†2 I shall not endure that this new comer shall in the least put her out of favour. In a former letter to Mr Clarke I told you that there appeard noe reason to me to apprehend that your nurses being rickety when she was a child should make her milke lesse wholsome now if she be otherwise healthy and of a good constitution now, that being a disease which though it criples pore children yet when age and strength gets over it makes them not that I have observed weaker or more unhealthy men and women. I wish you and all yours an happy new yeare, that every day of it may bring additions of satisfaction to you till it deliver you up to greater happyness in the following and soe on till you see severall generations I am
Madam
Your most humble and most faithfull servant
J L

775. James Tyrrell to Locke, [c. 23 February 1684] (768, 842)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 50-1. Date from Locke's endorsement, and by calculation from the thaw.
Dear C.
I perceive mine was so long before it was answerd, and the answere has bin so long upon the way, that I was afraid either that our letters had miscarryed, or els what was worse, you had not bin well; and that the extraordinary sharpnesse of the season might have wrought some ill effect upon your lungs: but yours has dispelld all those suspicions, and makes me hope that you are now as well as almost agone when you writ your last†a- of the-†a 26th: of Jan: and therefore I will not keep it long in my pocket without an answere: especially since I am goeing for London within this week, and therefore would give you timely notice of it, that if there be any thing I
― 610 ―

can serve you in there; you may write to me thither, for I intend to stay in Towne, or near it about a fortnight: as for your Patient†1 (who is now walking by me about the roome) she remembers her service to you with many thanks for your great concerne for her health: She was pretty well all the frost: but this last thaw,†2 has set her blood, (like other liquors) on a fresh ferment; so that she has bin full of paines, and windy stitches all up and downe for this fortnight, but I hope it will goe off againe: as the weather settles, and grows drier.
She intends as soon as her Asse Foals to begin another of her soveraign remedyes, Asses milk. As for Jemmy, notwithstanding the care wee have had; yet he could not escape some ill effects of this cold winter; for he got an Ague, (or intermittent) about 6 weeks agone; which after 5, or 6 fits wee drove away with the Cortex; but after a fortnights intermission it returned againe as violent as before; but wee have put it off agen after 5 fits by the same medicine, and I hope it will not returne, for wee give him the powder now for prevention: he is very well at present and much your servant. (as are also the other two) he is goeing next week to school agen before I goe for London, now the days grow long, and the cold weather is over. but I am sure he has great reason to thank you for your kind advice: and now my small concernes are over (which I should not trouble you with but as your kindnesse has made them somewhat to you) I shall now tell you farther concerning your papers,†3 which I have read over with all the care I could a second time, and like them better then at the first, which I take to be one maine signe when I am not fed with empty notions instead of things and I have made bold since it is your foul copy to note it on the blanck pages whene I doubt any thing; or where I think I can illustrate any thing you have sayd by a fitter example; but whether those scribleings will signify any thing to your work now it is put into another order, I know not but
― 611 ―

shall leave them to your Judgment when you look them over: If they doe not I have my end however which was to please my self in the writeing my present thoughts: and I can tell you farther that I have likewise read lately what Du Hamel,†1 or Mr: Hobs have†a done†a (who in his little tract of humane nature†b †2 has done the best hitherto on that subject) and I find as much difference, as between a Short Epitomee, and an exact work: besides the newnesse of a great many notions which I cannot find by what I have read have bin ever started before, so that I think you will have very little reason to lay by any thing for being stale. so that if your thinking has bin your hunting, and hawking this winter, I may safely say it has bin mine to read what you have thought on and put together with so much Judgment: so that I long for that happy hour when a warmer season may bring us together againe; and that I may see your excellent work in its utmost perfection: but I long more to see the Authour, who if he likes the place within a mile of an Ivy Steeple†3 better then France, or the long dark entry,†4 I suppose it is because there is a little more sincerity here, then in the former; and somewhat more chat, and light then in the latter. tho' it be like that but a dull melancholy place (God knows) when C. is not here, to whom I imagined my self talking i<n>†c a full carrere, till I am come to the end of my tedder, and have no more <to ru>nne,†c then to adde that I am yours
J T
I thank you for the favour of your books but shall not make use of it untill I returne from London. you may direct yours to Mr: Hickss if you write within these 3 weeks. I hear L. is very well at Gl:†d and will be up this spring†5
Address: For Mr: John Lynne†e †6

776. Locke to Edward Clarke, 7/17 March [1684] (773, 780)
Rand, pp. 106-8. Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. The year from the mention of the severe winter and from what appears to be a reference to this letter in no. 808. The endorsement shows that the date is new style.
Amsterdam, 17th March
Sir,
Yours of the 26th February with the former mentioned in it are all come safe to hand. And by one I received from your Lady to-day I find that one of mine, as I feared upon the notice of your journey it would, came the next day after you were gone. I find she intends to trouble you with it in the country. I have therefore taken this shortest way I could imagine to acquaint you that I would not have you disturb your affairs there with any thoughts of my matters of that kind I then desired, for concluding you would begin before your letter would come to your hands I have taken care to have it done in another way. If I should contrary to my custom write news, I should tell you that I think that an evil spirit possesses people everywhere. Here, too, people are writing against one another as hot as may be,†1 and there are every day pamphlets published here that deserve as well to be burnt as the History of the Growth of Popery,†2 or No Protestant Plot,†3 or the like, in other places. Tares and divisions sowing everywhere, and methinks the tares take root and spread apace. Whether the late great conjunction in the heavens†4 make these divisions on earth I know not astrology enough to resolve, but I wish King James's maxim were more in credit on this side the water, and beati pacifici†5 would pass among Christians for good gospel, as I think it would be good policy in defence of Christendom against the great event of war with the Turk.
― 613 ―

But you know I have little skill in politics and therefore may mistake, and so I leave these matters quae supra nos——.†1
I have since my last inquired most particularly of a very skilful man concerning abele†2 and lime trees. He tells me of the abele trees there is but one sort, and in them you cannot be mistaken. Of lime trees there be two sorts, but the best is that which they call the female lime tree. It is that which bears the flowers, and the bark looks a little reddish and is not altogether so sad as the other. The offsets from the roots will grow. If I can light of any here in time enough I will send you some by a ship that is going hence for Exeter, which I conclude will be much more convenient than London and all the long cartage by land. I have not yet got the lime seeds which were promised me, for our highways, that is rivers and canals, are scarce yet quite open. And now I consider you in the country I can not but be talking to you of those innocent designs of building houses and planning walks: the latter is my theme at present. I desire you to make your walks broad enough, that is, let the bodies of the trees stand in two lines twenty foot in each side wider than the outside walls of your house, and then another row on the outside of those twenty further. On the front I think lime trees would do best, on the east side elms, and on the north witch elms, which is a better sort of trees than we commonly imagine. So much at present for walks.
They have no water here but rain water from their houses fit for kitchen uses, and therefore every house has a cistern made of plaster of Paris†3 to hold their rain water. I am learning the way to make them, for methinks that it would do well at Chipley.
Mr. Doem†4 remembers kindly to you. He lately by my encouragement made use of your name to Mr. Codrington†5 in High Street, Bristol, to desire a kindness of him, something about merchant affairs. I desire you to write to Mr. Codrington, and to own it and encourage him to do Mr. Doem any good offices he can in that town. You see I find the way to you wherever you are. I shall be glad to hear from you from hence, and am
your most humble servant,
J. L.
― 614 ―

If you return by Sutton, pray enquire of my cousin Stratton of my affairs, and let him pay to you what money he hath of mine. If you show him these three lines th[ey will] be authority enough. My service to all my friends. I shall be glad to hear if my uncle†1got well over this very sharp winter.
 
Address: For Edward Clarke, Esq., at Chipley.
Endorsed by Clarke(?): J. L. his letter. Received the 15th of March, 1683-4.
― 615 ―

777. Locke to Mrs. Mary Clarke, 8/18 March 1684 (774, 806)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 13. Printed in Rand, pp. 109-10. The postmark shows that the date is new style.
18o March 84
Madam
I am now indebted to you for two letters which I thinke is a shame for†a- an old-†a Batchelor to a young Lady But which very much increases the debt they are two very kinde letters, and such as need a litle allowance to be made to the very great civility of the writer to make them to be understoode without some litle suspition of complement since they cary soe great expressions of thanks for courteseys, which in truth are but some poore acknowledgments of those many I have received from you. I threatend in a former letter to Mr Clarke to quarell with you about it as I found reason I had to doe with him, But it would perhaps be not very handsome to set upon you now you are alone, And if I mistake not it is more becomeing as well as more justifiable for us batchelors to make love then quarell when the husband is away. I thanke you for the good news that the litle ones as well as you your self are all well. I remember I askd a good while since whether Master and my mistris were in towne or noe, but to that I yet finde noe answer. You know or at least ought to beleive that when I have a mistris I am very tender of her. and therefor if my pretty Mis†bBetty be ordered otherwise then I thinke convenient father and mother and all will be sure to heare of it. Perhaps this is but an ill and unpractised way of makeing ones addresse But who can help it we old batchelors are as positive as you maried women and thinke it some times as reasonable to have our wills. Had I known Mr Clarke had been goeing into the country soe soon I should not have troubld him with that letter which you received since his departure. pray trouble him not with it when he is amongst his worke men, it will keepe cold well enoug till he comes to town. Now this terrible winter is almost over (for the Ice is now goeing apace) methinks you and I have had two very good deliverances, you have been well deliverd of a fine girle†1 and I of a scurvy cough, which I thinke, had I been on your side the water this feirce long
― 616 ―

cold weather, would have deliverd me over to the wormes but I thanke god I have had more mastery of it this very contrary season here, then in England I used to have in the most favourable, soe that I cannot repent my journey the greatest inconvenience has been the want of yours and Mr Clarkes good company. I hold you in a tale of my cough and an old pair of rotten lungs in revenge for your not telling me any news of my Lady,†1 nor Mrs Waller,†2 Nor Mrs Cudworth nor Susan†3 nor none of our freinds. Are there noe Amours; noe Gallants; noe marrying nor giveing in mariage; noe storys amongst all our freinds? or doe you thinke we on this side care not what becomes of you on that side the water? If you have thought soe far amisse repent and reforme your heresy and beleive me
Madam
Your most humble and most obedient servant
J L
Pray doe me the favour to send the inclosed to Mr Hicks's by your foot man
Address: These present To Mrs: Mary Clarke at the Lady Kings in Salisbury-Court in Fleet street London
Postmark: MR 11

778. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, 14/24 May 1684 (721, 781) with a note written by Raymond Formentin
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, f. 139. Year from Locke's note. The letter appears to respond rather to a message sent by Locke through Trenchard than to a letter from Locke.
+
ce Jeudi 24. May†a
[Formentin:]
Le Capitaine†4 est infiniment obligé a Monsieur Locke de l'honeur de son souvenir. Monsieur Locke luy fait assurement en cela quelque justice, n'y ayant personne au monde qui l'honore plus que
― 617 ―

luy. Il y a deja trop de pieces inutiles dans son Arsenal, et il seroit fasché de donner la pene a Monsieur Locke de luy en envoyer de nouvelles. Il reçoit neantmoins avec toute la reconnoissance dont il est capable les offres qu'il luy fait, et en contreschange il le prie d'estre persuadé qu'il ne se tiendroit jamais plus heureux que s'il trouvoit l'occasion de luy marquer avec quel respect il est son tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
FORMENTIN.
[Toinard:]
Ceque dessus seul peut vous certifier amplement combien on a de joie en ce pais cy de la decouverte que j'ay faite. J'en ay l'obligation a monsieur Trinchard†1 qui m'a fait lhonneur de me venir voir ici, ou j'ay bien vu d'autres de vos messieurs d'outre mer, comme monsieur Fall par deux fois, et Les mylords Douglas et autres, mais pas un ne ma repondu positivement sur votre sujet, et devant d'entrer en autre matiere le capitene vous prie aussi de nous mander quel est le francois que vous avez vu de sa connoissance.†2
A l'egard du service harmonique cest que j'ay un Breviarium Chronologicum in duodecimo. Ægidii Strauchs Wittebergæ 1657.†3 qui cite de lui une Dissertatio de Nativitate Emmanuelis,†4 qu'il n'anticipe que de deux ans, (mais je me suis encore bien afermi pour trois ans depuis mes epreuves faites,)†a et il cite aussi de lui une Dissertatio de Paschate σταυρωσίμῳ†5 ou il est de meme opinion que moy pour le 3. d'Avril de la 33. de l'Ære vulgaire. Je crois que ces livres ne sont pas de grand coust, c'est pourquoi je prens la liberté de vous prier de vouloir me les trouver, avec ce meme Breviarium chronologicum, que l'on m'a dit etre plus ample que l'edition de 1657.†b
Mandez moi aussi si mr Henri Westein qui a succedé à mr Elzevier, est de retour de Francfort: il m'a ecrit et fait ecrire pour imprimer mon harmonie, mais comm'il ne m'ofre rien de positif,
― 618 ―

je n'ay pas pu entrer en traité avec lui, et vous pouriez pendant votre sejour la ou vous etes, negocier cela, mais ne dites point ceque vous en avez.†1 Il y a des caracterismes à changer que je vous marqueray une autrefois.
Il m'est arivé comme a vous une infinité d'aflictions depuis l'interruption de notre commerce, et pour chercher quelque consolation dans ma douleur, j'ay traduit le petit traité de Josephe Περὶ Αὐτοκράτορος Λογισμοῦ, mal intitulé De Maccabæis. Vos messieurs d'Oxfort m'en ont refusé les Variæ Lectiones, quoique je leur eusse fait tenir un exemplaire lavé en eau d'alun sur lequel ils n'auroient eu qua les ecrire une fois.†2 mr L'Abé Renaudot et autres de mes amis leur en savent mauvais gré, et cela n'invite pas à de pareilles communications. Il entre dans les notes sur ce petit traité, deux belles questions l'une de Annis Sabbaticis, savoir si eles portoient abolition ou seulement surseance de detes, L'autre de quel texte de l'ancien testament se servoient les Juifs en tems de J. Ch.
J'ay une joie que je ne saurois exprimer de ceque je vous possede encore.
J'ay fait une Harmonie de Josephe†3 comme vous en avez vu de ma facon d'autres parties de la bible. Je vous en enverray quelque page.

779. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 16 June [1684] (763, 784)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 114-15. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Could I have knowne that it would have beene more Acceptable to you to have done otherwise, you have Reason enough to beleive
― 619 ―

that I would not have beene Silent, Nor have sent you other Peoples Words without any of my owne to Accompanie them; my Fault therefore if I was Guiltie of any, I Appeal to your self was of Invincable Ignorance,†1 and as such, Knowing you to be Just, I do without asking it, Venture to assure my self of your Pardon; As for mine you certainly long since had it, since I have almost forgot those Resentments you tell me of, and every thing else that was in that Letter; tho I thought I had rather expres'd my self in it to be in a very good Humour, then an Ill one, and that I was better Sattisfy'd with my Solitude at that time,†2 then I had of a long while before beene: I am now going to it againe, and wish that I may be but as well Pleas'd with it now, as I was then; The little Pleasure that I have taken of late in any Company has made it extreamly desirable to me, Yet I indeavor what I can, not to lose all my old Aversion to it, since I find the Cure to be much worse then the Disease, it being oweing to the Greatest Discontent that I ever yet received, and to the most Real Disgust of the World, occasion'd by the Misfortune, or extreame Folly more truely, of a Person that has always beene to me the Dearest Part of my self, Hee to whom you was Pleas'd to write, or Designe it, about a Yeare since, which Letter (if you did) hee had not received when he writt His to mee which came very lately.†3
I am now I hope Absolutely Cur'd of Promiseing my self any great Pleasure in this World, tho it depended upon so many Contingences before, that I think I deserv'd to be Punish'd for but Flattering my self with an Imagination that it may be it might bee.
If I ever did Act any Part upon the Stage of this Earth in the Anti-diluvian State of it,†4 that Golden Age, I wish it were Possible for me now to Remember it, that I might have no Temptation to Quarrel with Providence for giveing me Inclinations so little Sutable to this, and so unlike ever to be Gratify'd; Tho if I could have Faith enough to beleeve Helmonts Opinion,†5 and Could
― 620 ―

with as strong a Fancie conceit my self to have beene Methuselah (as its said a great Philosopher did Him self to have beene One who was Slaine at the Seige of Troy)†1 I think it might do all <but>†a as well, and I could not sure then want Patience to Compleate my Thousand Yeares either now, Or in any other Age of the World; The Truth is, with the Present I have beene much more out of Conceite for these Ten Days, and feare I shall continue so, then when I had the Designe that you Know of turning Stoick; I see more then ever, that it is a Base, False, Foolish World; and that Vertue, Honour, and Friendship, are but Names in it, Whilst People sell theire Honestie for Imaginarie Profit, and theire Happiness for the Senceless Reputation of being Wise. But this is our World, and as it Appears to me in the Discontented Humour that I am in; I should be very glad to heare a Better Account of yours; which if you cannot give, Pray inform me a little about your Neighbors in Frieze Land, the L'abadies,†2 Since tho I be ever so far Distant from them, it would much Reconcile me to the World to know that there were but somewhere in it a better sort of People then those where I am; I desire therefore that you will tell me what theire Manner of liveing is; and Whether it be that, or any Peculiar Principle, or Opinion, in theire Religion which Unites them
― 621 ―

together; What that is; Whether they be Learn'd, or Unlearn'd; and whether in theire Lives, and Conversation one amongst Another they do really differ from the rest of the World, and do appeare to have more true Honestie amongst them.
As for the Inquiries which you make at the end of your Letter I can onely refer you for the first of them to the General Fame that has beene in all Ages Concerning that Matter, which I think has spoke Loudly in theire Praise. As for my self, If I may be Allow'd to make a Judgment of what I was then by what I am now, I must be Permited to say that I cannot beleeve that in that Particular I came short of any of them, But that I always was, and always shall be, a Constant Lover of my Friends whilst they Continue to be so; More I suppose you will not think it Reasonable that they should expect from me; and so much they may assure themselves of; as you may that I am very much
Your Humble Servant
June the 16th
You†a cannot write to me whilst I stay in Towne Pray therefore when you do Inclose it with a Direction to Mr Thomas Andrews†1 at the Crowne in Cornhill who will send it to me.
Address: To Mr Lock.

780. Edward Clarke to Locke, 1 July 1684 (776, 782)
Rand, pp. 110-11. There printed from a copy made by Clarke. Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. Answered by no. 782.
London, 1st July, 1684.
Sir,
Being on Thursday next†2 to begin my journey into the West, I cannot omit this opportunity of telling you that my wife and children are in perfect health and give their best services to you. And that you have highly obliged my wife by your noble present of the Bible, which she hath now in her possession very finely bound
― 622 ―

by Powell†1 according to your direction. But her acknowledgments for that and all other your public and private favours bestowed on her you may expect hereafter as opportunity will leave, but at present she hopes the hurry of so near an approaching journey will excuse her silence and induce you to take notice of her hearty thanks she returns you by me, and likewise of the earnest invitation we both give you to Chipley in case you make England happy with your presence this summer. We design to continue at Chipley until towards the latter end of October, and then return hither if nothing in the meantime happens to alter our resolutions. And I choose the rather to go down the Bath road, and to make three or four days' stay at Sutton,†2 [that I may] do you some small service there, which I shall endeavour with ...
I think I told you in one of my former letters that I have placed your £5 in Mrs. Smithby's hands as you ordered. And the key of your scriptor is sealed up with another small key of yours and left with Mr. Lynn†3 and directed to you; and I have left one hundred pounds of your money in ... Perce's†4 hands, to be paid out as you shall direct or appoint, from whom if you come over you will be informed where your goods are placed that were removed from the Doctor's.†5 Which is all that I can think of material to acquaint you at present, therefore conclude with my hearty prayers for the continuance of your health, and remain,
your most faithful friend and servant,
E. C.

THE LETTERS ON EDUCATION
In no. 782 Locke begins a series of instructions to Mr. and Mrs. Clarke for the bringing up and education of their son Edward, and more generally of their other children. The series continues in nos. 799, 803, 807, 822, 829, 844-5, 929, 943, 999, 1098, and 1370; some letters belonging to it are lost.
Locke probably made a connected version of what he had written up to date between 15 October and 18 November while he was at Leyden: no. 800; and probably about the end of November sent Clarke a copy of it (no. 791; this version was preserved at Nynehead in Rand's time); and a fresh copy of it, with an additional passage, in January 1685 (no. 804; now B.M., Add. MS. 38,771; published by Sir Frederic Kenyon as Directions concerning Education, Roxburghe Club, 1933). He perhaps elaborated and extended this version while he was in Rotterdam: no. 1638. Eventually the connected version and the letters served as a foundation for Some Thoughts concerning Education. Many passages reproduce the letters verbatim; others have been expanded or altered; there are no specific references to the young Edward. The first and second editions of Some Thoughts appeared in 1693, the second copying the first so closely that it is not known which is the first and which the second. There are notable additions and alterations in the third edition, 1695. The alterations in the fourth, 1699, and fifth, 1705, are slight.
The significant versions are here distinguished as K for the British Museum Directions as edited by Kenyon; A for the text of the first or second edition; C for the third edition. The citations are by paragraph numbers (the enumeration in D and E, the fourth and fifth editions, is the same as in C). In comparing the letters with these versions duplicate keys are used (in each case the same number repeated) at the beginning and end of each passage. My alterations of Rand's readings and emendations are based on K and A.
782. Locke to Edward Clarke, 9/19 July [1684] (780, 786)
Rand, pp. 111-15. 'The whole of this letter is in very bad condition; the ink is faded; and the paper, rotten and in pieces, has turned brown': Rand; see
― 625 ―

also below. Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. The year from Clarke's endorsement and contents; the day is presumably new style. Answers a lost letter and no. 780.
This is the first of the Education letters.
19th July
Sir,
... With my services tell Madam I very much approve her carrying the boy†1 to Chipley with her, and leaving the child with Nurse Trent.†2 If she think it matters not whether I like this ordering of the matter or not, pray tell her though she be my mistress she cannot hinder me from loving her and her children (that would be contrary to all ... and reason), and that I cannot love them without concerning myself about them. And therefore tell her that as I shall take care to please her as becomes a most obedient galley [slave], in this matter she must have a care not to displease me unless she [expects to] hear of it, and I can scold cruelly.
I thought the young man†3 had been well enough behaved already not to need any new instructions. But since as you tell me my cousin does want a dancing master, I could ... him to take one from this side the water. France I think a good place for those that want reinforcements of good breeding and behaviour, but I fear I should lose my labour if I should [advise] travel to one so wedded to his own country ... I wish him as well as any relation I have, and pray assure him of it when you see him.
This much in answer to yours of the 17th June; and now I turn to that of the 1st instant, which I received on Tuesday last†4and the hamper of wine the same day. I thank you exceedingly for both. The wine is excellent, good, and came safe. Mr. Pierce†5misinformed you came away later and arrived here. Madam need not trouble herself to thank me for any public services nor for any private favours I have done her. In the matter of ... between her and me, I can pretend to nothing but to be on the receiving side. Though I have never found other, but her promise to be very kind when I come to Chipley has strong temptations in it, and I know
― 626 ―

not whether I shall be able to resist such temptation. This and my wish would complete my ...†a
<INSTRUCTIONS FOR THE EDUCATION OF CLARKE'S SON.>†1
1. †2- Mens sana in corpore sano is a short but full description of the most desirable state we are capable of in this life. He who has these two has little more to wish; and he that wants either of them will be but little the better for anything else. Men's happiness or misery is for the most part of their own making. He whose mind directs not wisely will never take the right way; and he whose body fails his mind will never be able to march in it. I confess there are some men's constitutions of body and mind so vigorous, and well framed by nature, that they shift pretty well without much assistance from others; by the strength of their natural genius, they are, from their cradles, carried towards what is excellent. But those examples are but few, and I think I may say of all the men we meet with, nine parts of ten, or perhaps ninety-nine of one hundred, are what they are, good or evil, useful or not, by their education. 'Tis that which makes the great difference in mankind. The little and almost insensible impressions, on our tender infancies, have very important and lasting influences; and there it is, as in the fountains of some rivers, where a gentle application of the hand turns the flexible waters into channels that make them take quite contrary courses; and by this little impression given them at the source they come to arrive at places quite distant and opposite.
2. I imagine the minds of children are as easily turned this or that way as water itself; and I think [with parents should be] their first care.... But though this be the principal part, and our main care should be about the inside, yet the clay tenement†3 is not to be neglected. I shall therefore begin with the case, and consider first the health of the body, as that which perhaps you may rather expect, from that study I have been thought more peculiarly to
― 627 ―

have applied myself to; and that also which will be soonest dispatched, as lying, as I imagine in a very little compass.
3. How necessary health is to our business and happiness, and how necessary a strong constitution, able to endure hardships and fatigue, is to one that will make any figure be anything considerable in the world, is too obvious to need any proof.†-2 
4. †1- Your son seems to me to be of as strong principles of <nature>†a as any child I have seen, so that one and the hardest part touching the body is spared. We need not trouble ourselves how to invigorate a weak or mend a faulty constitution. We have nothing to do but to preserve a good one, and help it to continue suitable to so promising a beginning; and that perhaps might be dispatched all in a word, by bidding you use him as you see one of our ordinary tenants does his children.
5. But because that perhaps may seem to you a little too spare, and to your Lady a little too hard,... who will be ready to say, 'tis apparent he has no children of his own, I shall explain myself a little more particularly, laying this down in the first place as a general and certain observation for Madam to consider of, viz. that most children's constitutions are either weakened or spoiled by cockering and tenderness. I say not this to accuse her, for I think her not guilty, but to fortify against the silly opinions and discourses of others.-†1
6. †3- The first thing then to be had a care of is, that he be not too warmly clad or covered in winter or summer. The face is no less tender than any other part of the body when we are born. 'Tis use alone hardens it, and makes it more able to endure the cold. And therefore what the Scythian philosopher said to the Grecian [is significant], who wondered at his going naked in the cold of winter in so cold a country. 'How can you endure your face exposed to the sharp winter air?' said the Scythian. 'Because it is used to it,' said the Greek. 'Think me then all face,' replied he.†4 There is nothing more certain than that our bodies will be brought to bear anything and be reconciled to any hardship, if from the beginning it be by constant [degrees] made familiar. I think it therefore time now, if
― 628 ―

we have not before done so, to leave off his cap, and perhaps†a- no more <to put it on> again,-†a unless about twenty years hence, if it be thought fit, <to put on>†b a thin holland one for fashion's sake to please the young lady when he goes a-wooing.†-3 
7. †1- I think it would also be of great advantage to have his feet washed every night in cold water, and to have his shoes so made that they may leak and let in water whenever he treads on any marshy place. Here, I imagine, I shall have both Mistress and maids about my ears. One perhaps will think it too filthy, and the other too much pains to make his stockings clean. But yet truth will have it, that his health is much more worth than all this little ado, and ten times as much more. Must my young master never dirty his shoes? and if it cost the wash of a pair of stockings or two more in a week the trouble may be borne and the thing be worth it, if we consider how mischievous and mortal a thing taking wet in the feet proves often to those who have been bred nicely. When a fever or consumption follows from just an accident, for wet in the feet will sometimes happen, then will he wish he had, with the poor people's children, gone barefoot, and so 'scaped the danger and perhaps death which a little unhappy moisture in his feet hath brought upon him; whilst the hardened poor man's son, reconciled by custom to wet in his feet by that means, suffers no more by it than if his hands were put in water. And what is it, I pray, that makes this great difference between the hands and the feet, but only custom? And I doubt not, but if a man from his cradle had been always used to go barefoot, but to have his hands close wrapped up constantly in thick mittens and handshoes (as the Dutch call gloves)†2 over them; I doubt not, I say, but such a custom would make taking wet in the hands as dangerous to him, as now taking wet in their feet is to a great many others. To prevent this, I would I say have him wear leaking shoes, and his feet washed every night in cold water, both for health and cleanliness sake. But begin first in the spring with luke warm water, and so colder and colder every night till in a few days you come to perfectly cold water, and so continue. For
― 629 ―

it is to be observed in this and all other alterations from our ordinary way of living, the change must be made by gentle and insensible degrees; and so we may bring our bodies to any thing without pain and without danger.†a †-1 
You know I am a meddling man in all your affairs, though not much in other ways. [I have written in] very great haste ... or purpose your house more than ... what is necessary. Were it not for this I had ere now sent you a draught of some things made here, that look very much like carved wood and gilded, that look very well and last as long as if they were wood. They are much cheaper and serve instead of gilded ..., as you have seen often in rooms hanged with plain stuff, and are much handsomer. It is a sort of plaster made in ... I hope my cousin Stratton has got in all my accounts. What has happened to ... troubled about him.
Address: For Mr. Edward Clarke at the Lady King's in Salisbury Court, near Fleet Street, London.
Endorsed by Clarke: J. L.'s letter with instructions about the education of my son, etc. Received the 24th of July, 1684.

784. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 25 August [1684] (779, 787)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 116-17. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Whether the World was always the same it is, or no, in its Antediluvian State, or since, I leave to the Author of the new Theorie to determine,†2 But this I am very Confident of that you
― 631 ―

are still the same you always was ever since I Knew you, and that no Change of Climate or any thing else is able to make one in your Humour.
It is not to your Praise that I tell you this, Since to Confess the Truth I made Account so Melancholy a letter as mine (at lest one that expres'd me with so much Reason Afflicted) should for those few moments that you were thinking of me have a little suspended that Pleasantness which is so natural to you, and I should yet quarrel with you for its not doing so, did I not Justly Apprehend that you would excuse your self by laying all the Blame upon Astrea,†1 and tell me over againe that Friendship, as well as Vertue, and Honour, being of Her Retinue, forsook the World when she did; If it be so wherefore Should I come into Freezeland? and what is there to be found There that is not to be had as well where I am? Notwithstanding the Character which you have giv'n of the Labadies I acknowledge that I like very well, But should have thought it an Excellent One had not the Notion I then had of them been quite alter'd since I writt to you last, I haveing beene inform'd since (but how Rightly I know not) that they are so far in Realitie as well as in theire Pretences (if that be true which you say of them) from being better then others, that they are indeed so much worse as under a show and Appearance of Religion there are not really greater Libertines in the World; like some Here in England formerly of whom I suppose you have heard,†2 They were a sect in Particular very Prevailing with the Women of the Place, and therefore notwithstanding your Advise I think it will behoove me to be Very Cautious how I enter into Acquaintance with the like till you have made further Inquiries Concerning them, although I partly suspect alreadie in what you did write that you had a mind to try how far my Credulitie might be Abus'd. In the meane time I find my self much more Dispos'd to see Holland, then Freezland; and can't but fancie that the Sight of a Place where Love, and Business, may be so well reconcil'd, is as much worth my Curiositie as that of the Labadies; and Yet how good Opportunitie soever I may ere long have of doing so, I shall†a scarse be incourag'd to it by all that you have yet said, There being Convenient Lime Treese, and Canals Large enough, if there be occasion for them, much
― 632 ―

nearer hand, Unless you let me know that there are some Idle People there were you are besides your self, Business you know, being as Mr Cowley says, the Thing which I of all things Hate;†1 and that I have a Perswasion that All There have nothing else in them no more in theire Heads, then in theire Hearts; If you say that this is an Errour, and can find me but any Acquaintance such as you Promis'd me in France I may Possibly ere it be long come and learne some of those fine Dishes you talk of, Otherwise they will be no Temptation to me not haveing any Designe at Present to become a Housekeeper, any more then a Labadie. How Time may Dispose me either way I know not, For for the last I would not have you think by any thing that I have said that I am so Prejudic'd against them that I should not be willing to heare any Ill that I have heard of them Refuted, and to entertaine a good Opinion of them. I do also much desire to see the Book you tell me of,†2 and Wonder you have found no Opportunitie of sending it me all this While, as it may be you may that I have beene thus long of writeing to you, The Reasons of which I cannot give you without telling you a great many sad stories which I know cannot be Pleasant to any Body, and which would serve for nothing but to indanger my being Angry with you againe whenever you are so well Dispos'd as to write to me next. I shall therefore say no more to you of them but onely desire you to beleeve that if I have beene silent longer then in Civilitie I ought it is to be Attributed to nothing else but a Succession of Misfortunes extraordinarie, and Uncommon,†3 too great to Permit me to think of any thing but themselves, Since your Governess is I assure you the very same you ever Knew Her, as Impertinent as ever, and as much
Your Humble Servant
PHILOCLEA.
August the 25th.
Address: To Mr Lock.

(Original Text) Distinguished and excellent Sir,
I have no doubt that you have now received my recent letter; I hope you may satisfy the desire I have expressed in it. For the present I am sending you the contents of Dr. Wepfer's reply†1 to my letter, which I received yesterday.
'My best greetings, distinguished and excellent Sir.
(Original Text) 'We find that for intermittent tertian and quartan fevers there is hardly a more effective antidote than quinquina bark, notably this autumn, when many people are affected by them. In two quartan and several tertian cases I have administered sometimes the following powder ... and sometimes the following ... Some poor people have been benefited by the following powder ... Such is the dosage I give on a quiet day, at
[p. 634]
5 in the morning and 5 in the evening; on the day of a paroxysm patients are to be fed 5 or 6 hours before the attack; half an hour or an hour before it they are to take the draught I have mentioned, and another again when the paroxysm is passing off and sweating has commenced; when the sweating is well over they may have a meal. It offers good hope of a speedy cure if the sweat comes out quickly, but not violently, after the draught; on the patients' quiet days we feel safe in allowing them wine; we very rarely purge, and that not unless there is serious aggravation of the stomach, and then we usually employ an emetic. For some years I have advised no more than a laxative. The Illustrious Antony Count of Furstenberg†1 suffered from epilepsy as a boy; the attack was brought on by colic and teething; I gave him an enema of milk and almond-oil, and then a draught ... as often as he was able to swallow; I anointed his abdomen with ... I held Balsam. succin. to his nostrils, but did not anoint them. I heard from Rhodius†2 at Padua that manna is often adulterated with juice of scammony; I have seen that leaves of spurge have been mixed with that plant. See on this Donatus ab Altom.,†3 where he gives the right method of gathering it, which gatherers will scarcely ever observe. Oil ex florib. Slotan. is described in the Letter to Paul Crocoverus which is to
[p. 635]
be found in the works of Fabricius Hild. p.656/1043 m., sc. after Cent. 6. Obs.†1 Some years ago I learnt that a substitute for moxa is artemisia, which is also confirmed by Heer Ten Rhyne in the treatise which I possess through your generosity and for which I continue to be obliged to you.†2 I frequently use it for cauterizing parts that are painful but not inflamed, even the hairy scalp and the temples; this time I have treated the knee of a certain cobbler afflicted with very severe gout in that part, giving him immediate relief, but not by the Oriental method; I do not allow the skin to be deeply burned; the moment they feel the heat of the glowing cinder I flick away the moxa; I have observed a beneficial effect when the skin is simply branded with a yellow patch; I therefore have no need of plasters or anything else when the moxa is struck off. I applied it to the cobbler in 3 or 4 places on a single occasion. If I could find time I would gladly let you have an augmented and less faulty edition of my Historia de Cicuta aq.,†3 which might be furnished with a more accurate index; the one that Dr. Harder of Basel made is worthless. I have written something on the bites of poisonous animals, but I am not satisfied with myself on many points; I do not get enough opportunity of experimenting, and if I did learn anything more in that way I should not be able to make it public, for I should certainly end by being called a poisoner. Redi mentions
[p. 636]
among his experiments†1 an oil that is immediately lethal; but he keeps it dark, no doubt for the same reason; some say that it is oil of tobacco; I have made some attempts with that oil distilled by descent,†2 but without success. I am particularly eager to know by what kind of death animals die when wounded with poisoned knives or needles; is it attended by convulsions or does it happen by syncope? What is the character of the blood in their heart and larger arteries? The flesh of fowls killed with knives smeared with wolf's bane is rendered tenderer, according to Thuanus.†3 I killed several dogs instantaneously by a new experiment in infusory surgery, and recently at St. Blasius,†4 with the assistance of my son-in-law Dr. Brunner,†5 a she-goat; they were slightly convulsed at first but soon lay motionless with no remaining sign of life; I found traces of the substance I had introduced in all parts of them, even in the brain; but I shall make still more tests, which will perhaps help to clear up some of the more obscure points in practice. My son has tried the same thing on two dogs with equal success. These experiments might with advantage be added to those on bites and on water-hemlock. Dr. Screta†6 has written an excellent treatise on malignant fevers, which is to
[p. 637]
be printed, unless I am mistaken, at Tübingen, with Latin notes. Good-bye excellent Sir, and believe me to be
Your most obedient servant
JOH. JACOB WEPFER, M.D.
(Original Text) Schaffhausen 20 Aug. 1684.'
Since, however, I shall shortly be answering this letter of Dr. Wepfer's I should be very glad if you would tell me of anything new and worth knowing on which it might be permissible to get information from this learned man; so I earnestly beg you to let me know of it when you write. Some days ago, too, a certain young woman put herself under my care; she has been suffering from haemorrhoids for the past two and a half years; they are external and painful, though no longer bleeding, but are swollen to the length of a finger-joint; she suspects that she contracted this malady from intermission of the motions whilst suffering from fever, and owing to the frequent purges she resorted to at that time. A relation of hers, a married woman who had a rather difficult child-birth six months ago, is also suffering from the same sort of haemorrhoids, but bleeding a good deal. They have employed various remedies without success; I should therefore be glad if you would tell me whether you have any certain specific against haemorrhoids which they could use. Many such are of course recommended in text-books
[p. 638]
such as fig-wort, etc., but I have never yet tried them. With this I must break off, as I have made this letter longer then I intended. Meanwhile good-bye, excellent Sir and best of helpers, and believe me to be
Your most obedient servant
C. SIBELIUS, Doctor.
(Original Text) Deventer, 14 October 1684
(Original Text) N.B. The haemorrhoids I have mentioned can indeed be introverted by local treatment, but they come out of the anus again afterwards; hence they must be treated in such a way that they will not appear externally any longer but be retained inside. I seek your advice on this point.

787. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 8 October [1684] (784, 805)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 118-19. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Tho the quarrel that I had with the World when I writt to you from L——†1 was not of the Nature of those (as most Commonly
― 639 ―

they are) after which People love it but the Better, But Reasonably enough Grounded to be Lasting Yet has not my Desire of retireing from it beene of late any thing so great as it uses to be; Not that I am not as much as ever I was a Stoick; and less that the Stars have inform'd you aright; Since on the Contrarie for the first I cannot but think my Courage (for so it is) an effect of my improvement in that Philosophy, And for the last do assure you I am so far from any such thoughts that I have beene in much greater Likelihood both from my owne Inclination, and the Perswasion of others, (tho for different Reasons) of makeing a Resolution never to have any such whilst I live. But Considering that if I did so I should for that very Reason have had an Invincible Temptation of doing otherwise, I have with much ado forborne, and am now so far come off from it as to have a great deal the better Opinion of your Neighbours in Freezeland†1 for not doing so neither, Of whom a more Particular Account would have beene very Pleaseing to me, that do not Perhaps as you say inquire onely out of Curiositie, since tho I am growne more Hardie, Or thro the Continuance of the Evills I complain'd of less sensible, and so can better indure this Wicked World then formerly Yet it follows not from thence that I always will do so, and therefore I may (notwithstanding your Opinion to the Contrary) in time Possess the Place that you have taken up for me, Besides that you have given me a New Temptation to do so, since most Certainly if ever I come to be Perfectly reconcil'd to Matrimonie againe I shall have an extreame Desire to Marry a Labadist, and be one my self for that very Reason. For if the Notion I have of them is right, and there be any Happiness to be found in Marriage it must Certainly be amongst them, who I suppose Consider nothing in it but to Please them selves, To Whom

Joynter, Portion, Gold, Estate,
Houses, Housholdstuff, and Land,
(The Low Conveniences of Fate)
Are Greek they do not understand.†2
Who Know no Interest Contrary to theire Inclination; and Who are Wiser either in Marrying or not Marrying, then to Rate theire Happiness by the Estimation that others make of it more then theire owne. It is thus that I fancie them as to this matter, and am
― 640 ―

almost in Love with some unknowne Brother alreadie; But when you write next you must let me know whether or no I am not mistaken in them, as also whatever else you can think of that concerns theire Manner of liveing, tho by the Way if they are so shy of informing those who inquire onely out of Curiositie I doubt you had not much Conversation with them, since whatever it was that Carry'd you into Freezeland I suppose you would not impose upon them so much as to Perswade them that it was with any Designe at all of Becomeing Better; tho some way or other it has Certainly beene Advantageous to you, since I cannot but Fancie by your Letter that you have learnt more Scripture there then ever you Knew in your whole life before, whom I little thought once would ever have writt me a letter not to be understood without turning to St Paul, and St Peters Epistles.
The Booke you sent me (for which I returne you my Thanks) I received but a Week since,†1 and have yet had but very little Leisure to look in it, Mr Loggan†2 haveing beene willing to spend some time with me to instruct me a little in Perspective, that so I may be able to send them over a Draught of my Chamber at Wieuwert when I shall be there. For any other Books I leave it to you to do as you Please, not knowing whether they will signifie any thing, or not, since I perceive that which I should be most desireous to see is not writt in a Language which I understand.†3
I was in Hopes that before this I should have had an Answeare from You to my last letter, and have received some incouragement to come into Hollond. But I find you are not in such hast to see your Governess (whatever you would have her Beleeve) as she would be did it Depend on Her. I will not for that Reason say to see You, But the Fine things that you told me of; Although I Hope you do beleeve that she notwithstanding is as much as ever she was
Your Friend and Servant
PHILOCLEA.
Oct: the 8th.
Address: To Mr Lock.
Endorsed by Locke: Philoclea 8 Oct.84

788. William Charleton to Locke, 16 October 1684 (736, 816)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, f. 58. Damaged: cover torn off, affecting some words of text.
London the 16th October 1684
Deare Sir
I am now I hope like to get rid of a verry sore distemper that has Confin'd me to my chamber almost this moneth, the griping of the gutts,†1 the epidemicall disease of the towne, your favour of the 18th September came verry opportunely to perfect I hope my recovery for I received it with all imaginable satisfaction and pleasure, fearing least you might have been under the same circumstances as my self. Leonardo de Capoa shall be kept carefully for you, I had bought at Paris Moreri's Dictionary, but shortly after a bookeseller a freind of mine acquainted me that it would verry speedyly be reprinted, upon which I thought it my best Course to part with it, which I did at the same rate it Cost me, not long after Carew†2 my old implacable adversary Came thither and was verry solicitous to have me joyne with him in order to obtaine letters of reprisall against the Dutch from the French Court, which I refused to do alleadging as it was verry true that his Majesty the King of England had seen fit to call in the letters already granted him, and withall stricktly forbid any of his subjects to endeavour to procure others from any Prince, or state, without his permission, or the Lords of the Admiralty's, but I promised him not to obstruct him though he did act without me, he went twice or thrice to Versailles to mr Colbert de Crecy†3 but found a Cold reception. In the meantime I suspecting my Gentleman put all my meddalls†4and things of value out of his reach, and twas well I did, for he had obtained surreptitiously an order to seize on my effects without giving security for their being restored in case he was cast, to be short after about 4 moneths waging of warr, I got the better, and
― 642 ―

by a decree in Parliament he is no more to trouble their Courts of Judicature, his cause being cast out and damages allowed me. this affaire hindered me from buying another Moreri's Dictionary, but if you will be pleased to leave it now to my care I shall as soone as may be get you one. Your seeds were sent by a verry honest Gentleman one Dr. Sloane†1 who delivered them to Dr. Goodalls Lady†2 for you, if you please I shall enquire farther about them. Dr. Barbyrac is alive and ha's this yeare caused to be printed at Lyons a small peice in octavo though not in his name which ha's for title Traite des Maladies de la poitrine.†3 I will see if I can get it when I goe abroad, If you hold not a corispondency with Hamburgh I can tell you it may be a peice of news, our mode<st>†a bashfull freind Mr Wall,†4 is said to have got a Yokefellow, a rich widdow, had he been an old Testame<nt>†a preist, I supose this sort of chewed meat would have been no more permitted him to have tasted of, then of a Camelion or a Lizart,†5 I wish him all the hapynesse that can atend that state of lif<e>†aand none of the many vexations that are but frequently the companions of wedlock, if yo<u>†a write to him pray present him my service, and ob<lige>†a me in laying frequently your Commands upon
Sir
Your most Affectionate obliged humble Servant
WILLIAM CHARLETON
Sir never any things were in greater order or received lesse dammage then those of mine, that you were pleased to take into your Care, the bottles of Eau d'Ange, and mille fleurs, sufferr'd only by the Extremity of the weather, I wish I had found the things I left when I went abroad in as good Condition it would have been a 100 ll. in my way.

790. Locke to Nicolas Toinard, 13/23 November [1684] (789, 796)
B.M. Add. MS. 28,753, ff. 24-5. Printed in Ollion pp. 112-14. Year from Toinard's note and contents. Answers no. 789; answered by nos. 796, 802.
Amsterdam. 23 Nov.†a
Croiez vous que le monde est autre chose qu'il n'estoit il y a deux mil ans. le meme chanson qu'on chantoit pour lors de la Fortune ne sera pas mal a propos dans nostre temps, mais je souhaite que vous n'ayez pas sujet de chanter vos vers Greques a Monsieur l'Abè que j'avois l'honeur de voire dans la Bibliotheque de Monsieur de Thou quand vous me procurasts l'honeur de faire la reverence a M L.P D.C. Mais je m'etonne que vous que trouvez la Fortune, (qui est le plus changeant de touts les dieux) la même aujourdhuy qu'elle estoit avant tant des seicles, traitez l'Amitie d'une autre maniere, car en veritè ou est il que vous trouverez parmy vos Greques, qu'on seroit faschè de payer le port de une letre qui apporta les nouvelles de son ami s'il n'y avoit quelque chose ajoutèe qui pourroit avoir raport au profit. PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH AND THE REMONSTRANTS
When Locke was in Paris in 1678 he became acquainted with Dr. Pieter Guenellon, a physician from Amsterdam (p. 738, n. 2). When he came to Amsterdam in September 1683 he renewed the acquaintance, and thanks to Guenellon met other physicians and in January 1684 Philippus van Limborch, in his time the leading divine among the Remonstrants, the persuasion to which Guenellon belonged. Van Limborch was to become one of Locke's principal friends.
The Remonstrants regarded Erasmus as a precursor. With him they sought the source of theology in the New Testament and especially in the Gospels. Christianity was interpreted mainly as a pious and virtuous life; with this went a large tolerance for those who differed in their opinions. In the sixteenth century many Netherlanders were attracted by this kindly spirit but the fighters against Spanish tyranny required a sterner creed; they found it in Calvinism. An intolerant Calvinism prevailed in most parts of the United Provinces, but in Holland the great merchants from whom were drawn the governing bodies of the towns, the regents, were more liberal. In general they were Calvinists but they had absorbed Erasmian principles of tolerance; they were acquainted with men of other creeds; as traders they rejected the restrictions that orthodox Calvinist economic doctrine would have imposed on them; as laymen they would not suffer clerical domination. The divergence between precisians and liberals (preciesen and rekkelyken) became manifest towards the end of the century when Jacob Arminius set out his views on predestination. Calvin 'maintained that Christ's atoning death was offered for the elect alone. He added to the gratuitous predestination of the elect the equally gratuitous and positive reprobation of the damned, to whom salvation is denied from all eternity without any fault on their part.'
― 649 ―

Arminius regarded this as unbiblical. 'The Divine sovereignty was compatible with a real free-will in man; Jesus Christ died for all and not only for the elect.' Johan van Oldenbarneveldt, the Landsadvocaat of Holland and leader of the States party, tried to establish toleration. The Calvinists would not have it. Their ministers protested angrily. Some were expelled from their pulpits, and their congregations from their churches. Conciliation proved impossible. Arminius died in 1609. For a conference at The Hague in 1610 his disciples prepared a Remonstrance in which they set out their own views in five articles. The Calvinists replied with a Counter-Remonstrance.
Meanwhile an entirely secular conflict was developing, on the one side Oldenbarneveldt, on the other Prince Maurice of Orange, Stadholder of Holland, Zealand, and three other provinces, and commander of the army of the United Provinces. The principal question at issue was peace or war with Spain; the increase of trade and prosperity or the military security of the republic. Eventually Oldenbarneveldt's acts were likely to imperil it. Thereupon Maurice effected a revolution. Oldenbarneveldt was arrested in August 1618; in the next few weeks Maurice changed the governing bodies of the towns of Holland and secured control of its Estates.
Both Remonstrants and Calvinists had wanted a national synod for the settlement of ecclesiastical affairs. The Synod of Dort opened on 13 November 1618. The Remonstrants soon learnt that the Calvinists had come not to discuss but to condemn their views. They were deprived of their offices. The Synod closed on 9 May. Four days later Oldenbarneveldt was the victim of a judicial murder. Grotius, one of his principal adherents, was imprisoned in the castle of Loevestein. In July the States General silenced the Remonstrant divines. Of the 200 removed from office about forty were reinstated on signing the articles of belief drawn up by the Synod; about seventy promised to live quietly; at least eighty preferred exile. For some years the Remonstrants were subject to active persecution and mobviolence.
Arminius was succeeded in the leadership by Simon Bisschop, known as Episcopius (no. 926 n.). While he was in exile he drew up for them a confession, a declaration of belief and not a rule of faith, which was published in 1621. In his teaching he 'emphasized the practical nature of Christianity, affirmed that the Church is based on a minimum of speculative beliefs, remonstrated against current Calvinist dogmas of predestination and original sin, stressed the responsibility of man, not God, for sin, and taught a reduced view of the divinity of Christ and a subordinationist doctrine of the Trinity' —one which regards either the Son as subordinate to the Father or the Holy Ghost as subordinate to both. This last exposed him and the Remonstrants to accusations of Socinianism and the holding of Unitarian views. In the seventeenth century any questioning of the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity was apt to be regarded as blasphemous and provocative of the wrath of God. Hence the Remonstrants, while prepared to tolerate what they regarded as the speculative errors of the Socinians, and on occasion to come to their defence, insisted on the falsity of the accusation that they shared their views.
In 1625 Prince Maurice was succeeded as Stadholder of Holland and Zealand by his half-brother Frederick Henry. The persecution ended. Public
― 650 ―

worship was now permitted; the ministers returned from exile; churches were built. In 1632 the rulers of Amsterdam had established the Doorlugtige School (or Athenæum Illustre), an institution for further education which was to develop in the course of time into the University of Amsterdam. This led the Remonstrants to establish in Amsterdam a seminary for training their ministers; they could study literature and philosophy at the Athenæum and theology at their own seminary.
They were now secure. The changes made by Maurice among the regents in 1618 had scarcely affected the general character of the class. The influences that had determined their predecessors' attitude were still potent; the Calvinists' victory at the Synod of Dort did not lead to a Calvinist established church such as the Church of England. The Remonstrants had no legal status as a religious body, but in practice were little affected by civil disabilities. They were always probably few in number.†1
Philippus van Limborch's earliest known ancestor lived in Maastricht in the earlier part of the sixteenth century. His son, probably for religious reasons, moved to Emden in 1557. In 1595 a son of the refugee settled in Amsterdam, where his son Frans was born in 1597. This Frans was for a time a merchant and later an advocate. In 1623 he married Geertruidt, daughter of Rem Egbertszoon Bisschop, a merchant, the elder brother of Simon Episcopius and as a leading Remonstrant occasionally a sufferer in the cause. In 1632 when the Remonstrant church was established in Amsterdam Frans van Limborch was elected an elder. There were three sons of the marriage, Philippus, born on 19 June 1633, and his elder and younger brothers Rem and Simon, who both studied law and obtained official positions.
Philippus, after attending the grammar (latijnsche) school, went in 1647 to the Amsterdam Athenæum. He was baptized on 9 June 1651 (the Remonstrants prefer adult to infant baptism). He then, while continuing to attend the Athenæum, studied theology under Étienne de Courcelles (Curcellæus) at the Remonstrants' seminary. His various teachers were acquainted with Descartes's works; Courcelles had known him and had published an edition of the Discours de la méthode and the attendant pieces in 1644; while few of them accepted any part of his views they must all have been influenced by his method. Van Limborch spent some months in 1653-4 at the university of Utrecht, where Descartes's most thoroughgoing Dutch opponent, the orthodox Calvinist Gisbertus Voetius, was professor of theology. He was examined in theology in the Amsterdam seminary in August 1655. Later in the year the Remonstrants at Alkmaar invited him to be their pastor; wishing to continue his studies he refused the call, but accepted one from Gouda in 1657 (Gouda was notoriously a city of refuge for heretics). He now began his literary career. He also entered into correspondence with some English divines and notably with the Cambridge Platonists Henry More and Ralph Cudworth. He had much in common with More and Cudworth, and later with Tillotson and his fellow Latitudinarians. He remained at Gouda until 1667, when he accepted a call from Amsterdam. In the following year he
― 651 ―

was appointed professor of theology in the Remonstrants' seminary. He held the chair until his death in 1712. He married for the first time in 1660; his wife died in 1664, leaving him a daughter who died in 1679. He married again in 1674; his second wife, who outlived him, brought him a daughter Geertruydt, who died unmarried in 1743, and a son Frans, whose incompetence was to be a source of anxiety to his parents.
Van Limborch was an able and industrious author and editor. His tasks were to define the tenets of the Remonstrants and to defend them and their holders in an intolerant and hostile world. His first great achievement was to edit, in conjunction with Christiaan Hartsoeker, a collection of 332 letters from Arminius, his friends, and successors; Praestantium ac Eruditorum Virorum Epistolae Ecclesiasticae et Theologicae Varii Argumenti, 1660. He edited part of Episcopius's theological works (1665) and some of his other pieces; to a collection of his sermons published in Dutch in 1693 he prefixed a Life of Episcopius; a Latin translation of the life appeared in 1701.
His principal work was the Theologia Christiana, ad Praxin Pietatis ac Promotionem Pacis Christianae unice directa. It was written at the desire of his English correspondents the Cambridge Platonists and of his Dutch fellow-believers. Published in 1686, there were further editions in 1695 and 1700; four more after van Limborch's death and Dutch (1701-3) and English (1713) translations. It was followed by another expository work, De Veritate Religionis Christianae (1688), written as part of a friendly discussion with a learned Jew, the physician Isaac Orobio. While it was in preparation one of Locke's friends obtained control of a manuscript recording the proceedings of the Inquisition at Toulouse from 1307 to 1323. It was decided to publish it and to it van Limborch prefixed his Historia Inquisitionis (1692), an account principally of the constitution and procedure of the Inquisition, based almost entirely on the writings of a number of Inquisitors. Ostensibly directed against the Roman Catholic Church and the Spanish Inquisition of its time, its underlying moral is the detestability of all religious persecution. Orobio had given van Limborch an account of his sufferings while he was a prisoner of the Inquisition; what was more relevant was the treatment to which divines who uttered Socinian and other heretical views were liable to be subjected by orthodox Calvinists. Locke had good reason to write the Epistola de Tolerantia for him.
Of all Locke's correspondents van Limborch responded most fully to his religious aspirations. Each of them had particular beliefs which the other did not share. But they held similar views on the relations of reason and revelation and on the conduct of Christian life, and when they differed discussed their differences in an inquiring and friendly spirit. Both men brought sociability and ready pens to the common pursuit of truth; the continuance of the friendship was due largely to van Limborch's goodness of heart which surmounted Locke's irritability and bursts of ill temper.

He is on terms of friendship with men in this city who are renowned for scholarship, especially those of the medical profession, all of whom are as full of praise for his unsullied character as they are of respect for his learning. It was in this way that I was fortunate enough to make his acquaintance and to become his friend. If after tasting the pleasure of his society you should see fit to introduce him to some leading persons you will be doing what is worthy of your erudition and courtesy and what will be most gratifying to him. Good-bye, eminent Sir, and never cease to adorn our age with your learned labours.
