795. Thomas Herbert, eighth earl of Pembroke, to Locke, [c. 24 November 1684] (452, 797)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 191-2. Printed in King, p. 158. Herbert succeeded as eighth earl of Pembroke in 1683. Answered by no. 797.
This is the first of a group of letters relating to Locke's expulsion from Christ Church. The exact date is problematical. The course of events is as follows:
6/16 November. Sunderland orders Fell to deprive Locke of his studentship.
8/18 November. Fell summons Locke to appear at Christ Church by 1 January 1685.
8/18 November. Locke goes from Leyden to Amsterdam en route for Utrecht.
11/21 November. The king orders Locke's immediate deprivation.
15/25 November. Locke is deprived of his studentship.
20/30 November. Locke still intends to go to Utrecht (no. 792).
It was apparently not until after he had written to van Limborch on 20/30 November (no. 792) that Locke learnt of the summons to Christ Church. There is nothing to show how word of it reached him; it might have come through Old, Tyrrell, or Pawling, or have been sent by Fell or the College
― 658 ―

officers, or it might have come in some other way. He presumably wrote immediately on hearing the news to either Pembroke or a common friend, announcing that he intended to return to England. The present letter appears to be Pembroke's response, the notice of his 'generous concern' mentioned in no. 797. It reached Locke at the same time as the news of his deprivation. Locke apparently wrote his answer, dated 28 November/8 December (no. 797), within a few hours of receiving it and the news of his deprivation. The post at its best took three days between London and Amsterdam. This gives as date for this letter 24 November/4 December or the succeeding day.
There are two possible objections. First, the long time between the proceedings at Oxford and Locke's hearing of them. This may have been due to weather. Secondly, Pembroke appears not to have heard of Locke's deprivation when he wrote this letter. There appears to be nothing to show that the deprivation attracted any attention outside Christ Church. (In view of the alteration Locke's endorsement cannot determine whether it was in November or December that he received the letter; the new-style December is the more likely.)
Sir
You might very well expect that I who have had so much satisfaction in the friendship I have so many years contracted with you†1 would be pleased at your design of coming hether this winter but when I consider how prejudicial it may be to your health to leave that Cuntry (which I have often heard†2 has much increased it) I can't but use my endeavor you should not remove till Spring. I was much surprised when I heard the reason of your coming so soon, but as soon comforted myself when I considerd how many men of good reputation by being accused have had an advantage publicly to prove themselvs honest men: certainly I who know your Actions should be to blame to give credit to others Words; you may be assured nothing shall hinder me from haserding all I am worth when it may be advantageous to such a friend, I perceive my great concern has made me say more then is needful, I would otherwayes have been contented only to have subscribed myself
Your friend
PEMBROKE.
Address: For Mr. Lock.
Endorsed by Locke: E: Pembroke Nov:†a 84
― 659 ―

A l'egard de la recete pour les yeux, Mr†a- L'Abé m'a dit qu'il n'est pas tout a fait necessaire que la Tutie soi preparée, il faut en metre quelques petis morceaux, gros en tout environ comm une petite noix dans l'eau distillee, et puis boucher la bouteille. cete Tutie sert à purifier en luy communiquant en même tems sa vertu. L'eau devient trouble et la Tutie se precipite en bas au bout de quelque tems, apres lequel l'on filtre l'eau, ou bien l'on la verse doucement par inclination. Elle est presque bonne a tous les maux des yeux, et quoiqu'il y ait des ingrediens chaux, elle guerit à merveilles toutes les inflammations et fluxions tartreuses et c.
Au reste la preparation de la Tutie qui alors est un bon collyre, se fait en cete maniere.
Metez Tutie en poudre ou morceaux dans une ceuïller de fer sur le feu, et y jetez de l'eau roze tirée sans feu, et quelques racines toutes freches de chelidoine: et laissez cela sur le feu jusques à siccité. voila votre Tutie preparée.
Puis que me voila sur ce sujet, j'ajouteray que pour les inflammations des yeux, il faut couper un grand fenouïl au dessous d'un nœud lorsqu'il commence a grener, et remplir sa cavité de sucre candi en poudre quand le soleil ne donne plus dessus, et boucher la tige avec de la cire ou mastic, et laisser le tout fondre 24. heures ou environ: puis le verser.-†a
Cete maniere a du raport à ceque vous m'avez autrefois apris pour l'oppium.
J'ay fait imprimer ici il y a plus de deux ans une grande table pour les receuils et j'en ay fait une infinité d'amis ausquels tous j'ay dit que je la tenois de vous. Le Capitaine de marine en est ravi, et le precepteur de monsieur L'Abé de Coislin†1 neveu de monseigneur l'Evesque d'orleans. Je vous prie d'en regaler le public le plus
― 660 ―

prontement que vous pourez. j'estime que vous devez la faire imprimer in quarto en beau papier et fort: et j'ay assez peu de honte pour vous en demander une douzaine d'exemplaires. J'en ay fait une en Grec pour mon usage, il faut 7. pour 5 dans le Latin. Vous en toucherez un mot dans l'instruction.
Il seroit bon aussi qu'en la faisant imprimer, vous fissiez tirer quelque nombre d'exemplaires de la table pour en donner a vos amis afin de servir à leurs receuïls.
Vous avez cy inclus un modele de celle la†a moitié†a que j'ay fait imprimer en in folio. Les vignetes†1 marqueés de rouge sont egales entr'elles et plus grosses que celle qui separent les letres: et cela ne fait pas un mechant efet. Vous pourez m'envoier par la poste une epreuve et je vous en diray mon sentiment. Vous suppleerez dans ce modele les lignes qui divisent chaque voiele.
Nota que vous devez donner a votre ouvrage une bonne marge interieure, car ne pouvant pas etre gros, il sera plus aisé à etre broché.
Vous pouriez aussi le faire en in octavo, mais sur tout donnez de lui de la marge au fond pour la raison cy dessus, et que les vignetes qui divisent les letres soient les plus menües qu'il se poura afin de manger peu d'espace de haut en bas, et que les reglets soient bien fins. Ils reussissent bien en cela en Holande.
Je vous avoüe que j'ay de l'impatience de voir cela achevé, ou tout au moins une epreuve de la table.
Je nescai point le prix ny la bonté des livres Delphiniques.

797. Locke to Thomas Herbert, earl of Pembroke, 28 Nov./8 Dec. 1684 (795, 828)
Christ Church, Oxford. Previously in the Sanford collection at Nynehead. Excerpt printed in Christie, Shaftesbury, i. 261 n. (reprinted in Fox Bourne, i. 487-8). The letter was probably sent through Clarke: no. 801. Mr. Laslett argues that Clarke did not deliver it but kept it: ed. Two Treatises, p. 41 n.; this is perhaps based on the provenance. Both Mr. Laslett and Professor Cranston (pp. 247-50) consider the letter disingenuous if not untruthful. One passage probably refers to no. 795.
Amsterdam 8 Dec: 1684
My Lord
In my passage through this town from Leyden (where I had been for some time at an auction)†3 to Utrecht (where I designed to passe
― 662 ―

this winter) I was surprised with the news of a moneo, summoning me to appear at Ch: Ch: by the first of January.
The occasion, and circumstances of it, I suppose, your Lordship may have heard; and therefor I shall not trouble your Honour with the recitall of them. When I was prepareing to comport my self to that citation as became me, the next post brings the news, that I am actually expeld; but with it brings also the notice of your <Lordships>†a generous concerne for an unfortunate and exposed innocence. My Lord I have had the honour to be known to your Lordship these many years, both at home and abroad; and I appeale to your Lordship, whether in all my conversation (which if it trespassed any way I am sure it was not in being over reserved) your Lordship ever observed the least appeareance of any thing in me of the kinde I am charged with; but quite the contrary. I appeale likewise to my Lord Bishop of Oxford†1 whether my cariage in the colledg, for soe long a time, caryed in it any the least mark of undutifull against the government either of the church, state, or Colledg it self; or whether there were any appearance of turbulency, faction, or sedition in my nature. Afterwards when chance, and not my owne seekeing (as your neighbour Dr Thomas†2 can informe your Lordship at large) threw me into my Lord Shaftsburys acquaintance and family, I chalenge any one to say my behaviour was otherwise. If it had been, it would have belyd my minde and temper; and therefor I cannot but thinke it hard, that any imputation that lyes upon him should draw suspitions upon me. For though either through attention, or good luck, I happend to doe him some acceptable service in that great, and strange disease, when he was opend. soe that he was afterwards pleased to own, that he owed his life to my care; and possibly the memory of that, might make him treat me ever after (as I confesse he did) with great civility and kindenesse; Yet some of my freinds, when they considerd, how small an advancement of my fortune I had made, in soe long an attendance, have thought, that I had noe great reason to brag of the effects of that Kindenesse.†3 I say not this, my Lord, to complain of my dead master, it will be noe way decent in me, But in this extremity, I cannot but complain of it as an hard case, that haveing reaped soe
― 663 ―

litle advantage from my service to him whilst liveing, I should suffer soe much on that account now he is dead.
For if I had spent those years I lived with him, in the publique practise of physique, I beleive, I may say without boasting, that I might have made my self an other maner of establishment, then now I have; at least I should have been rich still in my students place, which I always soe valued, as the highest convenience for a retired single life, that the keepeing of it (which was always my great care) was what most satisfied me in the not geting other things: and I imagin had I spent my time, just as I did, in any but my Lord Shaftsburys house, I might now search my health, and injoy my pittance, and privacy any where, quietly without being suspected of libells, or any other miscariages,†1 though in every thing else, but barely liveing in his family, my actions had been all exactly the same they have been now. For I never did any thing undutifully against his Majestie or the government: I know noe thing in my life scandalous, or am conscious of any thing that ought to give any offence; I have never been of any suspected clubs or caballs, I have made litle acquaintance, and kept litle company in an house where soe much came, and for that litle my choyse was of bookish not busy men. All this my Lord is known to be soe, and the constant course of soe many years cannot but be visible. And indeed such a course was the natural†a product of my unmedleing temper, which always sought quiet and inspired me with noe other desires, noe other aimes then to passe silently through this world with the company of a few good freinds and books. And therefor to remove my self as far as might be from any publique concernes, I in the late†b unhappy times pitchd upon the study of physique. But my Lord one accident of my life (my falling into a great mans family) and one fault in my health (a consumptive indisposition which forbad me a setled abode to looke after others health and gave me worke enough to take care of my owne) have (I know not by what witchcraft) confounded the quiet, I always sought; and the more I endeavour to get into some quiet retreat, the more still I finde my self in a storme. For now, when with some degree of health (which has improved here beyond my expectation) I hoped to enjoy some repose, in a separation from almost all conversation, I am suspected to write divers
― 664 ―

scandalous and seditious libells.†1
I have often wonderd in the way that I lived, and the make I knew my self of, how it could come to passe, that I was made the author of soe many pamphlets, unlesse it was because I of all my Lords family happend to have been most bred amongst books. This opinion of me I thought time and the contradictions it caryed with it would have cured, and that the most suspitious would at last have been weary of imputeing to me writeings whose matter, and stile have I beleive (for pamphlets have been laid to me which I have never seen) been soe very different, that it was hard to thinke they should have the same author, though a much abler man then me. This suspition however follows me, it seems, here, where I hoped to be out of the way of all publique concernes, for that made some part of my satisfaction in those many solitary howers I spent alone, industriously avoiding company, to that degree, that it was reproachd to me here, that I was a man by my self. And it is a very odde fate, that I should get the reputation of noe small writer, without haveing donne any thing for it. For I thinke two or three copys of verses of mine, published with my name to them,†2have not gaind me that reputation. Bateing those I here solemnly protest in the presence of god, that I am not the author, not only of any libell, but not of any pamphlet or treatise whatsoever in print good bad or indifferent.†3 The apprehension and backwardnesse I have ever had to be in print even in matters very remote from any thing of Libellous or seditious, is soe well known to my freinds, that I am sure I can in this have many compurgators. As to the company I am said to keepe at Coffee houses, the honour of your Lordships acquaintance flatters me, that your Lordship beleives me not a natural†a foole, which I must
― 665 ―

needs be, if I should come hither to make acquaintanc<e>†a now, and keepe company with men, whom every one that would be safe shuns, and who were never any of my associates in England, when they were under much better circumstances.
Those who are particularly named for my Companions, I assure your Lordship with the truth I would speake my last breath, I never saw out of England, nor in a long time before I left it.†1 Coffee houses it is well known I loved and frequented litle in England, lesse here. I speake much within compasse when I say I have not been in a Coffee house as many times as I have been months here, haveing noe great delight either in the conversation or the liquor, and when I went there, which I remember I was once forced to doe three or fower times in one weeke, it was only to speake with some merchant I had businesse with. My time was most spent alone, at home by my fires side, where I confesse I writ a good deale, I thinke I may say, more then ever I did in soe much time in my life, but noe libells, unlesse perhaps it may be a libell against all mankinde to give some account of the weaknesse and shortnesse of humane understanding, for upon that my old theme de Intellectu humano (on which your Lordship knows I have been a good while a hammering), has my head been beating, and my pen scribleing all the time I have been here except what I have spent in travelling about to see the country.†2 It has been asked too, why I chose Holland, and not France for change of aire (For this consumptive poor shadow of a man moves noe where without a noise) The reasons in short were, I had tried France and it would not prove a cure, it only kept my cough at a pretty tolerable abatement, but silenced it not quite. And this country I had not tried, which I now finde more effectuall, and I have reason to hope in time a perfect cure. Besides wine always sensibly hurts my lungs, and water since my last sicknesse gives me the colique, and there is but litle beare in France, none in the southern parts, These considerations made this choise necessary†3
― 666 ―

My Lord though this be the second letter I have given my self the honour to write your Lordship since I left England,†1 yet when I consider the length of this, I am apt to feare, I am more then a dayly importuner. It was my duty and designe to return your Honour my most humble thanks for your Lordships most generous continuation of your favour and kindenesse to me in this my disgrace. But instead of it I see I have troubled your Lordship with a tedious account of my self, and am falne into such a stile as I was not wont to use with your Lordship. Tis a great part of the misfortune of the unhappy that they are full of noething but their own misery. And those who thinke they have not merited the hardships they lye under would willingly finde a patron to tell the story of their innocence to, I perswade my self I might have spared my long one to your Lordship, and that your owne knowledg of me would have justified me in your Lordships thoughts. But your Lordships good opinion and favour is of soe mighty a value and comfort to me that my concerne to preserve it could not expresse it self in fewer words; And when I cease to be a loyall subject, or an honest man, may I (as the last of miserys) loose that too. I am
My Lord
Your Honours most humble most obedient
and most obleiged servant
J. LOCKE
My Lord if it were not too great a presumption on your Lordships goodnesse to suppose you continue the same willingnesse to see my odde notions when in some tolerable order as you were pleased to expresse formerly I would with your Lordships permission take the boldnesse to present to your Lordships view by the first oportunity a part of what I have been doeing here.†2
Address: To the Right Honourable Thomas Earle of Pembroke these Humbly present
― 667 ―

799. Locke to Edward Clarke, [mid-December 1684?] (791, 801)
Rand, pp. 115-17. 'The whole of this letter is in a very bad condition.' Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. The date of the endorsement is suspect. In no. 801 Locke writes that he is glad that Clarke approves of his method of keeping Master free from being costive. If the method is that set out in the present letter, Clarke must have written not later than 19/29 December. One of the education letters: p. 624
[Amsterdam, Dec. 1684.]
Sir,
Yours from Chipley I answered about ten days since.... One†3- thing since has come to my mind relating to your son's health, and which perhaps may be of use to you also, which is that I would have him go constantly to stool once a day. I expect you should
― 668 ―

think it [strange that I] propose this as if it were in his or any body's power else, and I [think in] great measure it is, and more perhaps than you would imagine. I myself being naturally costive, and considering a great part of our diseases come from a want of a due excretion of what was to be separated in the several c ... tions of the body, cast about for a remedy. Purging medicines I knew were so far from helping those that were used to be bound, that they increased the disorder. Laxative diet is neither always to be had nor fit always to be used. I first, then, considered that a great many motions of our body that seemed natural and almost wholly involuntary, might yet, by a use and constant application, in a good measure be made obedient, and particularly that of the peristaltic motion of the guts which caused that excretion I saw might be restrained.†a ... Therefore after my first eating, which was seldom till noon, I constantly went to the stool, whether I had any motion or no, and there stayed so long that most commonly I [attained] my errand; and by this constant practice in a short time the habit was so settled, that I usually feel a motion; if not I, however, go to the place as if I had, and there seldom fail (not once in a month) to do the business I came for. This is one of the greatest secrets I know in physic for the preservation of health, and I doubt not but it will succeed both in you and your son, if with constancy and patience at first you put it into practice.†-3 You must pardon this homely discourse. For nature not having thought fit to make us all civet cats, physicians that are nature's interpreters are forced sometimes to talk even to ladies of other things than perfumes.
Since the receipt of yours of the 7th from London, I am in great pain till I hear again what becomes of my little Mistress, and whether the indisposition you then mentioned proved the small pox....†b
Your being out of town and in my ramble†1 made me forget the mentioning to you the <matter> of the money left in Mr. Pierce's†2 hands. Therefore pray deliver him up his note, and when it may be ... better advantage ... your money paid there will produce most here; pray return the book again to the same person here as Mr. Pierce did, and that for my use. I am not in great haste, and therefore
― 669 ―

you may do it when your convenience, and your business of exchange, which you will learn there amongst the merchants at any time. My humble service to my Mistress and young Master, and believe tht I am perfectly,
Sir,
your most humble servant,
J. L.
Address: For Mr. Edward Clarke at the Lady King's in Salisbury Court, Fleet Street, London.
Endorsed by Clarke: J. L. his letter about my son's health. Received the 25th December, 1684.
800. Locke to Dr. later Sir, Thomas Molyneux, [22 December 1684/1 January 1685?] (1531)
Dr. G. K. Woodgate. On deposit in the Kent Record Office, Maidstone. Transcribed from Xerox print. Printed by (Sir) William R. W. Wilde in Dublin University Magazine, xviii (July-December 1841), 489-90. The date is uncertain. It is not clear whether it was Locke or Molyneux who added the letters 'O.S.' to the date. It would have been unusual for Locke to use an old-style date at this time; on the other hand unless the letter was exceedingly slow in transit, or Molyneux dilatory in reply, the date must be old style. An old-style date fits also with no. 801: when Locke wants to send Clarke a fresh copy of his 'Directions' for the young Edward he finds that he has lost his draft of them.
Thomas Molyneux, 1661-1733, was born in Dublin. He graduated M.A. and M.B. of Trinity College in 1683, and was now studying at Leyden. He graduated M.D. of Dublin in 1687 and was elected F.R.S. later in that year. He was active as a physician mainly in Dublin. He was created a baronet in 1730: D.N.B., and the articles by (Sir) William R. W. Wilde in Dublin University Magazine, xviii (1841).
In 1692 Locke entered into a correspondence with Molyneux's elder brother William (no. 1515, etc.).
Utrecht, 22o Dec: 84†a
Sir
I hope you and the rest of your good company had a good journey back again to Leyden, where I often wish my self with you: haveing not passed any of my time on this side the water soe pleasantly as there for which I am indebted to the civility of those gent I had the honour to converse with there, and particularly to yours: of
― 670 ―

which haveing had soe much experience I venture to give you a new trouble. which is to enquire of Mrs. Terry's people whether none of them saw any papers that I left any where about the chamber or the presses there when I came away. A freind of mine haveing an only son that he is very tender of sent to me for some directions about him, which I made an hasty draught of whilst I was at Leyden.†1 The father of the childe lately writ to me again to the same purpose, and when I now designed†a upon this new instance, to revise those papers I there writ in haste and send them him, I finde them misseing. I cannot thinke of any place I was soe like to leave them as upon one of the shelves there, where I laid them the last time I remember I saw them. Though they were hasty directions huddled up in the vacancys of the auction†2 and particularly adapted to a child of between two and three years old†3 and soe not worth the reading to any body else, yet you would doe me a singular favour if you could retreive them, they being writ when all the circumstances were fresh in my memory, and if they be lost I shall very much disappoint the father. I know you have civility enough to excuse this trouble which I hope may be a provocation to you to use the same freedome with me in†b any occasion wherein I may shew with what readynesse I am, Sir,
Sir
your most humble servant
JOHN LOCKE.
Pray present my most humble service to all those Gent I had the happynesse to know and converse with at Mrs. Terrys
Be pleased to direct your letter to me at the Wedue Gremons†4 op het Hoek van Het oude Kerk hof tot Utrecht.

801. Locke to Edward Clarke, 22 December 1684/1 January 1685 (799, 803)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 14. Badly faded; guarded with transparent paper. Printed in Rand, pp. 117-21. Many readings are conjectural; the passages in pointed brackets are mainly Rand's readings.
Utrecht 1o Jan: 85
Sir
I have been very unfortunate and other people very malitious to raise Suspitions upon me without any ground but their owne misinterpretations of my most innocent actions. For I am more and more confirmed in my opinion that my being much in my chamber alone the last winter and busy there for the most part about my enquiry concerneing Humane Understanding†a a subject which I had for a good while backwards thought on by catches and set downe without method severall thoughts upon as they had at distinct times and on severall occasions come in my way and which I was now willing in this retreat to forme into a lesse confused and coherent discourse and adde what was wanting to make my designe intelligible to some†b of my freinds who had desired it of me and to whom I had promised a sight of it when it was a litle out of the rubish, and to that purpose had brought those papers along with me into this country,†c †1 and I was glad I did soe since they not only gave me an innocent and (as I thought) a safe imployment for my solitary howers here, but I was also satisfied I should scarce any where else, where I had had the company of my freinds, and where soe much time had not lain upon my hands, ever have had the patience to have revised and new formed my old scatterd notions it takeing up more time and pains with lesse pleasure and profit then the pursuit of new ones. This however innocently it then helped me to passe away my time with some satisfaction in the absence of my freinds and almost all company I am confident has been the occasion of my misfortune. The more I consider it the more I am confirmed in this opinion, and I phansy I could guesse pretty neare the very person who tooke an oportunity from my being constantly almost writeing to give a rise to that suspition which has soe much
― 672 ―

ruined me.†1 For why should I thinke those that I have known busy in other peoples affairs and free of their misrepresentations and wrong reports should be more civil to me, Into the acquaintance with some such unavoidable accidents brought me here.
But a <man>†a that thinkes noe ill is apt to feare none, and therefor knowing my actions and intentions cleare I had noe apprehensions of any thing like what has befallen me. I know not whether this may bring my prudence in question I am sure it cannot my innocence: He that had designed to write libells would have been more <cautious and not> put himself into a house where he knew he should meet with such as would not <be backwards to give information.> I wish all that I have writ here were seen by those that most suspect me or wish ill to me (if there be any such for I deserve it from noe body) they would then see my <head was> imploid about speculations remote enough from any publique <or>†b politique concern and was not teemeing with any thing for the presse here. For I tell you again with that truth which should be sacred betwixt freinds that I am not the Author of any treatise or pamphlet in print good bad or indifferent and therefor you may be sure how I am used when people talke of libells. Two or three copys of verses indeed there are of mine in print as I have formerly told you <but>†c those have my name to them. But as for libells I am soe far from writeing any that I take care not to read any thing that lookes that way, I avoid all commerce about them and if a letter from a freind should have in it but the title or mention of any libell, I should thinke it a sufficient reason to burne it immediately what ever else of concernement there might be in it, and to quarrell with him that writ it and I desire noe other usage for my letters or my self from my freinds. But to keepe myself far enough from that I have never any commerce of news with any absent acquaintance, and inquire not after it†2 amongst those I am with, I have scarce read soe much as half a dozen gazet since I have been here and those only when other people have put them into my hands, not that I thinke it a fault, but haveing resolved not to medle in the least
― 673 ―

with any publique affairs, I decline as much as I can the discourse of them and the rather because forainers (for with those I choose rather to converse then with my countrymen) being apt to aske an English man concerning English news I may truly tell them I know not any.
Though all I said in my long letter to E:P†1 be all true yet it is not all I have to say for my self. For to mention but one thing more to you. Can any one thinke I should lay out soe much mony in books as I have since I came hither (above 50l and should have donne more) which would be an intolerable burden to a wanderer, and at the same time by libels and other miscariages have shut up the way to my returne into England and forfeit my place at Ch: ch: which I knew any displeasure might take from me, and now that it is gon I know not what to doe with my books haveing noe where to place them. Before this calamity I considerd my purchase of them with pleasure but now with regreat, It displeases†a me as often as I thinke on them, and if my innocence did not give me some hopes of my place again I thinke I should disburthen my self of them presently. But though the consideration of his Majesties great†b clemency†b and of my own innocence give me reason to hope a restoration, yet I doe not thinke it convenient to move <in it yet. Great men doe not love to have> innocence pleaded in the first heat of their <suspition, however raised by misinformation> when I am satisfied that it is a proper time to stir in it I will <in>†c another long letter to him make my innocence yet clearer, but <neither is it fit to load him with such a letter, nor is it> yet a proper time to move, at present there is no remedy but patience, and therefor pray manage his forward kindenesse soe as dexterously to put it off from stiring in it till a fiter season, least by too much hast the businesse be sp<oi>led†d and I loose the benefit of his assistance afterwards at a more proper time. For <you may> let him know I have a great deale more to say for my self but that I cannot thinke it reasonable to tire him with long storys haveing soe lately offended that way already. For this reason I would not have Mr Somers†e †2 say any thing to him or any of my
― 674 ―

freinds of what I guessed in mine of 8 Dec.†1 I had just then at my return from Leyden first heard of that <malitious thing I there mentioned>†2 and presently after was surprised with the news from Ch:Ch: and the circumstance of the time led my then perplexed thoughts into that conjecture, but had I heard then what I have <since>†a concerneing it I should not have mentiond it nor troubled Mr Som: with that uselesse conjecture which could serve to noe purpose to be mentioned, but an innocent man under the surprise of an unexpected and undeservd misfortune must be pardond if he cast about on all sides and thinke whence soe strange a mischeife most probably appears to come. Did E P take notice to you of the postscript of my letter and expresse any willingnesse that I should send him any part of my discourse De Intellectu humano which I have been at worke about here to put it into a forme that one may now see the designe and connection of the parts. <I>f†a he did I will finde some way to send it; if he did not there is noe farther mention to be made of it.
I am glad you approve of my es ...†b the†b method for keeping your son from being costive without <giving>†c him physique.†3I beleive you will finde it effectuall, and I thinke it a thing of great moment to my health, therefor I recommend it to you for your own practise a<s w>ell†a as for your son. Though I tend the young sprout yet I would have the old stock also preserved as long as I could. What <I>†c say in mine that inclosed E P's long one and also in another to the same purpose I doe not upon second thoughts soe well approve as being not of a peice with the rest, and therefor pray burn them, saveing them cannot be of any use. If you had receivd the dir ...... pers at large concerneing the management of your sons health I sent about <th>e†a end of November†4 you would then have seen a great part of my thoughts ...†d much better then in stragling pages writ at distant times which you have received, which some times crosse out the and seeme to con what was writ. If those be miscaried as your silence gives me reason
― 675 ―

to suspect, let me know, and then I shall repeat them again with my stragling additions and shall make this advantage of the losse that then you shall have all my thoughts togeather in that matter, and thus†a seeing them all togeather I shall be sure to make them of a peice.†1 It will be when all togeather at least 4 or 5 sheets and therefor too big to be sent by the post, and cost that way more then it is worth and therefor to prevent a second miscariage take order with Mr Perce†2 that what comes to his hand for you be conveyd to you by a sure messenger on purpose, for I find the penny post way has lost several of my letters which came safe to London, for though I care not who sees what I write, yet I would have those also see it to whom I write it, especially what cost me some pains in writeing, and I thinke may be of some use to those I send it, as I hope this discourse concerning your son will be, or else I would not give you the trouble to read nor my self to write so much on that occasion. If your Lady approve of it when she sees it I will then obey her commands in reference to her daughters, where in there will be some though noe great difference, for makeing a litle allowance for beauty and some few other considerations of the s<ort>†b the  †c of training†d of boys and girles especially in their younger years I imagine should be much the same. Je vous ecris, monsieur, de chez monsieur L'Abé comme secretaire d'un triumvirat†1 qui a bu a votre santé ad multos annos.†2 le capitaine de marine, le croiriez vous? est celui qui en cela officie le plus mal, mais il a d'autres qualitéz qui recompensent ce defaut. 805. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 15 January [1685] (787, 815)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 120-1. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Tho you do not Chide me for not Answearing the letter I received from You Dated from Deventer†1 I cannot sattisfie my self not to Make some Apologie for it, and to let you know that my Eyes were for above a Month after so Weake that I durst not use them at all either to Write, or Read, Since when I have never beene in a Humour Good enough to Answear a Letter that so severely reprooves me for being in an Ill One. Whatever Occasion there might be for it, I durst not therefore write to you for my Life for feare of makeing some Complaints that you would have beene sure to have thought Unreasonable, as I suppose you will now think it for me to have beene so Long out of Humour, and Yet methinks Wageing War with the World, and the Flesh (as you say I do) should not seeme to you so easie a Matter but that it may very well serve to Justifie me for it. It is so long since the 8th of Oct:†2 that I know not now what it was that I then said to you, nor what my Thoughts were. But I assure you since then, whatever you may think, I have beene much more a Stoick then you ever knew me, and have now such a Zeal for the Sect I have embrac'd, that I never was so sorry as since I had your letter that I am neither Handsome nor Witty; since you think such an Example would do so much Good in the World. But it is not my fault I am sure and so I indeavour to sattisfie my self, who tho I am now altogether a Stoick as to my Philosophy Yet may I Hope be a Labadist too if I see it Convenient, there being no Inconsistencie I think, but a very Good Agreement betweene them. Should I ever resolve for Matrimonie, You have so far improv'd my Reasons and Arguments for it that I should Certainly then go into Freezeland, But should I do the Contrary I beleeve you will think it best that I stay where I am, especially since if Men should ever become my Aversion, or that I should grow extraordinarie Devout and Religious, things that sometimes Happen in that case, Here is a Friend of yours who doubts not in a little time but that she shall see her selfe an Abbess,†3 With
― 679 ―

whom I Question not but you have sufficient Interest to Procure that I may be one of Her Nuns.
The Difficultie therefore lyes in makeing this Choise, and since it seemes I have so far alreadie Trusted you as to Confess to You that I am but Half Arm'd against Matrimonie I cannot fancie that I can Pitch upon any Body better, to Advise me by which of my Halfs it is that I ought to be Determin'd which till you have done I meane to Converse indeed in this Present Evill world, but with such a Stoical sort of Indifference that the Brethren in Freezeland shall have no Reason to say that Damaris has forsaken them and to Convince you that there is alreadie a very great Change wrought in me I assure you I cannot remember that any discourse of Mine since I came to Towne has beene able to tend at all to Mr Clarks Edification Concerning the fasions Or that Mrs Clarke and I or any other Lady have once sat in Councell about that Matter. Tis true, I am not yet got into a Tammy Petticoat and Wastcoate, nor a Say Apron,†1 But the Reason is that if I should continue onely to be a Plaine Stoick I cannot yet Determine my self whether it may not be as agreable, or more so, to the Severitie of our Sect to go without any Cloaths at all, since Certainly They are a Part of, at lest Depend upon the Goods of Fortune. I Hope therefore you will be Convinc'd now that I am true to my Principles, and that a Proselite is not Lost, Also since My Quarrel with the World is so Lasting, that it is more likelie it was occasion'd for want of a Servant,†2 then through any falling out with any that I Had. You know I have Liv'd Lately a great while in a Place where it has been a Complaint (as you may remember) that there was no Occasion for a Heart,†3 and therefore the thing is not at all Unlikely. However since perhaps it may not be so much for my Honour to have it thought so, I think I am Concern'd if it were but on that Score to Continue the same Here that I use to be in that Duller Aire, which for a Thousand New Reasons I was not a little glad to Quitt at this time, but should have beene much more so could I have had any Hopes of Meeting you Here. I have not yet seene Mr Clarke to inform my self what it was he said to you of me, But if it
― 680 ―

were that I think of my Pupil much oftener then he dos of his Governess I dare say it was nothing but Truth. However though I am a little Jealous and suspicious in this matter I am notwithstanding as much as ever his Real Friend and very Humble Servant
P.†1
Jan: the 15th

806. Mrs. Mary Clarke to Locke, 16 January 1685 (777, 809)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 179. Printed in Rand, pp. 121-2. Answered by no. 809.
London January the 16th. 1684
Deare Sir
I have Receved a thousand Favours from you for which I ought to returne you my thankes by every opertunity, but now in perticuler I am to thanke you for the Great Care you have taken in writing and sending the directtions How to Bring up my Little Boy,†2 by which you have Infineatly oblidged both his Father and mee who shall be very Carfull to observe and Follow every perticuler of it, and I hope that will incorage you to wright a second part and that will be as Great a sattisfacktion as can be next Conversing with you in person, I am in Great hopes when you returne hither a Gen we shall have as much of your Company as any of your Frends, and that you will oblidge us in makeing use of that apartment that you made Choyce of in our House†3 and is ever since reserved a purpose for you and I am sure you cann take noe better a way to keepe mr Clarkes vapors from returning then to Lett him see that his Building proves any ways serviceable to one that he has soe Great a vallew For as your selfe; and I have one thinge more to tempt you which is the best turnips and Carretts that ever wase eat, and insteede of makeing walkes of them, I thinke they have walked, for all our Frends theare†a abouts have
― 681 ―

robbed us of them, and that they might be sure not to be denyd, Great bellied women have pretended to Long for them, and I cannott blame them, for If you will beleve me I thinke them the best that ever wase eat. Pray pardon the tediousness of my Letter and Give me Leave only to add my desires to you to take Great care of your health and beleve me to be,
Sir,
your Most affecttionate Frend and Faithfull humble servant,
M CLARKE.
My Sone and both my Daughters are your humble servants, and your mistres is now very prety Company, Sir I hope my carrectter of the tarnups and your Good nature will be the occation of your sending some more of the same sorts of seedes

807. Locke to Edward Clarke, [24 January/3 February 1685?] (804, 808)
Rand, pp. 244-6. 'This letter is in very bad condition and in part perished.' Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. The letter is dated by Rand '[12th] February [1688]'. It belongs early in 1685. Locke mentions mislaying his own copy of the 'Directions' for Master's education and the copy sent probably in January: pp. 670, 680; and two trunks that are identifiable as those mentioned on pp. 698 and 708. He is to send Mrs. Clarke some directions for girls; he sent her some in no. 809, which dates probably from 28 January/7 February. February
Sir,
I am glad to hear by yours of 20th Jan. that my opinion on children has at last come to hand. But I hope you have ere this received a more perfect copy [of the portion] lost I took care to send you. Indeed I was in some trouble for several days [in trying to] find the original copy and so being [thereby able] to retrieve it again.†1 For if I were to be hindered at this rate I could not write to you on the same subject again anything you or I could with patience read, because whenever I should set myself to write my
― 682 ―

thoughts would hunt in my memory for what pleased me when I writ before, and not in any reason whereby I should be able to make nothing of it. I am glad also to find by yours of 16th Jan. that it so well pleases both you and Madam. But yet though one can but be satisfied that what one does proves acceptable to a friend one loves, yet I once more beg you to look on it as a discourse that fell into your hands by chance and to have no consideration of the author but of your son in the case, for I had much rather you should find me in a mistake than commit any yourself by my advice in a business of such concernment to you as is the right ordering of your son.†1
One thing I have thought fit to add or alter concerning your [method of teaching your son] to read, which therefore if you value and think it worth the transcribing you may add to the end of the former papers. Instead†2- of the ivory polygon, a polyhedron mentioned p.... to paste the letters of the alphabet on; a shorter and better way will be to get some of the largest dice (4 will serve for the 24 letters) you can, and either peeke out the marks, or, which is better, have them plain without any. On one of these at first paste an A and a B, drawing lines under them as here to show which way they must stand to be looked at. Then have the same letters in pieces of paper and lay them on apples, raisins, almonds or any of those kind of things he loves, and you have a mind he should have, and so after dinner or supper the company, and amongst them he, play for them, so that who first throws A is to have what A is laid on, etc. When by this way of playing he is perfect in these two letters you may add C, and so on. Another way may be with pigeon-holes as they call them: at these twenty-four holes, over the first paste an A, over the second a B, and so laying a like a and b to the things you play for, let that be won which has the letter you first hit.-†2 This has variety and more exercise than the other....†a
I must therefore desire you to excuse my silence till I get a little leisure to talk to her concerning my pretty little Miss and her other daughter, wherein if I can satisfy her as well as she persuades
― 683 ―

me I have about her son I shall think myself very happy. And since you continue to think my old bachelor's advice concerning your son's education as he [proceeds] is worth the having, you may be sure that I who so forwardly thrust myself into this affair will not be backward to go on now you desire it ...†a The next thing therefore to be done is to observe his temper whether bold or timorous, careless or curious, steady or unconstant, friendly or churlish, etc., for your having once established your authority and got the ascendant over him, the next thing must be to bend the crooks the other way if he have any in him, and apply proper methods to his peculiar inclinations.†1 Pray tell me in your next whether his cap was left off and whether his feet have been washed every night in cold water as I advised in the beginning of summer, and how it has succeeded with him.
There is at Mr. Old's an hair portmanteau trunk with deeds in it and the box you nailed up and sent thither when you did me the favour to go to Paulton.†2 I desire you to let him know there are things in them both that you shall have occasion to make use of for me, and therefore desire him to send them both to you very carefully. He has besides a very little red trunk of mine, not a foot I think nor eight inches long, which I desire him to lock up in the hair portmanteau trunk (for as I remember he has the key of it), and send it in it When I hear you have them I will tell you what I would have done with some of the deeds in them....†b

what the two last sorts are I know not. they say the sugar ray roots being boiled may be either eaten hot butterd as Turneps, or cold with oyle and vinegar as a salad. Sarsafey I have eaten in England they are pleasant and commended for wholsome.

If I had your coat of Armes in Colours I would get it donne in glasse to be set up some where at Chipley, being very well acquainted with a good glasse painter here.
I remember Adrian sent me word he could not get the key into the locke of a chest of mine where in were some clothes. This has some times happend to me for there is a square spike in the locke which goes into the hollow of the key, which if it stands not right the key will not goe in, and then the spike in the locke must be turned a litle with a pair of nippars or compasses soe that the square of it may stand right with the square of the hollow of the key to goe into it and then the key will goe in. But when the key is in there requires yet some skill to open the locke. to which purpose I left with him a circle drawn with markes. pray remember that
this marke Δ stands for Degrees and
This ♁ for Minutes.

I thanke Susan†1 for my Flanen†2 Shirts. Pray appease her wrath for I thought she would not be displeased with my recantation. to shew her that I have noe malice I desire her to get me fower flanen shirts more just as the former only the collars I would have single and at least three fingers broad or more where as these I have were double and narrow. when they are donne I would desire to have my Cissars at John Hicks's, the litle bottle Musidore left with you and an other he has or will send you wrapd up and sent in them and the shirts sent as the last were.
Now we are come to discourse of trees again I cannot forbeare to repeat what I thinke I mentioned formerly,†3 that is, to be sure to set the inmost row of your trees that lead to your house on either side, 20 foot without the line of your house this will be much best when the trees are grown up and if you thinke it will be a fault to looke along your walke by the side of your house in the meane time that I thinke will be cured by planting one tree at the end of the walke next your house just in the line of your house. I doe not approve Abells for walkes up to your house, they will doe better down about your ponds and by the brooks side. The walkes leadeing to your house on the 4 sides I would have of these fower sorts. Lime in the front and on the three other sides Oaks, on one Elmes on the other, and witch Elmes on the third as you like best and for winter greens if you will be ruled by me use none but Ewe and Holly, they will make hedges or standars as you please will endure any cuting and weather, whereas all other as phylyrea, alaternus cypresses etc are commonly one in 20 years cut downe to the ground by a severe winter, examine the gardens and see how many of them were left last sommer.†4 I am Sir your most humble servant J L

809. Locke to Mrs. Mary Clarke, [28 January/7 February 1685?] (806, 908)
Rand, pp. 102-6. 'This letter is in very bad condition, being discoloured and very much faded, even since 1877, when a copy which accompanies it was made. It is here printed from the copy of 1877, as the greater part of the original letter is now hopelessly illegible.' Words in square brackets supplied by Rand. His date is questionable. The passage relating to the bringing-up of girls is a sequel to that for boys in no. 782 or the revision in Locke's 'Directions' (nos. 791, 804), and makes good the promises of nos. 801 and 807; other passages answer no. 806; and the ten sorts of seeds connect with the list in no. 808. Following Rand I have given the day as the 7th of the month, though it conflicts with that of no. 808.
7 <February>†a 1683[-4].
Madam,
... [This] is not the first by many I have received from you without having any other title to them but barely [your goodness]. To make some acknowledgment, 'tis fit I acquit myself of my promise to you in reference to my little mistress ... [and] you will think that speaking with [the sincere] affection I have for the softer sex I shall not think of any rougher usage than only what [her sex] requires. Since therefore I acknowledge no difference of sex in your mind relating ... to truth, virtue and obedience, I think well to have no thing altered in it from what is [writ for the son]. And since I should rather desire in my wife a healthy constitution, a stomach able to digest ordinary food, and a body that could endure upon occasion both wind and sun, rather than a puling, weak, sickly wretch, that every breath of wind or least hardship puts in danger, I think the meat drink and lodging and clothing should be ordered after the same manner for the girls as for the boys. There is only one or two things whereof I think distinct consideration is to be had. You know my opinion is that the boys should be much abroad in the air at all times and in all weathers, and if they play in the sun and in the wind without hats and gloves so much the better. But since in your girls care is to be taken too of their beauty as much as health will permit, this in them must have some restriction, the more they exercise and the more they are in the air the better health they will have, that I am sure: but yet 'tis fit their tender skins should be fenced against the busy sunbeams, especially when they are very hot and piercing: to avoid this and yet to give them exercise in the air, some little shady grove near the house would be convenient for them to play in, and a large airy room in ill
― 687 ―

weather: and if all the year you make them rise as soon as it is light and walk a mile or two and play abroad before sun-rising, you will by that custom obtain more good effects than one; and it will make them not only fresh and healthy, but good housewives too. But that they may have sleep enough, which whilst they are young must not be scanty, they must be early to bed too.
Another thing is, that of washing their feet every night in cold water and exposing them to the wet in the day. Though my reason is satisfied that it is both the healthiest and safest way, yet since it is not fit that girls should be dabbling in water as your boys will be, and since perhaps it will be thought both an odd and new thing, I cannot tell how to enjoin it. This I am sure I have seen many a little healthy [child do in] winter, and I think that had I a daughter I should order water to be put in her [shoes] when she put them on, and have her feet well washed in cold water. But this must not be begun at any time of the year, but in the hot weather in May, and then begin only with one dabble the first morning, two the next, and so on. If continuing in this custom ... benefit to nature ... about thirteen or fourteen as others have†a , and as I could not at all doubt, I should do her a very great kindness by preventing the mischiefs, that others (who used to keep their feet warm and dry) very often receive by taking wet in their feet, whereof in your sex there are daily examples. But since I affect not to go out of the ordinary road, and there are many healthy women without it, I do not advise it for my pretty little Mis[s], though if there should be any inconvenience in it, the very leaving of it off would remove it.
Their heads, I think, should never be covered, nor their necks within doors, and when they go abroad the covering of these should be more against the sun than the cold. And herein you may take notice how much it is use that makes us either tender or hardy, for there is scarce a young lady so weak and tender who will not go bare in her neck without suffering any harm at a season when if a hardy strong man not used to it should imitate her it would be intolerable to him, and he would be sure to get a cold if not a fever.
Girls should have a dancing master at home early: it gives them fashion and easy comely motion betimes which is very convenient, and they, usually staying at home with their mothers, do not lose it again, whereas the boys commonly going to school, they lose
― 688 ―

what they learn of a dancing master at home amongst their ill-fashioned schoolfellows, which makes it often less necessary because less useful for the boys to learn to dance at home when little: though if they were always to play at home in good company I should advise it for them too. If the girls are also by nature very bashful, it would be good that they should go also to dance publicly in the dancing schools when little till their sheepishness were cured; but too much of the public schools may not perhaps do well, for of the two, too much shamefacedness better becomes a girl than too much confidence, but having more admired than considered your sex I may perhaps be out in these matters, which you must pardon me.
This is all I can think of at present, wherein the treatment of your girls should be different from that I have proposed for the boys. Only I think the father [ought] to strike very seldom, if at all to chide his daughters. Their governing and correcting, I think, properly belongs to the mother.
You need not take so much care to bespeak me to a man and company to which my own inclination so much carries me. But if once I get into possession of my apartment, as you are so kindly pleased to call it, can anybody tell whether it will be easy to get me out again? The pleasures of the place and the agreeableness of the conversation may, for ought I know, so charm me, that perhaps by that time will have his belly-full of wandering, that he may not probably ... go ... out of it. This I can assure you, that if it be a pleasure to be with those one extremely loves and values, I could not be so happy anywhere as at Chipley when you and Mr. Clark are there with your little ones; though there were no such temptations of a like opportunity, if he might have never any greater occasion to raise vapours than that house. I am sure you will be forever free from them, both of you, for I have [never seen a] house that I have liked better and that in all respects I have thought so prudently built and suited to all purposes.
You make no show of it, and you do good offices when you seemed but to compliment. For it is you, I find, who by magnifying the turnips to that degree have raised them above lime and abele trees, and when Mr. Clarke had reason to reproach me for this sort of plantation for walks, 'twas an obliging artifice to stop his mouth with turnips. This deserves that I should at least [supply] your garden with such kind of furniture. I have therefore provided
― 689 ―

you another parcel of seeds of turnips and other roots of this country. If they come safe there are ten sorts of them. Your gardener will take care to sow them so as to observe which genus will suit you, and have [the] excellency in them worth the sending for, that so we may take care there has to be provided from hence [only] such Dutch seeds [as are] better than our own. Sarsafras is a root lately come into use. It is very pleasant and very wholesome, and your gardener may also succeed [with it] and set your neighbours' mouth a watering after them too....
But [what of] an arrant country Lady†1 a few hundred mile from court or any thought of London you ... like. Blame Mrs. Cudworth: she solemnly protests she has not had one discourse with you [since she came] to town.†2 What is the matter, I beseech you? Whence rises and on what side lies their trouble? The mortification [of it] is as much and almost as cold as freezing a bed, and looks as strange as if coaches were going on the Thames....†3 But will there not a thaw come, and will you not think of the spring glittering and garniture, with a gaiety again? Anything but old father winter with a garland of his turnips and carrots about his head†4that in them ... will not always do. I have [hopes] the reason of the town and better thoughts will dissipate it, and then consultation about [it] will be renewed again. If it be not, I will pronounce you duller than they are here....
My service to Mr. Clarke and your little ones and to Mrs. Cudworth and ... And, let me be angry or pleased, she ought to write.
I am, Madam,
your most humble servant,
J. L.
Address: For Mrs. Mary Clarke at the Lady King's, Salisbury Court, London
Endorsed: J. L. letter to Mrs. Clarke received ... 1684.

However, after much thought and long hesitation as to what was the best thing to do I have at last decided on a plan which perhaps you expected least of all; yet when you have carefully considered the matter in all its bearings you will, I hope, come to agree with me that there is no better way I could have thought of for getting this method published. Here, then, is the gist of my plan:
(Original Text) 1. Since this subject could not possibly amount to the bulk of a regular volume, and as it would be absurd to augment it with irrelevant matter, I felt that it must necessarily be inserted in some one of those miscellanies that are now appearing everywhere; our English miscellanies are in fact hanging fire at the moment or rather are carelessly managed; the German are a long way off. But in fact a publication of this kind requires the presence
[p. 692]
either of the author or of someone who understands the matter equally well. Accordingly I have entrusted it to your hands for insertion in your periodicals, if that seems convenient.†1
(Original Text) 2. I have written it in English, as that is the language I can express myself in best and most succinctly; I do not know French well enough to be able to turn out a pamphlet like this in proper style. Here it is for you in English, then; you need not be surprised, for you know about it already, and there are so many of your countrymen to be found who understand English that you will not want for an interpreter; he can go over it with you, either rendering it word for word or giving you a rather more studied translation; thus, I feel sure, you will grasp my meaning and will write it out in clear and lucid French, as your way is. You seem troubled about the provision of an index. I do not myself feel that this need be considered; there is no way in which it could be made to square with volumes of different form. I do not mean only those in folio, quarto, and octavo, but not even all in folio, so great are the differences in the [size of] paper. A much better way, I think, is for the first two pages of the book itself to be divided into twenty-five equal parts, as you see done in my own draft; everyone can then draw these lines to suit the
[p. 693]
size of his own book; this can be done without difficulty even in lead pencil, unless one should prefer to draw every fifth line in ink for the sake of clearer distinction, as you see has been done in my accompanying table. Be guided by your own instinct rather than by any advice from me; in my own books I add no distinctions in ink between the written entries other than the slightest, such as you can see at the foot of the table. I want these pages to contain not only a description but an example of my method; and I should advise that this description be printed in the same manner; for examples are more informative than instructions. What I have added at the end about the method of citing authorities you can omit if you like, as it possibly does not deserve publication; it is only that I should not wish to leave you in the dark about any detail of my practice in this matter. Well then, I put it entirely in your hands; decide on anything you like about any part or about the whole of it. If you think I have omitted anything I will add it; if you consider me too concise and obscure on any point I will take your advice and give a fuller explanation; if you disapprove I will correct. But why so much about these trifles when your own Harmony, the object of all desires, continues to hang fire? What is to be done about it, tell me, at long last? it is certainly held in the highest esteem here; scholars who have seen specimens of the work are most eager for its appearance.

813. Locke to Edward Clarke, 12/22 March 1685 (808, 817)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 16. Faded; covered with transparent paper. Printed in Rand, pp. 124-7.
Utrecht 22o Mar 85
Deare Sir
The unwellcome news of your Ladys sicknesse came first to me yesterday by yours of 6o instant that being the only one I have yet received from you since that of 3o Feb: I am very sorry for her illnesse and should be much more soe if I apprehended it a disease that were like to be long in its continuance or dangerous in the event, but being an ague and this the spring I should not suspect very much perill were there noe Dr Goodall within call nor noe Cortex Peru: in England but though I am pretty secure of the issue, yet the trouble and languors of repeated fits of an ague in a freind I love soe well are not indifferent things to me and therefor I shall be in pain till I heare she is perfectly well. Cortex Peru: is soe safe a remedy espetially if one begin to take it as soon as the fit is over and soe continued on in good large quantity till after the time of the next fit that I never saw it doe harme but allways found good successe. after the fits are off the use of it should be persisted in for a long time else they are apt to returne. Only I advise her to take it in pills because the ungratefulnesse of the tast to some pallats gives such an aversion and loathing when taken otherwise that the stomach is often apt to check at it and it cannot afterwards be
― 697 ―

gott down. But I suppose the Doctor abovesaid is with her and then I need say noething. only besure she thinke herself not perfectly cured too soon, but continue takeing on†a the medecine at least a month after she has had but any grumbleing of a fit.
This is another reason besides those I formerly mentioned to you why you should not thinke of your journey†1 till the begining of May at soonest, for the accidents and incommoditys of travell will endanger a relaps and you will be greatly perplexed should she fall ill by the way. The seeds I hope you have ere this but the trees we are very unlucky in, for when I beleived them at Exeter I received a note that told me that they were not to be got where I was promisd them and therefor I was advised this was the place I must furnish my self. I then presently sought the nurserys here, where I found none but what were a litle above the size you desird and infinitely above the price I expected for they stood upon eighteen pence a peice for such as were about the bignesse of ones thumb or a litle biger. I was loath to give 15l sterling for 200 Lime tree plants which considering the latenesse of the season and the uncertainty to meet with an Exeter ship†2 ready to saile presently twas oddes would not grow one of ten of them if any at all. I advise you to furnish yourself among the gardeners and seeds men in and about London with the seeds. In the meane time pray send me word what price such lime tree plants beare in England, for I imagin it was but the cheating strangers price they asked me and had it not been soe late in the year and under the circumstances I mention I should not have left the matter soe, though I was at two or three places, but I will take such order that if they be any thing reasonable, another yeare you shall not misse them, and that we may trie both sorts I will take care that you shall also have seed from hence. Pray returne my thanks to my cosin Somerton†3 for his soe ready complying with my occasions, the circumstances and every part is extreamly obleigeing, But pray tell him if any losse should happen (as in his freindly manner of proceeding tis possible there may) I must make it good to him, pray assure him this from me and say to him besides
― 698 ―

whatever you thinke should be said from a gratefull to a good man and an excellent freind.
Your dispatch in one part of my businesse haveing out donne my expectation I make noe doubt but you have with a like care and kindenesse donne in every point what I desired in mine of 22 Feb:†1 espetially in that part which mentions some deeds. I refer you again to that letter not because I suppose all was not donne that I there in desired but because it may help you not to forget when you write next those other things where in you have obleiged me, which the hast you were in made you omit in your last letter, and will possibly be omitted in your next if you make not that letter your monitor. For such Lawyers as you who take noe fees please your selves with dispatching your freinds businesse and doeing the kindenesse and then are content it should be forgotten and mentioned noe more. The hair trunke of deeds when you had donne with it I suppose you lodgd at my Name sakes†2 unlesse you had some particular reason to the contrary; Pray thanke and gratifie him for what he did for me in Mrs: Richards businesse†3 when you were last year out of town. Besides that I looke on him as a very fair and understanding man this consideration inclined me to that place viz because it seemed to me the most commodious to have any writeings from, which there might be occasion to send for into the country should we light upon such a chapman for Buckhill†4 as we were put in hopes of the last yeare or should there be occasion to make any other alterations. The box that accompanied that trunke conteineing noe thing but lumber, it is placed I presume with the lumber I left in Warwick lane.†5 Pray thanke Mrs: Perce for her care of those things.†6 In your next pray let me know where this trunke and box are in case of Mortality. If the trunke be not at my namesakes I suppose then they are both trunke and box togeather in†a some†a other place. The bills are come safe to hand, Mr Oakley†7 hath 32l in his hands ready at call, two words
― 699 ―

from you will make it be paid where you please, this and what I expect from Stratton I would have applyd presently towards the reibursing†a my cosin†a . I am
Sir your obedient†a and†a humble servant J L
Your Cosin ownes himself infinitely obleiged to your kindenesse to him and desires to be remembred with all respects to you and your Lady, he cannot help wishing her here he says, soe naturall is it for people who have found any thing advantageous to their owne health, to offer and wish it their freinds. He says she should be very wellcome to him and he is now in a pretty good condition to receive her, he thinkes too if she came you would not stay behinde nor the litle ones he soe much longs to see, nor should I be sorry to kisse her hands here, but dare scarce propose such a voiage to her though a litle seasicknesse would not doe her much harme. But I see the journey lies Westward hay, pray let me know when you thinke to be goeing that I may know how to order my letters.

Cum iterum Amstelodomum rediero oleum illud orientale quod laudas sollicete quæram, usus tua me docebit amicitia. Sed ad Adversaria
(English ) Davus sum non Aristoteles;†1 Obtemperare in animo habui non fallere. non ego is sum philosophus ut verba dare vellem, rem tenere; ἐκδέδωκα κὰι μὴ ἐκδέδωκα†2 non mihi videtur tam scitè quam malignè et angusti animi dictum. Verum irascor popularibus meis qui cum iis opus habeas nulli sunt. Non dubitavi Dominum Cox†3 apud vos sedes ad aliquod tempus fixisse, et cum jam longâ dissuetudine sermo Latinus mihi non tam facilis nec familiaris, ad methodam meam describendam magis oportunam credidi Anglicanam, quia putaram ex illius Angli interpretatione eo modo tibi magis omnia dilucida fore, verùm cum illud consilium tam male successit, descriptioni Latinæ jam incumbo quam tibi propediem promitto, legas oro diligenter, et siquid in re vel sermone erratum corrigas, siquid adjectum, demtum, mutatum velis, moneas rogo. Cum ad mentem tuam castigatum habuerimus exemplar, de editione videbimus, sive Ephemeridibus vestris (Journal des Scavans) Gallicè inserendam censeas, sive hic seorsim Latine imprimendam, tuo omnia permitto judicio Totus enim Tuus sum J L

our spiritual friend's†1 divine plaster as soon as I got it, and if skill in the
[p. 700]
physician and faith in the patient are any guarantee I shall have health for certain and without delay. The precious pieces that were cut away whilst I was fitting the plaster to the spot I am keeping for other uses, which you will tell me about. But one job gives rise to another; you have just doctored my body; I now commend my mind to your care, begging you to do all you can to save me from mental sickness whilst in bodily health and from inward distress at any suspicion of ingratitude towards the excellent Abbé. My own powers of expression are no match for such services; I need all your wealth of eloquence in this matter, and all the favour that you enjoy with him. I require all your care, diligence, and zeal to ensure that he is fully persuaded of the infinite gratitude I feel towards him, as in duty bound, even if I cannot thank him adequately for his kindness. There is a bold demand to make of you, but it suits my case; for you already hold me under such obligations for all you have done for me this long time past that I have no hope or desire left of freeing myself from them; so why should I be modest any longer in my requests? There is also a matter in which I am outrageous enough to want my revenge on you; for whenever in your letters I come upon the mention of your triumvirate I burst with envy; I have the greatest possible affection for each of you taken by himself, but when I think of you united I do not have the patience to bear my absence from your company. Indeed it seems to me the greatest proof of my own virtue that in all my wretchedness of absence I can still pray so sincerely for the prosperity and happiness of you all who are enjoying the blessings of each other's society. When I get back to
[p. 701]
Amsterdam again I shall seek carefully for that eastern oil that you praise; your friendship will please instruct me in the use of it. But to the Adversaria:
(Original Text) I am Davus, not Aristotle;†1 my purpose was to comply with your wishes, not to deceive you. I am not the sort of philosopher who might be disposed to give empty words whilst withholding the actual thing; 'I have published and not published'†2seems to me not so much a sagacious remark as the indication of a niggardly and narrow mind. Really, though, I am angry with my countrymen who are not there just when you need them. I never doubted that Mr. Cox†3 had settled down with you for some time; and since Latin is neither easy nor familiar to me owing to having been so long out of practice with it I thought English would be more suitable for the description of my method, as I supposed that everything would so be made clearer to you by his explanations. However, that plan has gone wrong; so I am now busy on a Latin version, which I promise to let you have shortly. Please read it carefully, and if you find anything to correct in the subject-matter or the language, or if you wish anything to be added, removed, or changed, please let me know. As soon as we have a copy emended to your satisfaction we will see about publication, whether you think it should be inserted in French in your periodical (the Journal des Sçavans), or else printed separately here in Latin. I leave everything to your judgement, being entirely yours JL
