815. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 20 March [1685] (805, 823)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, f. 122. Year from Locke's endorsement.
The identification of the persons mentioned in the present letter puzzled Locke and, owing to the loss of letters, is uncertain. There are relevant passages in nos. 805, 817, 819, 820, 822, 823, 839, and 950. I assume (i) that the 'Abbess' in nos. 805 and 950 is the same person; that no. 805 is the 'last letter' of no. 815, and consequently that she is Locke's 'Mistress' and a widow; she is here identified as Mrs. Grigg; (ii) that Philoclea's malicious and prophetic friend in no. 815 is the Urgunda of nos. 823, 839, and 950; she is here identified as Mrs. Stillingfleet. Philoclea was clearly lodging elsewhere than at Lady King's, where Mrs. Clarke lodged. Mrs. Grigg mentions visiting a lady identifiable as Philoclea at Dr. Stillingfleet's house: no. 820; Philoclea says that a person, apparently the Abbess, visited her at Urgunda's: no. 950; I assume that the two notices relate to the same occasion; if it is the visit of the present letter Philoclea was lodging with Mrs. Stillingfleet.
Philoclea's acquaintance with Stillingfleet about this time is established by her statement that it was at his house while he was dean that she learnt about Fell's misgivings regarding Locke's expulsion from Christ Church: her letter to Le Clerc, 12 January 1704/5. An allusive passage in no. 817 may mean that she was lodging with him. She was married in his church, St. Andrew's Holborn, in June of this year. Mrs. Stillingfleet was a third cousin of Sir Francis Masham.
A Certaine Lady, a Mistress of Yours, that I had an Occasion to Mention to you in my last Letter, made the other Day a Visit to Her of this House where I am;†1 Mrs Clark Happen'd to be just come in before Her to see me; and there was in the Company (Besides many others) a very good Friend of mine who has no other Fault but that she is upon occasion much dispos'd to be a little Malicious, which Perhaps you will think is none whilst you are far enough out of the reach of it. This Lady who it seemes can have Revelations whenever she Pleases, finding that the Widdow
― 703 ―

would have it so do what I could, took a Fancie to Perswade Her in good earnest of what she Herself had onely spoken in Jest, Haveing a Certaine spightfull thought that it might Possibly Vex Her as she knew it must needs do me on another Account.
To this good End then she has Maintain'd with All the Confidence of Inspiration that You Love me Exceedingly; So Much as ought to give a Jealousie to any one who was either yet willing to be Lov'd themselves, Or was but Barely Unwilling that another should; which after Sixteene Yeares†1 is as much as I think in Reason ought of either side to be expected, But However that be she Fancy'd Her designe to Have succeeded; and was not a little Pleas'd with it, whilst Mrs C——†2 who bore a Part that she Knew not of, had I doubt not in Her owne Minde the Pleasure of Laughing at us both, Yet nevertheless put in sometimes so Pertinently, and Opportunely, that to the rest of the Company who were equally strangers to us All, I question not but we Appear'd as three Rivalls who Had all Had, or Thought we Had, some Reason in our Time to beleeve we had a sufficient Interest in you; and there was a Mightie Whispering About to know who the Happy Gentleman was in whom both Maids, Widdow, and Wives, had such a Concerne; Nor for my Part do I expect any less then to see my self very shortly in a Ballade for your sake. However I see clearely that the most Honourable Part of it will be Mine, which dos not a little Rejoyce me, How little Reason soever there be for it, since of all the things in the World I should the most Hate to be thought a Neglected Mistress, and to Heare my Misadventure Sett to the Tune of the Forsaken Maid.†3 Tis therefore for Feare of some such sad Fortune as that, that I have never yet had any thing but Friends, in which I shall now more then ever beleeve my self to have beene in the Right since without being so Enthusiastical as to Credit the Revelation I told you of I have been able without Jealousie to see One that I am inform'd You have done and I suppose still do Esteeme above All besides, and in the opinion of others to see Her a little Jealous of me too, For which I beg your Pardon if it really be so, which you will I am sure grant me on the Considerations of its being very Contrary to my Intention, and How much I am likely to suffer for your sake. For though my Part as I said I think will be the Best, yet I find
― 704 ―

that it is likely to be so very Kind a One as would be sufficient (if Kindness can do it) to supply for the Defect of All Manner of Merrit besides, and to Justifie your Choise Abundantly.
You will think me perhaps Altogether in Jest in what I now say. But I assure you there is a great deal of Truth in it, and I have beene Really Vex'd, Tho not so much as that any share in your Friendship dos not make me sufficient Amends for it. Or that I am ever the less Pleas'd in telling You that I am your most Real Friend and servant
PHILOCLEA.
March the 20.
I sent you a letter since that which I mention as my last, I suppose by this time you have received it from the Gentleman to whom Mr C——†1 gave it.
Endorsed by Locke: Philoclea 20 Mar 85
816. William Charleton to Locke, 24 March 1685 (788, 821)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, ff. 59-61. The mutilation of this letter and of no. 821 and the allusive passage in no. 817 suggest that Locke was alarmed at this time. Charles II was succeeded by James II on 6 February, O.S. Thomas Chudleigh, the English envoy to the States General, was recalled about this time; Bevil Skelton was sent over on 17/27 March to replace him: James II to the Prince of Orange, in Sir James Dalrymple, Memoirs, etc., 2nd ed., 1790, pt. i, bk. ii, app., pp. 13, 14.
The use of Mr. Somerton, 'your cousin', etc., in the correspondence with Clarke, and the mutilations of later letters, seem rather to spring from the desire for privacy.
London March the 24th 1684/5
Deare Sir
Both your letters of the 4th January and 14th Instant came in due time to my hands, for my not giving you so speedy an answer to the former as I ought I beg your pardon, desiring you to give me directions as to the sending you Leonardo di Capoa, and Moreri's Dictionary. Since I wrote to you I have vissited Mr. <Justel>†a †2
― 705 ―

and have had his Company at my Chamber in the Temple, and to my great astonishment speaking accidently of you he expressed himself in such a manner that I perceaved he was none of your freinds, and consequently not the man I suposed him to be, I tooke not the least notice to him of the freindship that was betwixt us, not thinking it needfull, but though it may be that I am one of the most averse to tale bearing that lives yet I thought my self obliged to give you this account that you may not take an enemy for a freind.
I most heartyly thanke you for the acquisition you have made for me of 2 such great rarities as the clove, and cinamon tree branches, and wish I had any thinge to make a return to the gentleman that gave them you; if they would let you know what things these parts afford worthy of their acceptance I should be extreamely pleased, Inclosed I send you a small Catalogue of what I have or presume I can meet with, which if either of your freinds like of I shall send as you shall inorder me, of doubles I have preserved in spirit of wine which I had at Montpellier (and as well conditioned as when first put into the glasses) a black, and grey scorpion, a strange sort of locust, a large peice of chrystall with mosse in it, and a small parcel†a of rich silver ore, as others come in my way you shall have notice. In Swammerdams collection (a Catalogue of which I have seen)†1 there are severall things that I have already, so that if they be not to be sold a part I shall not thinke of them, I heare there is lately a great Collection to be sold by auction at Amsterdam of one Roiter's amongst which are 2 Remoras if to be had at reasonable rates I would willingly have them both, and what fine colloured Indian birds there may be amongst his things, the Insects that are Exotick of all kinds will be verry acceptable, espicially the great Phalangium,†2 the teeth of which are usually set in gold to make tooth picks of, the Tarantula of the spider sort found in the Kingdome of Naples, for the other is a kind of Lizart and common all over Italy, the Stella arborescens†3 if to be meet with I should desire you to procure for me, amongst the seamen things may be had at easier rates then when they come

I take my leave and am
Deare Sir
Your most obliged and most affectionate humble servant
WILLIAM CHARLETON
I thanke God I am now in pretty good health but returne you my humble thankes for your advice as to a Physitian.

817. Locke to Edward Clarke, 26 March/5 April 1685 (813, 819)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 17. Faded. Printed in Rand, pp. 127-30.
Utrecht: 5o Apr. 85
Sir
I perceive by your litle note of 10th: of March: that came inclosed in Musidores, as well as by other instances, that the things I send you hence come very slowly to your hands, I am glad however that those cuts at last got to you and that they were acceptable to the Ladys I sent them to. I heare there are other plates a graveing relateing to the same cabinet if there are I shall get them and send them too. In the meane time the slownesse of things in their passage makes me apprehend what is become of the seeds I bought for you in January last for though I have writt severall times to Amsterdam about them to hasten their sending and to have an account they are gon, yet I can get noe answer but soe it generally happens when one is not upon the place to looke after things ones self. I am extremely obleiged to you for your enquirys after Mrs Richards and her children. Mr Bray†1 you say in your last of 17o Mar yet hears noe thing and I begin to thinke that I shall never heare any thing of that I expected. I am very glad that you and I jump soe right about your journey into the country, But though your Ladys ague be now gon again, yet let me prevaile with you; not to venture upon that journey till the warme weather of May, agues are apter to returne this spring then ever I knew them and upon very litle accidents. I have of this a cleare example in my servant who has been well of a tertian (he got last Autumn) ever since November last and has now within these three or fower days even in very warme weather got it again and that by a very litle and inconsiderable oversight. I therefor beg you not to thinke of your journey till the warme weather in May be steady and setled. If I thought you would be inclined to doe other wise I would write to Madame and two or three other she freinds I finde I have in towne, who would keepe you in order if you were stubborne in the point and preferd the country aire to their satisfaction. For I am by a letter I just now received from my C: Mis†2 confirmed in the opinion that I was
― 708 ―

wrapd abundantly in my mothers smock†1 but it was still but the upper end of it.
She tells me of a conference lately at her lodging amongst some Ladys amongst which your Lady was one whereof I was the main subject. She tells me amongst other things that there was one amongst them that maintaind with great confidence that I was exceedingly in love with my C: Mis: and that with a malitious designe against a very discreet widow that made a part of the conversation. Your Lady and her self she names, the widow I guesse. But who was that other lady that had such revelation and could soe certainly tell where I disposd of my heart she perfectly conceales and I would gladly know. Though I doubt not but there is a great deale of railery in this, yet the way she writes it makes me see there is some truth in it, pray learne from your Lady for I long to know that I may beare my part in the mirth with them. Would you not advise me to get here a good dull Dutch indifferency? for if I should returne gay and Amorous what would become of my heart and lungs too amongst soe many Mistrises. I writ to you in my last that your Lady should take on the Cortex Peru: at least a month after her ague is quite gon to prevent relaps's, but if she should thinke she should not need it on that account for we in England are always well too soon, yet it would doe her good upon other accounts and this I write to her as a most devoted servant to a most esteemd Mistris.†a I am concerned that my cosin Somerton†2should be soe bacwards to comply with my desires about thos drugs and preparations he found in the red trunk. If there were any books amongst them I confesse I had forgot them and meant them not and he will obleige me if he keepe them. But to satisfie him that I am not mistaken in the other things, and that I doe know what was there that I gave order about, he will finde in the least parcel marked. 2. if he examine it, nuts, acorns, shineing pebles ambergris and such other things of natures production as she her self offers to humane use. this parcel he may keep also if he please.†b In an other bigger parcell (carying the figure. 1. as I remember) he will finde things relateing to the animal Kingdome as it is divided in the begining of Gen: into the three great provinces viz Fishes of the sea fouls of the air and beast
― 709 ―

cattle and creepeing things that creepe upon the earth: An other which is the bigest parcell made up in a long bundle is all of artificiall things more exalted and refind into spiritality†a by art, whereof one part was of the Doctors prepareing where you tell me (in your last) one of my Mistrisses†b now lies, and the other of my owne though for the most part marked by an others hand who was my operator when I kept†c- my bed.-†c†1
I know them also to be the same I intended by what my cosin†2 says of them, for to speake freely to you, the same reason that makes him desire to keepe them makes me desire he should not. But since he puts such a value as he seemes to doe upon trifles some whereof are not very safe to be medled with and is soe desirous to keepe them I am inclind to humor him soe far (for in truth he is a very good man and deserves from me particular respect for his exceeding great kindenesse on all occasions) as to consent he should keepe one half of them, provided he can remember the way of ordering them in the devision which I once shewd him an example of in things of the like nature, which way of keepeing them he seemd mightily pleased with when I once enterteind him for several howers in my chamber in town with the sight of such kinde of preparations to his great satisfaction. The other half I would have him put to others of the same kinde, put up in the way and ...†d abovesaid, in a drawer I mentiond to him in the Country as their repository. If he can remember and will be at the trouble to doe this I cannot refuse soe far complyeing with the fondnesse he has for them. But rather then he should keepe them altogeather unseparated in the terrible posture they are now I positively insist on it to have the two last mentiond parcells immediately disposed of according as I directed in mine of 22 Feb:†3 which I desire you not only to prevaile with him to doe but to see donne your self, for I am concerned for his litle ones if any mischeif should come to them through his carelesnesse and delay in this point, but pray manage this businesse soe with him that he may perceive I am sensible of the kindenesse he intended by that which he calls his disobedience and that I take not those things out of his hand out of any stinginesse or unkindenesse to him but quite the contrary.†e Mr Oakley in his last to me desired some turnep and carot seeds from hence which I perceive
― 710 ―

some body has recommended to him tis too late now to thinke of sending him any from hence for this yeare, if you can therefor conveniently let him have a small parcell of some of your sorts you can best spare for his present supply and I will take order against an other yeare. My service to Madame whose recovery from her ague and geting of strength again exceedingly pleases me, but pray tell her she must now be orderly for a good while and have a care of the cold evening aire, cold drinke, and must now and then drinke a glasse of wine more then she used. She may be sure she may drinke wine when I recommend it. I am
Sir your most humble servant
J L

819. Locke to Edward Clarke, 20/30 April 1685 (817, 822)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 18. Faded. Printed in Rand, pp. 131-3.
Utrecht: 30 Apr 85
Deare Sir
The news of your sicknesse from Mrs Cudworth†2 put me out of the dumps my minde was in under the apprehensions of some indispotion in your family into a reall trouble for your ague and yet perhaps if I were with you I should not make that hast to rid you of it as you would expect from a man who tenders your health as much as his owne. Unlesse it treats <you s>everely,†a and pulls you downe too much I should let it run out a litle while at this time of the year, when it seems to be an efflorescence of the bloud, which†b- should have a litle vent,-†b which I would indeavour to rectifie by diet rather then medecins, espetially if it had noe presseing or dangerous symptoms. But I talke in the darke and therefor you must not heed me in this point but be governd by your physitian†3 who is upon the place, and sees and weighs all the circumstances. Only this I am positive in that let him treat you what way you will
― 712 ―

you must not thinke of goeing out of town this month at least, for I will assure you it will be apt upon every the least occasion to returne. and when you doe goe out of town (after haveing experimented by your stay that you are perfectly well) I would have you take fower of the pills I here send you the discripsion of every other morning exerciseing an hower or two after in the open aire a foot or on hors back if the weather permitt: and continue the use of them at least till January next, and the bitter wine drinke†a with them, only defering the use of that till the begining of August, because we are now in the growing part of the yeare and it may be too hot till that time. For since your ague may as I suspect make you have more need of the waters this yeare then any one since I knew you: even that, that we were at Tunbridg togeather,†1 but yet utterly forbid the use of them since they will certainly bring your ague again, nor can you safely purge or bleed. I know noe thing you can better doe for secureing your health then follow the course I here direct you if you will adde to it the method of goeing to stoole I directed in my advice about your son. which I would have you observe, whether you take my pills or noe. for I would have you shew my bill to your Doctor and have his opinion upon it. for there may be reasons that I see not to forbeare, or alter something in that method, which if there be when I know them from the Doctor I shall know what to say.
Though I said above that I should perhaps if I were there let your ague run out some time, yet the concernment I have for your health makes me long to heare speedily that it is gon. I hope your next which will be an answer to mine of the 5th: instant will set my minde perfectly at rest with the news of yours Madame and all your healths for in that is included all things. If Madame will consent to take them when she goes into the country I will send her also a direction for some pills to prevent the returne of her ague but they must be different from yours. My service to her, Young master my pretty Mistris and the rest of my freinds. Besides a thousand other things, I am indebted to you I perceive for the discovery of the Lady I enquired after, but if I knew her as well as I doe somebody else she should not have all the talke and laughing to
― 713 ―

her self I would have some part in the conversation for who knows what diversion the womans talent might also give one? By the inclosed you will finde I writ to Mrs. Clarke the last post supposeing she was ill. <I hope>†a that letter found her well as I hope this will you. there is noe thing I am more concerned for since I am with the utmost sincerity and obligation
Sir
your most affectionate and most humble servant
J L
If you finde your wine too bitter or too hot in August you may dilute it with good small beare or alle or good spring water, but you must not put in too much water, espetially when the cold whether begins to come in, for then it will be best to allay the bitternesse with pure wine.
If the pills should be too big you may then have them made lesse but then you must take the more soe that they may amount to the wait of fower of that size I prescribe.
Dureing this course eat as you use to doe and drinke a glasse of wine at meales as you use; the farther you are past midsomer the larger, but drinke not hard be sure at any time and let your supper be lighter much then your diner

B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 149-50. Part of f. 150, including most of the address, is torn away.
Deare Brother
I have with the firce spirit of true friendship complain'd of your silence, and when our friend in Theams street†1 and I met we rail'd at you titely, from her House I once writ to you, but so like one desperatly provok'd that tho I had fitted it for its transportation upon a revieu, a considerat vapour seas'd me and spoyl'd its voyage, To speak truth I express'd myself with that firceness that you could not but conclude you had disturb'd the sweet reposs of my mind, but least I should revive too quick a sens of a silence that tried my patience, ile say no more of whats past, but respectfully and kindly answer your make peace Epistle and in the first place tell you that no body is more joy'd to receave the good newes of your health, and to recompence you for it doe assure you that I am reconcil'd to my old friend whose concern for me suffers no decay by absence, this relation gives you right and
― 715 ―

title to a true information how it fairs with me, and my darling, You must know then that by ways most innocent and without designing my own private intrest the present Bishop of Ely†1 has bin privie to my most retired thoughts, and is become the best friend I have in England, has disposs'd of my son in Jesus Coll: in Cambridge†2 where he is a favourite, and if God preserve the best Church in the world as I trust he will†3 your little friend is in a hopefull way, and that nothing might inconvenience me, my Lord has fix'd me in his own sanctuary where his pious Mother†4 and the prittiest virgin his only child†5 are as fond of the little woman as is possible to imagin.
So that I have now no complaints to make, but am surrounded with such blessings as bespeak an obedient and thankfull heart, in truth all things being well considred I know no woman whose circumstances I like better, and if ever I move from Ely House†6 it will be hard to reconcile me to a life of hury again (so quiet are we and orderly). I confess I sometimes think without being melancholy that a country life near such as would be anything the better for me would suit my humour; But to that Divin goodness which ever determins best may I still refer myself, in the meane time I indevour to be as unperplexd with the world as ever I can, and had rather be thought dul than curiously prie into unhappy prospects. I hope er long you will find the way to us, and then I expect a large shar of your conversation, being two great a lover of myself to be contented with short or infrequent vissits from you when tis in your power to make them such as I covet. All this while I forget to tell you that I was lately to visist a fair and intolerably Witty Lady†7 at the Dean of St Pauls†8 whose severity they say makes you afraid to apear, but be of good chear, she whispred in my Ear that she most heartily long'd to see you, this
― 716 ―

hint I told her I would make good use of, and by vertue of it bespeak your quick return, not doubting but my intrest in you would bespeak me one in her, and the reputation of being endured by you both would I doubt not make me considerable, but to be serious I just begin to know and admire Mrs C—— and expect to be better acquainted with her, which I should not covet were she not so worthy the esteem of the most criticall judges, All that I can devise to tempt you back I would make use of, so sensible am I that tis my intrest to be your Auditor, tho most commonly you preach against me, but tis so luckeyly that it allways dos me credit. I am as I have bin above 16 yeares†1
Your faithfull friend and sister
A G
I will take care that W Grigg may receave safely your kind rememberance, which will adorn his smale palace, where he is so infinitely pleas'd having a Study and compleat apartment to himself that he's as happy as a Prince, may he learn to convers so wisely with the Books you send him as to be able himself to speak good sense, and thank you as decently as your constant care of him deserves. All our friends in the West†2 and in the town are very well
April the 20th 85
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur†a

821. William Charleton to Locke, 21 April 1685 (816, 843)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, f. 62.
London the 21th April 1685
Deare Sir
Your extraordinary kind letter of the 9th Instant is with me, and though I have omitted the returne of an answer till now, yet there was not a pacquet parted towards you since I received it but which I did intend should have caryed my thanks along with it, and though I have been thus long silent hereafter I shall be more exact in that part of my duty, and therefore I hope you will excuse me. The
― 717 ―

gentleman I writ to you about†1 ha's been with me 2 or 3 times since but we had no farther discourse concerning you, at the time you were mention'd by him he seemed to be dissatisfied in that you refused to†a ... <if> ever I am so happy as to see you I shall give you a more full account. Moreri's Dictionary and Leonardo di Capoa are now in my chamber, and shall be kept till farther order, I am promised the small Treatise writ by Dr. Barbyrac when I receive it you shall have notice. Pray let me know how I may send the things†b- I have-†bby me to you, what you send me be pleased to adresse to mr. William Jarret merchant In Limestreet, you are verry much in the right in what you say in reference to the rates of curiosities, but since you seem to desire my explaining myself in that particular I shall only Instance in the prices of these few following things: for the Phalangium spider, the Stella arborescens, the Remora, and the true Tarantula I should willingly give twenty shillings a peice, but what I writ to you in relation to these kind of things as I have already hinted, was in case they came accidentally in your way and therefore by no meanes do not think of travelling about the countrey to gratifie my Curiosity. I take my leave and remaine
Deare Sir
Your most affectionate and most obliged humble servant
WILLIAM CHARLETON
822. Locke to Edward Clarke, 23 April/3 May 1685 (819, 829)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 19. Faded and torn. Printed in Rand, pp. 133-7. One of the education letters: p. 624.

Sir
Yours of 20 Feb: and 17o Apr with the cissars you did me the favour to send <m>e†c came to me yesterday togeather. I am very glad to heare you are got rid of your ague since it treated you soe very severly. I had n<ew>s†c of it by a letter from my C Mistris†2

before, and thereupon writ to you the last post my <o>pinion†a concerning your disease.
That pa<rt>†a which concerned the leting it run out some time I am glad was otherwise orderd for the feircenesse of it required quicker d<isp>atch:†a as you will finde by that letter. But as to the other part concerning your staying in town till the end of May I <here>†b repeat it and  †c in it, being dayly more and more confirmed in the opinion I formerly writ you when I heard Madame had an ague, <that a>gues†a are this yeare very apt to returne. My servant has had three relapses of an ague he <fir>st†a got about the end of last August and he is now but newly out of the last returne though I cannot much <co>mplain†a of any very irregular management of himself. Therefor pray doe not you nor Madame thinke your selves <p>erfectly†a safe as soon as you finde the ague gon and your stomach and strength begin to returne. In my letter also by the last post I sent you directions for pills and bitter wine to take when y<ou>†a goe into the country. which I th<in>ke†a very necessary for you to take as I there directed to prevent any inconveniencys from your ague or spleen, but pray have your Doctors advice upon them and let me know what he says. I am very glad my cosin <S>omers,†a as you tell me, will punctually comply with my desires concerning the drugs and chimical pre<p>arations†a I writ about pray obleige me soe far as to take care with him it be not delaid. Though you cannot (as you say) in your neighbourhood finde a chymist of that name I mentiond in mine of 9o Apr: ye<t>†a you will finde amongst the books at Mrs: Perce's†1 two in quarto of an author of that name which I desire you to put into the Cedar box. Though the bottle of phosphorus and the flanen shirts are not yet come, yet I hope they will in good time. I can patiently wait for them for they are not things that I have present need of, only I would not have them quite lost. I had hea<r>d†a from my C: Mistris before the receit of your letter who was the Chairewoman of the committee of Ladys who w<e>re†a soe kinde to make me the subject of their discourse,†2 but as she confessed in that letter she told it me at your instance. I know not why she would make a secret of it since I thinke myself mightily obleiged
― 719 ―

to that La<d>y†a who though unknown to me takes soe much care of my concernes.
I wish I knew her soe well as to begin a correspond<e>nce†a with her. that I might have the diversion of hers as well as I have had of her mans pen, for I dare lay two to <one>†a on natures side and that she would be much more in the right in matters of the flesh then he has been in those of the <sp>irit,†a but to speake fairely of his endeavours what could a man doe more then to write pro and con, to hit it?†1 I desire my hat may have as neare noe stiffening in it as may be. I beg your pardon for troubleing you with this ci<r>cumstance†a but my weake head will not beare a stiff hat besides that they are cheats and never weare well. I am gl<ad>†a to finde by your letter that was as slow in comeing as my directions were in goeing, that you at last received those pap<e>rs†aconcerning your son.†2 I am affraid your kindenesse byasses you in the interpretation and assent you give them, but be that as great as it will I can assure you it cannot be greater then the good intention wherewith I writ them and I am not a litle satisfied that his mother too approves of my rules, but p<ray>†a remember that he weare thin stockings as well as leaky thin shoes as well as have his feet washd. I have <su>fferd†a soe much by a cough my self that I always thinke it worthy to be lookd after wherever it is and I hope his is of noe ill consequence, but yet pray let Madame or Mr Shipton†3 make as strong an infusion as possibly <t>hey†a can of alehoof otherwise cald ground ivie, and of that infusion with <a>†a sufficient quan<tity>†a of sugar make a syrop. which let him take in a decoction of Veronica or speedwell. and sometim<es>†a if you will in a draught of small beare, but pray let me know whether his cough was worse in the cold of win<ter>†a or since the warmer weather of the spring came in. But be sure send him abroad in your coach into th<e pa>rke†a every morning whilst you stay in town. you know he is at noe time to drinke wine <or>†a strong drinke, but <no>w†a espetially he is carefully to be kept from it, and when he coughs te<a>ch†a him to spit out what rises in his throat. The account you give me of his disposition is
― 720 ―

such as I gues<se>d†a it to be. and such as one could wish. a temper in a child curious resolute and good naturd will if set right <p>roduce†a any thing I imagin.
Incourage†1- his curiosity as much as you can by satisfying him and makeing him un<der>stand†a as much as he is capable the things he desires to know and is fit for him to know, and let noebody trifle with him and deceive him with false reasons or wrong accounts of things it will but teach him the trick to <d>issemble†a and make excuses. But the things that are not fit for him to know, it is a great deale better when he would prie into them, to deny them him directly but kindely by telling him he is not yet fit to un<d>erstand†a those matters. But if childrens curiositys were incouraged and led on as I thinke it might be, they would know a great deale more before they were 14 years old then we usually let them. and would be them<s>elves†a pleased with it, and put themselves forwards.-†1 But I see I am falling into a long discourse espetially if I should proceed to those other qualitys you mention but that must be the matter of another chapter only I cannot he<r>e†a forbeare to mention that when†2- ever he parts with any thing out of civility and good nature care should be taken that he should not loose any thing by it, but should perceive how it <returnd>†bhim advantage togeather with l<o>ve,†a esteem and commendation, which is what you must take all occasions to make him in love with.-†2 Though†3- he knows the letters of the Alphabet already, yet I would have my method or some thing like it made use of to make him reade, for I proposd it not that I thought him uncapable of learneing the ordinary way, but because I would not have learning to reade made a businesse to him, but that he should get it in <sp>ort†a and play, and therefor he and his sister should play with letters and syllables for the fruit they had and such other things they desired, which may be donne by letters and syllables printed on thick strong paper, which may be drawn by lott or thrown up like crosse and pile as well as by the dice for one might contrive twenty sorts of play of that nature.-†3 You have been too liberal of the seeds I sent you to Mr Oakley, not that I would not have sent him share†c enough, but his soile I am sure is unfit for roots and they will never be go<od>†a there, or else I should formerly have sent
― 721 ―

him, but he haveing mentiond them to me and it being too late, <I>†a would have had him have had a few of yours for triall but now I feare you have not left en<ough>†a for your owne use. Pray take care to get from him my Zinar or Persian planetree†1 at a convenient season and when you have it let your gardiner set it <in>†a a place where he may propagate it by layers or which is a better way as I thinke by grafting some of the grafts of the same tree on some of the small branches of its owne roots underground, whereby I thinke you will quickly have an increase of young ones without hindering the growth of the main tree. I would have you also in your nursery have a good stock of yew trees both for hedges and standards, that and holly are the two best winter greens, will endure all cuting and all weather and noe thing covers a wall better, Jacob Bobert†2 has an admirable way to raise them from seeds, let our freind enquire of him the ways of raiseing transplanting and ordering them. One thing in your letter of the 20 Feb: falls out unluckyly to†b- be soe long a comeing-†b in that it brings me news that E.P†3 has a desire to see my notions de Intellectu humano, they are now grown to at least three quires of paper and the writeing over of such a bulke is not of easy dispatch: and I shall not be able to compasse it before you goe out of town whose hand I would have it passe by. However I will doe some thing before you goe wherin I will endeavour to satisfye him. I am
Sir
Your most obleiged humble servant

June
823. Damaris Cudworth, later Lady Masham, to Locke, 5 June 1685 (815, 827)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, f. 123.
As Impertinent as my Letters Usually are, your last makes me think You value them so much that I am Almost Angry With my self for not haveing writt to You againe All this while†1 and especially the Care you take of my Health seemeing to Oblige me to it, as it would have done But that I thought you could not by what I writt in my last Concerning it, beleeve my Ilness had any Danger in it, and that I could not till very lately, if I had writt, have sent you word that I was any thing better, Who was not Certainly in a more Stoical Humour when I sent my first letter to you, Then you was when you writt the first of Those that I have now by me, and Yet Perhaps at this Time I go farther then you did then, For when you Compare the World to a Dutch Inne etc: You onely do it upon a supposition that there were no such thing as Friendship in it, But I Allowing for That, and Valueing it Perhaps as much as any Body, Can yet Beleeve it at the very Best, to be no better then an English one. Like Betty Ainsworths†2 indeed if you will, where one may be sufficiently well Treated tis true (Considering that you are yet but upon the Road) But must Pay a Most Unconscionable Reckoning for it. However methinks (for All That) wee have no Reason to Quarrel with it, since it seemes to me Notwithstanding, to be very Fitt, and Just, that Things should be as They Are; and that we ought to be extreamly well
― 723 ―

Sattisfy'd, and Pleas'd with It; as I shall be if you still After so much Absence, and Distance, Continue Your Governess in the Number of Those Few, that give you the Best Thoughts of it; who can never be less your Friend then she ever was, and whom though you may easilie change for a more Deserving One, You never can for One more Sincere, and Faithfull.
But you will Perhaps think that I am got into a Wonderfull serious Humour, Which if your first Letter Put me In; Your last should have brought me out of; But it will not Do; Gravitie has the Ascendant I Confesse, and neither your Extraordinarie Bed, nor Hogen Mogen Gyant with Dejected Whiskers,†1 can do any more then Just make me smile: and Yet I fancie Him at Urgunda's†2Feet as much as is Possible, who is indeed a great Diviner, and Predicter, But you Know very well that her skill is not Always Infallible. Notwithstanding I Allow that she Merits extraordinarie Homage; and I my self will Pay it Her if on the Twentie second Day of This Month,†3 I find that she Foreknew in the Last what was to Come to Pass in my Heart. In which should she Prove in the Right (as Yet I cannot Think) That Puzling Difficultie about Matrimonie might Perhaps be soone Resolv'd; and Your Governess (Following the Example of some other Soveraine Powers) might after a Long and Glorious Reigne Perchance Resigne Her Authoritie, and submit Her self Henceforwards to the more Humble Qualitie, and Condition, of a Subject. In which (If she should) she would not I hope Appeare to You Less Worthy of Your Esteeme at Least, then she has Hitherto had the Good Fortune to do; Since though All This, be but Fancie, without Realitie, The Bare Imagination that she would, if it were so, would be a Considerable Addition to that Uneasiness of Mind that I am in at Present Upon Diverse Accounts, which Yet Cannot hinder me (as You see) from telling you that I Constantly am
Your Real Friend and Servant
PHILOCLEA.
June the 5th 85.
Endorsed by Locke: Philoclea 5 Jun. 85

824. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, [summer 1685?] (810, 825)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 255m. Printed in Ollion, pp. 163-4. This letter and no. 825 were evidently written by Locke while he was living in hiding in Amsterdam. They are datable between his arrival there on 13/23 May of this year and his departure for Cleves about 5/15 September: these dates from Locke's Journal. They are unlikely to be earlier because there was no occasion for Locke to go into hiding prior to the request, 7/17 May, of Bevil Skelton, the English envoy, for his expulsion from the United Provinces and extradition: King, pp. 154-6. They are unlikely to be later on account of the spelling of van Limborch's name in the address: in earlier dated letters (nos. 798, 810) Locke uses the same form; from 18/28 September (no. 831) onwards he invariably uses the correct spelling.

Monday
(Original Text) Distinguished Sir,
I receive on all hands strong proofs of your kindly and friendly disposition; trusting in this and relying on my own experience I have made bold to ask you for fresh favours. I am most eager to see you, for I have much to say to you. If you care to call on me this messenger will show you my lodgings at what hour you please. But if you think it more convenient that I should call on you, I will be at your house this evening after nine o'clock; meanwhile please say nothing about me. I am your most obedient servant

826. Mrs. Ellen Dare to Locke, 14/24 July [1685]
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, f. 190. The date is presumably new style; year from Locke's endorsement. The writer is evidently the widow of Thomas Dare (p. 623, n. 4), who was killed at Lyme Regis on 13/23 June, at the outset of Monmouth's rebellion. On 11/21 August 1686 Locke sent seeds by her to Mrs. Clarke: Journal.
July 24th
Worthy Sir
I am sory that I cannot answar your desier, but att presant, I am so out of mony that I know not what to do, haveing a bill returned of 71ll which my husband drew Just before he left mee†1 and 50 drawn on him in a week after, which I was forst to pay, Sir the goods is not sold as yet but as soon as ever it is, your mony shall be payd, for ther is nothing more a trouble to mee than not being able to pay all persons ther deu att demand. Mr Le Blon†2 has promised mee to do his best to disspose of itt, with my humble servis is all from
your servant
ELLEN DARE
and iff you leave these parts pleas to oder to whome I shall pay itt to and I will take care to do itt

August
827. Lady Masham, formerly Damaris Cudworth, to Locke, 14 August [1685] (823, 830)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 124-5. Year from Locke's endorsement. For Sir Francis Masham and his family see pp. 470-1.
You cannot more Condemne me then I am Vex'd at my self for not Haveing writ to You all this While and yet I have really ever since I received yours Had so little the Command of my owne Time that it has beene next to impossible for me to do otherwise. Do not Therefore I Beg of you think me Alter'd, Although it be true that there is no longer any Mademoiselle C: in the World that I know of, Nor would your letter have found any had it come but one Half Houre later then it did, it being in the very Church that she received it, and
― 727 ―

Almost at the very same moment that she was going to quitt that name for Another Under which you will Always find her as much your Friend as she ever was, or as you can Desire that she should be.
I dare not say more, for Feare of Frighting you again and makeing you send for your Taylor, Although the Flatterie of your Distick I confess did not at all Displeas me, being Willing to Beleeve there may be a little Truth <amongst>†a a great deal that is not so, and that you Have Assur'd me in Plaine Prose (which Generally is more sincere then Verse) that I still am in the number of Those who make you Prefer the World to a Dutch Inne. My Value of it, is still much at the Old Rate, As my Philosophy is still the same, However you Reproach me as not being true to my Principles; But Fortune who is more Just then you, and who Knows (it seemes) How well I Merrited to be a Weiwert Sister, has on this side the Water found for me a Friend of L'Abadies; so that whenever your Health Permits you to come into England You may Possibly Have as great an Inducement to bring you into Essex,†1as I should have to see F:†2 if I were with you, who if you Remember Have sometimes said that you thought Me very well Qualify'd to bring up a new sect; I may therefore with much more ease improve upon the Old Foundations Do not then think that the Spirrit of Care, and Familie Affairs shall Intirely Possess me How deepe soever I may seeme to Have ingag'd my self in them I am at this time Willing to Beleeve what Has beene sometimes told me, That in some sort I am Capable of any Thing that I Have either a mind to Or that it otherwise Befits me to do. However my Predominant Inclinations will I am certaine Always be the same and I shall never Help being well enough Opiniated of them Neither to oppose Them Or be Assham'd to Owne Them. The Love of my Friends Therefore and the Best Kinds of Usefull Knowledge†3 so far as I am Capable of it, will still Possess my Heart as much as ever They did; However
― 728 ―

I deny not But that I Have had a Thousand Perplexing Imaginations of another Nature (Tho not about Those Weightie Matters You Fancie) and that my Head was never so much Distracted by the Thoughts of this World, and Pittyfull Life, as it has of late beene; Nevertheless if my letter was so Grave as you say it ought not to be Attributed wholly to that Cause, since my Feares of a Misfortune which since has Prov'd but too True were sufficient to forbid me Mirth and Railerie; I dare Hardly Trust my self with the Mention of it to You, it being too great to be Complain'd of, But if you think me yet more serious then is usual to me to be, it will be sufficient I suppose that you Know my Brother in the I: is Dead,†1 without being Acquainted with any of those Circumstances that Aggravate so great a Loss, The Reflection upon which will scarse Permit me to finish this Letter However not to Answeare some Part of Yours as I otherwise should But if you are still as much my Friend as you was You will be Content with me in All Humours, and I am certaine it cannot displease you to be Assur'd in a very serious One that I shall not be sattisfy'd with nothing But Good Wishes without Knowing what They are, and that if You would have me think you still my Friend You must Continue to Tell me so, who am very much Yours, as Also (without a Compliment)
Your Humble Servant
PHILOCLEA
Aug: the 14th

Address: To Mr Lock

828. Thomas Herbert, eighth earl of Pembroke, to Locke, 20 August [1685] (797, 982)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 193-4. Printed in King, p. 158. Year from Locke's endorsement. Pembroke enjoyed James II's favour at this time: he was lord lieutenant of Wiltshire; had distinguished himself at Sedgemoor; and James now wanted William of Orange to appoint him commander-in-chief of the English and Scottish regiments in Dutch service: H.M.C., Rutland MSS.
― 729 ―

ii. 92; Cal. S.P., Dom., 1685, nos. 1269, 1459; etc. James spent the night of 28 August 1686 at Wilton: Luttrell, i. 384. The letter may not have reached Locke before he set out for Cleves.
London August 20th.
Sir
I have often writt to you with great satisfaction in hopes of an answer, you will easily therfore conclude with how much more I write now since it will be the occasion of injoying your Company here in England: I need not tell you that I have omitted no oppertunety of contradicting all false reports to the King, and (as in so good a cause none can but succeed) I have so satisfied the King that he has assurd me he will never believe any ill reports of you, he bid me write to you to come over, I told him I would then bring you to kiss his hand and he was fully satisfied I should: pray for my sake let me see you before this summer be over, I believe you will not mistrust me I am sure none can the Kings word; you having so many friends least you should mistake who I am I must subscribe my self
Your friend
PEMBROKE.
Address: For Mr Locke.
Endorsed by Locke: E Pembroke 20 Aug. 85
829. Locke to Edward Clarke, 22 August/1 September 1685 (822, 844)
Rand, pp. 137-42. One of the education letters: p. 624.
1st Sept. 1685.
Sir
Your son's temper by the account you give of it is I find not only such as I guessed it would be, but such as one would wish, and the qualities you already observe in him require nothing but right management whereby to be made very useful.
Curiosity†1- in children is but an appetite after knowledge, and therefore ought to be encouraged in them, not only as a good sign, but as the great instrument nature has provided, to remove that
― 730 ―

ignorance they brought into the world with them, and which without this busy inquisitiveness would make them dull and useless creatures. The ways to encourage and keep it active and vigorous are, I suppose, these following:
1st. Not to check or discountenance any inquiries he may make, or suffer them to be laughed at; but to answer all his questions and explain matters he desires to know, so as to make them as much intelligible to him, as suits the capacity of his age and knowledge. But confound not <his>†a understanding with explications or notions that are above it, or with the variety or number of things that are not to his present purpose. Mark what it is he aims at in the question, and when you have informed and satisfied him in that, you shall see how his thoughts will proceed on to other things, and how by fit answers to his enquiries he may be led on farther than perhaps you could imagine. For knowledge to the understanding is as acceptable as light to the eyes; and children are pleased and delighted with it exceedingly, especially if they see that their enquiries are regarded, and that their desire of knowing is encouraged and commended. And I doubt not but one great reason why many children abandon themselves wholly to silly play, and spend all their time in trifling, is, because they have found their curiosity baulked and their enquiries neglected. But had they been treated with more kindness and respect, and their questions answered as they should to their satisfaction, I doubt not but they would have taken more pleasure in learning several things, and improving their knowledge, wherein there would be still newness and variety, which they delight in than in returning over and over to the same playthings.
2nd. To this serious answering their questions, and informing their understandings in what they desire, as if it were a matter that needed it, should be added some ways of commendation. Let others whom they esteem be told before their faces of the knowledge they have in such and such things; and since we are all even from our cradles vain, and proud creatures, let their vanity be flattered with things that will do them good; and let their pride set them to work on something which may turn to their advantage. Upon this ground you shall find that there can not be a greater spur to anything you would have your son learn or know himself, than to set him upon teaching it his sisters.
― 731 ―

3rd. As children's enquiries are not to be slighted, so also great care is to be taken, that they never receive deceitful and <eluding>†a answers. They easily perceive when they are slighted or deceived, and quickly learn the trick of neglect, dissimulation, and falsehood which they observe others to make use of. We are not to entrench upon truth in our conversation, but least of all with children. Since if we play false with them, we not only deceive their expectation, and hinder their knowledge, but corrupt their innocence, and teach them the worst of vices. They are travellers newly arrived in a strange country of which they know very little: we should therefore make conscience not to mislead them. And though their questions seem sometimes not very material, yet they should be seriously answered; for however they may appear to us to whom they are long since known, enquiries not worth the making, they are of moment to them who are wholly ignorant. Children are strangers to all we are acquainted with, and all the things they meet with are at first unknown to them, as they were to us; and happy are they who meet with kind people, that will comply with their ignorance, and help them to get out of it.
If you or I should be set down in Japan, with all our <prudence>†b and knowledge about us, a conceit whereof makes us perhaps apt to slight the thoughts and enquiries of children; should we, I say, be set down in Japan, we should no doubt (if we would inform ourselves of what is there to be known) ask a thousand questions, which, to a supercilious and inconsiderate†1<Japaner>,†c would seem very idle and impertinent; and yet to us would be very material, and we would be glad to find a man so kind and humane, as would answer them, and instruct our ignorance.
When any new thing comes in their way, children usually ask the common question of a stranger, What is it? Whereby they commonly mean nothing but the name; and therefore to tell them how it is called is usually the proper answer to that demand. The next question usually is, What is it for? And <to>†d this it should be answered truly and directly: the use of the thing told, and the way explained, how it serves to such a purpose, as far as their capacities can comprehend it; and so of any other circumstances they shall ask about
― 732 ―

it; not turning them going, till you have given all the satisfaction they are capable of, leading them by the answers into farther questions. And perhaps to a grown man such conversation will not altogether be so idle and insignificant as he may imagine. The native and untaught suggestions of inquisitive children do often offer things that may set a considering man's thoughts on work. And I think there is often more to be learnt from the unexpected questions of a child, than the discourses of men, who talk in a road, according to the fashions and customs of their country.
4th. Perhaps it may not, however, be amiss to exercise their curiosity concerning strange and new things in their way, on purpose that they may enquire and be busy to inform themselves about them; and if by chance their curiosity leads them to ask what they should not know, it is a great deal better to tell them plainly, that it is a thing that belongs not to them to know, than to pop them off with a falsehood, or a frivolous answer.†-1 
†2 Surliness†3- in a child joined with good nature I take to be a fault that will of itself yield in time to plain dealing without any mixture of a dissimulation; but being a quality much less tolerable in a man than a child, and least of all in a gentleman; it may deserve your care. If you observe that it begins to wear off of itself, and that age and good company, as I am apt to think, does insensibly lessen this natural roughness, and render your young gentleman more complaisant, the best way is neither to trouble yourself nor him about it, but leave your care to time and his own observations and the example of others about him. But if you find this natural stiffness confirm itself by age, and growing up with him, you must try to shame him out of it. Be not yet too hasty in this case, for as I said before, unpolishedness of manners and want of well-fashioned civility should be your least care whilst he is young. If you fill his tender mind with respect for you and his mother, which consists in love, and esteem, and a fear to offend you, for that reason, the respect will of itself teach to him those ways of expressing it which he observes most acceptable to you. Be sure to keep up in him the principles of good-nature and kindness, and encourage them as much as you can, by credit, commendation, and other rewards that
― 733 ―

accompany that state: and when they have taken root in his mind, and are settled there by practice, the ornaments of conversation and the outside of fashionable manners, will come of themselves.†-3 
One†1- thing I have observed in children, that when they have got possession of any poor creature, they are apt to use it ill, and they often torment and treat ill very young birds, butterflies, and such other poor things, which they get into their power, and that with a seeming kind of pleasure. This, I think, should be watched in them, and if they incline to any such cruelty they should be taught the contrary usage. For the custom of tormenting and killing of beasts will by degrees harden their minds even towards men, and they who accustom themselves to delight in the suffering and destruction of inferior creatures, will not be apt to be very compassionate or benign to those of their own kind. Our law†2 takes notice of this in the exclusion of butchers from juries of life and death. Children, then, should be taught from the beginning not to destroy any living creature unless it be for the preservation and advantage of some other that is nobler. And, indeed, if the preservation of all mankind as much as in him lies, were the persuasion of every one, as it is indeed the true principle of religion, politics and morality, the world would be much quieter and better natured than it is. But to return to our present business; I cannot but commend both the kindness and prudence of a mother I know, who was wont always to indulge her daughters when any of them desired dogs, squirrels, birds, or any such things, as young girls <use>†a to be delighted with. But then, when they had them, they must be sure to keep them well, and look well after them, that they want nothing, or were not ill used; for, if they were negligent in the care of them, it was counted a great fault which often forfeited their possession; or at least they failed not to be rebuked for it, whereby they were early taught diligence and good nature. And, indeed, I think people should be accustomed from their cradles to be tender to all sensible creatures, and to spoil or waste nothing at all.-†1
When†4- your son has by the easy and gentler ways before mentioned learnt to read a little, some pleasant book of little stories suited to a child's capacity, such as Æsop's Fables, if it be in English,
― 734 ―

or the like, should be chosen for him to read in, where the entertainment of what he reads might draw him on, and reward his pains in reading. It will add delight, if one talk with him afterwards of the stories he has read, that so he may find that there is some use and pleasure in reading, which in the ordinary method I think they do not till it be late; and so take books only for impertinent troubles that are good for nothing.†-4 
For†1- the Lord's Prayer, the Creed, and the Ten Commandments, they should be taught him by somebody repeating them to him by heart; and not out of the primer, or be mixed with his reading, which should be made as little troublesome to him as may be.-†1
But it is time to give off, having already exceeded the bounds of a letter. Besides that, I am just now packing to go I know not whither,†2 to find, if I can, a place to enjoy my health with quiet. For I cannot but think it an odd persecution of my stars, that I who meddle with no affairs but my own, that seek nothing but retirement and books to pass the remainder of my time in an air that favours my health cannot be permitted it.
I am, Sir,
your most humble servant,
J. L.
Address: To Edward Clarke, Esq., at his house at C[hipley].†a To be left at the Post-house in Taunton, Somersetshire.
September
830. Lady Masham, formerly Damaris Cudworth, to Locke, 15 September [1685?] (827, 837)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 134-5. Year from contents.
Your last Letter seemes to me to Differ so much from the stile of your former ones, that I cannot help being Dissattisfy'd with you for it, notwithstanding the many obliging Things You have said to me in it; And you make such distinctions betweene Friendship, and Respect, Your Governess, and my Lady — that if I were at all naturally Suspicious would Incline me to beleeve you was
― 735 ―

growing Wearie of the Former. But as I am not so, I confess I cannot find either in you, Or my self, any Reason that should induce me to be of that Opinion; You haveing too much Judgment to be mistaken in the Choise of a Friend, and I too much Value for your Friendship to neglect Preserving it by any thing in my Power; However the Appearances, But, of Some Things, are Displeaseing; and I would not (Therefore) any more But seeme to see my self Treated by You at a Greater Distance then befitts your Friend; Which is a Title I hope You do so much Right to my Judgment, as to Beleeve that I am Proud to Owne. But methinks you have almost Infected me, since I find in my self some Inclination at this Time to forget the Libertie of your Governess and to write to you in a stile that more Befits the Greatness of my Respect, and Esteeme, for You. However it being but the first Temptation of this Kind, in Hopes also it may be the Last, I Resolve to Prevail with my self to withstand it, Although I cannot but Hope that you Think in this Case what Mrs Phillips as truely says in Another,

That Freind
's a Name which all the Rest dos Comprehend.†1
You see that I cannot yet forget my Poetry upon occasion, and I Assure you the Vehicles†2 of the Platonists (whatever the Vortices of Des Cartes were) were Always much more my Favourites then the Muses; And it is not for Guilded Coaches, and Embroider'd Beds, Nor Yet the more important Considerations of a Familie, and Children, How Bountefully soever stor'd with Them, that will with me make them give Place to those Others, There being no Inconsistencie I hope betweene being still the same Philoclea, and indeavoring to Acquitt my self as my Lady — But that is a Name which we will lay aside if you Please till you are Better Reconcil'd
― 736 ―

to it, and Have seene (which I cannot but Hope you once will, and that, ere very long) How Perfectly she Resembles your Governess. In the mean time Remember that in the Learned Dulness of this Place†1 there is Yet more Societie then in the Countrey And that amidst the Impertinent Wrang'lings of the Schools One may sometimes Heare something more Edifying (at least more Diverting) then in the Repeated Entertainments of the Price of Corn, and the Best Managment of a Dairie; and Consequently that I shall have more need now of the Conversation of my Absent Friends then ever I have had Here, How much soever I have formerly Complain'd, and that Justly enough too Yet think not for This that I am Confin'd to a Desert neither, Since I am but within Half a Days Journey of the Great World at any time, Nor much more from Hence.†2 But you know it is not Places I have ever lov'd; Or Crouds that I have Thought Company; Twoo, or Three, of my Friends therefore may bring the Towne to me whenever they Please and leave London a Desert; at lest as Mr Cowley says


(A Village less then Islington)†3
Who were enough to make One even in Love with a Countrey life Had he found in it afterwards, the Sattisfaction he Promis'd Himself beforehand; But the World it seemes is the same every where; and the Honest Simplicitie of the Golden Age was no more to be found at Chelsea,†4 then in the Courts of Princes, Neither do I any more expect (though remov'd at something a Greater Distance from them then He) that Philoclea should find an Arcadia till the next Revolution.†5 But There are surely Better Eliziums then that was And without the Assistance of Faith I think wee may very well Hope for a more Noble Paradice then the Antediluvian One†6
You see I am geting againe to the Platonists notwithstanding what you Say; Whether it be in Contradiction to you or No, I cannot tell; but to my Knowledge I never had so Great a Desire as
― 737 ―

now to Talk to you of a Vehicle; But You shall not smile upon so serious a Subject; Since I Know after All, it would but serve you for a more Ingenuous Railerie; and in the Humour I am at Present in, I should not Acquit you of Prophanation; For Know that in the Solitude of a short Widdowhood, I Have shutt my self of the World, and Retireing into my self, am Mounted as far Above it, as an Inhabitant of Clay can be; Where I look downe with Pitty on All Things Below me; and where even Witt it self seemes but an Unvaluable Bauble; Where my Ideas are too Sublime to beare the Mixture of any thing that is Material; and where the Objects of all my Thoughts are of an Immortal Nature; and such without doubt is Friendship, since I find that There; But Alass! it is of a Friendship so Pure, Great, Generous, and Perfect, that I Dispaire of ever finding any lively Resemblance of it Here Below. However Reason Teaches me (for I would not have you Think that I am Mounted Above That too) to be Contented with the World as it tis, and to make the Best of every thing in it; Feare not then but that I shall Descend againe from this Pitch of Altitude; and Accept without Disdaine of such a Friendship as You can afford me.
But whether am I Run? And what a Pretty Answear is This to All the Complement you have sent me; But I onely Defer it; You shall stay for it till you are Newly Marryd and then I will Beg Philander†1 to Assist me in it; who in the Meane time will I Hope Answeare All the Kind, and Sincere, Part of it, in supplying by His owne Thoughts whatever my Words have been wanting in Acknowledgment.
But is it not time to Conclude? Or shall I Lengthen yet this Long Letter by makeing an Apologie for it? In which, I have nothing to say for my self but that it is the last you are like to Have a great While; I meane not the last letter, but the last long one; Since I go very suddenly into the Countrey, where you must Allow me for some time to be more then Ordinarilie employ'd, Where I shall have a Great deal of Real Business, and Where if I Had none I must However seeme Busie to Acquire the Necessarie Reputation of a Good Countrey Houswife; Which should I in earnest come at length to Deserve I will Have Affidavit made of it by the most skilfull of my Neighbourhood, and send it to you to Publish for the Honour of the Muses; Who I dare say will think it no Disparagment to them;
― 738 ―

and for whose Reputation I cannot but have a Concerne since the World Here, will Beleeve me to be a Votarie of Theires whether I will, or No. But I think verylie instead of a letter I shall write a Book to You, The Title of which must I think be Miscellanies; But I will now have done; and therefore to avoid any more Impertinence, I will Conclude like other Authors,
Finis.
Sept: the 15th.
I cannot Help improving this little Remainder of my Paper by a Postscript to let you know that I am exceeding glad of your owne Good Health and that I Know nothing lately either of Mr C—s†1 or His Ladys. The last that I Heard of Him was that he was gone into the Countrey to her; and that he got well Thither.

28 Sept
(Original Text) You will readily believe that when I wrote to our friend Mr. Guenellon†2 ten days ago I did not omit to send greetings to yourself, Distinguished Sir.
[p. 739]
But in truth a consideration of my duty and of your kindness demands of me some other way of greeting and thanking you, lest I should seem to perform what is so highly incumbent upon me either casually or negligently. This is especially so since our friend Guenellon's silence makes me doubt whether my letter has reached him. I should certainly not wish it to have been lost, lest I should seem to all of you, to whom I am obliged on so many accounts, either forgetful or ungrateful, and lest you should think that an interval of a few hours had erased from my mind the memory of so many and so great acts of kindness, which in fact no lapse of time will ever efface. I also mentioned in my letter how courteously your friend Vander Key received me, and how obligingly he assisted me; I am moved to thank you for this once again by that gentleman's great courtesy, though that is a small matter compared to the kindnesses with which you yourself have loaded me. I cannot easily find words in which to remember myself to Mr. Veen†1 and his excellent wife, as there are none which could match either their acts of kindness or the gratitude that I feel
[p. 740]
and shall always feel for them; I beg you, however, to express my feelings as warmly as you can. I told Mr. Guenellon in my letter how I have been detained here and prevented from proceeding further by reasons of health. The pleasantness of the place and if not laziness, at any rate a love of peace and quiet, as well as aversion to the discomfort I experienced on the journey, still detain me.†1 There are very pleasant walks here, with which I take revenge every day for my preceding spell of rest, but they would be much pleasanter if I had the company of some of you on my excursions; I wish for this continually as well for your sakes as for my own, especially in this fine weather; I do not think it would do you any harm, especially to Mevr. Guenellon; I feel sure that this calm and clear air†2 would be most beneficial for her weak lungs and not too robust health. I beg that you will give my most respectful regards to her as well as to your own excellent wife. Please write and tell me what is happening with you, particularly in regard to our friends. I hope especially that you will let me know that you and our friends are well. I am
Yours most respectfully

(English ) Præstantissime Vir
Recte te valere avide et cum gaudio ex tuis, nobis longe gratissimis, intelleximus. Literæ tuæ priores ad D. Guenellon recte curatæ sunt; ad quas jam præcedente dië Martis†3 responsum, cui ego ob nimiam festinationem exiguum adjunxi epistolium, misit, ipseque, ne aberraret, tabellario tradidit: Itaque miramur tibi illud nondum exhibitum fuisse ante vigesimum octavum Septembris, quo postremas tuas ad me scripsisti. Hæc præmitto, ut de literis tuis securus sis. Spero nec D. Guenelloni responsorias intercidisse, sed jam fideliter tibi redditas. Hisce addo alteras a D. Guenellon, aliasque ex Anglia ante triduum, me absente, ad ædes meas perlatas. Gratulamur
― 742 ―

tibi valetudinem meliorem, quam loci amœnitas, aërisque salubritas procul dubio confirmatiorem reddet. Omnes nos hactenus, Deo sit gratia, recte valemus. Salutavi amicos: Verum nimia tua humanitas nobis omnibus ruborem incutit: Exigua officiola, meritis tuis longe inferiora, in immensum exaggeras; quæ dum tibi præstamus, majorem nobis thesaurum, amicitiam tuam, lucrati sumus; quam ego longe majoribus, siquidem potestatis meæ esset, comparare beneficii loco censerem. Vidi ego alias loca, quæ nunc quotidie a te calcantur: Verum si aliquando te illic videre, tecumque montium ac sylvarum anfractus contemplari detur, spectaculum hoc, alias oculis meis gratissimum, longe gratius reddet tam amici viri præsentia: Et si in sequentem usque æstatem (nisi forte ad nos, quod malumus, reverti placeat) ibi subsistas, credo me cum amicis nostris te visurum. Vidi ego Hagæ Comitis fratrem meum:†1 fractura est in acromio: Verum ipse valet, nullaque symptomata sensit: itaque brevi restituendum spero. Hoc addo, quia sub discessum tuum de ipsius casu infœlici audivisti. Nova vix habeo quæ addam; et si quæ sint, a D. Guenellon scripta credo. Fui Lugduni Batavorum: Tractatum illum Gallicum contra P. Simonis
― 743 ―

Historiam Criticam valde a Theologis exagitari audio: Indignissime ferunt scriptum illud, quod Epistola undecima et duodecima exhibetur.†1 Autoritatem Scripturæ eo convelli clamant. Sane meo judicio audacius est; crediderimque ego, ejusmodi sententias mature esse examinandas, rationumque, quibus fulcitur, momenta prudenter ponderanda, antequam in publicum emittantur: Imo, etiamsi veræ forent, expendendum an ejusmodi veritatem, cum totius ferme orbis Christiani offendiculo, in lucem emittere expediat. Occurrunt sane phrases aliquot, meo judicio, duriores; quas emollitas oportuisset, ne sententia, per se satis odiosa, verbis ac phrasibus durioribus ingratior reddatur. Si ego ejusmodi editionis conscius fuissem, eam dissuasissem, ne crabrones irritarentur. Nunc alea jacta est, et exspectandum, quid objiciatur. Quando doctissimas tuas considerationes in tractatum meum de Ecclesia†2 relego, doleo maxime discessu tuo occasionem mihi ereptam, reliqua, et præsertim responsum Judæo oppositum,†3 sagacissimis tuis oculis ac limatissimo judicio subjiciendi: Quæ ego magno labore frustra
― 744 ―

quæro, ea profunda tua eruditio ac fœlicissimum ingenium nullo negotio tibi subministrant. Interim pro accuratissimo judicio grates habeo maximas; quas duplas tibi me debiturum profiteor, si scriptum, cujus mihi legendi potestatem fecisti, ultimam tuam manum expertum unquam lucem adspiciat.†1 Vale vir præstantissime. Salutat te D. Veenius cum uxore, uti et uxor mea.
Tui Observantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH
(English ) Amstelodami Cal. Octobris
 
(Original Text) Eminent Sir,
We learnt with great pleasure from your very welcome letter that you are in good health. Your previous letter to Mr. Guenellon was duly seen to; he sent a reply last Tuesday,†3 to which I added a short note of my own, being pressed for time; he gave it personally to the post-boy in case it should go astray. I am therefore surprised that it had not reached you by 28 September, the date of your last to me. I tell you this much so that you may have no anxiety about your own letter. I hope too that Mr. Guenellon's answer has not been lost but has been duly delivered to you. I send herewith another from him, also one from England, which was delivered at my house in my absence
[p. 742]
two days ago. We congratulate you on your improvement in health, which will doubtless be confirmed by the amenities of the place and the healthful air. All of us are well up to the present, thanks be to God. I have remembered you to our friends; but to tell the truth, your excessive kindness puts us all to the blush; you make much too much of trifling services which fall far short of your own deserts. In rendering you these we have won for ourselves a greater treasure in your friendship; for myself, if it had been in my power to purchase this with far greater services to you I would have counted myself well rewarded. I have on other occasions visited the places where you are now taking your daily walks; but if ever I may be fortunate enough to see you there, and in your company to view the winding ways of hills and woods, that prospect, grateful as it is to my eyes at any time, will be made doubly so by the presence of such a valued friend. Indeed, if you are to stay there till next summer—unless perhaps you decide to return to us, as we should prefer—I believe I may hope to see you there together with our friends. I have seen my brother†1 at The Hague; his fracture is at the point of the shoulder; but his health is good, and he has felt no further symptoms, so I hope he will soon be fully restored. I mention this, as you heard of his unfortunate accident just before your departure. I have little more news to give you; if there be any, I am sure that Mr. Guenellon will have given it to you. I have been to Leyden; that French treatise against Father Simon's Histoire
[p. 743]
critique is, I hear, meeting with severe criticism from the theologians. They are particularly scandalized by the matter of his eleventh and twelfth Letters,†1 which, they asseverate, destroys the authority of Scripture. In my own judgement, to be sure, it is somewhat rash; I feel that such sentiments should be thoroughly examined and the arguments on which they rest carefully weighed before they are made public. Indeed, even if they were true, yet it is a matter for consideration whether it is expedient that truth of this sort should see the light when it is likely to give offence to almost the whole Christian world. I find in it a number of expressions which seem to me unduly harsh; these should have been softened lest an opinion distasteful enough in itself should be rendered even more unwelcome by asperity of language. Had I known that such a publication was in prospect I would have advised against it, in order to avoid stirring up a hornet's nest. Now the die is cast, and one must await the counter-throw. When I reread your scholarly observations on my treatise on the Church†2 I deeply regret that your departure deprived me of the opportunity of submitting the rest, notably my reply to the Jew,†3 to your discerning scrutiny and fine judgement. What I seek in vain to achieve by hard labour is supplied to you without
[p. 744]
trouble by your profound learning and natural aptitude. Meanwhile I am deeply grateful for your careful criticisms; and my debt, I declare, will be doubled if the work which you permitted me to read should some time see the light after receiving the finishing touch from your hand.†1 Good-bye, my illustrious friend. Dr. Veen and his wife send you their greetings, as does my own.
Your most obedient servant
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH.
(Original Text) Amsterdam 1 October 1685
