Si duabus tuis amicissimis epistolis parum vel nihil a me responsum est. id instanti Tabularii†a discessui imputes rogo, nec credas me tam rebus meis intentum, tuæ vero consuetudinis et jucundissimi juxta ac doctissimi sermonis negligentem ut omnia de meis negotiis, de tuis gratissimis literis nihil dicerem, nisi gravis aliqua subesset causa cur de adventu Comitis Pembrokiæ quam fieri potuit citissime certior fierem. Sed jam quo maxime propendet animus ad te Vir Optime et Scripta tua redeo in quibus primo accuso amicitiam tuam, de me et meritis meis tam magnificè, de vestris erga me officiis et beneficiis tam exiliter loquentem. hi sunt fateor magnæ et non fictæ amicitiæ aliquando errores de quibus ideo queror ut mihi aliter de iisdem rebus sentienti ignoscas, et me credas amicitiæ et gratitudinis dictata sequi cum in eâ persistam sententiâ, aliqua me apud vos accepisse beneficia quibus respondere verbis nec possim nec debeam. et nisi vos omnes, in re, contra quam par est,
― 747 ―

voluntati meæ obstare viderem tuam ego hic opem implorarem ut hanc mihi velles eximere ægritudinem, et tuâ authoritate, qua plurimum apud præstantissimum Veenium polles, huic querelæ tam justæ finem imponeres. Si quod videris promittere, sed heu longum abest, his in collibus et sylvarum umbra, tua frui daretur et amicorum nostrorum consuetudine, crederem ego specimen aliquod aurei rediisse sæculi, nam virtus benignitas pax et fides in sylvis solum degebant, quibus in urbanorum hominum frequentiâ vix datur locus. Sic cecinerunt poetæ. an aliquid aliud nos docent historici hoc tempore non est mihi inquirendi animus. Gaudeo fratrem tuum convaluisse et sine graviore aliquo symptomate. Locum illum epistolæ tuæ ubi scriptorum tuorum memineris non sine mærore legi, sentio quantam ex decessu meo fecerim jacturam et voluptatis et eruditionis quod non legerim reliqua tua scripta ex quibus non minorem mihi lucem promitterem quam ex jam lectis multo cum fructu percepissem. Si vis ut sincere et aperte dicam nullibi reperi opiniones magis dilucide propositas, argumentorum rationibus melius subnixas, a partium studiis longius remotas et veritati per omnia magis conformes. Hoc me ex animo proferre dubitare non potes, cum me tam importune tam deditâ operâ criticum tam paucis potuisse dentem malignum imprimere patet. Sed me miserum,
― 748 ―

magnam partem fructus quem ex istâ meâ criticâ severitate mihi proposui, perdidi. Plurima enim quæ inter legendum notavaram non tam tui corrigendi quam mei informandi feci animo, de quibus tecum ulterius inquirendum statueram. Non est igitur quod mihi tanto Ardelioni†1gratias agas, satis est si vehementi nimis inquisitori et culpandi ansas studiose quærenti ignoscas. Quanquam non male pictæ tabulæ indicium est si quis cogatur in ea quærere nævos. Utinam quæ ego meditor eo essent scripta ideomate ut tu poteris vices rependere, reperires te ulciscendi copiosam materiem.†2 Quod scribis de Critici Critico†3 facile credo, quamprimum enim attigi istum undecimæ epistolæ locum videbar mihi audire obstrepescentium exclamationes quasi de religione omnino actum esset, nosti hujusmodi hominum mores, quo minus heterodoxum aliquid possint refellere ne nihil in causa dei agere videantur, tanto magis clamoribus incusationibus calumniis insurgunt. Fateor argumentum illud modeste proponendum fuisse, et caute tractandum, sed tamen ejusmodi est ut mereatur tandem summâ cum acribiâ discuti. Si omnia quæ in sacris libris continentur pro theopneustis pariter habenda sine omni discretione, magna sane
― 749 ―

præbetur philosophis de fide et sinceritate nostra dubitandi ansa. Si e contrario quædam pro scriptis purè humanis habenda, ubi constabit scripturarum divina authoritas? sine qua corruet religio Christiana; quodnam erit criterium? quis modus? adeo ut in hac quæstione, si quæ alia, maximè fundamentali, summâ cum cautione, prudentiâ, modestiâ agendum præsertim ab eo cui uti credo jam non nimium favent ecclesiasticæ potestates et Theologorum classes,†1 sed signa cecinerunt et expectandus est conflictus. Ego qui ubique solam quæro veritatem, eamque quantum capere possum sive inter Orthodoxos reperio sive heterodoxos pariter amplector, fateor aliqua esse in eo scripto quæ mihi plane†a non satisfaciunt, alia quibus respondere non possum, de illis ab authore libenter responsum acciperem, si commodum existimas, de his tuum quæro judicium. 1o Ni fallor author sæpius utitur contra Apostolorum continuam inspirationem hoc argumento, quod sc: multa ab illis dicta invenimus

Itaque metuo ne homines suspicentur hoc argumentum potius quæsitum quam e re natum.

Cleves 6 Oct. 85
(Original Text) Distinguished Sir,
If I answered little or nothing to your two most friendly letters you must please charge this to the imminent departure of the post-boy; you may believe, too, that I would not have been so intent on my own affairs and so neglectful of your companionship and your delightful and scholarly conversation as to say everything about my own business and nothing about your most welcome letters unless I had had a serious reason for wishing to be informed as quickly as possibly about the arrival of the earl of Pembroke. But I now return to my chief interest, to yourself, honoured Sir, and to your letters; in these I first of all bring a charge against your friendship for speaking so handsomely of me and my deserts, while you say so little of the services and kindnesses I have received from you all. These are sometimes, I admit, the mistakes made by great and unfeigned friendship, and I complain of them only that you may forgive me for feeling otherwise about those same things; I would have you believe that I am following the dictates of friendship and gratitude when I persist in the opinion that I have received at your hands some benefits that I neither could nor ought to acknowledge by mere words; and if I did not see that you are all unjustly opposed to my wishes in this
[p. 747]
matter I would here implore your help, begging you, if you would, to relieve me of this distress, and by using the great authority that you have with the excellent Veen to put an end to my just complaint. If what you seem to promise, but, alas, at a very long date, might be fulfilled; if it might be granted me to enjoy among these hills and shady woods your own society and that of our friends, I should believe that some likeness of the golden age had returned. For forests used to be the only abode of virtue and benevolence, peace and good faith, for which there is hardly a place in the crowded cities of men. So poets have sung; whether historians teach us anything different in these days I am not minded to inquire. I am glad that your brother has recovered and without showing any more serious symptom. That passage in your letter where you mention your writings caused me some regret when I read it; I feel what a great sacrifice I made by my departure of both pleasure and instruction, seeing that I did not read the rest of what you had written, from which I could have promised myself no less enlightenment than I had received from what I had already read with great profit. If you wish me to speak openly and sincerely, nowhere have I found opinions more clearly set forth, better supported by reasoned arguments, further removed from party feeling, and in all points more conformable to the truth. You cannot doubt that I am expressing my genine feelings, when it is plain that, persistent and purposeful critic as I am, I have been able to find so little on which to exercise
[p. 748]
a spiteful tooth. But woe is me! I lost a great part of the reward I promised myself from that critical severity, for most of my observations in the course of reading were made not so much with the idea of correcting you as of informing myself on points I had decided to consult you about later. You have therefore no reason to thank such a great busybody†1 as myself; it is enough if you will pardon an over-strenuous inquisitor and diligent seeker of handles for faultfinding. For that matter it is no sign of a badly painted picture if one is compelled to look for blemishes in it. I only wish that the work I am engaged on were written in a language that might enable you to repay me in kind; you would find abundant material for your revenge.†2 I can readily believe what you say about the Critic's Critic;†3 the moment I came upon that passage in the eleventh letter I seemed to myself to hear cries of protest as if it meant the end of all religion. You know the ways of such people: the less they are able to refute some heterodox opinion, the more they are roused, in their anxiety not to appear idle in God's cause, to outcries, accusations, and calumnies. That argument should, I admit, have been put forward with moderation and handled with caution; all the same, it is after all of a kind that deserves to be discussed with the greatest exactness. If everything in holy writ is to be considered without distinction as equally inspired by God,
[p. 749]
then this surely provides philosophers with a great opportunity for casting doubt on our faith and sincerity. If, on the contrary, certain parts are to be considered as purely human writings, then where in the Scriptures will there be found the certainty of divine authority, without which the Christian religion will fall to the ground? What criterion will there be, or what measure? It comes to this, that on this question, which is, if any, in the utmost degree fundamental, it was proper to proceed with the greatest caution, prudence, and moderation, especially for a person who, I believe, was already not too favourably regarded by the ecclesiastical authorities and†b- the theologians in the presbyteries.-†b†1 But the trumpets have sounded and one must expect the conflict. For myself, who am everywhere in search of the truth alone and to the best of my understanding embrace it with equal readiness whether I find it among the orthodox or the heterodox, I confess that there are some things in that tract that I am positively dissatisfied with and others to which I cannot find an answer; I would be glad to have the author's reply about these, and I would like to have your own opinion on them, if you think proper to give it to me. 1. Unless I am mistaken, the writer in disputing the perpetual inspiration of the Apostles not infrequently uses the argument that we find many things said by them which could have been said
[p. 750]
without the assistance of the Holy Spirit; if this is admitted, however, it proves nothing against the divine authority and inspired character of Holy Scripture. It is maintained that constant and infallible truth is to be found throughout in Holy Scripture. Now, if St. Paul in Acts 23 (see p. 241)†1 says something that had not been revealed to him from Heaven this in no way detracts from the certainty of Scripture, for the matter was of a kind that he could know certainly and infallibly without divine revelation. In matters of which the Apostles were assured by their senses and their certain knowledge there was no need of revelation for the account of them transmitted by the Apostles to be held indubitable. I therefore fear that men may suspect this argument of being sought ut rather than naturally presenting itself.
(Original Text) 2. The explanation of that promise in John 16: 13 which he gives at length on p. 256 cannot possibly, it seems to me, be applied to the Apostle Paul, if one reads his story attentively as given in Acts 9 and following.†2 For how was that enemy of the Gospel, and, as he somewhere himself confesses, an ignorant man, able so quickly to become an interpreter and proclaimer of the mysteries of the Gospel unless by supernatural and divine inspiration (see Acts 9: 19, 20)? These are some of the points that did not satisfy me in
[p. 751]
the course of reading; there were others that I have forgotten; but I should be glad to know what the writer has to say about these. But since there are in fact a number of other passages which appear to cast doubt upon the general infallibility and inspiration of Holy Scripture, and to which I confess that I cannot find an answer, I earnestly beg that you will not find it too troublesome to explain to me your own feelings on the matter. Many things that I have come across in the canonical books, long before I read this treatise, have kept me in doubt and anxiety, and you will be doing me a most welcome service if you can relieve me of these scruples. Kindly hand the enclosed to my excellent host,†1 with the fullest expression of my friendship, gratitude, and respect. Please remember me to his wife and your own as well as to Guenellon's, and to all our other friends. Good-bye, and forgive me for writing long letters; for I find it difficult to stop talking with you.
Your most devoted
J L
(Original Text) I have just received a letter from my friend Guenellon, dated the 5th, with the enclosed letter. Please give him my thanks, for I do not wish to weary all of you at the same time with long letters.

(English ) Amplissime Vir
Tuis postremis, quæ mihi Hagam abiturienti Amstelodami redditæ sunt, non respondi, quia id solum scribere potuissem, me, quod a me requiris, Hagæ curaturum probe, quantum in me esset. Inquisivi hic de adventu Comitis Pembrochiæ: Creditur huc adventurus circa reditum Principis Auriaci, qui e Geldria huc reversurus exspectatur circa initium Novembris. Interim dum hic sum, accurate, quantum possum, apud alios tempus illud expiscabor, et Tibi indicabo. Adfuit mihi nuper Helmontius, post quadriennalem in Anglia commorationem redux in patriam nostram.†1 Totus nunc in eo est, ut nos duodecies in hunc mundum reducat. Vix aliud nunc videtur sapere. Ostendit mihi manuscriptum Latinum, continens ducentas quæstiones, quibus sententia ipsius, ejusque fundamenta, explicantur: eundem ajebat esse, quem Anglico idiomate emiserat. Nunc in Batavia typographum quærit, ut
― 753 ―

etiam Latine ab Angliæ linguæ ignaris legi possit.†1 Alium mihi dedit tractatum Anglicum, varia continentem, cujus non exigua pars hac quæstione occupatur.†2 Ita etiam nobis sperare licebit, si nunc simus separati, ante quadringentos annos rursus fore conjunctos; quæ conjunctio, si non potu lethæo omnis nostræ amicitiæ memoria prorsus deleta fit, multo erit gratior futura, quando post tot annorum decursum dextras jungere dabitur, notasque audire et reddere voces.†3 Quæsivit me etiam Domini Preston Legati Regis Angliæ ad Regem Galliæ sacellanus,†4 dum hac transiens Angliam repeteret. Literas habebat ab amico quodam Gallo mihi inscriptas. Deprehendi virum esse eruditum, et amicus meus, cui fuit familiarus, laudat prolixe ejus non tantum eruditionem, sed et erga dissentientes moderationem. Etiam se talem apud me explicuit. Uterque doluimus ob Legati subitum discessum occasionem nobis præreptam sæpius conveniendi, et de variis conferendi: Ulterius ego animum ejus de variis explorassem, præsertim de moderatione in negotio religionis. Omnes adhuc bene valemus, quod Te ex literis D. Guenellon
― 754 ―

jam probe intellexisse nullus dubito. Salutat te quam amantissime uxor mea, quæ mecum Hagæ est: Uterque omnia Tibi fausta precamur. Vale.
Tui Observantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH
(English ) Hagæ Comitis 8 Octobris
 
(Original Text) Excellent Sir,
I did not reply to your last letter, which reached me at Amsterdam just as I was setting out for The Hague, since I could only have told you that I would attend to the matter of your request there to the best of my ability. I have made inquiries about the arrival of the earl of Pembroke; it is believed that he will be here about the time of the Prince of Orange's return, who is expected to be back here from Gelderland about the beginning of November. Meanwhile whilst I am here I will do my best to find out from other people the time of the earl's arrival and will inform you of it. I was recently visited by van Helmont, who has returned to our country after a four years' sojourn in England.†1 He is now entirely wrapped up in his design to bring us all back twelve times to this world. He seems at the moment to have no other idea in his head. He showed me a manuscript in Latin containing two hundred questions, in which his theory and the grounds of it are set forth; he told me it was the same as that which he had published in the English language. He is now looking for a printer in Holland, so that it may also be read in
[p. 753]
Latin by those who know no English.†1 He gave me another pamphlet in English on various subjects, a considerable part of which is taken up by his theory.†2 So it seems that we too may hope that if we are to be separated in this life we may meet once more in four hundred years' time; such a reunion, unless all memory of our friendship is to be entirely obliterated by the draught of Lethe, will be all the pleasanter when after the lapse of so many years it is granted us to clasp hands and to 'hear and return familiar speech'.†3 I also received a visit from the chaplain of Lord Preston, the king of England's ambassador to the king of France,†4 when he was passing through here on his way back to England. He had a letter from a French friend addressed to me. I found him to be a scholarly man, and my friend, who knew him well, gives him unstinted praise, not only for his learning but for his tolerant attitude towards those who disagree with him. He proved himself such to me as well. We were both sorry that the ambassador's sudden departure deprived us of the opportunity of meeting oftener and of discussing various topics; I would have searched further into his opinions on a number of things, especially on the question of toleration in matters of religion. We are all still well, as no
[p. 754]
doubt you have already been told by Dr. Guenellon in his letter. My wife, who is with me at The Hague, sends you her affectionate greetings; we both wish you all happiness and prosperity. Good-bye.
Your most obedient servant
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
(Original Text) The Hague 8 October

836. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 8/18 October 1685 (835, 838)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, f. 4. Answers no. 834.
(English ) Amplissime Vir
Utramque meam epistolam Hagâ missam fideliter tibi traditam nullus dubito.†1 Nudius tertius in novellis nostratibus legi, Comitem Pembrochiæ jam navem conscendisse, ac propediem hic exspectari. Hodiernæ de eo plane silebant. Perendie prodituræ forsitan
― 755 ―

adventum ejus nuntiabunt. Ex hisce liquet, aut jam appulisse Comitem, aut brevi appulsurum. Certius nihil resciscere potui.
(English ) Prolixius nunc tibi destinaveram responsum: Verum negotia, non quidem magna, sed multa, quæ me Haga redeuntem ferme opprimunt, id in sequentem hebdomadam differre cogunt. Prælegi autori critices in Simonem†1 partem epistolæ tuæ, quæ ipsum concernit: Putabat se facile difficultatibus tuis occurrere posse, et promisit mihi responsum, quod ad te mittam. (Ille tamen ignorat, a Te epistolam missam). Hodie autem, uti promiserat, non attulit: credo aliis impeditum, quia in alias ædes ipsi heri immigrandum fuit. Dubito tamen, an ita facile se expedire possit. Alia ego ipsi objeci: Videri mihi rem scripto ipso comprehensam accurato examine dignam: Verum autorem oportuisse eam prudentius, distinctius et clarius tractasse: Debuisse distincte proponere, quid Apostolis adscriberet, quid iisdem denegaret: ut ita controversiæ status clare et dilucide esset propositus, neque dissensus major videretur, quam revera est. Addebam, ipsum aliquando pugnare argumentis debilibus valde, quæ facile refelli possunt: quorum tum quædam indicabam. Fatebatur: sed addebat, licet illa per se non
― 756 ―

multum valerent, aliis tamen validioribus juncta pondus suum habere. Regessi ego, præjudicium ita fieri veritati: refutatis enim quibusdam argumentis infirmioribus, facile et alia ab imperitioribus rejici. Concludebam, oportuisse scriptum illud in multis refingi, antequam esset editum. Respondit, se, in alieno scripto, cujus tantum interpres fuit, tantum sibi juris non ausum arrogare. Regessi ego: præstitisse aliquamdiu editionem illius differri, et interim scriptum ita emendatum ad autorem remittere; ut postea prodeat minus scabrosum. Undique enim, ajebam, in te insurgent Theologi, teque, si non autorem, saltem approbatorem dicent: Interim de tota hac quæstione libens judicium meum perscribam: Verum temporis angustia graviores illas et serias meditationes, et scriptionem prolixiorem non permittit. Ea tamen lege judicium meum scribam, ut tu criseos meæ sis epicrita. De amica illa concertatione quæ inter nos est, nihil addam: Tu te nobis obstrictum censes: nos officiola nostra, meritis tuis longe inferiora, nimis a te extolli credimus, et plura tibi debere profitemur. Uterque sensu suo abundet, et sinceræ amicitiæ ac amoris infucati actibus inter nos certemus: sic licet locorum distantia corpora nostra separet,
― 757 ―

animos nunquam divellet. Verum abrumpere cogor. Vale Præstantissime Vir: uxor plurimam tibi dicit salutem, mecumque omnia fausta precatur.
Tui Observantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH
(English ) Amstelodami 18 Octobris
 
(Original Text) Excellent Sir,
I have no doubt that both the letters which I sent you from The Hague have been duly delivered to you.†1 I read in our newspaper of the day before yesterday that the earl of Pembroke had already embarked and was expected here shortly. Today's paper has no word about him. The day after tomorrow's, when it appears, will perhaps announce his arrival. From this it is clear that
[p. 755]
the earl has either landed by this time or will shortly do so. I have not been able to obtain any surer information.
(Original Text) I had intended to answer you now at greater length; but affairs, not serious indeed, but numerous, which are taking up almost all my time on my return from The Hague, compel me to defer this till next week. I read over to the writer of the critique on Simon†1 that part of your letter which concerns him. He thought he could easily meet the difficulties you raise, and promised to give me a reply to send to you. (He does not know, however, that the letter was yours.) He has failed to bring it today as he promised, having been prevented, I imagine, by other business, since he had to move into another house yesterday. I doubt, however, whether he will find it so easy to extricate himself. I put other objections to him: it seemed to me, I told him, that the subject dealt with in the treatise deserved careful consideration, but that the author should have handled it with greater prudence, precision, and clarity. He ought, I said, to have set forth distinctly what he attributed to the Apostles and what he denied to them, that so the point at issue in the controversy might be seen in a clear light, and that the difference of opinion might not appear greater than it really is. I added that he sometimes employed very weak arguments, which could be easily refuted; I pointed out some of these to him at the time. He admitted this, but added that, although such
[p. 756]
arguments might not be very strong in themselves, yet they had their due weight when taken together with other and stronger ones. I rejoined that this was to the prejudice of the truth; for if certain weaker arguments were refuted it might easily happen that others too would be rejected by less informed readers. My conclusion was, I said, that that work should have been reshaped in many respects before it was published. He replied that in the case of another person's work of which he was only the interpreter he had not presumed to take so much upon himself. To this I rejoined that it would have been better to defer the publication of it for a time, and meanwhile to send back the work so emended to the author, so that it might appear later in a less rough and uneven form. 'For the theologians', I told him, 'will rise up against you on all sides, and they will say that if you did not write it, at any rate you approve of it. Meanwhile I will gladly put in writing my own opinion on the whole question; but the short time at my disposal does not permit me to give it the earnest and serious study I should wish and to state my views at greater length. On one condition, however, I will write it for you, namely if you undertake to pass your own judgement on mine.' On the subject of that friendly dispute of ours I have no more to say; you consider yourself under obligations to us; for our part, we believe that you make too much of our small services, which are far short of your own deserts, and we maintain that we are the deeper in debt to you. Let each of us cherish his own belief, and let our contest be in acts of sincere friendship and unfeigned affection; thus though distance may separate our bodies it will never sunder
[p. 757]
our hearts. But I am forced to break off. Good-bye, my honoured friend; my wife sends you her warmest greetings and joins with me in wishing you all good fortune.
Your most obedient servant
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH

837. Lady Masham, formerly Damaris Cudworth, to Locke, 14 November [1685] (830, 839)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 126-7. Year from Locke's endorsement.
I have several times begun to write to You since I received Yours But the Necessitie of Household Affaires will have it so that I could never Yet finish one Letter; what the Fate of This will be I Know not, But I have in my designe set apart this Day to Discharge my self to my Friends of All Obligations of this Kind; In the first Rank of whom I Hope you doubt not but you stand It being Altogether impossible for any thing whatever to incroach upon the Place You have theire, whilst I may Beleeve I have any in Yours, And yet I cannot but Acknowledge that as to some Things Matrimonie and Familie Cares have Alter'd me very much. Though I was Always Dull, I find that I am now a Thousand times more so then formerly; And the little Knowledge that I once had, is now exchangd for Absolute Ignorance; I am taken off of All that I once did Know, and Understand; and Have nothing at All in lieu of it; Tis in Vain that you bid me Preserve my Poetry; Household Affaires are the Opium of the Soul†1 and it is impossible for me to make use of that
― 758 ―

Preservative unless I can Recover first from this Lethargie that am now in. Which that you may have some Hopes of However, Know that I am at Present All alone in that Place I told you of except the Gentleman you Kno of, a Young Man of 16, a Child of 5, and a Girl between both that speakes not yet a Word of English;†1 For These last you may judge what conversation They are; and for the first the Business of this World Almost wholly imploys him when he is at Home, so that I have very little of His Company. All my Friends and Relations have just left me, and the Badness of the Season Permits not now any Visits from the Neighborhood which However are not very Desireable. These things with the consideration of finding every Thing New About me may perhaps be some excuse for the Present, and afford some Hopes that when some of them are remov'd, and that I am Accustom'd to the rest I may returne to my self againe, which I heartilie wish; since whatever Value I in my last set upon the Accomplishment of being a Countrey Housewife, I owne I slight it as much now; which is however Perhaps but the last Shift of Prudence in me who may be (as Davenant has it) What I would Prize

When I find I can't get, seeme to Dispise.†2
But I find I am geting into Poetry alreadie before I Have thought of it, I cannot therefore but Hope well of my self Though Certainly nothing but the Aire of Essex†3 would have brought this Poet to my Mind. That, where You are, has had a Much better effect sure upon You, tho I should not have Hop'd for so much from it, since how it comes about otherwise I Know not, but you are
― 759 ―

methinks of late growne a most Wonderfull Platonist Tho by your leave you greatly mistake in your Accusation of the Platonique you mention,†1 if you think she has any Way Profan'd those Misteries, or Degenerated from theire Principles; Souls are not fetch'd from those Happy Abodes, before they have forfeited Them; Nor clad in Clay, whilst they are Capable of Acting in any better Vehicle.†2 The former, is but the meanes to restore them againe to the latter, and she is so far therefore from being any way guiltie upon that score, that it is indeed the greatest Act of Platonique Charitie that she was Capable of Performing, and The Omission of it so long, the greatest thing she ought to Repent of; But it is not a yeare yet since she writt her Recantation, and Promis'd Amendment, (which I would now send you, since you desire Verse, but that it is too long)†3 and she has so Honestly Kept Her Word since, that I hope she has sufficiently Merrited her Pardon for that Sin of Ignorance
But how shall I do to forgive all your Abuse of me, as well as Her, Since I can neither make any Verses at this Time, nor remember any to the Purpose. But be Assur'd your Punishment is but Defer'd, since if ever that Humour come on me againe You shall Wish for Finis a Thousand times before you find it; I will set the Affronted Countrey Ladies too upon you, and They shall Abuse you Ten times more then I can, for All your Contempt of Theire Sublime Ideas of Goose Pye, and Bag Puding. This would bring me again now to the Chapter of Household Affaires, and my imployments; but that I am awearie; However for All my quarrel with you I cannot help telling you that there is scarse any thing I would not give to see you Here in my Closet where I am now writeing to You; I can but Think how you would smile to see Cowley and my Surfeit Waters Jumbled together; with Dr More and my Gally Potts of Mithridate and Dioscordium; My Receits and Account Books with Antoninus's†4 his Meditations, and Des Cartes Principles; with my Globes, and my Spining Wheel; for just in this order They at present ly, and tis not without Reason I think that I designe to Draw Curtains over this Fantastical Furniture. Neither is it so, that I may beleeve you Tyr'd by this Time as well as my self; who you see cannot forbeare writeing long letters where ever I am; whatever I say to the Contrary. But I will now put an end to
― 760 ―

this, and since you will Have it so, Conclude as I use to do with telling you that I am your Humble Servant
PHILOCLEA.

839. Lady Masham, formerly Damaris Cudworth, to Locke, 14 December [1685] (837, 847)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 128-9. Year from Locke's endorsement.
It is Methinks a Long while since I writt to You and I Have not since Heard Any thing of You; Sometimes I Fancie You are not well But I more often Think that it is a Wilfull neglect of your Governess that occasions Your silence. Pardon me if I cannot Help being a little Jealous; I think you never was so long without leting me Heare from You but Once before. Methinks I still Deserve from You as much as I ever did, since I am still the same I ever was in Respect of my Friends, Unless that the loss of some of them Has made me more Covetuous of Preserving those that are left; to which you must lay the Blame of my importuning you now with Another Letter before you Have Answear'd the last which as I remember was indeed Dull enough not to Merit it. However I cannot make Amends for it at this Time since You have Put me out of Humour and it is but fitt You should be Punish'd for it
I Dreamt of Heareing from you last Night and I wish'd for it All This Day when In comes a Double letter to me just now from my Brother,†1 who never used to write to me But to inclose yours. I Began to Admire my Good Fortune extreamly; and Open'd it with All the Hast imaginable expecting All the Diversion which your Letters use to Afford me, when in stead of That†a I find nothing But a Long Weding Compliment from a Countrey Cosen that without question has beene studying for it This Half Yeare; Judge
― 762 ―

you now whether this was not a great Disappoint†a and Whether I can forgive You for it without makeing me a large Amends, That is, by writeing me a letter Twice as Long as His without makeing any notice of Matrimonie, for I am quite sick of that subject by way of letters; and I should be very glad instead of being Wish'd Joy any more that you will indeavour to give me some by saying something that is more new to me.
I Assure you in this Winters Solitude it will be a great Charitie, since I have not so much as the Diversion of my Dairie, and am Forc'd now (and Therefore I Hope it will be without Offence to the Good Housewifes of my neighborhood) to seeke my entertainment in Books Altogether; and that Principally in Poetry, to which the Present Fancie most inclines me, and Therefore know at this Time that it is out of pure Crosness that I send You none, since I Hardly write of Late to Any Body but your self in Prose. Yet do not Blame me for it, since I Have Alreadie told you that I am Jealous and it is impossible there should be any good Humour left where that Passion is. How ever perhaps you may see me in Print in a little While, and then need not be Beholden to me, it being growne much the Fasion of late for our sex, Though I confess it has not much of my Approbation because (Principally) the Mode is for one to Dye First;†1 and at this time if I might Have my owne Choice I Have no Great Inclination That Way Tho whether it be with Haveing Converst so much of late with Urgunda†2 that she has imparted any of the spirrit of Prophecie to me, or otherwise, I Know not, But I am not without some Apprehensions that I am to do so in a little Time As within Half a Yeare or There abouts,†3 which if I should out live I then Fancie I am settled in for a Pretty while However for Feare of the First let me Advise you for so long time at least to Retaine All that Regard which you ever Had for your Governess, since should I go before you with Another Perswasion, I assure you I shall not onely be very stout when I meet you There, But Also give a very Ill Character of You to Those Platonical Spirrits whose Friendship I am sure you will Desire There, whatever you think of them now. But I Designd to Have writt but 3 lines to you, and I Have Almost
― 763 ―

Blotted All my Paper. I will Therefore Conclude with onely telling you that Though I am not good Friends with you, I am yet much your Humble Servant

(Original Text)
Last day of the year
(Original Text) Distinguished Sir,
The business matters which I know have engaged your attention these days are reason enough for my not having so far seen either thee or tea. However, as it may happen (I know how ready you always are to do things for me) that this purchase has possibly been made, I should not wish to neglect the approach of Janus, under whose auspices I hoped, in accordance with custom, that this trifling gift which I had intended for my hostess might find favour. So there; you have my plan of campaign, and this was why I have sent my servant to bring me the tea if it has already been bought. But if your manifold affairs have willed otherwise we can wait, and no harm done. Meanwhile please forgive my tiresome importunity; I promise not to offend again in the same way this year. This language seems to exhibit a certain amount of
[p. 764]
restraint; but please remember that the new year is upon us tomorrow, and that your company, conversation, advice, and help are so necessary to me that I would not dare to promise that I can abstain a day longer from calling on you. This is not to be understood of the purchase of the tea; if not bought yet let it be bought when it suits you; I only ask that it may be of the best quality. I wish you and yours every sort of happiness and prosperity in the coming year; and to make it a happy one for me continue to love me.
Your most affectionate
J L

23 Jan. 86
(Original Text) Distinguished Sir,
I am too well acquainted with your feelings towards me for it to be possible that a few days' silence should trouble me in any way. If I had felt any anxiety on that score I would have put the blame on your affairs, as I should have preferred, or on illness, which I am sorry to find that I can do with reason; anything would have entered my head sooner than doubt about your friendship.
[p. 765]
You have surely indulged that friendship too far by imposing for my sake the fatigue of writing upon a head not yet sufficiently settled after illness and a hand that is still weak. I am sorry that instead of my servant, whom I am sending with this, I cannot be with you myself, to sit beside you as you recover and sometimes to while away a languid hour. There is no need to mention the reasons, which you have indicated sufficiently yourself. But enough of this; I will speak of other things elsewhere; for you must be spared reading no less than writing. Only see to it that you get well; that you may do so as soon and as thoroughly as possible is the earnest wish of
Your devoted
J L

842. James Tyrrell to Locke, 20 January [1686] (775, 889)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 52-3. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Cam:†1 Jan 20th.
Dear C.
It is high time to answere your last kind, as well as large, letter, in which you sufficiently attone for your former short one; as allso for your half years silence; and, to let you see how well the physic you have prescribed hath wrought with me; Ile assure you I have purged off all that bilious matter that lay upon my spirit: and to make it work upward as well as downeward; shall let you see (since it belongs to your profession to contemplate such matters) what it was that (to carry on the metaphor in latine) did too much movere
― 766 ―

stomachum. first I could not but call to mind that I heard you say that you liked not to leave your papers, and writeings in London, because of fire, and other accidents: and yet you could send for all you had left with me; to be consigned to a hand that had no place els at that time to keep them in. whether they have bin since removed to any safer place I never inquired.
since it is none of my businesse. but if that Gentlemans papers had bin seized (as they were not long since like to have bin)†1 I know not in what condition yours might have bin in likewise. not for any dangerous matter that was in them: but for the difficulty, of haveing them againe: I doe not speake this that I desire such a charge; (since I am trusted by you with enough already. onely it vexed me a little to see another hand perhaps not so long knowne; so much preferred before mine. (when to use your owne phrase) I could see no reason for such a distinction: so likewise that last summer you could forbid my writeing to you untill you gave me notice of your returne from your Tour;†2 and then could continue 6. monthes silent without ever leting me know whether you were dead or alive; which troubled me very much, being then alarmed with so many false reports concerneing you, not fit to be committed to this paper. and then, when I could not speake with Mr: C.†3 or any one els that kept correspondence with you, whereby to be better satisfyed. therefore tho' I had wrot†a you a long letter by the command of your right honourable Friend;†4 and at a time when he had no leasure to write himself, wherein I gave you a full account of the state of your affaires; and what course your Friend then advised you to take. yet because you ordered me not to write againe to you untill etc. I never sent it. but in excuse for your silence you tell me you had forgot you writ any such advertisement: and therefore wondred I did not write againe: but had I bin in Cs case I should sooner have beleived that M had written†5 and that his letters had miscarryed; (and therefore should have sent him two for his one)
― 767 ―

then that he had neglected me so long in a duty, which is a far greater pleasure then burthen to performe: and that when your letter came, tho it was full of a great many expressions of kindnesse to my wife; yet I found none to myself: (not that I am jealous of her, but you) nor would I have you think I take it at all ill that you made the calling in of your money allmost the onely subject of that letter; since it is lawfull to doe what you will with your owne; and I had had it long enough in my hands: and hope I shall as honestly discharge my self of it againe: and Mr: C.†1 can tell you that I offred it to pay it him; the last winter when you called in for your other moneys but he refused to meddle with it; not haveing your particular order. so to doe: therefore since as the proverbe is even reckonings make long friends: I thought fit at once to set all accounts as well spirituall as temporal even between us: and tell you in what I look upon you as debtor to me in point of Friendship as well as I must owne my self beholding and obliged to you in all other circumstan<ces,>†a and therefore, I must in the first place beg your pardon for my mistake; in supposeing the ten pounds I owed you upon note of my hand to be included in the 32l†2you demanded by Mrs: Smithesby for the truth is I had forgote the receipt of the first quarters allowance which I received of Mr: P.†3 but haveing now sent to Jo: C:†b †4 into the Countrey for the Almanack in which the account between us was written doe now find it according to this in <closed>†c note, which I desire you to keep as well for your owne satisfaction as my justification: thereupon I have taken up the former note of my hand which I gave Mrs: S:†5 and have given her another for which is all that is due to you upon the account of your CC.†d
allowance:†6 and as for the note of my hand for the 10l. it is in hair trunk in a book. but tis time to lay aside businesse <and>†e to give you some account of that which you desire viz: the health of your Friends. as for my wi: she has bin much after the old rate still indisposed in her head stomach, or both: yet lookes pretty well God be thanked: and I see change of air has not that effect upon her I could wish; and so wee are goeing downe into
― 768 ―

the Countrey againe by the midst or end of next month at farthest: in the meane time she remembers her service to you, and has sent you the†a enclosed†a receipt for the puddings: and wishes the Lady you intend them for may please your palate as well with an English pud: at Amst: as ever you have bin at O.†1 as for Friends Dr: S.†2 and Dr: T.†3 are both well I hope for they were so lately: and so I hope is honest L. at G.†4 I saw him the begining of this winter.
I thank you for the account of the bookes you sent me; and if those of Controversy would please you I would send you over the papist misrepresented with the answere, replications, and replye.†5 very well worth the readeing for those who desire a true state of that controversye: I could allso send you some papers lately here published under the name of the late Dutchesse of Y: and those attested by his present Majesty and said to be found in the late Kings box and Closet after their decease conteining their reasons for their leaveing the church of E. and turneing to the R.C.C.†6 but these are of too great bulk and weight to be trusted by the Post, and unlesse you desire them and could direct me to a private hand to send them by are not to be ventured. as for my Lord Ps:†b life, or the letters:†7 they are now got into Sir R.L.s hands†8 for a License; and when they will be got out againe I know not: if you desire to know how things are like to goe here I recommend his observatour,†9 to your reading: and you will by that see what heresyes in Politicks are most prevalent here. but I have no more paper now left. then to
― 769 ―

assure you, quarrells as well as complements apart I am your really Friend, and servant. M.

843. William Charleton to Locke, 26 January 1686 (821, 856)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, f. 63.
London January the 26th 1685/6;
Deare Sir
Before I received your letter of the 1th: Instant I had returned my thankes to our freind at Amsterdam†3 for the care he tooke in Conveying the things you were pleased to procure me, which are mention'd in your letter, and were extraordinary welcome being verry great rarity's, I confesse my self extreamely to blame for not giving notice of my having received them sooner for though my Indisposition of health has been verry great and continues still yet that was no sufficient reason to be alleadged by me for so long a silence, the truth is I had Casually mislayed his letter and could not find it till of late, but I shall for the future be more carefull beging yours and his pardon for what is past, the next weeke I hope I shall send towards him some few bookes and a meddall of K. Charles the 2d: the last of his that was made†4 being a poore return for the curious present I received. I desired him (as I earnestly do you) that he would be pleased to let me know what bookes he liked or other things that I might not make an ill choice, and so send what might not be acceptable. I have still by me Moreri's Dictionary and Leonardi's booke and want but your orders for dispatching them
― 770 ―

towards you which if you have not by you pray let me know by the next who am assuredly
Deare Sir
Your most affectionate as well as most obliged humble servant
WILLIAM CHARLETON
Endorsed by Locke: W Charleton 26o Jan 85/6;
844. Locke to Edward Clarke, 29 January/8 February [1686] (829, 845)
Rand, pp. 142-50 and B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 162. Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. Locke wrote to Clarke on 29 January/8 February, accompanying his letter with instructions for the education of his children. The instructions break off abruptly, and Locke sent Clarke the remainder, with a further letter, on 5/15 March. Rand printed the two letters, with the instructions between them: pp. 142-62. I follow him in printing the instructions without interruption, though strictly the later part belongs with no. 845. The text here is that of Rand for the earlier part; of the letter of 5/15 March for the later.
The second part and the succeeding letter of 5/15 March are written on a single sheet of paper and, apart from the subscription, were written by Syl, but with corrections, etc., by Locke. According to Rand the first part of the instructions was written by Syl, with corrections by Locke; the preceding letter, dated 8 February [N.S.], is 'on the page opposite of the same sheet' as that on which the first part of the instructions is written, and is written by Locke. Syl was copying the instructions presumably from Locke's manuscript: no. 849. He made some mistakes, but some may be due to Rand. The year of the letter is established by no. 849, and more generally by parts of the contents.
