8th Feb. 1686.
Sir,
Yours of the 2nd Jan. brought me the good news of the safe delivery of your Lady, and the increase of your family by a lusty boy†1 was not a little welcome to me. I am rejoiced with all the circumstances of it, and though I hope you will live to see young Master happily married and have children, yet it is a satisfaction to have two strings to your bow. I wish they may be as great blessings to you as children can be to a father. Pray remember me
― 771 ―

to your Lady, to whom I wish the same.
I hope this letter will find her up, and well, and at work again about such another piece of night arras. Methinks she has so good a hand at it that she ought to continue. I am glad Nurse Trent is with you, for I think her a very fit woman for the employment. But pray let not your house corrupt, nor make her, if she suckle her child, eat and drink those things, which she would have been a stranger to at Ditton. Nor if she bring up the child by hand, make her give him that which she would not have had there. Your children have had such good success in that plain way, that if reason had nothing to say for it, yet our own experience ought to make you exactly follow it. I had within this very month occasion to observe a child under an year [so often given] sugar candy to please him, that at last nothing but what was very sweet [was desired by him] [There was] nothing but perpetual crying and bawling, and the child from his hunger and craving after sweet things was perpetually uneasy. I told his mother she giving him those licorish things to quiet him when he cried was but the way to increase it, [un]less she could resolve to feed him wholly with them, which would certainly destroy his health; and that the only cure was to endure for a day or two his crying without appeasing [his desires. After] some time, finding that ill increased by those ways that at present [permitted the] child [to gratify his] appetite, she resolved to take away from him at once all sweet things, and <when>†a he cried [to give him] nothing but what she judged wholesomest and best for his health. This made him impatient the first day, but when he saw he got not his desire by crying he left it off, and in two or three days, he, that before could not be quieted, when he saw either sugar, or sugar candy, or apples until they were given to him, so that they were fain carefully to hide them from him, was brought by this means, when apples or the like which he loved came in his way, only to show his desire of them, but not to cry for them, and this in a child wanting one or two of twelve months old. Which example confirms me in the opinion you know I am of, that children find the success of their crying, and accordingly make use of it to have their will sooner than is usually imagined; and that they should be accustomed very early not to have their desires [always granted], and that they should not be indulged in the things they cry for, where they were not absolutely necessary.
― 772 ―

You will find one part of this paper filled with the continuation of my opinion in reference to your son. It breaks off abruptly for want of room. But the remainder you shall have whenever you desire it; and when I know how far our rules have been put in practice, and with what success, or what difficulties have hindered. I shall in my next also add what may be convenient, or upon trial you have found deficient, or perhaps impracticable in what I have formerly writ on this occasion. For it often happens that the speculations which please a contemplative man in his study are not so easy to be put in use out of it. If also his particular temper or inclination require any further peculiar application, that also shall be considered. In the meantime I wish you, your Lady, and little ones perfect health and happiness, and am very much respect,
Sir,
your most humble servant,
J. L.
I heard nothing of Adrian or Susan.†1 The Cortex Peru, and what else you mentioned in your letter, came all safe to hand, for which I thank you. I hear nothing how they do at St. J ...†2 I hope my Valentine†3 and all are well.
Address: For Mr. Edward Clarke at the Lady King's in Salisbury Court, Fleet Street, London.
Sir,
The kind reception you have given to my former papers on this subject, and the desire you express that I should go on with it, gives me the confidence to proceed in my advice concerning the education of your son. For though it be a business with which my course of life has made me little acquainted, yet the service and obedience I owe you ought to make me attempt anything which you let me know may be acceptable to you.†4
― 773 ―

I†1- suppose by this time he has, by the ways before mentioned, learned to read pretty well, or if he has not, it is no great matter, so it be not without hopes that he will. If he goes on though slowly I think it better than tormenting him about it, and if he stand not quite still one may be assured that in time the skill of reading will perfectly be gotten. We have also agreed that the books he should at first read should be pleasant, easy and suited to his capacity, and yet not such as should fill his head with perfectly useless trumpery, or lay the principles of vice or folly. And therefore I made choice of Æsop's Fables, which being stories apt to delight and entertain a child, may yet afford useful reflections to a grown man; and if his memory retain them all his life after, he will not repent to find them there amongst his most manly thoughts and serious business. And if you and others talk with him sometimes about these fables, it will be an encouragement to his reading them.†1
What†2- other books there are in English of the sort, fit for children, I confess I cannot tell, having never before had any occasion to make any such reflections, much less any enquiry after them. And I am apt to think, that children, being generally delivered over to the method of the schools, where the fear of the rod is to enforce, and not the pleasure of the employment to invite them to learn; this sort of useful books amongst the number of silly ones that are of all sorts, have yet had the fate to be neglected; and nothing has been considered in this kind out of the ordinary road of the hornbook, primer, psalter, Testament and Bible. However, perhaps some such books [as I pro]pose may be found if you enquire.-†2
As†3- for the Bible, which children are usually employed in, to exercise and improve their talent in reading, I think the promiscuous reading of <it through, by>†a chapters as they lie in order, is so far from any advantage to children, either for the <perfecting>†b of reading, or principling their religion, that perhaps a worse could not be found. For what pleasure or encouragement can it be to a child to exercise himself in reading in a book where he understands nothing? And how little are the history of the creation, the law of
― 774 ―

Moses, the Psalms of David, and the Epistles in the New Testament (to omit the prophetical parts of both Old and New) suited to a child's capacity? And though the history of the evangelists, and the Acts, have something easier; yet, taken all together, it is very disproportionate to the understanding of childhood. I grant that the principles of religion are to be drawn from thence, and that they are best also delivered to children in the very words of the scripture. But it is far from this to read through the whole Bible, and that for reading's sake. And what an odd jumble of thoughts must a child have in his head concerning religion, who in his tender years reads all the parts of the Bible indifferently, as the word of God,†1 without any other distinction. I am apt to think, that this, in some men, has been the very reason why they have never had clear and distinct thoughts of it all their life time.†-3 
And†2- now I am by chance fallen on this subject, give me leave to say, that there are some parts of the scripture, which may be proper to put into the hands of a child to engage him to read; such as are the story of Joseph and his brethren, of David and Goliath, of David and Jonathan, etc., and others, that he should be made to read for his instruction; as that 'What you would have another do unto you, do you the same unto them'; and such other easy and plain moral rules, which, being fitly chosen, might be sometimes made use of both for reading and instruction together. But the reading of the whole scripture, or any part of it indifferently, is I think very inconvenient for children, till, after having been made acquainted with the plainest and fundamental parts of it, they have got some kind of general view of what they ought principally to believe and practice.†a ...-†2
When your son can read English perfectly, the next thing, of course, to be learnt is Latin,†4 which however necessary I allow it to be, yet†5- the ordinary way of learning it in a grammar school, is that, which having long had thoughts about, I can by no means approve of. The reasons against it are so evident and cogent, that they have prevailed with some intelligent persons you have known
― 775 ―

to quit the ordinary road, not without success, though the method made use of was not exactly that which I would have proposed.
Mine in short is this: to trouble the child with no rules of grammar at all, but to have Latin, as English has been, without the perplexity of rules, talked into him. For if you will consider it, Latin is no more unknowne to a child, when he comes into the world, than English: and yet he learns English without master, rule, or grammar: and so ought he Latin too, if he had somebody always to talk to him in this language. When we so often see a Frenchwoman teach a young girl to speak and read French perfectly, in a year or two, without one rule of grammar, or anything else, but prattling to her; I cannot but wonder how gentlewomen have overseen this way for their sons, and thought them more dull and incapable than their daughters. If therefore a man could be got, who himself speaks good Latin, who would always be about your son, and talk constantly to him, that would be the true and genuine way of teaching him Latin; and that that I could wish adopted as the easiest and best way of learning him a language without pains and chiding, which children <use>†a to be whipped for at school six or seven years together: he might at the same time not only form his mind and manners, but instruct him also in several sciences, such as a good part of geography, astronomy, anatomy, besides some part of history, and all other parts of knowledge of things, that fall under the senses, and require little more than memory. For there, if we would take the true way, our knowledge should begin, and in those things be laid the foundation; and not in the abstract notions of logic and metaphysics, which are fitter to <amuse>†b †1 than inform the understanding, in its first setting out towards knowledge. In which abstract speculations <when>†c young men have had their heads employed a while, without finding the success and improvement they expected, they are apt to have mean thoughts either of learning or themselves, to quit their studies, and to throw away their books, as containing nothing but hard words and empty sounds; or else concluding, if there be any real knowledge in them, they themselves have not understanding capable of it. And that this is so, perhaps I could assure you upon my own experience. Amongst other things to be learnt by a young man in this method, whilst others of his age are wholly taken up with Latin and languages, I
― 776 ―

may also set down geometry, for once having known a young gentleman bred something after this way, able to demonstrate several propositions in Euclid before he was thirteen.†-5 
But†1- if such a man cannot be got, who speaks good Latin, and being able to instruct your son in all those parts of knowledge, will undertake it by this method; my next best is to have him taught as near this way as may be, which is by translating the two languages Latin and English, forwards and backwards, one into another, and that at first out of some easy Roman author, and by using him to read Latin and nothing else. For the doing of this it will be convenient to know the declining of the nouns and the formation of the verbs, but more than this I would not have him know of grammar. But the learning of Latin being nothing but the learning of words, a very unpleasant business both to young and old, join as much other real knowledge with it as you can, beginning still with that which is most obvious to the senses; such as the knowledge of minerals, plants, and animals, but more especially trees, their parts and ways of propagation, wherein a great deal may be taught a child, which will not be useless to the man.-†1
But†2- if, after all, his fate be to go to school to get the Latin tongue, it will be in vain to talk to you concerning the method I think best to be observed even in schools. You must submit to what you find there, nor will the Imper.†3 have it changed for your son [since what is] established in his <Dominions>†a is as unchangeable as the things of the Medes and Persians. But yet by all means obtain, if you can, that he be not employed in making Latin themes and declamations, and least of all verses of any kind. You may insist upon it to the learned Dom. if it will do any good, that you have no desire to make him either a Latin orator <or a>†b poet, but would barely have him understand perfectly a Latin author. And <that>†c you observe that those who teach any of the modern languages, and that with success, never amuse their scholars to make speeches or verses either in French or Italian, their business being language barely, and not invention.-†2
― 777 ―

But†1- to tell you a little more fully, why I would not have your son exercised in making themes and verses: 1st. As to themes, though they have, I confess, the pretence of something useful, which is to teach people to speak handsomely and well on any subject; which, if it could be attained in this way, I confess, would be a great advantage; there being nothing more becoming a gentleman, nor more useful in all the occurrences of life, than to be able on any occasion to speak well, and to the purpose. But this I say, that the making of themes, as is usual in schools, helps not one jot towards it: For 1st. Do but consider what it is in making a theme that a young lad is employed about; it is to make a speech upon some Latin saying as 'Omnia vincit amor,' or 'Dulces sunt fructus radix virtutis amara.'†2 And here the poor lad, who wants knowledge of these things he is to speak of, which is to be had only from time and experience, must set his invention on the rack, to say something where he knows nothing which is a sort of Egyptian tyranny, to bid them make bricks who have not yet any of the materials. And therefore it is usual in such cases for the poor children to go to those of higher forms with this petition, 'Pray give me a little sense'; which, whether it be more reasonable or more ridiculous, is not easy to determine. Before a man can be in any capacity to speak on any subject, it is necessary he be acquainted with it; or else it is as foolish to set him to discourse about it, as to set a blind man to talk of colours, or a deaf man of music. And would you not think him a little cracked who should require another to make an argument on a moot question, who understood nothing of our laws? And what, I pray, do schoolboys understand concerning those matters, which are used to be proposed to them in their themes, as subjects to discourse on, to whet and exercise their fancies?-†1
In†3- the next place, consider the language that their themes are to be made in. It is Latin, a language foreign in their country, and long since dead everywhere; a language which your son, it is an hundred to one, shall never have an occasion once to make a speech in as long as he lives (unless it be for exercise); and a language, wherein the manner of expressing one's self is so far different from ours, that to be perfect in that, would very little improve the purity and facility of his English style.-†3
― 778 ―

But,†1- perhaps, we shall be told, it is to improve and perfect them in the Latin tongue. It is true, that is their proper business at school; but the making of themes is not the way to it: that perplexes their brains about invention of things to say, not about the signification of words to be learnt; and when they are making a theme, it is thoughts they search and sweat for, and not language. But the learning and mastery of a tongue, being uneasy and unpleasant enough in itself, should not be cumbered with any other difficulties, as is done in this way of proceeding. In fine, if boys' invention is to be quickened by such exercise, let them make themes in English, where they have facility and command of words, and will better see what kind of thoughts they have, when put into their own language. And, if the Latin tongue be to be learned, let it be done the easiest way, without toiling and disgusting the mind by so uneasy an employment as that of making speeches joined to it.-†1
If†2- these may be any reasons against children's making Latin themes at schools, I have much more to say, and of more weight, against their making verses of any sort. For if he has no genius to poetry, it is the most unreasonable thing in the world to torment him and waste his time about that which can never succeed. And, if he have a poetic vein, it is the most senseless thing in the world to cherish and improve it. It ought to be stifled and suppressed as much as may be; and I know not what reason a father can have to desire to have his son a poet, who does not desire to have him an idle useless fellow: which is not yet the worst of the case; for if he prove a successful rhymer, and get once the reputation of a wit, I desire it may be considered what company and places he is like to spend his time in, nay, and estate too. For†3- it has very seldom been, that-†3 anyone discovers gold or silver upon Parnassus. It is a pleasant air, but a barren soil, and there are very few instances of those who have added to their patrimony by any thing they have reaped from thence. Poetry and gaming, which usually go together, are alike in this too, that they seldom bring any advantage, but to those who have nothing else to live on. Men of estates almost constantly go away losers; and it is well if they escape at a cheaper rate than their whole estates, or the greatest part of them. If,
― 779 ―

therefore, you would not have your son the fiddle to every jovial†a company,†a without whom the sparkes could not relish their wine, nor know how to passe an afternoon Idely. If you would not have him wast his time and estate to divert others and contemne the dirty acres left him by his ancestors I doe not thinke you will much care he should be a poet or that his schoolmaster should enter him in Versifying.†-2 
Another†1- thing there is very ordinary in the Vulgar method of Grammar Schooles of which I see noe use at all unlesse it be to baulke young lads in the way to learning <languages>†b which in my opinion should be made as easy and pleasant as might be, and that which was painfull in it as much as possible quite removed. That which I meane and here complaine of is, their being forced to learne by heart great parcels of the authors that are taught them wherein I can discover noe advantage at all espetially to the businesse they are upon. Languages are to be learnt only by reading and talkeing and not by scrapps of authors got by heart which when a mans head is stuffed with he has got the just furniture of a pedant and tis the ready way to make him one then which there is noething lesse becomeing a gent. for what can be more rediculous then to mix the rich and handsom thoughts and sayings of others with a deale of poore stuff of his owne which is thereby only the more Exposd, and has noe other grace in it, nor will otherwise recommend the speaker then a threadbare russet coat would, that was set off with large patches of scarlet and glittering brocard. Indeed where a passage comes in the way whose matter is worthy remembrance and the Expression of it very pat and Excellent (as there are many such in the ancient authors) it may not be amisse to lodg it in the minde of a young scholler and with such admirable strokes of these great masters sometimes Exercise the memory of schoolboys. But the learning of their lessons by heart as they happen to fall out in their books without choise or destinction I know not what it serves for but to mispend their time and pains and give them a disgust of their books wherein they finde noething but uselesse trouble.-†1
― 780 ―

When†1- your Son is got past words and languages and is to learne things the other sciences he may perhaps doe well to take a short view of and salute as a passenger, but those I would have him rest upon and make a through acquaintance with should be the civil law and History. I meane the more general part of the civil law such as is to be found in Grotius de Jure Belli et Pacis†2or Puffendorf de Jure naturali et Gentium†3 which I prefer to Grotius etc. If he be well versed in the general parts of the Civil law which concernes not the chicquane of private cases but the affairs and intercourses of civilized nations in general; Understands Latin well and can write a good hand you may turne him loose into the world he will finde imployment and esteeme any where.-†1These†4- 3 therefor the Latin tongue writeing a very fair hand and the general part of the civil law I would have him perfect in to which soe much Geometry as is conteind in the 6 first books of Euclid may be usefull; for more then that perhaps will but doe harme. But as for Arithmatique there is noe doeing any thing without it; It is use full in all the parts of life and of this he cannot have too much be sure therefore he be made very perfect in all the parts of Arithmetique.-†4
Merchants†5- accounts though it be not likely to help a Gent. to get an estate, yet possibly there is not anything of more use and efficacy to make him preserve the estate he has. Tis seldome observed that he who keepes an account of his income and Expences and thereby has constantly under view the course of his domestique affairs lets them run to ruin and I doubt not but many a man gets behinde hand before he is a ware or runs farther on when he is once in for want of this care or skill to doe it. I would therefor advise all Gent. to learne perfectly merchants accounts and not thinke it is a skill that belongs not to them because it has received its name and has been cheifly practised by men of trafick. And when my young master has got the skill of keeping accounts (which is a businesse of reason more then Arithmetique) perhaps it will not be amisse that
― 781 ―

his father from thence forth require him to doe it in all his concernments. Not that I would have him set downe every pint of wine or play that costs him money, the general name of Expences will serve for such things well enough; nor would I have his father looke soe narrowly into these accounts as to take occasion from thence to criticize <on>†a †1 his Expenses he must remember that he himselfe was once a young man and not forget the thoughts he had then nor the right his son has to have the same and to have allowance made for them. If†b- therefor I would have the young gent obleiged to keepe an account it is not at all to have that way a cheque upon his expenses (For what the father allows him he ought to let him be full master of) but only that he might be brought early-†b into the custome of doeing it And that that might†c be made familiar and habitual to him betimes which will be soe usefull and necessary to be constantly practised the whole course of his life. A noble Venetian whose son wallowd in the plenty of his fathers riches finding his sons Expences grow very high and Extravagant orderd his casheer to let him have for the future noe more money then what he should count when he received it. This one would thinke noe great restraint to a young gent.'s Expences who could freely have as much money as he could tell. But yet this to one who was used to noething but the pursuit of his pleasures proved a very great trouble which at last ended in this sober and advantageous reflection. If it be soe much pains to me barely to count the mony I would spend what labour and pains did it cost my ancestors not only to count but get it?†d this rational thought suggested by this litle pains imposd upon him wrought soe effectually upon his minde that it made him take up and from that time forwards prove a good husband. This at least every body must allow that noething is likelier to keepe a man within compasse then the haveing constantly before his Eyes the state of his affairs in a regular course of accounts.†-5 
Where†2- I speake above of writeing a good hand (which I thinke
― 782 ―

mightily convenient) I should have mentiond another thing which as it is something of Kin to writeing well soe it is also what I thinke very usefull to a gent. in severall occasions but espetially if he Travell and that is Drawing which helps a man often to expresse in a few lines well put togeather what a whole sheet of paper in writeing would not be able to represent and make intelligible. How many buildings may a man see how many machines and habits meet with, the Ideas whereof would be easily reteind and communicated by a litle skill in Drawing which being committed to words are indanger to be lost or at best are but ill reteind in the most exact descriptions. I doe not meane that I would have your son a perfect painter, to be that to any tollerable degree will require more time then a young gent. can spare from his other improvements. But soe much insight into perspective and skill in drawing as will inable him to represent tollerably on paper any thing he sees Except faces may I thinke be got in a litle time espetially if he have a Genius to it But where that is wanting unlesse it be in things absolutely necessary it is better to let him passe them by quietly then to vex him about them to noe purpose and therefor I say of this as I doe of all other things not absolutely necessary. Nihil invitâ Minervâ.†-2 
Musique†1- I finde by some mightily valued but it wasts soe much of ones time to gain but a moderate skill in it and ingages in such odde company that I thinke it much better spared And amongst all those things that ever come into the list of accomplishments I give it next to Poetry the last place. Our short lives will not serve us for the atteinement of all things nor can our mindes be always in tent on some thing to be learnt. The weakenesse of our constitution both of minde and body requires that we should be often unbent and he that will make a good use of any part of his life must allow a large portion of it to Recreation At least this must not be denyd to young people unlesse whilst you with too much hast make them old,†a you have the displeasure to see them in their graves or a second childhood sooner then you could wish And therefor I thinke that the time and pains alloted to serious improvements should be imploid about things of most use and consequence and that too in the methods the most easy and short
― 783 ―

that could be at any rate obteind and perhaps it would be none of the least secreat in Education to make the Exercises of the body and the minde the recreation one to another. I doubt not but something might be donne by a prudent man that would well consider the temper and inclination of his pupill for he that is wearyd either with study or Danceing does not desire presently to goe to sleepe but to doe something else which may divert and delight him. But this must be always remembred that noething can come into the account of recreation that is not donne with delight.†-1 Concerning†2- danceing I have (as you know already) a quite other opinion then of Musik It being that which gives gracefull motions all the life and above all things manlynesse and a becomeing confidence to children I thinke it cannot be learnt too early after they are once of an age and strength capable of it. But you must be sure to have a good master that knows and can teach what is gracefull and becomeing and what gives a freedome and easynesse to all the motions of the body. One that teaches not this is worse then none at all. Naturall unfashionablenesse being much better then apish affected postures and I thinke it much more passable to put off the hat and make a leg like an honest Country gent. then like an ill fashond danceing master For as for the Jigging part and the figures of dances I count that litle or noething.-†2
Fencing†3- and rideing the great horse are usually considerd as parts of breeding the later of the two I could never see any use of unlesse it were for a Captain of horse at the head of his troop at a muster. For what else is necessary on horse back a Country gent. in England I thinke need not be taught. the pleasure and the frequent occasion of rideing seldome failes to instruct them without a master and hunting to compleat them in it.-†3
As†4- for fenceing it seemes to me a good Exercise for health but dangerous to the life. The Confidence of it being apt to engage in quarels those that thinke they have some skill and to make them more touchy then needs on points of honour and slight occasions and young men in their warme bloud are forward to thinke they have in vain learned to fence if they never shew their†askill and
― 784 ―

courage in a Duell. And they seeme to have reason. But how many sad Tragedies that reason has been the occasion of the tears of many a mother can witnesse. A man that cannot fence will be more carefull to keepe out of Bullys and gamsters company and will not be half soe apt to stand upon punctilios nor to give affronts or fircely justifie them when given which is that which usually makes the quarell. And when a man is in the feild a moderate skill in fenceing rather exposes him to the sword of his ennemy then secures him from it And certainly a man of courage who cannot fence at all and therefore will put all upon one thrust and not stand parying has the odds against a moderate Fencer espetially if he have skill in wrastling and therefor if any provision be to be made against such accidents and a man is to prepare his son for duells I had much rather mine should be a good wrastler then an ordinary Fencer which is the most a Gent. can atteine to in it unlesse he will be constantly in the fenceing schoole and every day exerciseing.†-4 
But†1- to returne to our books again you will perhaps thinke it strange that I say noething at all concerning the study of the Law of England whilst I am formeing a Gent. who can (to confesse the truth) be noe way considerable in his country without it. But that being a study you understand soe much better then I, it would be needlesse for me to discover my ignorance in it. That province therefor I leave to you and him when he is got past Tutors and shall only say that the generall and publique part of the law and not the chiquan and wrangleing is that which I thinke becomes a Gent. who ought to seeke the true measures of what is right and not the arts how one may avoid the doeing of it.-†1
Rhetorique†2- and Logique being the arts that in the ordinary method usually follow immediately after Grammar you may perhaps wonder too that I have said soe litle of them the reason is because of the litle advantage young people receive by them for I have seldome or never observed any one to get the skill of reasoning well or speakeing handsomely by studying those rules which pretend to teach it and therefor I would have a young gent. take a view of them in the shortest systemes could be found without dwelling long on the Contemplation and study of those formalitys. Right reasoning is founded on something else then the predicaments and predicables
― 785 ―

and does not consist in talkeing in mode and figure itself But tis besides my present businesse to enlarge upon that speculation. to come therefor to what we have in hand if you would have your son reason well let him read Bacon,†a †1 and if you would have him speake well let him be conversant in Tully†3 to give him the true Idea of Eloquence and let him read those things that are well writt in English to perfect his stile in the purity of our language.†-2 
Natural†4- philosophie as a speculative science I thinke we have none and perhaps may thinke I have reason to say we never shall. The works of nature are contrived†b by a wisdome and operate by ways too far surpasseing our facultys to discover or capacitys to conceive to be ever reduced into a science.-†4 Not†5- but that there are many things to be learnt in natural philosophie which abundantly reward the pains of the curious with delight and advantage. But these I thinke are rather to be found amongst such as have imploid themselves in makeing rational Experiments and observations then writeing speculative systemes. such writeings therefor as are Mr. Boyles may perhaps be fitest for a gent. with others that have writ of husbandry planting gardening and the like But if he has a minde to lanch farther out into general speculations I would recommend Des Cartes principles not as perfectly true or satisfactory to an inquisitive man <but>†c yet perhaps the most intelligible and most consistent with it self of any yet to be met with.-†5
This†6- is all in short that I thinke at present concerning matters of learning and accomplishment. The great businesse of all is Vertue.
Nullum†d- numen abest si sit prudentia.-†d†7 Teach him but to get a mastery over his inclination and make his appetite hearken to
― 786 ―

reason and the hardest part of the task is over. To that happy temper of minde I know noething that contributes soe much as the love of praise and Commendation which therefor you should I thinke endeavour to instill in to†a him by all the arts imaginable. make his minde as sensible of credit and shame as may be and when you have donne that you have put a principle in to him which will influence his actions when you are not by and to which the feare of a litle smart from†b a rod is not comparable.†-6 
One†1- thing more give me leave to adde and then I thinke I have donne at this time and that is as he grows up to talke familiarly with him nay ask his advice and consult with him about those things wherein he is capable of understanding by this you will gain two things both of great moment. The†c one is that it will put serious considerations into his thoughts better then any rules or advices you can give him. The sooner you treat him as a man the sooner he will begin to be one and if you admitt him into serious discourses sometimes†d- with you-†d you will thereby raise his minde above the†e- usuall amusements of youth and those trifleing occupations it is usually wasted in,-†e for it is easy to observe that many young men continue longer in the thoughts and conversation of schoolboys then otherwise they would because their parents keepe them at that distance and in that low ranke by all their carriage to them.
Another thing of greater consequence you will obteine by such a way of treateing him will be his freindship. Many fathers though they proportion to their sons liberall allowances according to their age and condition yet they keepe them as much†aunacquainted with their estates and all other concernments as if they were strangers. This if it lookes not like jealousy yet it wants those marks of kindnesse and intimacy a father should shew his Son and noe doubt often hinders or abates that cheerfullnesse and satisfaction wherewith a son should addresse himself to and rely upon his father. Noething cements and establishes freindship and good will soe much as confident communication of concernments and affairs. Other†a kindenesses without this leave still some doubts but
― 787 ―

when your son sees you open your minde to him that you interest him in your affairs as things you are willing should in their turne come into his hands he will be concerned for them as for his owne, wait his season with patience and love you in the meane time who keepe him not at the distance of a stranger.
This will also make him see that the injoyment you have is not without care which the more he is sensible of the lesse will he envy you the possession and the more thinke himself happy in†2- the injoyment-†2 of soe favourable a freind and soe carefull a father. There is scarce any young man of soe litle thought or soe void of sense that would not be glad of a sure freind that he might have recourse to and freely consult on occasion. the reservednesse and distance, that fathers keepe, often deprives their sons of that refuge which would be of more advantage to them then an hundred rebukes and chideings: would your son ingage in some frolike or take a vagary were it not much better he should doe it with then without your knowledg? For since allowances for such things must be made to young men the more you know of his intrigues and†a designes†a the better will you be able to prevent great mischeifs and by leting him see what†b- is like to follow-†b take the right way of prevailing with him to avoid lesse inconveniencys. would you have him open his heart to you and aske your advice? you must begin to doe soe†a with him first and by your cariage beget that confidence But whatever he consults you about, unlesse it lead to some fatall and irremediable mischeife be sure you advise only as a freind of more Experience but with your advice mingle noething of command or authority noe more then you would to your equall or a stranger. That would be to drive him for ever from any farther demandeing or receiveing advantage from your counsell you must consider that he is a young man and has pleasures and phansys which you are past you must not expect his inclinations should be just as yours nor that at 20 he should have the same thoughts you have at 50. All that you can wish is that since youth must have some libertys some outleapes they might be with the ingenuity of a son and under the eye of a father, and then noe very great harme can come of it. The way to obteine this as I said before is (according as you finde him capable) to talke
― 788 ―

with him about your affairs propose matters to him familiarly and aske his advice and when he ever lights on the right follow it as his and if it succeeds well let him have the commendation. This will not at all lessen your authority but increase his esteeme and love to you. whilst you keep your estate the staff will still be in your owne hands and your authority the surer the more it is strengthned with confidence and kindnesse for you have not that power you ought to have over him till he comes to be more afraid of offending soe good a freind then of looseing some part of his future Expetation.†-1 Finis
March
845. Locke to Edward Clarke, 5/15 March 1686 (844, 846)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 162. Printed in Rand, pp. 159-62. Written by Syl apart from the subscription: p. 770 n., where the relationship of the two letters is set out.
Sir I must confesse I am Extreamly pleasd if I have donne you any service in reference to your children But doe not thinke that those mighty thanks you heap upon me for it in your last ought to make me forget the solid obligations I have to you For after all that you doe or can say in magnifyeing this Essay of mine I must consider it as but a faint offer at some kinde of acknowledgment for your favours and I beseech you to receive it as such from one who wishes for noething more then the opportunitys of shewing how sensible he is of them. upon this confidence and the good successe you assure me our method hath hitherto had I venture to trouble you with the remainder of my thoughts on that subject and in this one more long sheet you will finde I am come to the end of my tether For haveing conducted my young master to the age wherein he will be got out of the hands of masters and Tutors we are at the bounds of what is <thought>†a to concerne Education.
I doe not pretend though I am now come to the†b conclusion that I have given you a just treatise on this matter There are a thousand <other things>†a that may need consideration Espetially if one should take in the various tempers, different inclinations and particular
― 789 ―

defaults that are to be found in children and <prescribe>†a proper remedys to each of them. But in this tumultuary draught I have made for your son I have considerd him barely†b as†b white paper†1 as a peice of wax to be mou<lded>†a and fashond and therefore have only touchd those heads which I judgd necessary to the breeding of a young gent. of his condition in general and though I have with a great deale of freedom given you my opinion concerning all those things that came in my thoughts and appeard material yet I am too sensible of my want of Experience in this affair and the oversights I am liable to, to thinke what I have writ approaches any thing neare perfect, even in that kinde. You must not therefor though I am come to the end look on it as a treatise which I put into your hands for Compleat. it is well if being writ (as it has been) by scrapps†c at distant times and places it will hold togeather and be of a peice what parts you finde I have either wholy omitted or too slightly touchd on I desire you to minde me of. For since I shall not scruple to trouble you with any thing else on this subject which may at any time hereafter come into my thoughts you may be sure I shall much more readily doe soe when you shall set me†d on worke and propose any new matter you shall finde wanting, which your care and concerne for your deare litle ones cannot (I conclude) faile to suggest to you in abundance It being a fate that usually attends the speculations which contemplative men have pleasd themselves with in their studys, to be found very defective when they come to be put in practise.
As to remedys for peculiar disorders the account you give me of your son makes me thinke I shall have litle to say on that occasion. you will not suspect I flatter you when I say his temper is as one could wish and the love of reason he shews in his enquirys and discourses is as much to be preferd to that pratleing quicknesse which we are apt to be delighted with in children as a healthy well made body is to a gaudy suit and if it were necessary here I thinke I could shew you that that witty pertnesse†2- that appears sometimes soe early proceeds from a principle that seldome accompanys a strong constitution of body or ripens into a strong judgment of minde and if you desire to have him a more brisk talker I beleive I
― 790 ―

could teach you the way to make him soe. But I finde you had rather your Son should be able and usefull when a man then pretty company and diversion to others whilst a child though if that too were to be considerd I thinke I may say there is not so much pleasure to have a child prattle agreeably as to reason well. Incourage therefor his inquisitivenesse all you can by satisfyeing his demands and informeing his judgment as far as it is capable. when his reasons are any way tolerable let him finde the credit and commendation of it and when they are quite out of the way let him without being laughd at for his mistake be gently put into the right and take care as much as you can that in this inclination he shews to reason†1 about every thing noe body baulke or impose upon him For when we have all donne the right improvement and Exercise of that Faculty is the highest perfection of a man and furnishes all the true light which our mindes can attein unto.†-2 
I have formerly mentioned Esops fables or some such other book†a- of pleasant-†a storys to draw him on with delight in reading. I now adde that if it be possible you should get it with pictures which will in a temper like his (that if I mistake not is much more pleased with things then names) make the learning of characters and words goe down much easier when he sees that there is some use of it and that the knowledg of beasts and birds and such other things comes along with it.†b those visible objects children heare talked of in vain and without any satisfaction whilst they have noe Ideas of them. if therefor Esops fables or some such other book cannot be got with pictures, yet at least get him what pictures of animals you can with the names to them which at the same time will encourage him to read and afford him matter of enquiry and knowledg.†3
If you finde it with difficulty to meet with such a Tutor as we desire I doe not at all wonder. I can only say spare noe care nor cost to get such an one. all things are to be had that way and I dare assure you that if you get a good one you will never repent the charge but you will always have the satisfaction to thinke it the money of all other the best laid out. But be sure take noe body
― 791 ―

upon freinds or charitable noe nor bare great commendations informe your selves throughly whether he be for your purpose and when you finde him every way soe get him at any rate but whether he be such an one as I have formerly mentioned and your designe will need you alone can judg nor will the reputation of a sober man with learning enough (which with others is all usually that is requird in a Tutor) serve your turne. In this choise be as curious as you would be in that of a wife for him For you must not thinke of tryall or changeing afterwards that will cause great inconvenience to you and greater to him. when I consider the scruples and cautions I here lay in your way me thinks it looks as if I advised you to something which I would have you offer at but in effect not doe. But you know how much I am in earnest in this point only you will understand me a right if you thinke it a businesse you ought to be very nice in. when you have pitched on one after haveing had him a while with you tell me what kinde of man he is. I will then the best I can tell you what kinde of use you are to make of him.
As to the businesse with Stratton I have noething to say but leave it wholy to your judgment, for soe as you determin I know it will be well. Present my humble service to Madam and tell her I am glad the litle ones follow soe well the footsteps of their Mother that they begin to have a reputation soe early. I wish her and them health that she may long enjoy that growing satisfaction. I wish you with them all happynesse and am†a
Sir your most humble servant J L
15 Mar.
Address: For Mr Edward Clarck at the Lady Kings in Salisbury Court near Fleet street London
Postmark: M- 19(?)
846. Locke to Edward Clarke, March 1686 (845, 849)
Mentioned by Rand, p. 162 n., as too faded to be reproduced.
― 792 ―

847. Lady Masham, formerly Damaris Cudworth, to Locke, 13 March [1686] (839, 870)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 130-3. Year from Locke's endorsement. The letter ff. 130-1; the enclosed poem ff. 132-3.
Had I not been Hinder'd by Business That Grave Impertinence†1 I should not have staid for your second letter to be out of your Debt for your First, since I am Covetuous of Keeping you Always in Mine Provided you be not long in Arrears; I would have you (if I could) Always Paying, and yet Always Oweing, that so I may never be long without either the Enjoyment or Expectation of that Pleasure which yours give me; Mine that I wrote last I did Beleeve would not Come to you of a great while because I had Inclos'd it in one to Mr Cl:†2 who I thought had then beene in Towne But understood soon after was not. However I am glad you received it at last since it has brought me so large a Returne, Nor will any more be Angry with you (though you still persist in it) either for Abuseing me, or my Neighbours, Though I must needs say after all your Railerie upon them it is in my Opinion no small Peice of Confidence in You to expect that I should find you out a Mistress amongst Them; But you do not indeed Desire it, Neither is it my Systeme of Platonisme that has Converted You; Handsome Faces, and Good Voices, afford more perswasive Arguments by much then any drawn from Philosophie, and without Them, and those Greater Charms of Witt, and Good Humour, which I doubt not Accompanie Them, I might have Preach'd Charitie to you long enough, and Those Distres'd Souls that have Forfeited theire first Priviledges might long enough have Continu'd in Their State of Inactivitie ere you would have had a thought of Provideing them more suitable Habitations. But why must Holland have the Honour of Converting so Obstinate a sinner as you were? Were I now in a Condition of seeing it I should Certainly for this Reason Have much Greater Curiositie to do so then ever I have yet Had, But Mine at Present (as you Know) gives me thoughts of a farther Voyage then That, and my Time of Preparation is now but short.†3 If you have any messages therefore to send, you must do it Quickly Although I confess I shall not be displeas'd any more then you, if after All, it
― 793 ―

should Happen that I should not go of that Errand.
Nevertheless do not think that if I leave this World I do it with any Mightie Regrett, since though I could perhaps at some times have done it with less, I am yet very far from being in Love with it; I would not have you therefore Mourne for me, and on that Account, as well as another, am at a loss what Legacie to leave You, Since I have a very great Desire to leave you something. But a Haire Ring, as well as Black Cloaths, might perhaps give Offence to your Dutch Mistress,†1 and tho the Dead need not much to be Fear'd, none who Deserve to make such extraordinarie Conquests as she has done But on such an occasion would be Jealous of Them. It would trouble my Ghost exceedingly in whatever state it finds its self, to be the Cause of any Allay to your Happiness and not to be in a Power of Justifying You in a Matter wherein it knew you to be Perfectly Innocent. But to Digress a little from so Grave a Subject Let me Know I beseech you what you meane by the Amends that you suppose you have made me in Length, Breadth, and Thickness. I have a Guess at it that makes me very Uneasie in the Want of it since Haveing not received it in All this Time I feare it is lodg'd in other Hands. If it be so Pray take Care to Redeeme it for me since I shall at least be so much the Better for it as to be furnishd thereby for makeing a more Considerable Legacie to somebody then any that I now Can, and that You may not think it will be to any unworthy of it, Know that if no Accident send me Post before the Time tis amongst the Learned, and those Particularly that you have expres'd most Value for, that I intend to make my last Exit, If my Part upon this Stage be indeed at an End But this brings me before I thought of it to the Subject of Poetry, and to makeing my excuse for not Writeing in Verse, Since that Rhimeing Humour not onely went soon off But I have Almost forsworne ever Leting it come on Againe, Since what was intended onely for my Owne Diversion I find has Unawares (to Use Mrs Phillips's words) expos'd me to the Severitie of the Wise and the Railerie of the Witts,†2 Altho not in any Printed Volume, Or I Hope ever will, But by my owne
― 794 ―

Indiscretion in the first Place in Trusting to the Favorable Censure of my Friends, and theirs in the next in exposeing me to that of Those who were not so; Nevertheless I have sent you the Paper you Desire, that You may see I will not make any excuses to You, Although how far it is Pertinent to the Subject we were Upon I cannot tell, since it was writt some Months before ever I saw Sir F:†1 Neither can I tell now how I came to Mention it Unless for being reproach'd with it that very Day I Hapned to write to You which I well remember I was I have shortned it what I could, by Leaveing out the Begining, more Impertinent then the Rest, the Person it is Addres'd to Haveing as little share in it as Usually Friends in the Countrey Have, serveing in Reallitie but for Pretence. Whether any other Had more, or No, is not I think Material to Say, But if they Had, I Beleeve 'twill be Needless to tell you it was not any Philosopher of the Platonic Sect. I Hope now that I shall have Appeas'd You, and that You will for once give me Fritters, for my Fritters,†2 and let me have Both the French Sonnet, and Your Translation.†3 It is late, and I have writt till I am so sleepie I scarse Know what I say, I shall therefore onely Add the Returne of my Thanks to Philander†4 for All the Good Wishes I had sent me at the Begining of the Yeare by Paul Hobson. Pray Assure him that I wish Him All the same and more if it be Possible and that I am with as much Friendship as His Faire Platonick will give me leave
His Humble Servant
PHILOCLEA
Since I Have sent you the inclos'd you must not refuse to tell me If the Author were Unknowne to you what Judgment you should from thence make of Her; I have a Reason to Ask, and therefore desire you would tell me sincerely. Let it be what it will it shall not Displease me; since the Persian Rose Water being cast Away, I resolve to have no Occasion for the Engine.†5 You will see I am got now quite out of the Element of Housewifrie, and Therefore I hope will excuse me for Receits of Marmalade, and Puding, But let me see you in my Closet, and There you shall have Them All.
March the 13th.
― 795 ―

[The enclosure:]
Our Sins of Ignorance sure are Small,
If Any such Can be at All;
Else Mightie Love! what Hope Have I
Ere to Appease thy Deitie,
That Have a Thousand times, and more,
Laugh'd at, and Defy'd Thy Power?
And what is still my shame, and Woo,
Drawne others in to do so too;
But now Like Dyeing Penitent
That dos in Decent Form Repent,
Haveing First Pardon Ask'd of Heaven,
Then Faith Receiv'd that Hee's Forgiven,
Thinks His Last Breath the Best to spend
When He exhorts His Wicked Friend;
So I, Deare Sister, do so Too, }
And for the Worst Have Pick'd out You }
The Very'st Reprobate I yet ere Knew. }
Then First, and Foremost, to Begin
Know Unbeleif's a Deadly Sin;
Errours, and Faults, may be in All,
But Those of Faith can be but†a small;
Then say, Love's Prophets, what They Will,
I Charge you to Beleeve Them still,
Nor ever Ask your Reason Why?
Though They should give Themselves the Lye:
You'l Think Perhaps tis very Hard
To be from Reason quite Debar'd,
And strait will Cry, But Pray Why so?
Why? Prethee Fool, How should I Know?
Churchmen, and Lovers, Both Agree }
There's no Salvation else Can be, }
's'not That enough for Thee, and Mee? }
And since wee unto That are Come
Sister, methinks your Future Doome,
Howere You may Out-Brave it Here,
Should make your Harden'd Heart to Feare;
― 796 ―

For sure You're not Arriv'd to That, }
To Disbeleeve a Future State, }
Should you Dye Excommunicate, }
Where All Repentance is in Vaine,
But you for ever must Remaine
The Laughing stock of All Below,
Who did your Pride, and Folly Know;
Even the Ape you shall Lead There†1
Grimaces at you shall not spare
And Justly too, when't shall be Guess'd,
That You, not Hee, Has beene the Beast;
For 't has beene said without Controul
That not to Love is want of Soul;
And if't Be so, without Dispute,
Then who Loves Least, Is Most a Brute;
But not to Fright you into Love
Since Feare dos as Destructive Prove
To That, As True Religion
Which is by each Extreame or'throwne,
I nothing now will farther say
Of What you'l find Another Day
Unless you do in Time Repent,
But Urge your Reason to Consent;
Reason, say you, Why what d'ye meane?
Reason, I Thought had Banish'd Beene;
No Hold; Because that some Abuse it
It follows not Others may'n't Use it;
Nor do they think it any scorne
When Handsomely 'twill serve their turne;
To this If you Object the lest,
I will informe Your Parish Priest,
And Therefore now let me Go On }
Without more Interruption, }
To say the Thing I had Begun, }
Which is, in short, no more then This, }
Love, Equally unto us is }
A Duty, and a Happiness; }
Our Duty sure it needs must Bee,
For What else were Created Wee?
― 797 ―

The Text you'l find is very Plaine
Eve, was made onely for the Man,
Then How can you your self Deceive
And think you're not some Adams Eve?
Or on the Man Look with a Frowne
Who onely comes to Claime His owne?
And Begs but that You would Restore
The Ribb You Rob'd Him of before;
And though for th'Hall of Westmister,
The Man no Justice can have There,
Yet surely Sister it is Plaine
He ought to have his Ribb Againe.
Then Haveing with our Duty done
I to our Happiness go On,
For if one Word will serve the Wise
What I have said may well suffice.
But Sister first we must express
In What Consists True Happiness;
Tis in a Mind Content, say You,
To which, I say, tis very True;
Yet some Exception must be made,
To Please Old Epictetus' shade,
Which else would take it Ill, that Wee }
Should from his owne Philosophie, }
A Madman Prove as Wise as Hee: }
And therefore Sister, to be Plaine,
It dos Consist in Ease from Paine:
I meane not Outward Ones Alone,
As Feavours; Collick; Gout; or Stone;
But Also those which we do find }
In That which wee ycleep the Mind; }
Our Particles the most Refin'd. }
Whether to This You will Agree
Or Not, I cannot well Foresee,
But Howere 't Be, I'm sure I Know
That You for once will grant it so;
But is it Thus that You would Prove
Cry you, the Happiness of Love?
Why Love is an Epitome
Of All the Passions which there Be;
― 798 ―

Tis Anger, which Deforms the Face;
Nay Hatred too, that Foe to Grace;
Tis Wild Dispaire; and Cureless Hope;
That either Mad do make; or Mope;
Tis Feare; Desire; and Envy too;
With Passions which none else ere Knew,
That Complicated are of These,
And which want Names Them to express,
But Above All tis Jealousie,
From which the Lover nere is Free;
And How in Love then can you find
That Ease you talk of in the Mind?
No Sister, who would Happy Bee }
Must Certainly from Love be free, }
There are no Joys like Those of Libertie. }
Tis Thus, I Know that you would Preach,
And think you'ad†a made a Pretty speech;
But Sister, dont your Breath misspend,
Reserve it for some Better End;
Full Foure Love sighs 't would make, I guess,
And much, I'me sure, it can't be less:
Now That of Breath would be some Use,
Whereas This were a Meere Abuse;
And so Beleeve me is't of Reason
When we employ it out of Season,
That Proud, Imperious Facultie, }
That gives to All the rest the Lie, }
And with as much Authoritie }
As if she could Produce a Charter
For makeing such a Stirr and Quarter;†1
But Sister, as You are a Tory,
Pray make Her Learne Another Story;†2
Though not But that the Thing is Good
When Rightly Us'd, and Understood,
But as the Vulgar do Abuse it
I think 't 'were Best They did not Use it,
― 799 ―

And such We Reckon All They Bee, }
Whom Churchmen Call the Layetie, }
That's every Mothers Child; But Wee. }
And Therefore, what I said before
I find I must Repeat once more,
Which is that what weare Pleas'd to Say,
You'ld with Implicite Faith Obey;
And Reason tis You should do so,
For 'tis by Faith we're sav'd you Know,
But Pray what Faith make showne can wee }
If Wee'l Beleeve But what we see; }
And Think things as They seeme to Bee? }
And Therefore, Sister, Urge no more,
One Word of what you said before,
Nor on the Paine of Direliction
Beleive it any Contradiction
Or that it is more strange, then True,
A Thing may Be, and not Be Too.†1
And now that All the Force is gone
Of This Your Pert Objection,
Though did you thus far Hold Aright
That labour needless I think might,
Yet for Decorums sake Alone
I something farther should go on;
And in a True Pedantick Cant
Like a Right Cambr: Disputant
That Haveing Prov'd it is not This,
Dos Then Demonstrate what it Is,
I Haveing freed Love from the Wrong
Which You, and I, Have done it Long,
Its Mightie Praises should Declare,
And Tell you Largely what They Are.
But Here it Better dos Become
Notorious Sinners to be Dumb,
Till by Theire Practise They have showne
They do Beleeve the Truths they owne;
― 800 ―

Nor is't for Mee to Talk, and Rant }
Like Any Old Experienc'd Saint, }
That Am But yet a Penitent. }
But though I'm Silent on That score, }
I have a Proverb yet in store, }
That who says, least dos Think the more.†1 }
Address (f. 131 v.): To Mr Lock.
Endorsed by Locke: (i: on cover of letter): Philoclea 13 Mar 85/6; (ii: on the enclosure): Philoclea Verses Mar 85/6.
848. William Stratton to Locke, 8 April 1686 (767, 895)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, f. 24. Marginal notes written by Locke.
Sutton the 8th Ap 1686
Dear Cosin
After A long silence I Cannot give any good account of sum of your Conserns in our Countery for your tenant Robert Horrall proves a very bad hind and is behind hand two years Rent this our lady day and he promised me sum securyty which was I think sumthing that he hath for his oun life of your land and I thinke sum small matter more that he hath by the yeare since his mothers decease. when our lady day was cum he put me of, but doeth not refuse it, but desires me to stay till I heare from you and If you say that he shall doe it he will, I think if we live another yeare we must part, if it had not bean Robert Horrall I shold not have forborn soe long, he being An ould tenant and haveing sum hopes that this small estate will be securyty, it made me forbeare, but now shall be very quick with him as soone as I heare from you†a
I am doutful that mony that was dew to you from John Anthony when he dyed will never be paid accept the 20s that I Reseived
the tynings that Barns Rented proved very bad this two years past and he proved a very bad tenant and hath not paid all his rent yet, and I have let it this last yeare to James Atkins sonn†2
― 801 ―

whome I hope will prove a better tenant but I dout I must abate rent†a
as for the furs the extraordinary frost it was douted was the killing of it and the abuse of the Cottages and tenants that it is cum to a very small matter
Buck furlong the most that It would yeald was 4l pr year and at last I let it to Sledg whoe proves An onest tenant and payes mony when he hath it and oweth but what is dew this last half year our lady day for that and all the rest and he supposes that that estate is bought that he lives in Contrary to your knowledg for John Stickland hath Vewed it twise and cummends it and Sledg was informed that it was Bought†b
I have agreed with the Widdow Shatter for two lives after the state†1 that is in her hous for 15l: 10s provided that I am satisfied by sum freind of ours that hath seen him in london or els wheare that he is now liveing†c
I have an ofer from Thomas Veale of pensford for ould doun that he will give for three lives 28l: if you are willing to dispose of it, and I think he will be content to give 2s: 6d yearly lords Rent I am willing to sell it him, but loth within 30l for the poore this two years are soe incresed that it is 10s: pr year to the poore besids all other taxes and James Atkins left it at 50s: pr yeare but I did not abate the rent and I let it two years to Thomas Spence for the same rent and he was wery and now have let it to James Atkins againe for the same Rent I desire to heare from you as soone as you can what your purpose is conserning it†d
I allsoe desire a word under your hand home I shall pay your rents to till I see you and make up our accounts I have mony by me and shall pay as soone as I have order from you†e
My Father†2 have written to you lately hoe is now feeble but as harty as Cand be expeckted and is sumthing deff he desires to be Kindly Remembred to you My Wife presents her humble servis to you, with my Children, it hath pleased god to make a breach in my famely since I writ last to you and take away my sonn John
― 802 ―

which was a great aflicktion the lord help me to make a santified use of it this being all at presant I take leave
your very humble servant and afecktionat Kinsman
WILLIAM STRATTON
Address: For mr lock
Endorsed by Locke: Wm: Stratton 8o Apr. 86
― 803 ―



Index of Correspondents in this Volume
This index is by the numbers of the letters, italics being used as in the text to indicate letters not by Locke. A bracketed number is either for a letter between persons other than Locke, in which case it appears under the names of both writer (or writers) and person addressed, or for an item other than a letter. If there is correspondence in earlier or later volumes between Locke and a person in this index it is indicated by the citation of the next volume or volumes in which any of it occurs.
The citation immediately following a name is that of a biographical note on the person. For persons concerned with only one or two letters the citation is omitted sometimes if the biographical note occurs in the headnote and is insignificant.

Recurrent Designations other than Proper Names
This list is intended to enable readers to identify persons mentioned in the letters in this volume by nicknames and similar designations. These designations are variable and are sometimes reduced to initials ('mr G-', 'mr lA. G.', 'mr Labé', etc.); the contexts will establish the identifications.
Adrian or Uncle Adrian: Dr. David Thomas
Capitaine de Marine, le: Raymond Formentin
Carmelin: Locke
G-, or mr lA. G., etc.: the Abbé François Gendron
Jemmy: the young James Tyrrell
Lysis: Nathaniel Hodges
Master: the young Edward Clarke
Miss: Elizabeth Clarke
Musidore: James Tyrrell
Oakley, Mr.: James Tyrrell
Parthenice: Mrs. Honor Thomas
Somers or Somerton, etc., cousin: Edward Clarke
Syl: Sylvester Brounower
Triumvirat, le: Gendron, Formentin, and Nicolas Toinard
